t: Inotodiol and dexamethasone treatment induced apoptotic morphological changes, including cytoplasmic blebbing and nuclear fragmentation, in differentiated EoL-1 eosinophils.
Cleaved caspase-3 expression was significantly higher in EoL-1 cells treated with 10 µg/mL inotodiol compared to media alone.
Expression of apoptosis-related proteins TRAILR2, Fas, Bax, and phosphorylated p53 increased in EoL-1 eosinophils following inotodiol treatment.
The number of apoptotic (cleaved caspase-3+) eosinophils (Siglec-F+) in nasal mucosa was significantly higher in inotodiol- and dexamethasone-treated ECRS mice than in untreated NP mice.
Inotodiol treatment significantly increased the number of apoptotic eosinophils in SEB-stimulated dispersed nasal polyp cell cultures from CRS patients compared to media alone.
IL-13 production after SEB stimulation was significantly suppressed in inotodiol-treated dispersed nasal polyp cells harvested from eosinophilic CRS patients.
Inotodiol treatment did not significantly reduce the number of nasal polyps compared to untreated NP mice, unlike dexamethasone.

Inotodiol has been shown in prior literature to inhibit NF-κB activation, thereby reducing transcription of inflammation-related genes, a mechanism proposed to explain its anti-inflammatory effects in this study.

Prior toxicology studies cited in the discussion showed that 13 weeks of daily inotodiol (95% purity, 20 mg/kg) caused no organ abnormalities, mortality, lipid metabolism changes, hematological/biochemical abnormalities, or liver toxicity in mice.
Silibinin was identified via virtual screening as forming strong hydrogen bond interactions with PLCβ3, with a predicted binding free energy of -119.277 kcal/mol.
Silibinin effectively blocked the protein-protein interaction between FcεRIβ and PLCβ3, a coupling implicated in allergic inflammatory cytokine production.

Silibinin reduced production of a broad panel of allergic inflammatory cytokines/chemokines (including CINC-2a, IL-2, CINC-1, IL-1α, MIP3α, IFN-γ, activin A, GM-CSF, ICAM-1, IL-4, IL-13, FasL and TNF-α) without inducing cytotoxicity.
In IgE-mediated allergic response studies, silibinin decreased the surface expression of the IgE receptor FcεRI.
In an OVA-induced allergic airway inflammation mouse model, silibinin alleviated allergen-induced asthma responses and reduced infiltration of inflammatory immune cells into the lungs.

CD56 immunostaining of erythromelalgia skin biopsies showed diminished autonomic nerve fiber density around the eccrine coil and arteries, resembling the denervation pattern seen in small fiber neuropathy.
Skin biopsies from affected acral areas in erythromelalgia patients showed superficial vascular ectasia.
Microvascular deposition of C5b-9 (terminal complement complex) was observed in erythromelalgia skin biopsies, suggesting complement-mediated microvascular injury.
Endothelial cells in erythromelalgia biopsies showed variable upregulation of type I interferon expression, implicating an immune-mediated microvascular mechanism.
Three of nine erythromelalgia patients had a concurrent autoimmune disease diagnosis (vitiligo, lupus erythematosus, or psoriatic arthritis).
Primary erythromelalgia is caused by gain-of-function mutations in genes encoding sodium channels, leading to hyperexcitability of pain-signaling neurons.
Secondary erythromelalgia has been linked to autoimmunity and hematologic dyscrasias such as thrombocythemia.

CD56 immunostaining in skin biopsies from erythromelalgia patients showed reduced autonomic nerve fiber density around the eccrine coil and arteries, resembling the denervation pattern seen in small fiber neuropathy.

The combined biopsy findings of vascular ectasia and autonomic denervation suggest that erythromelalgia is a dysautonomia syndrome with potential links to both immune and nonimmune microvascular compromise.
Peripheral sensory neuropathy (large and/or small fiber) was found by quantitative sensory testing in 85.3% of SSc patients.
Large fiber neuropathy was present in 57% of SSc patients, a significantly higher prevalence than in healthy controls.
Small fiber neuropathy (thermal/pain sensory impairment) was present in 80% of SSc patients, significantly more than in healthy controls.
More than half of the SSc cohort had co-existing large and small fiber neuropathy, indicating frequent overlap of both fiber-type deficits.
Self-reported neuropathic symptoms (numbness, paraesthesia, stabbing pain, burning pain) were significantly more prevalent in SSc patients than in healthy controls.
SSc patients had significantly fewer foot sites with preserved tactile sensitivity than healthy controls.
A greater proportion of SSc patients had impaired tactile sensitivity than healthy controls.
Vibration perception threshold was significantly delayed (higher) in SSc patients compared with healthy controls.
The proportion of patients with pathological vibratory sensitivity showed a trend toward being higher in SSc than HC but did not reach statistical significance.
SSc patients had a significantly lower cold detection threshold than healthy controls, indicating impaired small fiber cold sensitivity.
SSc patients had a significantly higher warm detection threshold than healthy controls, indicating impaired small fiber warm sensitivity.
The warm-cold threshold range was significantly wider in SSc patients than healthy controls, reflecting broader small fiber thermal dysfunction.
A significantly greater percentage of SSc patients had impaired thermal sensitivity compared with healthy controls.
SSc patients showed a significant reduction in pain perception (higher heat-pain threshold rate) compared with healthy controls.
Heat-pain threshold was significantly higher in SSc patients than in healthy controls, consistent with reduced pain sensitivity.
Nearly one in five SSc patients with objectively confirmed PSN on sensory testing did not report any neuropathic symptoms, indicating a subclinical presentation.
Burning pain was significantly associated with a history of foot ulcers in SSc patients.
Stabbing pain severity showed a weak inverse correlation with both disease duration and patient age.
Vibration threshold (worse large fiber sensitivity) was independently associated with smoking history, history of foot ulcers, and older age on multivariate analysis.
Warm sensory threshold (small fiber impairment) was independently associated with corticosteroid treatment and older age on multivariate analysis.
Older age was significantly associated with the presence of both large and small fiber neuropathy, especially when the two conditions co-existed.
Small fiber neuropathy was more frequent in patients with limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc) and anti-centromere antibody (ACA) positivity.
SSc patients reporting paraesthesia, numbness, or stabbing pain had significantly worse physical disability scores (SSc-HAQ) than those without these symptoms.
Three-quarters of SSc patients had disabling foot pain according to the Manchester Foot Pain and Disability Index, which was more common among those reporting paraesthesia, numbness or stabbing pain.
SSc patients reporting paraesthesia, numbness or stabbing pain had significantly worse disease-specific quality of life (SScQoL), which also correlated weakly with cold sensory threshold.

Intra-epidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) in glabrous hind paw skin significantly decreased in mice at 16-25 weeks on the high-fat neuropathy-inducing diet compared to 2 weeks on the diet, confirming progressive small fiber loss.

The DEN transdermal electrode device detected distinct functional changes in nerve electrical activity as early as 2 weeks of HFND feeding, before IENFD showed any significant reduction, suggesting greater sensitivity for early-stage small fiber neuropathy than skin biopsy.

A multi-class machine learning classification model built on DEN wavelet-transform features predicted HFND diet-group with an average 5-fold cross-validation accuracy of 91.73%, and 96.94% accuracy for the 16-week HFND group specifically.

The rate and prevalence of EKG-synchronized spike train activity recorded by the DEN device significantly decreased at 2 weeks and 25 weeks of HFND compared to chow controls, potentially indicating cardiac autonomic neuropathy.

Simultaneous EKG and DEN recordings showed that the EKG signal accounted for only about 1% of the total mean spike rate in DEN recordings, indicating EKG contamination was minor relative to overall recorded nerve activity.

Three major types of putative action potential activity (spike trains, bursts, and single spikes) were identified via DEN recordings across all three recording zones in both control and HFND-treated mice.

In healthy human subjects, the DEN device recorded six distinct types of neural activity: single action potentials, spike train activity, trains of CAPs/CMAPs, individual CAPs/CMAPs, patterned bursts of CAPs/CMAPs, and EMG activity following foot-ankle flexion.
Both human volunteers reported minimal or no pain upon insertion of the 32G DEN microneedle array into the lower leg, and the device was barely felt once in place.

Insertion or removal of a thin silver wire inside the DEN needle electrodes made no difference in the prevalence or rate of electrical activity recorded from control mice, so wires were excluded from subsequent recordings.

Electrical stimulation was found unnecessary to record nerve activity via DEN electrodes, since spontaneous/random firing and action potentials were observed under basal conditions in mouse transdermal tissue.
Body weight and subcutaneous white adipose tissue (scWAT) weight increased progressively in mice the longer they remained on the high-fat neuropathy-inducing diet.

Continuous wavelet transform scalogram analysis of a DEN recording from a 25-week HFND mouse exhibited the same signature as theoretically simulated noise-free compound action potential trains, supporting that DEN captures authentic, low-noise nerve electrical signals.
PCA-based clustering of digital wavelet transform features extracted from DEN recordings produced discrete, separable clusters corresponding to duration of high-fat diet feeding.
The incidence of grade 2 (high-risk) gastric antrum on point-of-care ultrasound was significantly higher in diabetic patients than in non-diabetic patients.
Antral cross-sectional area, gastric volume, and gastric volume per kg were significantly higher in diabetic patients compared to non-diabetic patients.
A higher antral ultrasonographic grade corresponded to a higher cross-sectional area and gastric volume.
Among diabetic patients, female gender was significantly associated with a higher likelihood of having a 'high-risk' gastric antrum for aspiration.
Increasing age showed a trend toward association with a 'high-risk' antrum among diabetic patients, but this did not reach statistical significance.
Despite the higher-risk gastric ultrasound findings in diabetic patients, no cases of actual aspiration pneumonitis occurred in either group during the 24-48 hour postoperative follow-up.
Among diabetic patients, 40% reported symptoms suggestive of peripheral neuropathy and 16% reported symptoms suggestive of autonomic neuropathy.
Overall, 37% of diabetic patients were classified as having a 'high-risk' antrum (grade 2, GV >0.8 mL/kg, or solid contents) for aspiration.
CH50, reflecting total complement activation capacity, was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls, even after adjusting for BMI.
Serum C3 levels did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Serum C4 levels did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Serum IgG was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls, remaining significant after BMI adjustment.
Serum IgM was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls, remaining significant after BMI adjustment.
In an unadjusted additional analysis, hsCRP was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
After adjusting for BMI, the difference in hsCRP between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls was no longer statistically significant, suggesting BMI confounded the unadjusted association.
ANA positivity rates did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
CH50 was positively correlated with overall pain intensity (BPI) in fibromyalgia patients; this correlation was not among those confirmed significant after adjusting for sex, age, and BMI.
CH50 was positively correlated with low back pain severity in fibromyalgia patients.
CH50 was positively correlated with knee pain severity in fibromyalgia patients.
CH50 was positively correlated with fatigue in fibromyalgia patients, and this association remained significant after adjusting for sex, age, and BMI.
CH50 was positively correlated with trait anxiety in fibromyalgia patients, and this association remained significant after adjusting for sex, age, and BMI.
hsCRP was positively correlated with low back pain in fibromyalgia patients, but this correlation was not significant after adjusting for sex, age, and BMI.
hsCRP was positively correlated with knee pain in fibromyalgia patients, but this correlation was not significant after adjusting for sex, age, and BMI.
Total IgG showed no significant correlation with pain, fatigue, or psychological symptom scores in fibromyalgia patients.
A higher proportion of fibromyalgia patients had IgG levels below the lower limit of normal compared to healthy controls (20% vs 3%), consistent with a prior study.
A small proportion of fibromyalgia patients had IgM levels below the lower limit of normal, whereas no healthy controls did.
IBD patients carry TLR4 gene polymorphisms that are associated with dysregulated enteric nervous system circuits, elevated 5-HT levels, and altered neuroimmune crosstalk.
DSS-induced ileitis in wild-type mice caused delayed gastrointestinal transit.
DSS-induced ileitis caused ileal myenteric neurodegeneration in wild-type mice.
DSS-induced ileitis produced reactive gliosis in the enteric nervous system of wild-type mice.
DSS-induced ileitis increased release of proinflammatory cytokines (mRNA levels) in ileal tissue of wild-type mice.
During ileitis, wild-type mice showed enhanced cholinergic and tachykinergic excitatory neuromuscular tone.
During DSS-induced ileitis, WT mice showed increased iNOS-mediated relaxation of ileal smooth muscle compared to untreated controls.
DSS-induced ileitis altered 5-HT and 5-HT receptor-mediated neuromuscular responses in WT mice.
Genetic deficiency of TLR4 reversed most of the functional and morphological abnormalities (motility, neurodegeneration, gliosis, neurotransmission changes) induced by DSS ileitis.
The authors propose that the neuroimmune interaction between TLR4 and 5-HT signalling is a potential pharmacological target for treating enteric nervous system dysfunction in IBD.
Diabetic rats treated with saline showed significantly lower CMAP amplitude compared to non-diabetic control rats.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) treatment improved CMAP amplitude compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) treatment produced a greater improvement in CMAP amplitude than low-dose or saline treatment.
Diabetic saline-treated rats had significantly prolonged distal latency compared to control rats.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) reduced distal latency compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) reduced distal latency further compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
Diabetic saline-treated rats showed markedly increased sciatic nerve perineural thickness compared to control rats, indicating fibrosis.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) decreased sciatic nerve perineural thickness compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) produced a more pronounced reduction in perineural thickness than low-dose DCA.
Diabetic saline-treated rats showed significantly impaired motor function (lower maximum inclined-plane angle) compared to controls.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) improved motor function (higher inclined-plane angle) compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) further improved motor function compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
STZ-induced diabetic rats had markedly elevated plasma glucose compared to non-diabetic controls, confirming the diabetic model.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) reduced plasma glucose compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) reduced plasma glucose more effectively than low-dose DCA.
Diabetic saline-treated rats showed significantly elevated plasma MDA (lipid peroxidation marker) compared to controls.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) reduced plasma MDA levels compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) further reduced plasma MDA levels compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
Diabetic saline-treated rats had significantly elevated plasma FGF-21 compared to controls.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) further elevated plasma FGF-21 compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) produced the greatest elevation in plasma FGF-21 among treatment groups.
Diabetic saline-treated rats had significantly elevated plasma TGF-beta compared to controls, indicating tissue damage/fibrosis.
Low-dose DCA (5 mg/kg) decreased plasma TGF-beta levels compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
High-dose DCA (10 mg/kg) further reduced plasma TGF-beta levels compared to diabetic saline-treated rats.
Female sex was consistently associated with a higher likelihood of receiving a Functional Disorder diagnostic label across multiple study designs.

IBS patients who received a diagnostic label reported higher symptom frequency, higher visceral sensitivity, and poorer quality of life than IBS patients meeting criteria but without a label, with small to moderate effect sizes.
No differences were found between IBS patients with and without a diagnostic label regarding sex, health worry, relationships, and pain catastrophizing.
Fibromyalgia patients with and without a diagnostic label showed similar impact of symptoms on health status, quality of life, life satisfaction, paid work, and healthcare consultations.
Women were more likely to be in the labelled than in the unlabelled fibromyalgia group.

In a cohort study of seven FD labels, higher intelligence, more functional somatic symptoms, and female sex were associated with receiving an FD diagnostic label, while age and neuroticism showed no significant association.

Patients labelled with ME/CFS reported less favourable illness duration, more subsequent fatigue symptoms, and more primary care consultations than patients labelled with Post-Viral Fatigue Syndrome, possibly reflecting greater initial symptom severity in the ME/CFS group.
Patients with a diagnostic label of ME reported less favourable outcomes than those labelled CFS, despite no statistically significant differences in symptom severity before diagnosis.
Patients with fibromyalgia reported an average of three years to receive a diagnostic label, described as an extensive process of excluding other medical diagnoses.
Focus group participants with fibromyalgia reported that some physicians viewed the FM diagnostic label as a 'fashion label' or a 'women's label', which contributed to delays in diagnosis.
Receiving the fibromyalgia diagnostic label brought brief relief and easier communication with others for some patients, but disappointment for others due to stigma and lack of welfare support.

In patients with remitted IBD experiencing abdominal pain, some found the secondary IBS label helpful for guiding management, while others disliked it, believing it obscured a prior IBD misdiagnosis; those with a holistic illness view saw the label as redundant.

In-depth interviews found HCPs reluctant to assign a fibromyalgia diagnostic label due to fear of negative effects for patients (e.g., stigmatization, adopting a 'sick role') and personal doubts about the disease's existence.

Practice nurses believed an ME/CFS diagnostic label was helpful for patients and services, but consistency in labelling was hindered by the lack of a definitive diagnostic test, and the doctor's attitude influenced whether a label was given.
In a vignette study with manipulated patient gender, GPs were more likely to assign a fibromyalgia/unspecified pain diagnostic label to female patients (42%) than male patients (22%).

Medical trainees and students believed CFS was a more accurate diagnostic label than ME or Florence Nightingale Disease, and attributed medical causes more often to patients with an ME label than to those with CFS or FN labels.

The CFS diagnostic label was interpreted negatively (e.g., 'it's between the ears', 'you are faking it') by 9% of participants, more often than for somatic diagnostic labels like Pfeiffer's disease and multiple sclerosis.

Male university students reported higher sympathy and lower hostility, and were more supportive of treatment, toward hypothetical patients with a CFS diagnostic label compared to those without a label, while female students showed no such differences.
Acute cold pain stress (CPS) significantly decreased jejunal mucosal microbiota alpha diversity (Shannon index) from baseline to 90 minutes post-stress.
The stress-induced decrease in microbial alpha diversity was more pronounced in females than males, although the sex difference itself did not reach statistical significance.
Overall microbial community composition (beta diversity, Bray-Curtis) was significantly altered by the stress model (CPS vs sham) across all samples.
Sex was a significant determinant of overall microbiota clustering (beta diversity) in paired pre/post samples.
Pre- and post-stress microbiota samples showed greater similarity (less change) in males than in females, visualized as greater overlap of PRE/POST ellipses in males on the MDS plot.

Five bacterial species were significantly differentially abundant in jejunal mucosa after CPS: Prevotella melaninogenica, Prevotella salivae, Granulicatella spp., Defluviitaleaceae_UCG.011 spp., and Megasphaera spp.
A distinct set of 10 taxa showed significant sex-dependent differential abundance after CPS (Time x Sex interaction), differing from the taxa significant for Time alone.
A significant negative correlation between OCL (occludin) gene expression fold-change and beta diversity change after CPS was observed only in females, not males.

Males showed eight significant correlations between barrier/inflammation/stress/circadian gene expression fold-changes and beta diversity change after CPS, versus only one significant correlation (OCL) in females.
SOD1 gene expression fold-change was negatively correlated with overall microbiota diversity change after stress, but only in males.
Beta diversity (Bray-Curtis dissimilarity) change after CPS negatively correlated with OCL (occludin) gene expression fold-change.
Alpha diversity (Shannon index) change after CPS positively correlated with NR3C1 (glucocorticoid receptor) gene expression fold-change.
No significant correlation was found between overall microbiome composition change and plasma cortisol or ACTH levels after stress.
Changes in subjective stress rating (SSRS) correlated with beta diversity changes overall; when stratified by sex, six significant correlations were found in males and none in females.
No significant correlation was found between overall microbiome composition change and chronic life stress score, depression score, weight, height, or body mass index.

An unclassified species of the genus Alloprevotella showed a significant sex-dependent decrease after CPS, contrasting with a prior mouse study showing this genus increased with psychosocial stress in males.
Rothia mucilaginosa abundance significantly decreased in females after CPS; this species has been previously linked to oral contraceptive use and reduced in Crohn's disease.
Granulicatella spp. abundance decreased after CPS, a genus also previously reported as dysregulated in Crohn's disease patients after ileocolic resection.
Cold pain stress significantly increased systolic and diastolic blood pressure in both sexes with no significant difference between males and females.
Cold pain stress did not significantly increase heart rate, and there was no difference between males and females.
Cold pain stress significantly increased plasma ACTH and cortisol levels in both sexes with no significant difference between males and females.

Sham intubation without cold pain stress did not significantly increase blood pressure, heart rate, subjective stress score, or plasma ACTH/cortisol in either sex, indicating the observed physiological responses were specific to CPS, not the biopsy/intubation procedure alone.
At baseline (before stress), there were no significant differences between males and females in the relative abundance of jejunal bacterial taxa.
An iPSC line (SCVIi124-A) was generated from a 64-year-old female Loeys-Dietz syndrome patient carrying a heterozygous TGFBR1 c.1117G>A mutation.
An iPSC line (SCVIi125-A) was generated from an 18-year-old female Loeys-Dietz syndrome patient carrying a heterozygous TGFBR1 c.563G>T mutation.
Both LDS iPSC lines expressed NANOG and SOX2 mRNA at levels comparable to control iPSC lines and significantly higher than in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, confirming pluripotency.
Both TGFBR1-mutant iPSC lines successfully differentiated into all three germ layers, confirmed by immunostaining for germ layer-specific markers.
Karyotype analysis via the KaryoStat assay confirmed normal chromosomal integrity in both LDS iPSC lines.
By passage 20, residual Sendai virus reprogramming vector genome was greatly reduced in both iPSC lines compared to control iPSC at early passages.
Both iPSC lines tested negative for mycoplasma contamination and were confirmed authentic to their donor PBMCs by STR analysis.

A cited study reported that combination treatment with Activin A and rapamycin can rescue smooth muscle cell defects caused by pathogenic TGFBR1 variants implicated in LDS-associated aortic root aneurysms.

A cited meta-analysis of global clinical trials found that angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), alone or combined with beta-blockers, significantly reduce the rate of aortic root enlargement in LDS patients.
GzmB-positive cell numbers were significantly increased in both the upper and lower dermis of hypertrophic scars compared to healthy skin.
GzmB+ cell numbers in keloid scars were not significantly different from healthy skin, though a non-significant trend toward accumulation was seen in the lower dermis.
No significant difference in GzmB+ cell numbers was found between keloid and hypertrophic scars.
CD8+ T-cell numbers were low and not significantly different between keloid/hypertrophic scars and healthy skin.
A weak positive correlation was observed between CD8+ T-cell and GzmB+ cell numbers in the upper dermis of KS and HS.
No correlation was found between CD8+ and GzmB+ cell numbers in the lower dermis of KS and HS.
Mast cells, identified by tryptase expression, significantly accumulated in the lower dermis of hypertrophic scars compared to healthy skin.
Mast cell (MCT+) and GzmB+ cell numbers were strongly positively correlated in both upper and lower dermis of keloid and hypertrophic scars, indicating mast cells as the major source of GzmB.
Substance P-positive cells, a mediator of mast cell degranulation, were increased in the dermis of KS and HS compared to healthy skin, suggesting a mechanism for mast-cell GzmB release.
Decorin staining intensity was significantly reduced in the dermis of both keloid and hypertrophic scars compared to healthy skin.
LTBP1 was reduced at the dermal-epidermal junction in KS and HS, with more pronounced loss in HS (absent in 8/10) than KS (absent in 6/10).
GzmB+ and MCT+ cell numbers in the upper dermis were significantly higher in LTBP1-negative lesions compared to LTBP1-positive lesions.

Bioinformatic prediction (GrabCas) identified 7 potential GzmB cleavage sites in LTBP1, mostly in the central Ca2+-binding EGF domains, compatible with release of a C-terminal fragment containing the small latent complex binding site.
Recombinant GzmB directly cleaved LTBP1 in conditioned medium in a cell-free assay, reducing its molecular weight over time.
CHO-LTBP1 cells exhibited a partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal morphological switch when cultured with 100 nM GzmB, but not with PBS or lower (50 nM) GzmB concentration.
Treatment of keratinocytes with GzmB-digested LTBP1 conditioned medium increased Smad2 phosphorylation 1.7-fold at 24h and 2.8-fold at 48h compared to non-digested LTBP1 medium.
A pan-TGF-β neutralizing antibody completely abolished the Smad2 phosphorylation induced by GzmB-digested LTBP1, confirming a TGF-β-dependent mechanism.
GzmB alone at 200 nM did not induce Smad2 phosphorylation in keratinocytes.
Pre-digestion of purified recombinant human LTBP1 by GzmB resulted in a 2-fold increase in Smad2 phosphorylation in keratinocytes compared to non-digested rhLTBP1.

GzmB-digestion of LTBP1 conditioned medium did not change p38 phosphorylation but reduced p44/42 MAPK phosphorylation in keratinocytes, and this MAPK effect persisted despite TGF-β blockade, suggesting a TGF-β independent, LTBP1-mediated mechanism.
In primary human dermal fibroblasts, GzmB-pre-digested recombinant LTBP1 caused a 2-fold increase in Smad2 phosphorylation compared to non-digested protein.

Unlike in keratinocytes, GzmB alone (200 nM) markedly induced Smad2 phosphorylation in primary dermal fibroblasts, which was abolished by a pan-TGF-β inhibitor, indicating GzmB can directly activate latent TGF-β secreted by fibroblasts independent of LTBP1 pre-digestion.

Even after GzmB proteolytic activity was blocked with the specific inhibitor VTI-1002 (confirmed by loss of FGFR1 cleavage), strong Smad2 phosphorylation remained detectable in primary dermal fibroblasts, indicating pre-formed cleavage fragments drive persistent TGF-β signaling.
GzmB-digested dermal fibroblast conditioned medium increased Smad2 phosphorylation in keratinocytes 2- to 3-fold compared to non-digested medium.

GzmB did not cleave the LAP-β1 pro-peptide in fibroblast conditioned medium, but generated two other unidentified degradation products, suggesting TGF-β activation occurs via cleavage of a different secreted protein rather than direct LAP degradation.
A delayed total recall score (FCSRT) below -1.65 SD was a strong predictor of belonging to the ME/CFS group rather than the MS group.

A Trail Making Test B-A score of 1.65 SD or higher (indicating mental flexibility impairment) was associated with a lower probability of belonging to the ME/CFS group, suggesting greater executive slowing in MS.
A VAS fatigue score of 3 or higher was a major independent predictor of belonging to the ME/CFS group.
ME/CFS patients showed weak performance in immediate visual memory (visual span forward test, mean z = -1.34±0.6), representing a deficit common to the ME/CFS population.
ME/CFS patients showed weak verbal episodic memory performance on the FCSRT, with impaired free recall and delayed free recall scores.
ME/CFS patients showed weak selective visual attention on Zazzo's cancellation test (three-signs condition).

Both ME/CFS and MS patients showed slowed reading/processing speed on the Stroop color-naming and word-reading conditions, while neither group was impaired on TMT A, suggesting a specific reading-speed rather than general processing-speed deficit, possibly linked to eye-movement dysfunction.

K-means clustering identified three severity-based subgroups within the ME/CFS cohort forming a continuum from very mild (group 1, n=15) to moderate (group 2, n=12) to definite (group 3, n=14) cognitive impairment, with a shared deficit in immediate visual-sequential memory across all groups.

K-means clustering revealed two ME/CFS subgroups: Cluster 1 (n=27) had near-normal cognition, while Cluster 2 (n=13) showed pronounced impairments in episodic memory, cognitive flexibility, and inhibition alongside higher pain, fatigue, depressive symptoms, and BMI.
The delay between disease onset and neuropsychological impairment did not significantly differ between ME/CFS and MS patients.

Prior PET imaging using a TSPO radioligand (marker of microglial activation) showed a correlation between cognitive impairment in ME/CFS and neuroinflammatory signal in the mid-pons-to-thalamus region, supporting a neuroinflammation hypothesis for ME/CFS cognitive dysfunction.

Cognitive impairments in ME/CFS were not attributable solely to fatigue, pain, or depression, as cognitive decline paralleled but was not fully explained by these symptom measures in the multivariable model.
A prior systematic review found that activity pacing interventions for ME/CFS lacked methodological rigor, were brief, did not follow guidelines, and failed to integrate recommended technology.

Co-production workshops with ME/CFS patients and health practitioners identified a need for early support, healthcare provider training, and public education to address stigma and misconceptions about the condition.
Participants recommended integrating mHealth technologies, multidisciplinary teams, and research-informed practices into future ME/CFS energy management interventions.
Participants recommended a comprehensive approach to ME/CFS management incorporating sleep, diet, and psychological support alongside activity pacing.
Severely ill ME/CFS patients had significantly lower morning salivary cortisol than healthy controls.
The diurnal salivary cortisol decline throughout the day was flattened in severely ill ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
Severely ill ME/CFS patients had a higher cholesterol/HDL ratio in blood samples compared to healthy controls.
Severely ill ME/CFS patients had lower blood albumin levels compared to healthy controls.
Severely ill ME/CFS patients had lower total bilirubin levels compared to healthy controls.

No significant differences in antibody/antigen testing for common viruses (HHV-6/7, HSV-1/2, EBV, CMV, parvovirus B19) or bacteria (Borrelia burgdorferi, Bartonella spp., Mycoplasma pneumoniae) were found between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.

Whole genome sequencing of 20 SIPS patients yielded 2,798,019 high-confidence variants, of which 103 were classified pathogenic/likely pathogenic by ACMG criteria; after removing 7 common SNVs, 96 variants across 93 genes remained.
Nine genes (ACADL, BRCA1, CFTR, COX10, HABP2, MFRP, PCLO, PRKN, ZFPM2) carried recurrent pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants affecting at least 2 of the 20 SIPS patients.
Seven of the nine recurrently mutated genes (77.8%) have previously been linked to cognitive impairment or neurological function, supporting a genetic basis for cognitive symptoms in SIPS patients.
Genes linked to fatigue were significantly enriched (3.94-fold) within the SIPS disease module relative to DisGeNET disease-gene association data.
Genes linked to cognitive disorders were significantly enriched (2.29-fold) within the SIPS disease module.

The SIPS disease module intersected significantly with six KEGG neurodegenerative disease pathways (Prion disease, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, Huntington's, Spinocerebellar ataxia, ALS), with enrichment ranging from 2.48 to 4.61-fold.

Among 70 DIAMOnD reference disease modules, the SIPS disease module showed the greatest similarity predominantly to neurological disorders (e.g., muscular dystrophies, basal ganglia diseases, spinocerebellar degenerations, Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, motor neuron disease, cerebrovascular disorders, ALS, cerebellar ataxia).
Cancer disease modules showed minimal similarity to the SIPS disease module, serving as a negative comparison group.
The SIPS disease module overlapped with disease modules built from two independent ME/CFS cohorts (23andMe and UK-Nor) by approximately 40%, more than expected by chance.
A depression disease module showed minimal overlap with the ME/CFS disease modules, supporting genetic distinction between ME/CFS and depression.

Multi-gene set pathway analysis across ME/CFS disease modules identified enrichment of COVID-19, EBV infection, antigen processing and presentation, and MAPK signaling pathways as likely associated with ME/CFS.
The cortisol synthesis and secretion pathway was enriched within the ME/CFS disease modules, consistent with previously observed diurnal cortisol abnormalities in SIPS patients.

The largest intra-cluster network component from multi-gene set analysis was dominated by immune response pathways related to infection (EBV infection, cytokine signaling, positive regulation of immune response, TNF-alpha/NF-kappa B signaling, antigen processing and presentation).

An estrogen signaling pathway connection to ME/CFS was identified, consistent with prior 23andMe cohort findings on hormone-related SNPs and offering a possible explanation for female predominance of the disease.

The variant rs35767802 in ADAMTSL2 was the most prevalent among the 103 identified variants, occurring in at least one allele in 45% (9/20) of severely ill ME/CFS patients despite being common (>12% allele frequency) in the general population.

ADAMTSL2, the gene harboring the most prevalent variant in the SIPS cohort, is associated with Type VIIC Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, suggesting a possible comorbidity between EDS-related joint hypermobility and ME/CFS.
A GWAS of post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS) identified a suggestively significant locus with lead SNP rs77857587, located approximately 252 kb upstream of the IRX1 gene.
The same PTLDS GWAS identified a second suggestively significant locus with lead SNP rs10833979, located 325 kb downstream of the GAS2 gene.

The top PTLDS-associated SNP rs77857587 is in high linkage disequilibrium with a long-range pQTL SNP (rs111774530) for the MARC2 protein, whose expression has been negatively associated with several immune checkpoint regulators.
Neither of the two suggestively significant PTLDS loci (near IRX1 and GAS2) was associated with fibromyalgia or ME/CFS in separate analyses of these conditions.
No SNPs reached the genome-wide significance threshold (P < 5 × 10−8) for association with PTLDS.
FUMA functional annotation showed that all suggestive PTLDS-associated SNPs were intergenic or intronic, had CADD scores below 20, and RegulomeDB scores indicating minimal to no regulatory evidence.
Using an enhanced EHR algorithm combining discrete diagnosis codes and free-text note searches, 19.4% (695/3,585) of patients treated for Lyme disease met criteria for PTLDS.
PTLDS cases were on average 1.5 years younger, more likely to be women, and more likely to be Hispanic/Latino than treated-Lyme-disease controls.

Fibromyalgia cases (n=5,041) were on average 1.37 years younger than controls, had a higher proportion of women, a lower proportion of White/European Americans, and a higher proportion of Hispanic/Latino participants.

ME/CFS cases (n=2,268) showed a higher proportion of women than controls, with no significant age difference, and had significantly fewer African American/Black and Hispanic/Latino participants but more White/European American participants compared to controls.

In a sensitivity analysis applying a more restrictive PTLDS definition (requiring symptom evidence within a shorter 4-26 week look-back), 121 cases were reclassified and excluded, but the association results for both suggestive loci remained robust.
Pooled analysis of six RCTs (623 participants) found XYS-based interventions produced a significantly higher clinical effective rate than standard biomedical treatment alone.
In the subgroup comparing XYS alone versus SBT (2 studies, 223 participants), XYS produced a significantly higher effective rate than SBT.
In the subgroup combining XYS with SBT versus SBT alone (4 studies, 400 participants), the combination significantly improved effective rate.
Pooled analysis showed XYS-based interventions significantly improved fatigue symptoms (FS-14 scores) compared to SBT, with moderate overall heterogeneity.
In the XYS-alone subgroup (2 studies, 223 participants), XYS significantly improved fatigue symptoms compared to SBT with low heterogeneity.
In the XYS+SBT subgroup (4 studies, 400 participants), combination therapy significantly improved fatigue symptoms compared to SBT alone.
In three studies (340 participants), combination of XYS and SBT significantly improved anxiety symptoms (SAS scores) versus SBT alone.
In three studies (340 participants), combination of XYS and SBT significantly improved depression symptoms (SDS scores) versus SBT alone with no heterogeneity.
Combining XYS with SBT (mainly paroxetine) significantly reduced the risk of adverse events compared to SBT alone, with overall AE incidence of 13% vs 27.5%.

Preclinical studies cited in the discussion indicate XYS mitigates stress behaviors and balances energy metabolism in CFS animal models by protecting mitochondrial structure/function and increasing plasma amino acids involved in energy production.
Discussion cites evidence that XYS restores Th2/Th17 balance, enhances macrophage cytotoxicity, and improves IgA, IgG, and complement C3 levels while reducing negative immune regulators.
A clinical trial cited in the discussion found XYS significantly increased NK cell activity and IgG/IgM levels in CFS patients, bringing them close to healthy control levels.

Discussion notes neuroinflammation as a hallmark of CFS, and that XYS shows neuroprotective effects by reducing oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, and neuronal damage while promoting neuronal recovery, based on cited mechanistic studies.

Discussion states intestinal inflammation, linked to neuroinflammation in CFS, is ameliorated by XYS via modulation of gut microbiota and reduction of inflammation through pathways such as the NLRP3 inflammasome.

Discussion states XYS's antidepressant/anxiolytic effects involve normalization of HPA axis activity, modulation of neurotransmitter levels, and influence on the tryptophan-kynurenine metabolic pathway.
The introduction cites that the global prevalence of CFS among long-COVID patients is as high as 45.2%, highlighting substantial overlap between ME/CFS and long COVID.
The introduction cites that approximately one quarter of CFS patients are severely affected to the point of being unable to work, with a substantial fraction bedridden and requiring nursing care.
The introduction notes that only about 4% of CFS patients report steady improvement in their condition, underscoring the lack of effective treatments.
Female OEF/OIF/OND veterans were significantly more likely than male veterans to report a lifetime history of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Female OEF/OIF/OND veterans were significantly more likely than male veterans to report a lifetime history of irritable bowel syndrome/colitis.
Female OEF/OIF/OND veterans were significantly more likely than male veterans to report a lifetime history of migraine.

A modified RAND Corporation Fidelity Coding Guide (CBSM Coding Guide) applied to 146 videotaped group CBSM sessions for chronic fatigue syndrome patients and partners showed moderate overall interrater reliability across 23 adherence and competence items.
Three of the 23 fidelity coding items did not reach the moderate interrater reliability cutoff and were identified as needing more extensive operationalization and rater training.
The patient with hEDS developed a hematoma in the left lung presenting only as mild hemoptysis, a clinical presentation not previously reported in hEDS.
Whole exome sequencing performed on the patient failed to identify any causative genetic mutation despite clinical suspicion of hEDS.
During surgery, the patient's connective tissue exhibited abnormal fragility that made hemostasis difficult and prevented completion of the planned lobectomy.
In Wales, the prevalence of hEDS and hypermobility spectrum disorders (HSD) is approximately 1 in 500, with 70% of diagnosed patients being female.
Reported prevalence of hEDS among POTS patients ranges from 15% to 22% according to cited studies.

Oral or intravenous vitamin C is suggested to improve vascular fragility and reduce bruising in EDS, with a cautioned dose limit of no more than 500 mg/day, and the patient was given 100 mg three times daily.
hEDS is frequently associated with symptoms such as fatigue, urticaria, flushing, angioedema, rhinitis, and diarrhea, potentially linked to mast cell activation disorder (MCAD).
Psychological comorbidities including depression, anxiety, ADHD, and PTSD are frequently observed across EDS types.
Studies indicate a significant positive correlation between pain intensity and severity of depressive symptoms in EDS patients.
hEDS is often linked with autonomic dysfunction, which when affecting the cardiovascular system manifests as orthostatic intolerance including POTS, though this patient did not exhibit POTS symptoms.
Thirteen of the 14 EDS subtypes have identifiable genetic markers, but hEDS remains diagnosed based solely on clinical criteria without a known genetic cause.

About 10% of patients clinically diagnosed with classical EDS (cEDS) may not have an identifiable genetic marker, and some patients with mild COL5A1/COL5A2 phenotypes may be diagnosed as hEDS rather than cEDS.
Participants generally found the HOPE online pain management programme feasible, acceptable and appropriate for hEDS/HSD, though with caveats.
Participants who had lived with hEDS/HSD for many years ('veterans') felt the programme offered little new information, whereas those newly diagnosed perceived stronger benefit.
Participants in the study reported multiple comorbidities alongside hEDS/HSD including fibromyalgia, dysautonomia, gastrointestinal (bowel) bleeding and neck issues.
Participants described substantial psychological burden associated with hEDS/HSD, including fear, stress, panic, hopelessness and emotional volatility.
Several participants reported loneliness and social isolation related to their hEDS/HSD experience, including negative experiences in online peer support groups.

The majority of interviewed participants (10 of 12) described substantial difficulty finding healthcare professionals knowledgeable about hEDS/HSD, contributing to delayed diagnosis and eroded therapeutic alliance.
One participant reported spending an estimated AUD$40,000 over seven years on specialist appointments while searching for an hEDS/HSD diagnosis and appropriate care.
Several participants self-identified as neurodivergent, and the study authors note neurodivergence is common in this population, indicating relevance to programme design.
In a prior Delphi survey of 396 people with hEDS/HSD, 81% indicated that a condition-specific online pain management programme was important or very important.
The same prior Delphi survey found 69% of people with hEDS/HSD felt regular online contact with a healthcare professional was an important component of a condition-specific pain programme.

A cited prior study of an online positive psychology programme for EDS reported that 40% of enrolled participants never started the intervention and 82% did not complete post-treatment outcome measures.
Of 36 intervention-group participants, 7 did not start the HOPE programme; only two responded to follow-up, citing medical issues as the reason for non-start.
Some participants found the CBT module within the HOPE programme unhelpful and triggering, based on prior negative experiences with CBT.
Self-guided reflective checkpoints in the programme were viewed positively by some participants as helpful for emotional processing, but by others as disruptive or lacking personal relevance.
Up to 98% of people with hEDS/HSD experience pain, and those with severe pain experience greater disability, per cited prior literature.
Global prevalence of EDS is estimated at 1 in 5000, but a localized Welsh study reported hEDS/HSD prevalence as high as 1 in 500.
Females represent approximately 70% of diagnosed hEDS cases, potentially reflecting estrogen's effects on collagen metabolism and pain perception.
Proteomic analysis of hEDS fibroblasts found dysregulation of ATP synthase subunits ATP5O, ATP5C1, and ATP5L, indicating compromised ATP production capacity.
TCA cycle enzymes aconitase 2 (ACO2), fumarate hydratase (FH), and malate dehydrogenase 2 (MDH2) showed altered expression levels in hEDS cells.

Genetic variations in MT-CYB, MT-ND1, and ACAD9 — genes involved in the mitochondrial OXPHOS system — have been associated with hEDS, potentially impairing electron transport chain function and fatty acid beta-oxidation.
hEDS fibroblasts show a metabolic shift from OXPHOS toward aerobic glycolysis, with upregulation of glycolytic enzymes GAPDH, PKM, and LDHB, resembling the Warburg effect.
Enzymes involved in fatty acid beta-oxidation, ACADVL and ECHS1, were dysregulated in hEDS fibroblasts, potentially contributing to exercise intolerance and post-exertional malaise.
hEDS fibroblasts show upregulation of voltage-dependent anion channels VDAC1 and VDAC2, which mediate ER-mitochondria calcium flux, suggesting altered calcium homeostasis.
hEDS fibroblasts show increased ROS production alongside upregulation of antioxidant enzymes SOD1, catalase, and GPX1, suggesting a compensatory oxidative-stress response.
ROS-mediated activation of MMP9 was linked to ECM disorganization in hEDS fibroblasts.

hEDS myofibroblasts showed high levels of S100A4, a protein that can disrupt mitochondria and induce oxidative stress in mast cells; silencing S100A4 inhibits mitochondrial complex I activity and reduces cellular ATP.
A KLK15 missense variant (p.Gly226Asp) was identified in approximately 2% of hEDS patients, potentially affecting connective tissue structure.
Heterozygous mutations in TNXB are known to disrupt collagen organization and ECM integrity, relevant to hEDS pathogenesis.
A COL3A1 p.Gly637Ser mutation was identified in a single family with autosomal dominant hEDS phenotype, leading to reduced collagen secretion and collagen over-modification.
Variants in COL5A1 and COL12A1 disrupt type V and XII collagen respectively, leading to ECM instability implicated in hEDS.

A survey found that clinically confirmed hEDS patients received an average of 10 years of alternative diagnoses (commonly anxiety, depression, migraines) before correct diagnosis, with many rejecting the earlier diagnoses once diagnosed with hEDS.

A study by Schaefer et al. found that common mtDNA mutations, when present on an incompatible mtDNA background, can alter the nuclear epigenome and influence expression of numerous ECM genes, providing a mechanism linking mitochondrial dysfunction to connective tissue abnormalities such as those in hEDS.

A meta-analysis of 17 patient cohorts with mitochondrial diseases suggested a link between OXPHOS defects and signs of hypermetabolism, with associated fatigue and exercise intolerance across multisystem disorders.

A recent study showed that the TGF-β receptor mediates communication between the ECM and mitochondria, suggesting mitochondrial dysfunction may amplify TGF-β signaling dysregulation and disrupt ECM homeostasis in hEDS.

Estrogen modulates mitochondrial biogenesis and function via ERα signaling, potentially influencing ECM turnover, collagen cross-linking, and hyaluronic acid synthesis, offering a proposed explanation for female predominance in hEDS.
Studies have demonstrated that impaired mitochondrial energy production correlates with exercise intolerance and post-exertional malaise in hEDS patients.

The review proposes that CoQ10 supplementation, as an electron transport chain carrier, could improve mitochondrial efficiency and reduce fatigue in hEDS, based on effects observed in other mitochondrial disorders, though this remains speculative and untested in hEDS.
The review proposes that mitochondria-targeted antioxidants such as MitoQ or SkQ1 might specifically reduce mitochondrial ROS and oxidative damage in hEDS, as a speculative therapeutic strategy.

Most surveyed genetics clinics (77%) reported having explicit policies or practices in place to manage the volume of referrals for joint hypermobility syndrome/hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (JHS/hEDS).
18% of institutions did not evaluate patients for JHS/EDS unless other syndromic or vascular indications were present.
The vast majority of interviewees (93%) cited a perceived large and increasing volume of JHS/EDS referrals as the primary logistical motivation for developing referral-limiting policies.
Two-thirds of interviewees (67%) believed that JHS/EDS evaluation appointments took significantly longer than appointments for other, nonurgent indications.
80% of interviewees cited the current lack of a known molecular basis for hEDS as a reason they felt unable to significantly affect care for this patient population.
67% of participants reported that their institution's policy limited how many JHS/EDS patients they evaluated within a given period.
47% of institutions sent JHS/hEDS-specific educational letters to referring providers to explain diagnostic criteria and reduce inappropriate referrals.
53% of institutions used JHS/hEDS-specific pre-visit questionnaires, sometimes up to 20 pages long, to streamline intake and set patient expectations.
53% of interviewees reported utilizing additional support staff (nurses, NPs, PAs, genetic counseling assistants) to help manage JHS/hEDS referrals and evaluations.
20% of institutions implemented a 2-step appointment process, with a preliminary genetic counselor visit or phone call before a physician evaluation, to optimize physician time.
67% of interviewees reported longer wait times for patients with JHS/hEDS as a negative outcome of restrictive referral policies.
33% of participants expressed concern that restrictive referral policies could result in missed diagnoses, including potentially life-threatening vascular subtypes of EDS.
73% of institutions' JHS/hEDS referral policies were developed through trial and error rather than nationally recognized guidelines and were subject to ongoing change.
20% of institutions reported declining to offer long-term follow-up care to JHS/hEDS patients as a policy to limit time commitment, unlike for other clinically diagnosed conditions.
Upper cervical spine morphological deviations occurred significantly more often in hEDS patients (51.9%) than in healthy controls (15.4%).
Posterior arch deficiencies (PAD) of the upper cervical spine occurred significantly more often in hEDS patients (48.1%) than in controls (12.8%).
Partial cleft of the first cervical vertebra occurred significantly more often in hEDS patients than in controls.
Neither occipitalization nor block fusion of the cervical vertebrae was observed in either the hEDS group or the control group.

Uncorrected analyses showed a more extended head posture in hEDS patients compared to controls on several cranio-vertical and cranio-cervical angles, though this became only a near-significant trend after correction for multiple testing.

Uncorrected analyses found some craniofacial morphology differences (less maxillary and mandibular prognathism, larger cranial base angle in hEDS), but none remained statistically significant after correction for multiple testing.
Participants diagnosed with hEDS after the latest reclassification reported worse physical and psychological wellbeing outcomes than those diagnosed earlier.
A higher number of comorbidities was associated with worse wellbeing outcomes in people with hEDS.
Older age was associated with improved wellbeing outcomes among people with hEDS.
Participant demographic profiling revealed a broader range of comorbidities associated with hEDS than had previously been documented.
There was no evidence that the pathway/route by which people are diagnosed with hEDS has changed over time, including after the reclassification.
The study found ongoing limitations in the availability of effective treatment options for people with hEDS.

Using TAS-20 cut-offs, 28% of hEDS patients met criteria for alexithymia and an additional 36% showed borderline alexithymia, levels the authors note appear higher than in the general Italian population.
Among SF-36 quality-of-life domains, Role Physical and Vitality were the most impaired in hEDS patients.

Pain intensity (BPI) showed a significant negative correlation with the DERS subscale 'Difficulties Engaging in Goal-Directed Behavior When Distressed', the only significant association for this pain measure.
Pain interference with daily life (BPI) showed no significant correlations with any affect regulation or alexithymia measures.
Patient age was negatively associated with the SF-36 pain scale score.
Longer time since hEDS diagnosis was negatively associated with overall emotion regulation difficulties (DERS).
Longer time since hEDS diagnosis was negatively associated with the TAS-20 'Difficulty Describing Feelings' subscale.
Longer time since hEDS diagnosis was positively associated with externally oriented thinking, a counterintuitive result interpreted as a possible defensive/distraction coping strategy.

SF-36 Mental Health and Role Emotional domains showed inverse correlations with DERS and TAS-20 scores, i.e., better emotional quality of life corresponded to greater ability to regulate emotions and stay in touch with feelings.

A positive correlation emerged between the DERS 'strategies' subscale and pain perception interfering with affective life, suggesting greater coping demands are required as pain increasingly affects emotional life.

Pain perception interfering with affective life was positively correlated with the alexithymia factor 'Difficulty Identifying Feelings', although alexithymia factors were not significantly correlated with pain intensity.

A positive correlation was found between SF-36 physical function quality and difficulty in emotional awareness (DERS awareness subscale), and separately, higher BPI interference in daily life (affective domain) was significantly negatively correlated with the emotional regulation awareness strategy.
In healthy dermis, glycosaminoglycan (GAG) chains of decorin wrap around collagen fibrils forming incomplete ring structures, described by the authors as a 'segmented ring-mesh model'.

In the dermis of a patient with musculocontractural Ehlers-Danlos syndrome caused by pathogenic CHST14 variants (mcEDS-CHST14), GAG chains were linear and did not form the ring structures seen in healthy dermis.
In mcEDS-CHST14 dermis, the GAG chain composition shifts to become chondroitin sulfate (CS)-rich and more linear, increasing inter-fibrillar space and inhibiting dense collagen fibril packing.

A 67-year-old woman with diffuse coronary artery aneurysms/ectasia involving all three coronary vessels was found to carry a heterozygous variant of unknown significance in COL3A1 (p.P517R/c.1550C>G) despite not meeting clinical criteria for vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.
The p.P517R variant is rare in the general population (gnomAD), occurring only in the European (non-Finnish) ancestry group and at higher frequency among genetic females.
The p.P517R variant has previously been reported five times in the ClinVar database in association with varying extracellular-matrix-related pathologies.
In silico analyses predicted the p.P517R substitution to be structurally deleterious, with a Grantham score of 103 and a REVEL pathogenicity score of 0.717.

AlphaFold structural modeling of the mutant COL3A1 protein showed an altered orientation between the substituted arginine at position 517 and the neighboring arginine at position 518, likely reflecting steric repulsion between the two positively charged residues, hypothesized to affect triple-helix stability.

Despite carrying a COL3A1 variant and presenting with diffuse coronary artery aneurysms, the patient lacked physical exam features of vascular EDS (joint hypermobility, skin laxity) and did not meet minimal clinical criteria for the disorder.

The patient's diffuse coronary aneurysms/ectasia involving all three coronary vessels, including the left main coronary artery, represents a rare presentation estimated to occur in only about 0.1% of the population.

A previously reported Dutch cohort of 142 individuals with pathogenic or likely pathogenic COL3A1 variants identified five patients with spontaneous coronary artery dissection at a mean age of 39 years, one of whom lacked other phenotypic features typical of vascular EDS.

A cited study of 1231 individuals with heterozygous COL3A1 mutations found that single-nucleotide substitutions within the triple helical region, particularly glycine substitutions, accounted for over 60% of identified pathogenic mutations and were associated with the shortest average lifespan (51 years).

A 12-week combined functional power training and high-intensity interval training program for children with heritable connective tissue disorders was feasible and safe, with no serious adverse events.
Following the training program, 80% of participants achieved their individual training goals.
75% of participants improved their aerobic capacity following the training program.
70% of participants showed gains in strength and agility after the training program.
Participants reported reductions in pain and fatigue following the training intervention.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization using 7 SNPs as instrumental variables found no statistically significant causal relationship between genetic liability to Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and hallux valgus.
The paper states, as background, that aortic dissection is associated with genetic connective tissue disorders including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, and Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Arterial tortuosity syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC2A10 gene, which encodes the glucose/dehydroascorbic acid transporter 10 (GLUT10).
Whole-gene sequencing of SLC2A10 in the patient identified a homozygous pathogenic nonsense variant, c.685C>T (p.R229*), confirming the diagnosis of arterial tortuosity syndrome.
The patient exhibited multiple extravascular connective-tissue features including high-arched palate, scoliosis, spina bifida occulta, pectus excavatum, and joint hypermobility.

Echocardiography and CT angiography demonstrated a restrictive subaortic ventricular septal defect, bicuspid aortic valve, aortic coarctation, and severe tortuosity/elongation of the ascending aorta, aortic arch, subclavian arteries and pulmonary artery branches.
Surgical closure of the ventricular septal defect and correction of aortic coarctation, performed in Italy due to lack of local cardiosurgery services, was reported as successful.

The role of GLUT10 as a dehydroascorbic acid transporter remains unclear, but shortage of ascorbic acid in the secretory pathway may affect extracellular matrix protein production at epigenetic and post-translational levels.

Severe arterial tortuosity is described as a distinguishing feature favoring a diagnosis of arterial tortuosity syndrome over other connective tissue disorders with overlapping presentations such as Ehlers-Danlos, Loeys-Dietz, and Marfan syndrome.

Typical manifestations of arterial tortuosity syndrome, as summarized from the literature, include facial dysmorphism, soft and hyperextensible skin, cutis laxa, hernias, skeletal abnormalities, joint hypermobility, congenital contractures, keratoconus and generalized hypotonia.

Recommended active surveillance for ATS patients includes annual echocardiography and MRI/CT every 3 years due to increased risk of aneurysm and dissection, plus routine ophthalmologic and orthopedic evaluation.
Multiple studies found elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the cerebrospinal fluid of fibromyalgia patients.
Brain imaging studies show strong glial cell activation across large parts of the CNS in fibromyalgia patients, with degree of activation correlating with fatigue severity.
Peripheral nociceptors in skin and muscle show sensitization of vanilloid receptors (TRPVs), acid-sensing ion channel receptors (ASICs), and purinergic receptors in fibromyalgia.
Fibromyalgia patients often exhibit elevated CRP, a marker of low-grade systemic inflammation, though not all patients show this elevation and levels may be influenced by comorbidities like obesity.
CCL2, a pro-inflammatory chemokine, was found elevated in the plasma of fibromyalgia patients by ELISA.

An interferon gene signature was identified in fibromyalgia patients, with increased expression of interferon-regulated genes (S100A8, S100A9, VCAM, CD163, SERPINA1, ANXA1) in peripheral B cells, suggesting a possible autoimmune-like component.

Proteomic analysis of plasma, serum, and saliva identified differentially expressed proteins in fibromyalgia patients versus healthy individuals, including transferrin, fibrinogen chains, profilin-1, transaldolase, PGAM1, apolipoprotein-C3, complement C4A/C1QC, immunoglobulin components, and acute phase reactants, several implicated in chronic low-grade inflammation.
Increased serum levels of IL-8, IL-37, AXIN1, and SIRT2 correlate with fibromyalgia symptom severity, including pain and fatigue.

Plasma protein studies reported reduced levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-4 and IL-13 alongside elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines, associated with activation of immune cells including mast cells in fibromyalgia patients.
Flow cytometry showed fibromyalgia patients have an increased neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio and alterations in T lymphocyte subpopulations, including CD4+ T cells and NKT cells.

Fecal microbiota transplantation from fibromyalgia patients into germ-free mice induced pain hypersensitivity, whereas transplantation from healthy individuals did not, implicating gut dysbiosis in peripheral sensitization via increased IL-17/TNF-α and monocyte/lymphocyte activation.
Fibromyalgia patients show altered gut microbiota composition with imbalances in specific bacterial species including Flavonifractor plautii, Parabacteroides merdae, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii.

Elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines and neurotrophic factors (IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, TNF-α, BDNF, GDNF) were found in the CSF of fibromyalgia patients, reflecting central inflammation driven by glial activation.

S100 proteins may contribute to fibromyalgia pathophysiology by activating RAGE and TLR4 receptors on glial cells, triggering JNK/ERK/p38 MAPK signaling and downstream AP-1/NF-κB activation to promote pro-inflammatory cytokine release.

In obese fibromyalgia patients, adipose tissue macrophages secrete pro-inflammatory cytokines/chemokines (TNF-α, IL-6, CCL4, CCL13) that sensitize nociceptors and dorsal root ganglia and can cross the blood-brain barrier to activate microglia, sustaining neuroinflammation.
Higher leptin levels correlate with increased pain sensitivity and inflammatory markers in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting a link between adiposity and central pain processing.
A Cochrane review of six RCTs found that NSAIDs did not provide a significant pain-relief benefit for fibromyalgia compared to placebo, and EULAR does not recommend their use.

NSAIDs are more effective in fibromyalgia patients who also have comorbid inflammatory conditions such as osteoarthritis, migraine, or rheumatoid arthritis, likely due to greater underlying inflammation in these conditions.
Combination therapy with the NSAID celecoxib and the antiviral famciclovir has shown potential in some clinical studies for reducing fibromyalgia-related pain and fatigue.
A Cochrane review of six RCTs found that NSAIDs did not provide a significant pain-relief benefit compared with placebo in fibromyalgia.
EULAR guidelines do not recommend the use of NSAIDs for fibromyalgia management.
No Cochrane review supports the effectiveness of acetaminophen for treating fibromyalgia, despite its common clinical use.

NSAIDs are reported to be more effective in fibromyalgia patients who have comorbid inflammatory conditions such as osteoarthritis, migraine, or rheumatoid arthritis, likely due to a higher degree of underlying inflammation.
Combination therapy of the NSAID celecoxib with the antiviral famciclovir has shown potential in some clinical studies to reduce fibromyalgia-related pain and fatigue.

An anti-inflammatory FODMAP diet excluding gluten, dairy, sugar, and ultra-processed foods resulted in better patient-reported outcomes, including reduced pain, fatigue, and gastrointestinal symptoms, in fibromyalgia patients.
A personalized Mediterranean diet showed positive effects on pain reduction and quality-of-life enhancement in fibromyalgia patients.
A gluten-free/low-FODMAP and low-histamine diet (IGUBAC-Diet®) combined with an olive-tree-based supplement showed beneficial effects on fibromyalgia symptom severity.
The Dietary Inflammatory Index (DII) has been correlated with pressure pain thresholds in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting a lower-inflammation diet may reduce pain hypersensitivity.
Aerobic and strength training exercise programs have been shown to be effective in reducing pain, sleep disturbances, fatigue, and depression in fibromyalgia patients.
Regular aerobic exercise increases beta-endorphin synthesis and activates CNS opioid receptors, producing anti-inflammatory effects and raising pain thresholds in fibromyalgia patients.
Comorbid obesity in fibromyalgia is linked to worsened clinical outcomes, including higher pain intensity, reduced physical function, and increased fatigue.
Higher leptin levels correlate with increased pain sensitivity and inflammatory markers in fibromyalgia patients, suggesting a direct link between adiposity and central pain processing.

Inflammatory arthritis, chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU), and functional bowel disorders (FBD) are commonly encountered comorbidities alongside fibromyalgia, suggesting a shared underlying inflammatory pathway.
The degree of glial cell activation observed in brain imaging of fibromyalgia patients is highly correlated with the severity of patient-reported fatigue.
Fibromyalgia patients show gut microbiota imbalances involving specific bacterial species, including Flavonifractor plautii, Parabacteroides merdae, and Faecalibacterium prausnitzii.
Fibromyalgia prevalence in the general population ranges from 0.2% to 4.7%, with higher incidence in middle-aged women, though it can occur at any age including childhood.

PET imaging using [11C]PBR28, which binds TSPO on activated microglia, showed increased radioligand binding in multiple cortical regions in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls, with cingulate cortex uptake associated with fatigue severity.

A study using TSPO ligand [18F]DPA-714 found higher microglial-marker binding in the right post-central gyrus and right occipital/temporal grey matter in fibromyalgia patients, with increased binding in the right parietal grey matter associated with decreased quality of life, increased pain, and cognitive symptoms.

[11C]-(R)-PK11195 PET showed increased microglial neuroinflammation in fibromyalgia patients versus healthy controls in similar brain regions, decreased neuroinflammation in the medulla, superior temporal gyrus, and left amygdala, and distinct regional patterns compared to complex regional pain syndrome patients.

CSF studies show a neuroinflammatory pattern of increased IL-8 without consistent elevation of IL-1β in fibromyalgia patients, consistent with glial activation rather than prostaglandin-mediated pathways.
Endotoxin challenge produced an abnormal thermal response in women with fibromyalgia, suggesting an abnormally sensitive central immune system.
The most consistent plasma cytokine profile in fibromyalgia involves increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8, the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10, and the chemokine eotaxin.
Plasma IL-8 and MCP-1 concentrations correlated with pain severity in fibromyalgia but not with overall symptom burden.
Substance P is the neuropeptide most consistently found to be elevated in the CSF and plasma of fibromyalgia patients.

Anti-satellite glial cell (SGC) IgG antibodies are elevated in serum/plasma of fibromyalgia patients and correlate with disease severity (higher self-reported pain), though not with pain pressure threshold or disease duration, and are not elevated in all patients.

Anti-SGC IgG antibodies are also elevated in painful post-COVID syndrome but not in COVID-recovered controls or in osteoarthritis, a non-nociplastic pain condition, supporting specificity for nociplastic pain states.

Passive transfer of IgG from fibromyalgia patients to mice induced sensory hypersensitivity (increased sensitivity to mechanical and cold stimuli, increased nociceptor excitability), reduced locomotor activity, reduced paw grip strength, and reduced small fibre skin innervation; effects were absent with IgG-depleted serum.

IgG from fibromyalgia patients localized to mouse dorsal root ganglia (particularly satellite glial cells and nerve fibre tracts) but not spinal cord or brain, with evidence of increased satellite glial cell activity.
Serum from fibromyalgia patients acutely activated murine DRG pro-nociceptive cells more intensely and widely than serum from healthy controls.

Patient sera IgG autoantibodies bound rat DRG neurons in 37% of fibromyalgia patients but in none of the controls, with SGC binding associated with symptom severity, suggesting distinct immune-related fibromyalgia subgroups.
Anti-SGC IgG antibody levels showed a negative correlation with metabolite concentrations in the rostral anterior cingulate cortex and thalamus.
Skin biopsies of fibromyalgia patients show significantly increased numbers of mast cells in the papillary dermis compared to controls.

Adoptive transfer of neutrophils from mice with chronic widespread pain or from fibromyalgia patients conferred mechanical hypersensitivity in naive recipient mice, suggesting a pronociceptive role of neutrophils.

Fibromyalgia patients show reduced NK cell Mu opioid receptor expression in skin, increased NK cell activation ligand expression on subepidermal nerves, and depletion of CD56bright NK cells with increased adhesion molecule expression.
Fibromyalgia patients show an increased Th1-type signature of CD4+ T cell subpopulations with associated increases in IFN-γ and TNF-α production, correlating with disease severity.
Fibromyalgia patients treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy showed reductions in circulating Th1 cells, TNF-α, IFN-γ, and serotonin levels, alongside reduced disease severity.

Microglia can switch between pro-inflammatory M1 and anti-inflammatory M2 phenotypes, with M1 cells inducing nociceptive/nociplastic pain and M2 cells having inhibitory pain effects; the fibromyalgia cytokine signature may reflect a skewed M1/M2 ratio.
Skin biopsies of fibromyalgia patients show a significantly increased number of mast cells in the papillary dermis compared to controls.

Adoptive transfer of neutrophils from mice with chronic widespread pain or from fibromyalgia patients conferred mechanical hypersensitivity in naive recipient mice, suggesting a pronociceptive role of neutrophils.

Skin biopsies of fibromyalgia patients show reduced NK cell expression of Mu opioid receptors and increased expression of NK cell activation ligands on subepidermal nerves, with NK cells found near peripheral nerves.
Fibromyalgia is associated with depletion of CD56bright NK cells and increased expression of adhesion molecules on NK cells.

In animal models, CD4+ T cell depletion inhibits thermal hyperalgesia, tactile central sensitisation, and mechanical hypersensitivity following partial sciatic nerve ligation, alongside reduced stress-related behaviours.
Human fibromyalgia studies show an increased Th1-type signature of CD4+ T cell subpopulations, with increased IFN-γ and TNF-α production correlating with disease severity.
Fibromyalgia patients treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy showed reductions in circulating Th1 cells, TNF-α, IFN-γ, serotonin levels, and disease severity.
Serotonin transporter 5-HTTLPR polymorphisms are associated with increased T cell activation in fibromyalgia patients, supporting interaction between serotonin and the adaptive immune system.
Fibromyalgia and complex regional pain syndrome patients show reductions in cytotoxic CD8+ T cells that correlate with post-traumatic stress scores, without alteration of the CD4/CD8 ratio.
Fibromyalgia is associated with an altered gene-expression profile of peripheral B cells, including increased expression of interferon-related genes.

The neurogenic flare (Lewis triple) response produced by pro-inflammatory C-fibre peptide release is increased in fibromyalgia patients, and its extent correlates with allodynia severity, reduced pain threshold, slow-wave sleep deprivation, and increased fatigue.
Fibromyalgia patients with Raynaud phenomenon and/or livedo reticularis have significantly elevated levels of fibronectin, a tissue marker of endothelial activation.
Approximately 50% of fibromyalgia patients show small fibre pathology with reduced density of unmyelinated skin nerve fibres, reduced mean axon diameter, and C-fibre structural change.

In fibromyalgia, the presence or absence of small fibre pathology did not influence the sensory phenotype, unlike isolated small fibre neuropathy, where sensory loss and mechanical hyperalgesia predominated.
Fibromyalgia patients demonstrate sympathetic hyperactivity with decreased heart rate variability and blunted autonomic response to stress, with heart rate variability correlating with pain severity.
Noradrenaline injections evoke significantly more pain in fibromyalgia patients compared to patients with rheumatoid arthritis or healthy controls.

Fibromyalgia patients show alterations in gut microbiome composition, particularly in bacterial species involved in short-chain fatty acid and bile acid metabolism, as well as species with roles in immune modulation.
A rodent study demonstrated a causal role of the gut microbiome in fibromyalgia-like changes, though the causal relationship in humans requires further exploration.

Fibromyalgia is associated with dysregulation of circadian cortisol variation and response to corticotropin-releasing hormone, with potential correlation with symptom severity, though data remain inconclusive.
Fibromyalgia patients show low vagal tone alongside sympathetic hyperactivity, as evidenced by low heart rate variability.
Neither non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs nor glucocorticoids appear to suppress neuroinflammation or improve fibromyalgia symptoms.
