Low-dose naltrexone, a μ-opioid receptor antagonist, increases TLR4 signalling and modulates microglial M1/M2 switching in favour of the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype.
The dual serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor milnacipran reduces ventricular lactate levels, a possible marker of central neuroinflammation, in fibromyalgia.
Sympathetic nervous system activity is abnormally increased in fibromyalgia, evidenced by reduced heart rate variability and blunted autonomic responses to stress.
Injection of noradrenaline evokes significantly more pain in fibromyalgia patients than in rheumatoid arthritis patients or healthy controls.

Studies of the gut microbiome in fibromyalgia have found alterations in bacterial species involved in short-chain fatty acid and bile acid metabolism and immune modulation, with one rodent study suggesting a causal role of the gut microbiome in fibromyalgia.

The HPA axis in fibromyalgia shows inconsistent findings of both hyper- and hypoactivity, with dysregulated circadian cortisol variation and blunted response to corticotropin-releasing hormone, potentially correlating with symptom severity.
Low vagal tone, indicated by low heart rate variability, is present in fibromyalgia and is linked to reduced anti-inflammatory vagal signalling in the neuroimmune axis.

IL-6 inhibition may reduce disproportionate articular pain in rheumatoid arthritis patients, raising the possibility that this class could have analgesic effects via neuroinflammatory pathways.

Low-dose naltrexone, a mu opioid receptor antagonist, suppresses pro-inflammatory microglial activity and shifts M1/M2 microglial phenotype switching toward the anti-inflammatory M2 state via increased TLR4 modulation.
Serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors are recommended fibromyalgia treatments, with evidence of reciprocal pathways linking serotonin to inflammation and immune activation.
The dual reuptake inhibitor milnacipran reduces ventricular lactate levels, a possible marker of central neuroinflammation, in fibromyalgia.

Mindfulness-based stress reduction decreases cutaneous neurogenic inflammatory responses and modifies pro-inflammatory cytokine profiles in fibromyalgia.
Exercise-based interventions reduce pro-inflammatory biomarkers in fibromyalgia, particularly IL-8.
The Mediterranean diet, considered anti-inflammatory, improves fibromyalgia parameters including fatigue, disability, and anxiety.

A clinical trial of rozanolixizumab, a humanised IgG4 monoclonal antibody that reduces circulating IgG, is underway in severe fibromyalgia patients to test whether IgG reduction improves symptom severity.

CD20-positive B cell antibody depletion reversed nociceptive sensitisation in murine models of complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), implicating B cell-mediated mechanisms in nociplastic pain conditions.

Patients with fibromyalgia in a Spanish study were more likely to have central obesity and reduced cardiopulmonary function than individuals without FM.

Metformin exhibits anti-inflammatory properties via AMPK activation and inhibition of TNF-α and IL-1β synthesis, potentially diminishing neuroinflammation and offering therapeutic benefit for fibromyalgia pathology.
There is a higher prevalence of fibromyalgia among patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus, though no link was found between FM prevalence and diabetes control.

In a study of 100 diabetes patients, fibromyalgia was frequently observed in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes, with its occurrence potentially linked to the level of glycemic control.

CRP levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in controls, indicating systemic inflammation.
ESR was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in controls, indicating systemic inflammation.

In a subgroup of 13 fibromyalgia patients with complete metabolic data, all exhibited abnormalities in at least one insulin resistance marker, and the IR-FM relationship was reportedly unaffected by age, gender, or ethnicity.

Logistic regression showed HOMA-IR was one of the strongest predictors of SNRI treatment resistance in fibromyalgia patients.
MRGPRX2-expressing mast cells are enriched in the submucosal and muscularis layers of the healthy human colon compared with other colon layers.
MRGPRX2 agonists trigger mast cell degranulation and sensitisation of TRPV1 in the submucosa of healthy human colon, using live imaging of colonic submucosal plexus samples.
The frequency of MRGPRX2-positive mast cells in rectal biopsies was similar between IBS patients and healthy volunteers.
Submucosal mast cells from IBS patients showed increased degranulation in response to MRGPRX2 agonists compared with healthy volunteers.
MRGPRX2 agonistic activity was increased in rectal biopsy supernatants from IBS patients compared with healthy volunteers, and this was associated with increased substance P levels.
Mosaic loss of the Y chromosome (mLOY) was significantly increased in late-onset rheumatoid arthritis compared with controls.
mLOY showed a significant negative association with young-onset rheumatoid arthritis (YORA), contrasting with its positive association in late-onset disease.
Autosomal mosaic chromosomal alterations showed consistent negative associations with rheumatoid arthritis overall, late-onset RA, and young-onset RA.
Mosaic loss of X (mLOX) showed consistent negative associations with rheumatoid arthritis overall, late-onset RA, and young-onset RA.
The effect size of the RA polygenic risk score was lower for late-onset RA than for young-onset RA, indicating differing genetic contributions by age at onset.

In young-onset RA, the association between polygenic risk score and disease was independent of mLOY, unlike in late-onset RA.
Mosaic loss of chromosome X showed a negative (non-significant/protective-direction) association with young-onset RA, consistent with patterns seen in overall RA and LORA.
The effect size of the RA polygenic risk score on disease risk was lower in late-onset RA compared with young-onset RA.
A high cell fraction of mosaic loss of Y strengthened the association between the polygenic risk score and late-onset RA.
In contrast to late-onset RA, the association between the polygenic risk score and young-onset RA was independent of mosaic loss of Y status.
Mice exposed to ovalbumin during water avoidance stress and re-exposed to ovalbumin weeks later developed increased pain signaling in the colon and small intestine, despite lacking systemic allergy.
Using pharmacologic and genetic approaches, the authors showed that OVA-induced increases in pain responses required mast cells, IgE, and STAT6 signaling.

Sensory neurons incubated with ileum and colon supernatants from stressed, OVA-re-exposed mice showed a lowered threshold of excitability, indicating peripheral sensitization by gut-derived mediators.
The H1 histamine receptor antagonist pyrilamine blocked the increased sensory neuron excitability and reduced ileal afferent nerve firing to distension in stressed, OVA-re-exposed mice.

Meta-analysis identified a novel Japanese-specific risk locus at 6q27, 13kb upstream of CCR6, associated with increased NMOSD risk.
The CCR6 risk variant remained significantly associated with disease specifically in anti-AQP4 antibody-positive NMOSD patients.
The CCR6 locus association found in this Japanese GWAS was not observed in a previous European NMOSD GWAS.

The CCR6 risk variant showed NMOSD-specific dosage effects on CCR6 expression in CD4 memory and Treg cells, absent in healthy controls.
Cell-cell communication analysis showed enhanced CCL20/CCR6 signaling between monocytes and CD4 memory T cells in NMOSD patients.
The proportion of non-naive CD4T cells, including Th17 cells, was increased in NMOSD patients relative to healthy controls.
The CCR6 risk variant rs12193698 showed a pQTL effect on plasma RNase T2 levels, with the risk allele reducing its expression.

Among autoimmune diseases tested, only NMOSD showed a strong, significant association with mCAs (both CNA and CN-LOH), with an odds ratio exceeding that seen for hematological malignancy.
Somatic loss of chromosome 21q was found in three NMOSD patients and was an NMOSD-specific recurrently affected region, not associated with hematological malignancy.

Ligand-receptor communication from CD4 naive/memory T cells to CD8 memory/CTL cells was enhanced in NMOSD patients compared with controls.
Among 58 COPD patients studied, 38% had airway eosinophilia at baseline, defined as BAL eosinophils >1% of total leukocytes.
COPD patients with airway eosinophilia had more severe airflow obstruction and more radiographic emphysema compared with those without airway eosinophilia.
COPD patients with airway eosinophilia showed higher baseline epithelial expression of type 2 airway inflammation and IL-13 gene signatures compared to non-eosinophilic COPD patients.
Airway epithelial mast cell activation gene signature expression was higher at baseline in COPD patients with airway eosinophilia than in those without.
Epithelial expression of type 1 and type 17 airway inflammation gene signatures was similar between COPD patients with and without airway eosinophilia at baseline.
Gene set enrichment analysis identified upregulation of canonical pathways related to type 2 immune response and asthma in the airway eosinophilia group.
Twelve weeks of inhaled corticosteroid treatment reduced airway epithelial expression of type 2 inflammation gene signatures in COPD patients with airway eosinophilia.
Epithelial expression of the type 17 airway inflammation gene signature did not differ between COPD patients with and without airway eosinophilia at baseline.
Gene set enrichment analysis showed upregulation of canonical pathways related to the type 2 immune response and asthma in COPD patients with airway eosinophilia.
Twelve weeks of inhaled corticosteroid treatment reduced epithelial expression of the type 2 inflammation gene signature in COPD patients with airway eosinophilia.

IENFD was reduced in NIID patients at the distal leg, proximal thigh, and cervical area compared to other groups, indicating a non-length-dependent pattern of small fiber loss.
Autonomic nerve fiber densities (SGNFD and PNFD) were lower in NIID patients compared with PD, AD, DPN, and healthy controls.
All NIID patients had distal leg IENFD below age-normalized reference values, meeting diagnostic criteria for small fiber neuropathy.
IENFD showed near-perfect diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing NIID from PD, AD, DPN, and healthy controls by ROC analysis.
NIID patients had higher SFN-SIQ scores than AD patients and healthy controls, but scores were not significantly different from PD or DPN patients.

NIID patients had higher COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores than AD, DPN, and healthy controls, but similar to PD patients, with gastrointestinal, secretomotor, bladder, and pupillomotor domains most affected.
Nerve conduction studies in a subset of NIID patients showed abnormal large fiber function, with reduced CMAP, MCV, SNAP, and SCV in a substantial proportion of patients.
Among NIID patients tested with combined skin biopsy and NCS, over half showed mixed large-and-small fiber neuropathy while nearly half had pure small fiber involvement.
Small fiber damage was more extensive (100%) than large fiber damage (53.3%) in NIID patients.
Quantitative sensory testing showed impaired thermal sensation in NIID patients, with elevated warm/heat pain thresholds and reduced cold detection/cold pain thresholds compared to other groups.
Current perception thresholds at 2000, 250, and 5 Hz were higher in NIID patients than other groups, indicating impaired pain/small fiber sensory function.
Tilt table testing showed greater orthostatic blood pressure decreases and lower heart rate in NIID patients compared to other groups, indicating autonomic/vasomotor dysfunction.
Sudomotor function testing (Sudoscan) revealed worse electrochemical skin conductance (ESC) in NIID patients than other groups, indicating impaired sweat gland innervation.
TH-positive noradrenergic nerve fibers in the arrector pili muscles were markedly decreased in NIID patients compared with healthy controls.
VIP-positive cholinergic nerve fibers in sweat glands were reduced in NIID patients compared with healthy controls.
Peptidergic nerve fibers (CGRP- and SP-positive) in the dermis were notably reduced in NIID patients compared with healthy controls.

GAP-43 staining showed near-absent sensory nerve regeneration and reduced but present autonomic nerve regeneration in NIID patients compared with healthy controls, suggesting insufficient nerve regeneration underlies somatosensory fiber loss.

SGNFD and PNFD were positively correlated with each other, but IENFD did not significantly correlate with SGNFD or PNFD in NIID patients, suggesting sensory and autonomic small fiber damage may not occur in parallel.
SGNFD and PNFD were negatively correlated with SFN-SIQ and COMPASS-31 clinical symptom scores in NIID patients, while IENFD showed no correlation with these clinical scales.
IENFD correlated with quantitative sensory testing thermal thresholds and current perception thresholds in NIID patients, linking pathology to function.
SGNFD and PNFD were positively correlated with electrochemical skin conductance (ESC) in the sudomotor function test, linking autonomic nerve fiber density to functional impairment.

No significant correlation was found between the frequency of skin intranuclear inclusions and IENFD, SGNFD, or PNFD, suggesting small fiber degeneration in NIID may not be directly linked to inclusion formation.

There were no significant differences in IENFD, SGNFD, or PNFD among the four clinical subgroups of NIID (muscle weakness-dominant, dementia-dominant, movement disorder-dominant, paroxysmal symptom-dominant), suggesting SFN is a common feature independent of clinical phenotype.
All NIID patients carried abnormal NOTCH2NLC GGC repeat expansions exceeding 60 repeats, with a median repeat size of 112, confirming genetic diagnosis of NIID.

The most common small fiber symptom reported by NIID patients was changed sweating, followed by dry mouth, micturition problems, constipation, dizziness standing, and dry eyes; classic sensory symptoms of SFN (sensitive skin, sheet intolerance) were rare.
ROC curve analysis showed that IENFD, SGNFD, and PNFD each had high diagnostic accuracy (AUC > 0.800) for distinguishing NIID patients from PD, AD, DPN, and healthy control groups.
IENFD showed the highest diagnostic value among the three metrics, with an AUC of 1.000 differentiating NIID from PD, AD, and HC, and 0.994 differentiating NIID from DPN.
In NIID patients, sweat gland nerve fiber density and pilomotor nerve fiber density were positively correlated with each other.
IENFD was not significantly correlated with either SGNFD or PNFD in NIID patients, suggesting sensory and autonomic small fiber damage may not occur in parallel.
IENFD did not correlate with self-reported small fiber symptom severity (SFN-SIQ) or autonomic symptom severity (COMPASS-31) scores in NIID patients.
SGNFD was negatively correlated with SFN-SIQ and COMPASS-31 scores, indicating that lower sweat gland innervation is associated with greater symptom severity in NIID.
PNFD was negatively correlated with SFN-SIQ and COMPASS-31 scores in NIID patients, paralleling the SGNFD correlation.

IENFD correlated with quantitative thermal sensory testing results, being negatively correlated with warm and heat pain thresholds and positively correlated with cold detection and cold pain thresholds.
IENFD was negatively correlated with current perception thresholds measured at 5 Hz, reflecting unmyelinated C-fiber function.
SGNFD and PNFD were positively correlated with electrochemical skin conductance in the sudomotor function test, linking autonomic nerve fiber loss to impaired sweat gland function.

No significant correlation was found between the frequency of skin intranuclear inclusions and IENFD, SGNFD, or PNFD in NIID patients, suggesting small fiber loss is not directly driven by local inclusion burden.

Quantification of intranuclear inclusions within fibroblasts and sweat gland cells showed no significant correlation with IENFD or SGNFD, suggesting peripheral inclusion toxicity may not directly cause small fiber nerve damage in NIID.

Diabetes mellitus, including prediabetic states, is associated with development of small-fiber neuropathy, which may act as a precursor to large-fiber neuropathy, with prominent autonomic involvement.
Metabolic syndrome components, particularly hypertriglyceridemia, have been associated with small-fiber neuropathy.
Hypothyroidism may cause pain syndromes compatible with small-fiber neuropathy, as determined via QST sensory thresholds.
A large cohort study found vitamin B12 deficiency incidence to be higher in SFN patients than in the general population.
HIV infection can cause sensory neuropathies with prominent pain, related to loss of intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD).
Among hepatitis viruses, hepatitis C infection has been most commonly associated with the development of SFN.
A case-control study reported that neuropathic pain was a common complaint among patients with acute hepatitis E infection.
Post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS), a chronic phase after Lyme disease treatment with cognitive impairment and pain, has been related to both somatic and autonomic small-fiber neuropathy.
Post-herpetic neuralgia following herpes zoster reactivation has been shown to be caused by small-fiber neuropathy, commonly accompanied by pruritus.
EBV infection was described in a single case report of acute autonomic neuropathy.
Leprosy can cause clinical pictures dominated by neuropathic pain due to small-fiber neuropathy.
Post-COVID (long-COVID) painful syndromes have been shown to be partly related to small-fiber neuropathy.

SFN has been demonstrated in SLE patients with neuropathic pain, occurring in both length-dependent and non-length-dependent forms, the latter postulated to result from dorsal root ganglion pathology.
Pure SFN, though less common than large-fiber axonal neuropathy in Sjögren syndrome, is possible and has been suggested to be associated with a distinct immunological profile.
In sarcoidosis, SFN has been estimated to be the most common neurological complication and is associated with autonomic dysfunction.

Autoantibodies against trisulfated heparin disaccharide (TS-HDS) and fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR-3) have been associated with functional small nerve fiber dysfunction, neuropathic pain, and non-length-dependent SFN.
Oxaliplatin, a platinum-based chemotherapy drug, causes acute cold-induced paresthesias related to its effect on Na+ channels, as part of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neurotoxicity.
Bortezomib, used to treat multiple myeloma, has been associated with somatic and autonomic length-dependent small-fiber neuropathy.
Docetaxel can induce small-fiber neuropathy, as demonstrated by skin biopsy and QST.
Metronidazole and nitrofurantoin, antibiotics, can induce painful small-fiber neuropathy via neurotoxic effects.

SCN9A (Nav1.7) mutations underlie a spectrum of pain disorders: missense gain-of-function mutations cause primary erythromelalgia and paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, loss-of-function mutations cause congenital insensitivity to pain, and other gain-of-function mutations have been found in SFN patients with dorsal root ganglion hyperexcitability and in painful diabetic neuropathy.
SCN10A (Nav1.8) mutations, both gain- and loss-of-function, have been described in patients and families with painful and autonomic signs and symptoms.
SCN11A mutations underlie hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 7 (HSAN7), and SFN patients have also been found to carry mutations of this gene.

Fabry disease, caused by GLA gene mutations leading to globotriaosylceramide accumulation, presents with acroparesthesias and pain from childhood, exacerbated by extreme temperatures, with autonomic gastrointestinal involvement, and pathophysiology involving dorsal root ganglion dysfunction and small-fiber neuropathy.
Familial amyloidosis caused by TTR gene mutations is characterized by autonomic small-fiber neuropathy as well as large-fiber involvement.
Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, a group of connective tissue disorders, are often characterized by pain shown to be related to small-fiber neuropathy.
Fibromyalgia, an important differential diagnosis for SFN, has shown alterations of intraepidermal innervation in some patient subsets.
Approximately 50% of SFN cases remain idiopathic despite the wide range of identified etiologies.
Corneal confocal microscopy showed reduction in corneal innervation preceding symptoms of impaired corneal sensitivity in patients with diabetic polyneuropathy.

Cardiovascular autonomic testing (tilt testing, Valsalva maneuver) is particularly relevant when patients report orthostatic intolerance symptoms, which could be explained by orthostatic hypotension or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).

Neuropathic pain in SFN can be treated with gabapentinoids (pregabalin, gabapentin), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (duloxetine, venlafaxine), and tricyclic antidepressants as first-line options, with cannabinoids, topical capsaicin, and botulinum toxin type A as second-line approaches.
Autonomic symptoms of SFN can be managed with lifestyle measures (e.g., chewing gum for sialorrhea) or specific therapy such as fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension.

Missense mutations in SCN9A causing gain-of-function of Nav1.7 were the first genetic cause described for primary erythromelalgia, characterized by episodes of burning pain and redness of the extremities.
Missense mutations of SCN9A that prevent inactivation of Nav1.7 were associated with paroxysmal extreme pain disorder.
Loss-of-function mutations in SCN9A were found in patients with congenital insensitivity to pain.
Gain-of-function mutations in SCN9A were described in patients with small-fiber neuropathy, associated with dorsal root ganglion hyperexcitability.
SCN9A mutations have also been described in patients with painful diabetic neuropathy.
SCN10A mutations, encoding Nav1.8, have been described in patients and families presenting with painful and autonomic signs and symptoms of small-fiber neuropathy.
SCN11A mutations underlie hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 7 (HSAN7), and SFN patients have also been found to carry mutations of this gene.

Familial amyloidosis caused by TTR gene mutations is characterized by autonomic small-fiber neuropathy along with large-fiber involvement.
Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, a group of connective tissue disorders, are often characterized by pain that has been shown to be related to small-fiber neuropathy.
Fibromyalgia shows alterations of intraepidermal innervation in some patient subsets, complicating differentiation from other causes of SFN-related pain.
Approximately 50% of SFN cases remain idiopathic despite the wide array of associated disorders and pathological processes identified.

Neuropathic pain in SFN can be treated with gabapentinoids (pregabalin, gabapentin), serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (duloxetine, venlafaxine), and tricyclic antidepressants as first-line pharmacologic options.

Second-line pharmacologic approaches for SFN-related neuropathic pain include cannabinoids, topical capsaicin, and botulinum toxin type A, with cognitive-behavioral therapy as a complementary non-pharmacologic option.

Targeted sodium channel therapy against Nav1.7, Nav1.8, and Nav1.9 is proposed as a specific approach for neuropathic pain, though achieving channel specificity without impairing other voltage-gated sodium channels remains challenging, and gene therapy is a promising but demanding alternative.
Autonomic symptoms in SFN can be managed with lifestyle measures (e.g., chewing gum for sialorrhea) or specific pharmacologic therapy such as fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension when severe.

Among 111 patients diagnosed with SFN, 9 tested positive for antibodies against TS-HDS, FGFR3, or plexin-D1.
RT-SFN-SIQ scores showed a trend toward improvement following rituximab treatment, though not reaching statistical significance.
SFN-RODS disability scores showed a trend toward improvement following rituximab treatment.
COMPASS-31 autonomic symptom scores remained unchanged after rituximab treatment.
Rituximab's therapeutic efficacy was monitored via reduction in circulating CD19+ B cell levels measured by flow cytometry.
Among 86 patients with skin-biopsy-confirmed small fiber neuropathy, serum neurofilament light chain was elevated in only 9 (10%), indicating sNfL is typically normal in SFN.

Of the 9 SFN patients with elevated sNfL, 7 had co-existing neurological comorbidities (e.g., CNS disorders, large-fiber polyneuropathy, radiculopathy) that could explain the elevation, suggesting sNfL elevation in SFN patients often reflects another underlying condition rather than small fiber injury itself.

Two SFN patients with elevated sNfL and no identified neurological comorbidity had a history of hypothyroidism and endometriosis respectively, suggesting possible non-neurological contributors to sNfL elevation.
Serum NfL levels were elevated in only 9 of 86 (10%) patients with confirmed small-fiber neuropathy, indicating that most SFN patients did not show evidence of active axonal injury by this marker.
SFN patients with elevated sNfL more frequently had additional neurological comorbidities (24% vs 7%) than those with normal sNfL, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.
The magnitude of sNfL elevation (test/upper-normal-limit ratio) did not differ significantly between SFN patients with versus without neurological comorbidities.
sNfL levels did not differ significantly between SFN patients with symptom duration of less than versus more than one year.
All nine patients with elevated sNfL also had reduced epidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy, consistent with confirmed small fiber loss.
Genetic evaluation prompted by family history and/or Congo red staining identified a TTR pathogenic variant in two SFN patients, one with confirmed cardiac amyloidosis and one asymptomatic carrier.

The two SFN patients with elevated sNfL but no neurological comorbidities both had a history of endometriosis and hypothyroidism, suggesting these systemic conditions may relate to axonal injury signal in SFN.
Sepiapterin treatment induced a wrinkled, rougher bacterial surface morphology in Bacillus subtilis compared to untreated controls, consistent with biofilm formation.
Sepiapterin treatment caused a large increase in mucus protein MUC2 expression in the Caco-2:HT-29 epithelial layer of the co-culture compared to untreated controls.
Sepiapterin treatment increased epithelial marker CK20 expression and caused pronounced cytokeratin rearrangement in the Caco-2:HT-29 epithelial layer alongside massive mucus production.
Sepiapterin treatment of M0 macrophages (THP-1) in the co-culture caused a large increase in the M1 marker CD80, indicating M1 polarization.
Sepiapterin treatment did not increase the M2 marker CD163 or the pan-macrophage marker CD68 in THP-1 cells, supporting a dedicated M1 polarization rather than a general macrophage activation.

In monoculture, Sepiapterin caused M0 and M2 macrophages to morphologically shift from spherical/smooth to elongated, spindle-like structures with pseudopods characteristic of M1-type macrophages, mirroring the authors' prior finding of SEP-driven M2-to-M1 reprogramming in breast tumor macrophages.

The 3D Flipwell co-culture system reproduced synchronous, crosstalk-driven responses of gut bacteria, mucus, colon epithelial cells, and macrophages to an exogenous pharmacologic stimulus (Sepiapterin), supporting its utility as a gut mucosal microenvironment model.
Acetylcholine treatment reduced doxorubicin-induced cell death and contractile dysfunction in cardiac spheroids.
ACh-loaded nanoparticles (ACh-NPs) were developed as a non-invasive delivery strategy and, per the title, protected cardiac spheroids against doxorubicin-induced toxicity.
Co-culture with ACh-producing cholinergic neurons (CNs) was tested as one of three ACh administration strategies to counter doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity in cardiac spheroids.
ACh counteracted doxorubicin-induced downregulation of genes controlling myocardial fibrosis, and endothelial and cardiomyocyte dysfunction.
ACh counteracted doxorubicin-induced downregulation of genes controlling autonomic dysregulation in the cardiac spheroid model.
ACh-mediated cardioprotection against doxorubicin toxicity was dependent on nitric oxide (NO) signaling specifically in endothelial cells.
ACh-mediated cardioprotection against doxorubicin toxicity was not dependent on nitric oxide signaling in cardiac myocytes.
ACh-mediated cardioprotection against doxorubicin toxicity was not dependent on nitric oxide signaling in cardiac fibroblasts.
ACh treatment counteracted the doxorubicin-induced downregulation of genes controlling myocardial fibrosis in cardiac spheroids.
ACh treatment counteracted the doxorubicin-induced downregulation of genes controlling endothelial dysfunction in cardiac spheroids.
ACh treatment counteracted the doxorubicin-induced downregulation of genes controlling cardiomyocyte dysfunction in cardiac spheroids.
ACh treatment counteracted the doxorubicin-induced downregulation of genes controlling autonomic dysregulation in cardiac spheroids.
Sodium propionate treatment decreased neutrophil influx into implants by 54% relative to control implants.
Sodium propionate treatment decreased lymphocyte influx into implants by 25% relative to control implants.
Sodium propionate treatment decreased macrophage influx into implants by 40% relative to control implants.
MPO activity, a marker of neutrophil presence, was reduced by 24% in implants of SP-treated mice.
TNF-α levels in implants were reduced by 50% in SP-treated mice compared with controls.
The number of mast cells in implants was decreased in SP-treated mice compared with controls (3.0±0.3 vs 4.0±0.3).
SP-treated implants showed a marked reduction in the number of newly formed blood vessels compared with control implants (1.26±0.7 vs 6.7±0.7).
VEGF levels in implants were reduced in SP-treated mice compared with controls (0.09±0.06 vs 0.71±0.27).
Total intra-implant collagen content, measured by Picrosirius red staining, was markedly lower in SP-treated implants than controls (1,156,159±305,114 μm2 vs 3,118,482±740,566 μm2).
SP treatment shifted the predominant collagen fiber type in the fibrotic capsule from type I (control) to type III (SP-treated), suggesting a less mature fibrotic response.
Intra-implant TGF-β1 levels (by ELISA) were lower in SP-treated mice compared with controls (0.4±0.08 vs 1.3±0.4).
Western blot analysis showed decreased α-SMA protein levels in implants of SP-treated mice compared with controls (0.7±0.05 vs 1.0±0.1), indicating reduced myofibroblast activation.
Western blot analysis showed lower TGF-β1 protein levels in implants of SP-treated mice compared with controls (0.74±0.15 vs 1.3±0.2).
The number of foreign body giant cells was reduced in SP-treated implants compared with controls (median 1.5 vs 3.6), with treated FBGCs also showing fewer nuclei and reduced cytoplasm.
Fibrous capsule wall thickness surrounding implants was reduced in SP-treated mice compared with controls (194.8±23.5 vs 311.5±44.4).
SP treatment increased the proportion of GR1-Low/Neg patrolling monocytes in implants relative to control, while macrophages and GR1+ monocytes were reduced.
Oral administration of sodium propionate (100 mg/kg for 14 days) produced no observable signs of toxicity such as sedation, weight loss, or altered motor activity in mice.
Electron microscopy of diabetic mouse choroids revealed loosened myelin sheaths, axon atrophy, and vacuolated Schwann cell cytoplasm compared to non-diabetic controls.
Choroidal epinephrine levels were lower in diabetic mice than in non-diabetic controls.
No significant difference in choroidal acetylcholine levels was found between diabetic and control mice.
The ratio of epinephrine to acetylcholine, a proxy for sympathetic/parasympathetic balance, was greatly decreased in diabetic choroids.
Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) levels were decreased in diabetic choroids, indicating reduced sympathetic activity.
Choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) levels were increased in diabetic choroids, indicating altered parasympathetic/cholinergic signaling.
Neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) levels were increased in diabetic choroids.
Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) levels were increased in diabetic choroids.
Neuropeptide Y (NPY) levels were increased in the choroids of diabetic mice compared to controls.
CGRP levels were increased in the choroids of diabetic mice compared to controls.
Fewer TH-positive and DβH-positive neuronal cells were observed in the superior cervical sympathetic ganglia of diabetic mice, indicating sympathetic neuronal loss or dysfunction.
More CGRP-positive neuronal cells were observed in the trigeminal ganglia of diabetic mice.
Fewer TH-positive neuronal cells were observed in the trigeminal ganglia of diabetic mice.
Vaginal wall tissue from patients with POP showed loosely arranged, disordered collagen fibers and reduced, broken elastic fiber density compared with controls.
F-actin stress fibers in POP vaginal wall tissue were wavy, distorted, and structurally destroyed compared with the evenly distributed, filamentous fibers seen in controls.
COL1A1 and COL3A1 mRNA expression levels were relatively high in prolapsed tissue, possibly reflecting compensatory gene expression.
COL1A1 and COL3A1 protein expression levels were significantly decreased in POP vaginal wall tissue compared with control tissue, despite elevated mRNA levels.
Integrin-β1 protein expression was significantly reduced in POP vaginal wall tissue compared with control tissue.
TGF-β1 protein expression was significantly reduced in POP vaginal wall tissue compared with control tissue.
TIMP-1 protein expression was significantly reduced in POP vaginal wall tissue compared with control tissue, consistent with reduced inhibition of MMP activity.
MMP-1 protein expression was significantly increased in POP vaginal wall tissue compared with control tissue.
Pharmacological inhibition of integrin-β1 (GRGDNP) significantly reduced fibroblast migration compared with untreated control fibroblasts.
Integrin-β1 inhibition and POP status were both associated with significantly increased fibroblast apoptosis compared with control fibroblasts.

Treatment of fibroblasts with an integrin-β1 inhibitor decreased protein expression of COL1A1, COL3A1 and integrin-β1 compared with untreated controls, linking integrin-β1 expression to collagen production.
After 6 h of 15% mechanical stretch, integrin-β1 and COL3A1 protein were non-significantly decreased while COL1A1 protein was significantly decreased compared with unstretched (0 h) fibroblasts.
After 12 h of 15% mechanical stretch, COL1A1 and COL3A1 protein expression were significantly increased compared with unstretched fibroblasts.
Fibroblast apoptosis rate increased progressively with duration of cyclic tensile mechanical stress from 0 to 24 hours.
After 12 h of 15% mechanical force, integrin-β1, TIMP-1, COL1A1 and COL3A1 expression increased while TGF-β1 and MMP-1 expression decreased, compared with unstressed control fibroblasts.

Combining integrin-β1 inhibition with mechanical force stimulation lowered integrin-β1, TGF-β1, COL1A1 and COL3A1 expression and raised MMP-1 and TIMP-1 expression compared with mechanical force alone, indicating integrin-β1 blockade attenuates the mechanical-force-induced pathway response.

The percentage of normal slow waves progressively decreased across healthy, prediabetic, and diabetic stages, beginning in the fasting state after high-fat diet feeding and in the postprandial state after streptozotocin injection.
The normal postprandial rise in slow wave power seen in control rats disappeared starting 2 weeks after high-fat diet initiation and remained absent after streptozotocin injection.
The percentage of normal slow waves was negatively correlated with fasting blood glucose levels.

During oral glucose tolerance testing, the relationship between duodenal slow wave regularity and blood glucose switched from positive in rats with HbA1C below 5.0% to negative in rats with HbA1C at or above 5.0%.
Plasma pancreatic polypeptide, a marker of vagal activity, progressively decreased across the healthy, prediabetic, and diabetic stages.
Plasma norepinephrine, a marker of sympathetic activity, progressively increased across the healthy, prediabetic, and diabetic stages.

Sympathetic nervous system activity, assessed via ECG, increased equally in healthy controls, IBS patients, and FD patients during the public-speaking VR scenario compared with the unmanned-room scenario.

Subjective stress (measured by visual analog scale) increased similarly across healthy controls, IBS patients, and FD patients during the public-speaking VR scenario relative to the unmanned-room scenario.
Patients with IBS showed higher activity in the left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (VLPFC) during the psychosocial stress scenario compared with FD patients and healthy controls.
Patients with IBS showed lower activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) during the psychosocial stress scenario compared with FD patients and healthy controls.
Mast cell numbers were found to be increased in the intestinal mucosa of patients with ulcerative colitis compared with control subjects.
A greater number of mast cells was observed in hypertrophied and fibrotic tissue sites of Crohn's disease patients compared with normal gut, suggesting a role for MCs in intestinal fibrosis.
Tryptase secreted from human mast cells activates fibroblasts to differentiate into myofibroblasts that release more extracellular matrix proteins, contributing to fibrosis seen in IBD.
Ex vivo oxygenation of mucosal biopsies showed more pronounced tryptase-β and histamine exocytosis in inflamed intestinal tissue compared with noninflamed colon of IBD patients.
Urinary histamine metabolite levels positively correlated with the severity and extent of disease in IBD patients.
Degranulating mast cells release substantial amounts of TNF-α, IL-16, and substance P in the mucosa of the ileum and colon of IBD patients, supporting a role in disease pathogenesis.

A connective-like murine mast cell subset expressing Mrgprb2 increases in inflamed colon of WT mice and localizes near nerve fibers, while Mrgprb2-/- mice show reduced neutrophil influx and attenuated acute colitis.

Single-cell RNA sequencing identified a human mast cell subset expressing MRGPRX2 that contributes to ulcerative colitis via a positive feedback inflammatory loop, suggesting MRGPRX2 as a therapeutic target.
The intracellular bacterial receptor NOD2 was found to be up-regulated in intestinal mast cells of Crohn's disease patients, suggesting a role in mast cell recruitment/activation.

In mMCP-4-null mice, loss of chymase increased crypt depth and decreased expression of the tight-junction protein claudin-3 relative to wild type, indicating a homeostatic role for this chymase in intestinal epithelial architecture.
Weston and coauthors reported increased numbers of mucosal mast cells in the terminal ileum of IBS patients, an early link between mast cells and IBS.
Barbara and coauthors showed IBS patients had more mast cells in the left colon and rectum than normal individuals, many residing near nerve endings, linking MCs to pain and gut dysfunction.
Enhanced tryptase activity was shown in ex vivo colonic biopsies from patients with diarrhea-predominant IBS (IBS-D).
Patients with constipation-predominant IBS (IBS-C) show high levels of mast cell cysteine protease activity that positively correlates with disease severity and abdominal pain scoring.

Upregulation of the MRGPRX2 gene has been observed in colonic biopsies of some IBS patients along with high IL-1b and PTGS2 gene expression, suggesting a connective-tissue-like mast cell subset contributing to abdominal pain.
In a pilot study, 46% of IBS patients receiving the H1-antihistamine ebastine for 12 weeks reported significantly improved symptom relief and reduced abdominal pain compared to 13% on placebo.
A phase 2 randomized, placebo-controlled study confirmed ebastine improved global relief of hypersensitivity symptoms and abdominal pain intensity in IBS-D patients.
5-HT3 antagonists such as alosetron and ramosetron have repeatedly shown efficacy in reducing abdominal pain and discomfort in IBS-D patients.
In a phase II study on ulcerative colitis patients, the tryptase inhibitor APC 2059 showed symptom improvement in more than 50% of treated patients.
Disodium cromoglycate administration resulted in clinical improvement of symptoms in IBS-D patients by decreasing tryptase release, and also showed benefit in IBD.

Treatment with the mast cell stabilizer ketotifen showed beneficial effects in both IBD and IBS patients, though the overall effect of MC stabilizers across studies was described as weak and inconsistent.

Probiotic administration displayed positive effects in pouchitis treatment, induction of remission in ulcerative colitis, and reduction in symptoms/inflammation in IBS, though specific strains/mechanisms remain undefined.

IgE-mediated crosslinking of mast cell FcεRI due to a break in oral tolerance to dietary antigens in an inflammatory environment can trigger food-induced abdominal pain, though the responsible mast cell subset is not characterized.

The authors describe a patient with chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction (CIPO) occurring in the setting of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), highlighting autonomic peripheral neuropathy as a cause of GI dysmotility.
The paper notes that CIPO is diagnostically challenging and is frequently misdiagnosed, resulting in patients undergoing unnecessary abdominal surgery.

A supervised multi-omics factor (recovery factor) trained on convalescent-phase immune profiling data discriminated long COVID from minimal-deficit participants with an AUROC of 0.69 in the test cohort.
The Hallmark Heme Metabolism gene expression pathway in PBMCs was upregulated in long COVID participants during convalescence, as identified by gene set enrichment analysis.
Androgenic steroid metabolites were downregulated in long COVID participants compared to those with minimal deficits.
Serum DNER, a non-canonical Notch ligand implicated in wound healing, was significantly reduced in long COVID participants.

Multiple serum Olink inflammatory and myeloid-regulatory proteins associated with chronic inflammation and endothelial/vascular inflammation were negatively associated with the recovery factor (i.e., elevated in long COVID).
The oxysterol binding protein transcript OSBP2, a leading edge gene in the Hallmark Heme Metabolism gene set, was elevated in long COVID participants.

Five specific androgenic steroid metabolites (DHEA-S, epiandrosterone sulfate, androsterone sulfate, and two 5alpha-androstan-diol sulfates) were significantly lower in long COVID participants after adjusting for age and sex.

A combined geometric mean score of 73 unique features (43 heme metabolism, 12 androgenic steroid, and 26 significant SPEAR analytes) discriminated MIN from long COVID participants with greater significance than any individual feature set.

Heme metabolism leading-edge gene expression signature identified in IMPACC significantly differentiated persistent vs. resolved symptoms in an independent cohort (Hanson et al.) at multiple post-infection time points, validating the finding across cohorts.

During convalescence, B cells and CD161+ MAIT cells were positively associated with the recovery factor while neutrophils and classical monocytes were negatively associated, suggesting persistent monocyte/neutrophil elevation and B cell deficit in long COVID.

Anemia as a clinical complication at admission was negatively associated with the recovery factor, while baseline hemoglobin and hematocrit were positively associated, linking anemia to long COVID risk.

The recovery factor remained significantly associated with long COVID status even after correcting for acute disease severity trajectory group, indicating this biomarker predicts LC independent of acute severity.

Nearly half of female participants had long-term deficits compared to ~30% of males; the recovery factor discriminated LC vs MIN significantly in females but not males, and sex was a significant covariate in LC associations.
SARS-CoV-2 vaccination during the convalescent follow-up period had no significant effect on recovery factor scores, indicating vaccination did not confound the LC-associated immune signature.
Recovery factor scores computed from acute-phase immune profiling data were significantly higher in MIN versus long COVID participants as early as hospital admission, before LC diagnosis.

During the acute phase, CD4+/CD8+ T cell subsets, dendritic cells, eosinophils, basophils, and NK cells were positively associated with the recovery factor (higher in MIN), while monocytes, neutrophils, B cells, and plasmablasts were negatively associated (higher in future LC), reflecting reduced adaptive immunity and heightened innate inflammation in those who develop LC.

In the full IMPACC cohort (n=1,148), acute-phase recovery factor scores were significantly associated with acute disease trajectory group severity, being highest in milder disease courses and lowest in the most severe/fatal trajectories, but LC status remained significantly associated with recovery factor scores even after adjusting for trajectory group.

Predictive models combining recovery factor scores with clinical features (age, sex, BMI, hospital stay length, SOFA score, antibody titers, viral load, comorbidities) improved LC classification performance over clinical features alone, both in acute and convalescent phases.
A streamlined model using only the 26 SPEAR-significant analytes achieved comparable predictive performance (AUROC 0.69) to more complex models, suggesting utility as a simplified diagnostic panel.

The top androgenic steroid metabolites identified in this long COVID recovery factor strongly overlapped with an androgenic steroid signature found reduced in an independent all-female ME/CFS cohort compared to healthy controls, implicating shared endocrine dysregulation in overlapping fatigue-related symptoms.

FGF21, a serum protein elevated in long COVID participants in this cohort, has also been proposed as a biomarker of chronic inflammation in ME/CFS, a condition that overlaps clinically with long COVID.

The lead genetic variant rs9367106 from the long COVID GWAS, along with nearby correlated SNPs, was used as the instrumental variable for Mendelian randomization, with F-statistics greater than 10 indicating no weak instrument bias.
Two-sample Mendelian randomization found no significant causal effect of genetic liability to long COVID on global cortical surface area or thickness after FDR correction.

Mendelian randomization showed no significant causal association between long COVID genetic liability and surface area or thickness of any of the 34 regional cortical brain structures after multiple testing correction.

No significant causal relationship was found between long COVID genetic liability and volumes of 17 left/right subcortical brain structures after FDR correction, while combined hemispheric subcortical volumes could not be tested due to insufficient instrument variables.
Female sex was associated with a significantly higher rate of long COVID compared to male sex.
Participants who identified as white race were slightly more likely to report long COVID than non-white participants.
Having at least one baseline comorbidity was significantly more common among participants who developed long COVID.
Class 3 obesity (BMI>40) at baseline was more common among participants who developed long COVID.
Elevated baseline CRP at hospital admission was not associated with subsequent development of long COVID.
Presence of infiltrates on baseline chest imaging was not associated with subsequent long COVID.
Baseline respiratory/ventilatory support requirement and disease severity at admission were not associated with subsequent long COVID.
Use of steroids during acute hospitalization was not associated with a change in long COVID prevalence.
Remdesivir use during acute hospitalization was not associated with reduced risk of long COVID.
Post-hospitalization symptoms across cardiopulmonary, GI/neurologic/upper respiratory, and systemic categories were all reported more frequently in participants classified as having long COVID.

Machine learning models (bGLM, NNET, RF, SVM, XGB) trained on baseline clinical, symptom, antibody and viral load features achieved modest but significant predictive performance for long COVID on an independent held-out test set, with AUROC 0.64-0.66 and AUPRC 0.51-0.54.
Lower baseline anti-Spike IgG antibody titers at hospital admission were the most important feature predicting subsequent development of long COVID across all machine learning models.
Higher baseline SARS-CoV-2 viral load (as measured by N1 gene RT-PCR) at hospital admission was among the most important features predicting subsequent long COVID.
Baseline diabetes mellitus was identified as a significant risk factor for developing long COVID in the machine learning models.
Chronic respiratory disease at baseline was identified as a significant risk factor for long COVID.
Chronic cardiac disease at baseline was identified as a significant risk factor for long COVID.
Chronic neurologic disease at baseline was identified as a significant risk factor for long COVID.
Presence of acute-phase symptoms of cough, chest pain, and sore throat at baseline was associated with a lower risk of subsequently developing long COVID.
Age did not differ significantly between participants with and without evidence of long COVID.
Severity of COVID-19 disease at hospital admission was not associated with development of long COVID, consistent with reports that PASC also occurs after mild to moderate infection.

The authors show that the widely circulated global ME/CFS prevalence figure of 17-24 million people stems from a misattributed citation in Lim et al.'s Background section (referencing a multiple sclerosis study), and that the study's actual headline estimate of 0.89% prevalence, when applied to the global population of 8 billion, yields a corrected estimate of approximately 71.2 million people affected.
Memory and concentration problems are self-reported by the large majority of ME/CFS patients.
Low-grade inflammation, reflected by elevated blood CRP and pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNFα, is present in many ME/CFS patients.

Peripheral cytokine levels correlate with psychological variables and sleep disturbance in ME/CFS, with executive function linked to IL-1/IL-6, interpersonal function to IL-6/TNFα, and sleep to IL-1, IL-2, IL-6, and TNFα.
Subjectively reported cognitive difficulties in memory, attention, and information processing are significantly worse in ME/CFS patients than healthy controls.
A meta-analysis of 50 studies (1988–2008) identified deficits in attention, memory, and reaction time in ME/CFS patients.
A meta-analysis of 33 studies (1988–2019) found significant impairments in visuo-spatial, short-term, and especially immediate memory, consistent with a massive executive deficit.
Over a quarter of patients diagnosed using the 1994 Fukuda criteria report no difficulties with memory and concentration in daily life, highlighting heterogeneity.

A cognitive domain study found impaired attention and motor functioning in ~50% of ME/CFS patients, executive functioning/processing speed impairment in 40%, visual memory impairment in 30%, and verbal memory/problem-solving impairment in under 20%.
DeLuca et al. found that while ME/CFS patients showed reduced information processing relative to controls, memory impairment was more severe in those with sudden, presumed infectious, onset.
The severity of cognitive dysfunction does not appear to differ between ME/CFS patients with short versus long duration of illness.
Depression and anxiety occur more frequently in ME/CFS, but marked attention impairment remains after adjusting for mood.

Voxel-based morphometry showed a global reduction in grey matter volume in ME/CFS patients compared to age-matched healthy controls, with a positive linear relationship between daily activity and grey matter volume seen only in patients.
Perrin et al. found no abnormal patterns of brain atrophy, ventricle volume, white matter lesions, cerebral blood flow, or aqueductal CSF flow in 18 CFS patients compared to 9 healthy controls.
Ultra-high field 7T MRI showed increased brainstem structure volumes in both ME/CFS and long COVID patients compared to healthy controls.
After correcting for total intracranial volume, Finkelmeyer et al. found increased insular cortex and amygdala volume but decreased brainstem volume in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.

During a verbal working memory (n-back) task, ME/CFS patients showed significantly increased activity in periaqueductal grey, dorsal and median raphe, right midbrain reticular formation, parabrachial complex, and locus coeruleus compared to controls.
Resting-state fMRI showed increased connectivity between the right insular cortex (salience network) and orbitofrontal cortex in ME/CFS patients compared to controls.
A meta-analysis by Lee et al. found reduced activity in the insula and thalamus in ME/CFS, suggesting disrupted limbic system connections contribute to symptomatology.
A global reduction in cerebral blood flow has been reported in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, which may confound BOLD fMRI interpretation.
Brainstem grey matter volume shows a strong correlation with pulse pressure in ME/CFS patients, suggesting impaired cerebrovascular autoregulation.

Nakatomi and colleagues found a correlation between cognitive impairment and TSPO-PET neuroinflammation signal (especially mid-pons to thalamus) in ME/CFS, but a later study found no difference in TSPO binding between patients and controls.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated reduced N-acetylaspartate, a neuronal marker, in the hippocampus of ME/CFS patients.

Spectroscopic imaging found widespread alterations in ratios of Choline, myo-Inositol, and Lactate to Creatine, and significantly elevated brain temperature in the insular/frontal cortices, thalamus, putamen, and cerebellum of ME/CFS patients, thought to reflect neuroinflammation.

EBV-encoded deoxyuridine triphosphate nucleotidohydrolase (dUTPase) stimulates anxiety and sickness behaviour in female mice with altered expression of proteins/genes important for blood-brain barrier integrity, fatigue, pain, and synapse structure.
A subset of ME/CFS patients showed prolonged, significantly elevated serum-neutralising antibodies against EBV dUTPase that inversely correlated with their symptoms.

Kogelnik et al. observed significant improvement in physical and mental functioning in 9 of 12 ME/CFS patients with high EBV/HHV-6 IgG titres who received 6 months of valganciclovir in an open-label study.
HERV expression was detected in duodenal tissue from 8 of 12 ME/CFS patients and in all patients with gastritis, with HERV-gag/pol colocalising with dendritic immune cell markers.

Experimental IL-6 administration at levels equivalent to acute infection increased CRP, ACTH, and cortisol, reduced TSH, produced fatigue and reduced concentration, and altered sleep architecture including decreased REM sleep.
L-carnitine was found significantly helpful in a retrospective before-and-after analysis of ME/CFS patients, associated with improved serum serotonin levels.

Administering IL-6 at levels comparable to acute infection produced increased CRP, ACTH, and cortisol, reduced TSH, subjective fatigue, reduced concentration, and altered sleep architecture including reduced REM sleep.

Disrupted sleep promotes central and peripheral inflammation and reduces secretion of IL-7, which is critical for T cell memory and preventing recurrent infection, relevant to the non-restorative sleep seen in ME/CFS.

In Hepatitis C patients, IFNα/ribavirin treatment flattened the ACTH and cortisol slope, which correlated with depression and fatigue measures but not with increases in TNFα or soluble TNFα receptor 2.
Cameron et al. found no significant differences in viral antibodies or gene copy numbers for EBV, CMV, and HHV6 in ME/CFS patient samples, discounting their importance as ongoing active infections.
EBV/HHV-6A dUTPase protein inhibited replication of human PBMCs in vitro and increased production of TNFα, IL1β, IL6, IL8, and IL10.
The mechanism of dUTPase-induced immune activation involves binding to TLR2 and subsequent activation of NF-kappa B through recruitment of the MyD88 adaptor molecule.
HHV6 reactivation has been shown to induce mitochondrial fragmentation and impair ATP synthesis, which would be expected to reduce neural activity mediating cognition.
Peripheral injection of poly I-C (a synthetic double-stranded RNA analogue) can induce immune changes in the cortex, hippocampus, and hypothalamus.
Reduced muscle usage due to symptom-related activity avoidance is proposed to lower BDNF, a factor produced by functioning muscle tissue, contributing to impaired memory and cognition.
ME/CFS patients with concomitant joint hypermobility syndrome and POTS have impaired regulation of blood pressure and heart rate and significant cognitive dysfunction after postural changes.

Cognitive behavioural therapy and graded exercise therapy were considered beneficial for ME/CFS by Kim et al., but often at large financial cost and without definitive improvement in cognitive dysfunction.
L-carnitine was found to be significantly helpful in a retrospective before-and-after analysis of people with ME/CFS and was associated with improved serum serotonin levels.
An earlier study showed no benefit of an SSRI agent in any aspect of ME/CFS symptomology.
In an open-label study, aripiprazole improved brain fog as well as physical fatigue and unrefreshing sleep in ME/CFS patients, suggesting dopamine pathway modulation may be beneficial.
HHV6 miRNA and EBV dUTPase have been found in several regions of the brain in ME/CFS patients but not in healthy controls.
B cell depletion therapy based on autoimmune mechanisms was initially successful in a randomised control trial for ME/CFS.
A later multicentre RCT with 151 patients failed to show benefit of B cell depletion therapy in ME/CFS, possibly because only patients with definitive autoimmunity would benefit.
Immunoadsorption has been utilised and found clinically helpful to remove harmful proteins including autonomic receptor auto-antibodies in ME/CFS.
A small open-label study using nebulised administration of a mixture of anti-oxidant agents aiming to reduce NF-κB activation showed some benefit, drawing parallels with PASC treatment approaches.
Treatment of insomnia can improve chronic fatigue and improve cortisol recovery after stress.
Benzodiazepines, while sometimes helpful for reducing time to fall asleep initially, frequently cause daytime drowsiness and can exacerbate cognitive dysfunction in ME/CFS.
Melatonin can encourage normalisation of sleep chronobiology and scavenge reactive oxygen species central to neuroinflammation, though it has not been systematically investigated in ME/CFS.
Melatonin combined with palmitoylethanolamide has been reported to improve pain, sleep, and overall quality of life in patients with fibromyalgia, a condition frequently co-occurring with ME/CFS.

A combination of NADH, Coenzyme Q10, acetyl-L-carnitine, ubiquinol-10, guanidinoacetic acid, and glycerol supplementation was well investigated and found helpful for optimising mitochondrial energy production in ME/CFS.
Patients with ME/CFS frequently have at least one other chronic pain condition such as fibromyalgia, chronic low back pain, irritable bowel syndrome, endometriosis, and chronic migraine.

Kogelnik et al. observed significant improvement in physical and mental functioning in 9 of 12 ME/CFS patients with high titre EBV and HHV-6 IgG antibodies who received 6 months of valganciclovir in an open-label study.
Glatiramer acetate, used in multiple sclerosis, has been found to bind abzymes seen in some ME/CFS patients that can damage myelin basic protein, suggesting a potential repurposed treatment.
There is evidence of altered mitochondrial oxidation of TCA cycle and pentose phosphate pathway intermediates, as well as fatty acid β-oxidation and amino acid degradation in ME/CFS.
Pediatric ME/CFS prevalence is estimated at 0.10% to 0.75% across studies, and the illness appears more common in adolescents (12-18 years) than younger school-age children.
An estimated 836,000 to 2.6 million Americans of all ages suffer from ME/CFS.
Cognitive difficulties such as memory impairment, attention deficits, and concentration difficulties are commonly seen in children with ME/CFS in school settings.

Children with ME/CFS experience reduced participation in social, educational, and recreational activities, diminishing quality of life, and severe cases can leave students homebound or bedbound and unable to attend school.

After completing a case-based educational activity (video and slides) on pediatric ME/CFS, the proportion of Cohort 1 students who identified ME/CFS as a medical condition rose from 23% to 81%, while those believing it was both medical and psychiatric fell from 55% to 16%.

In Cohort 1, students' self-rated ability to diagnose a patient with ME/CFS increased from a mean of 1.0 to 3.5 (0-5 scale) after the educational activity, and confidence to communicate with a patient with ME/CFS rose from a mean of 1.4 to 3.9.

In Cohort 2 (medical students only), belief that ME/CFS is a medical condition rose from 21% pretest to 79% posttest, while belief it was both medical and psychiatric fell from 58% to 21%, replicating the pattern seen in Cohort 1.

In Cohort 2, medical students' self-rated ability to diagnose a pediatric patient with ME/CFS rose from a mean of 0.6 to 3.3, and confidence in communicating with a pediatric patient with ME/CFS rose from a mean of 1.4 to 3.7.

A meta-analysis of 21 studies reported that post-COVID conditions in children and adolescents had a prevalence of 25.24%, with the most common symptoms being mood changes, fatigue, and sleep disturbances.

The CDC developed a five-step Voice of the Patient (VOP) qualitative interview process, grounded in photovoice and hermeneutic phenomenology tenets, and produced eight ME/CFS patient/caregiver narrative stories over four years.
Many people with ME/CFS report difficulty obtaining a diagnosis and feel that healthcare providers do not take their symptoms seriously, with barriers to healthcare utilization also reported.
The VOP story series achieved substantial public engagement, with 196,229 page views to the VOP website section as of December 2023, accessed primarily via mobile devices, desktop, and tablets.
Participants reported that obtaining a diagnosis of ME/CFS was very difficult, often requiring visits to multiple healthcare providers before being believed or heard.

A participant emphasized that clinicians should assess level of function before and after illness onset and that a thorough medical history requiring adequate time is key to ME/CFS diagnosis, rather than it being inherently difficult.
ME/CFS is reported to occur at higher rates among women than men, though men are also affected, and the illness affects people of all racial/ethnic and socio-demographic backgrounds and ages.
Between 836,000 and 3.3 million adults in the U.S. and millions more worldwide are estimated to be affected by ME/CFS.
At initial presentation, 27 of 28 patients who developed ME/CFS after COVID-19 vaccination had insufficient or deficient serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels, averaging 16 ± 4 ng/mL.
Vitamin D replacement therapy (dietary counseling, sun exposure recommendations, and oral supplementation) increased mean serum vitamin D levels from 16 ± 4 ng/mL to 28 ± 5 ng/mL.
ME/CFS diagnostic symptom severity score decreased from a mean of 10.3 ± 2.1 to 3.3 ± 2.0 following vitamin D replacement therapy.
After vitamin D replacement therapy, 23 of 28 patients (82%) no longer met diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS.
Among ME/CFS symptoms, sleep problems showed the greatest improvement (71%) following vitamin D replacement therapy.
Autonomic symptoms improved in 68% of patients following vitamin D replacement therapy, the second-most-improved symptom category.
Bright light therapy for two weeks did not significantly improve fatigue compared to waitlist in the full crossover analysis.
Fatigue scores improved immediately after two weeks of bright light therapy, though this did not hold up in the overall crossover comparison.
Patients showed decreased reaction time (improved attention) on a Test of Attentional Performance subtest after bright light therapy compared to waitlist.
More than 45% of the ME/CFS study participants were also diagnosed with postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS).
Karnofsky Performance Status Index scores, reflecting overall functional status, were significantly lower among pwME/CFS compared with healthy controls across studies.
Weigel et al. found a significantly lower median Dr Bell's CFIDS Disability Scale score among pwME/CFS compared with healthy controls.

In the only longitudinal HRQoL comparison with healthy controls, Cambras et al. found that pwME/CFS maintained significantly reduced Global SF-36 and most domain scores at both baseline and follow-up, indicating persistent impairment over time.

SF-36 Physical Functioning, Role Physical, Bodily Pain, General Health, Vitality and Social Functioning domains were consistently significantly lower in pwME/CFS than healthy controls across all studies using MOS questionnaires.
The Role Physical domain of the SF-36 was consistently the most severely impacted HRQoL domain among pwME/CFS.
SF-36 Vitality (Energy/Fatigue) scores were markedly impaired among pwME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
SF-36 Role Emotional and Mental Health domains were the least impacted among pwME/CFS but findings on statistical significance versus healthy controls were inconsistent across studies.
All WHODAS 2.0 domains were significantly impaired (elevated disability scores) among pwME/CFS compared with healthy controls, with the greatest impact in Life Activities and Participation.
WHODAS 2.0 Self-Care was the least affected domain in pwME/CFS but was still significantly elevated (worse) compared with healthy controls.
EQ-VAS self-rated health scores were significantly lower among pwPCC compared with healthy controls across all studies using this measure.
EQ-5D-3L index values were significantly reduced among pwPCC subgroups compared with healthy controls in Ariza et al.
Mean Global WHODAS 2.0 scores indicated significantly greater disability among pwPCC compared with healthy controls.

Contrary to other PROMs, the SF-12 Global score did not significantly differ between pwPCC and healthy controls in one study, a null finding possibly attributable to poor baseline health in the control group.
A large majority of pwPCC reported functional impairment on the Sheehan Disability Scale Global domain, though the comparison threshold and significance versus controls were not clearly defined.
All EQ-5D-5L domains (Mobility, Self-Care, Usual Activities, Pain/Discomfort, Anxiety/Depression) were significantly impaired among pwPCC compared with healthy controls.
All WHODAS 2.0 domains were significantly impaired among pwPCC compared with healthy controls, with Life Activities and Participation the most affected.
Social Relationships scores on the WHOQOL-BREF did not significantly differ between any PCC cohort and healthy controls, despite significant impairment in the Physical domain.

Direct comparison of pwME/CFS and pwPCC in one study found no significant differences between the two groups on the Dr Bell's CFIDS Disability Scale, SF-36, or WHODAS 2.0, indicating comparable illness burden.

Despite having experienced only mild acute COVID-19 illness, mild-PCC patients showed worse HRQoL across nearly all domains than hospitalised or ICU-admitted PCC patients, likely reflecting their significantly longer illness duration.
A substantial proportion (40-60%) of people with Post COVID-19 Condition meet ME/CFS case criteria, supporting clinical overlap and a shared or common aetiopathogenesis between the two conditions.

Overall, across the 16 included studies, all HRQoL domains assessed were significantly reduced among both pwME/CFS and pwPCC compared with healthy controls, with the most profound impairments in overall health perception, physical health, and ability to perform daily activities, while mental health/self-care domains were comparatively less affected.

Gulf War Illness affects an estimated 30-40% of the nearly 700,000 Veterans deployed to Operations Desert Shield/Storm/Sabre, presenting with fatigue, mood/cognition changes, chronic pain, GI symptoms (often labeled IBS), respiratory issues, and skin issues.
The authors propose that GWI may be a post-viral syndrome analogous to ME/CFS and long COVID, based on similarities in symptomatology and proposed pathophysiology among the three conditions.

The authors hypothesize that Veterans with GWI may have had an antecedent infection with a virus related to SARS-CoV-2, potentially MERS coronavirus or an ancestor virus, noting that MERS antibodies have been detected in dromedary camels in Saudi Arabia from 1983 to the present, spanning the time of the Gulf War deployment.

In the 2022 NHIS cohort, individuals with ME/CFS had significantly higher odds of reported cognitive difficulty compared to those without ME/CFS, after adjusting for long COVID status and sociodemographics.

In the 2023 NHIS cohort, individuals with ME/CFS had significantly higher odds of reported cognitive difficulty compared to those without ME/CFS, after adjusting for long COVID status and sociodemographics.

In the 2022 NHIS cohort, individuals with long COVID had significantly higher odds of reported cognitive difficulty compared to those without long COVID, after adjusting for ME/CFS status and sociodemographics.

In the 2023 NHIS cohort, individuals with long COVID had significantly higher odds of reported cognitive difficulty compared to those without long COVID, after adjusting for ME/CFS status and sociodemographics.
Individuals with comorbid ME/CFS and long COVID appear especially prone to memory and concentration difficulties compared to those with either condition alone or neither.
Targeted serum metabolomics found downregulation of purine metabolism in both ME/CFS and Gulf War Syndrome patients compared to healthy controls.
Uric acid, the terminal antioxidant product of purine metabolism, is decreased in serum of Gulf War Syndrome patients.
ME/CFS patients showed significant reductions in serum hypoxanthine during post-exertional malaise compared with healthy controls.
Multiple oxidative damage markers (MDA, isoprostanes, 8-OH-deoxyguanosine, 2,3-diphosphoglyceric acid, thiobutyric acid, protein carbonyls) are consistently elevated in ME/CFS patients.
In patients recovering from EBV-induced infectious mononucleosis, pre-illness dysregulation of nucleotide and glutathione plasma levels was associated with more severe subsequent illness outcomes.
Sphingomyelin pathway products are increased in Gulf War Syndrome, potentially contributing to muscle fatigue.
Sphingomyelin pathway products are decreased in ME/CFS, potentially contributing to muscle fatigue.
Muscle biopsy studies found significantly reduced mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation activity at complexes I and II in GWS patients compared with healthy controls.
Ceramides are elevated in both GWS and ME/CFS and are implicated in activation of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6 and TNF-α.
Higher plasma levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine CSF2 correlate with increased physical and fatigue symptoms in ME/CFS patients.
Oxaloacetate, a TCA cycle metabolite, improved symptoms in ME/CFS patients in a treatment study.
AXA1125 (a combination of amino acids and N-acetylcysteine) produced marked improvements in fatigue scores in Long COVID patients in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial.
Tryptophan levels are consistently reduced in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.
Tryptophan levels are increased in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, potentially contributing to central fatigue.
Both ME/CFS and fibromyalgia are associated with reduced levels of kynurenine, a downstream metabolite of tryptophan.
Taurine levels are elevated in fibromyalgia patients relative to healthy controls.
Taurine levels are significantly reduced in plasma of ME/CFS patients relative to healthy controls.
Serum adenosine, a precursor for ATP synthesis, is significantly decreased in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.

Vigorous exercise challenge testing revealed that ME/CFS patients undergo a metabolic shift from a hypometabolic baseline state to a hypermetabolic post-exercise state, with significant changes in the urea cycle and glutamate/pyruvate metabolism.

SLC25A11, the mitochondrial oxoglutarate carrier, was found upregulated in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients compared with controls, potentially altering malate/2-oxoglutarate shuttling and complex I activity.

PBMC proteomics identified elevated 3-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase type 1 (BDH1) and acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase 2 (ACAT2), both involved in fatty acid and ketone body metabolism, in ME/CFS patients relative to controls.
Plasma proteomics in ME/CFS patients revealed upregulation of the ephrin signaling pathway, which regulates cell signaling, morphology, axon guidance, and energy metabolism.
Germain et al. (2021) found that all significantly altered plasma proteins were elevated (not decreased) in female ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.

A 7-protein machine-learning panel distinguished ME/CFS from healthy controls with 79.1% accuracy (AUROC 0.891); extracellular vesicle IL-2 and cathelicidin antimicrobial protein (CAMP) were among the elevated markers.
Within the same 7-protein ME/CFS diagnostic panel, IGLV1-47, CRTAC1, LRG1, IGF1, and TUBA1 were decreased relative to healthy controls.
Higher plasma levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine CSF2 correlated with increased physical and fatigue symptom severity in ME/CFS patients.
In a cohort of 39 ME/CFS patients vs 41 healthy controls, a subset of patients showed markedly abnormal IGHV3-23/30 protein levels (12 very high, 3 very low).

A systematic review of ten fibromyalgia proteomics studies across saliva, plasma, serum, and CSF found altered levels of transferrin, fibrinogen chains, profilin-1, transaldolase, PGAM1, apolipoprotein-C3, complement C4A/C1QC, immunoglobulin fragments, and acute-phase reactants relative to healthy controls.
Transaldolase, a pentose phosphate pathway enzyme generating the antioxidant cofactor NADPH, was elevated in saliva and serum of fibromyalgia patients relative to controls in two independent studies.
Serum calgranulin A, an S100 calcium-binding protein implicated in oxidative stress handling, was elevated in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.
Glucose levels were raised in fibromyalgia patients relative to healthy controls, possibly reflecting abnormal energy metabolism.
In fibromyalgia, plasma/serum markers of coagulation were increased, complement markers decreased, and fibrinolysis markers showed mixed changes relative to healthy controls.
CSF proteomes did not differ significantly between ME/CFS patients with and without comorbid fibromyalgia, although both groups differed markedly from healthy controls.
CSF proteome analysis found very similar protein differences shared between ME/CFS and Gulf War Syndrome patients relative to healthy controls, suggesting overlapping biology.

In a Gulf War Syndrome mouse model, brain tissue showed significant reductions in cardiolipin alongside astroglial/microglial activation in the hippocampus, indicating decreased electron transport chain activity.

Odd-chain acylcarnitines were elevated in plasma of both Gulf War agent-exposed mice and GWI veterans relative to controls, but not in brain tissue, suggesting a peripheral rather than central metabolic effect.

In a mouse model of GWS (pyridostigmine bromide and permethrin exposure), brain tissue analysis at 5 months post-exposure revealed decreased levels of respiratory chain complexes I, II, IV, and V, indicating mitochondrial protein damage.
Despite no overt inflammatory phenotype in the brain, systemic immune dysregulation was indicated by significant decreases in IFNγ, TNFα, IL-1β, and IL10 in the GWS mouse model.
Microdialysis-based proteomics identified 26 interstitial muscle proteins linked to stress response, muscle contraction, and immune pathways in fibromyalgia, most of which were downregulated.
Plasma ceruloplasmin, a key acute-phase reactant, was upregulated in fibromyalgia and correlated with pain severity.

TMT proteomics of PBMCs from fibromyalgia patients identified differential expression of proteins regulated by the liver X receptor-retinoid X receptor (LXR/RXR) pathway, which modulates lipid metabolism and inflammation.

Post-exercise MRI in ME/CFS patients showed a significant increase in blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal across various brain regions, indicating a global shift in brain metabolism after exertion.
Post-exercise, GWS patients showed decreased BOLD signal in the dorsal midbrain, right middle insula, and left Rolandic operculum, a pattern distinct from the generalized increase seen in ME/CFS.
MRSI studies found increased ventricular lactate levels in ME/CFS patients, consistent with mitochondrial dysfunction and increased reliance on glycolysis for ATP production.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy imaging studies show increased ventricular/cortical lactate levels in ME/CFS patients, suggesting greater reliance on glycolysis due to mitochondrial dysfunction.
Shungu et al. (2012) found significantly lower cortical GSH levels in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, indicating impaired brain antioxidant defense.
Ghali et al. (2019) found 44.7% of ME/CFS patients had elevated resting blood lactate, which correlated with greater PEM severity but not with fatigue severity.
CSF lactate levels measured by MRSI were higher in both ME/CFS and FM patients compared with healthy controls, but did not differentiate between the two conditions.
In a survey of 3,933 respondents diagnosed with POTS, 20% also met criteria for fibromyalgia and 21% for ME/CFS, showing substantial diagnostic overlap.
Transient POTS was reported in approximately one-third of Gulf War Syndrome patients, with a potential association with post-exertional malaise.
Castro-Marrero et al. (2013) demonstrated elevated oxidative damage and reduced antioxidant levels, particularly Coenzyme Q10, in ME/CFS patients.
Jammes et al. found elevated plasma markers of oxidative stress in ME/CFS patients both at rest and following exercise.
