Dietary supplementation with resistant starch reduced high blood pressure in spontaneously hypertensive rats compared to untreated SHR.
RS treatment reshaped the gut microbiota of SHR, leading to increased short-chain fatty acid production and reduced endotoxemia.
RS fiber treatment decreased sympathetic activity in SHR, linked to gut microbiota changes and reduced endotoxemia.
RS treatment restored the balance between Th17 and Treg lymphocytes in mesenteric lymph nodes and aorta of SHR.
Plasma levels of acetate and butyrate were elevated in RS-treated SHR and correlated with increased aortic expression of GPR41, GPR43, and PPARδ.
Aortic expression of the short-chain fatty acid receptor GPR41 (FFAR3) was increased in RS-treated SHR relative to untreated SHR.
Treatment of SHR with inulin-type fructans (ITF) failed to prevent hypertension or endothelial dysfunction, unlike resistant starch.
Fecal microbiota transplantation from resistant-starch-treated SHR donors to recipient SHR partially replicated the beneficial cardiovascular effects seen in RS-treated animals.
Resistant starch treatment restored the balance between Th17 and Treg lymphocytes in mesenteric lymph nodes and aorta of SHR.
Resistant starch supplementation reduced endotoxemia in SHR, likely via improved gut permeability.
Resistant starch supplementation decreased sympathetic nervous system activity in SHR, contributing to blood pressure reduction.
Overall, recovered COVID-19 patients showed decreased HRT slope and decreased percentage of normal (category 0) HRT, alongside increased HRT onset, compared to controls.

No significant differences were found between the recovered COVID-19 group and controls in age, hypertension, gender, smoking, percentage of abnormal HRT onset, abnormal HRT slope, category 1, or category 2.

In the severe COVID-19 subgroup (chest CT severity score 16-25), HRT slope was decreased and HRT onset increased, with significantly higher percentages of abnormal HRT onset, abnormal HRT slope, category 1, and category 2 compared to controls.
No differences in any HRT parameters were observed between the control group and mild (subgroup 1) or moderate (subgroup 2) COVID-19 recovery subgroups.

Severe COVID-19 subgroup (subgroup 3) showed significantly higher abnormal HRT onset/slope percentages, category 1/2 percentages, and HRT onset value, with lower HRT slope, compared with the mild subgroup (subgroup 1).

Severe COVID-19 subgroup showed higher HRT onset value and abnormal HRT onset percentage, and lower HRT slope and category 0 percentage, compared with the moderate subgroup (subgroup 2); no difference in category 1/2 percentages between the two subgroups.
Chest CT severity score in recovered COVID-19 patients correlated positively with HRT onset and negatively with HRT slope by Pearson correlation.
Spearman's rho correlation showed a positive correlation between recovered COVID-19 subgroup severity and HRT onset, and a negative correlation with HRT slope.
No meaningful correlations were found between HRT parameters and either the number of positive PCR tests for COVID-19 or the time elapsed since infection.
Recovery from severe COVID-19 was an independent predictor of abnormal HRT onset, with a 5.435-fold increased likelihood compared to controls and other subgroups.
Recovery from severe COVID-19 was an independent predictor of abnormal HRT slope, with a 4.756-fold increased risk compared to controls and other subgroups.
Linear regression showed that each 1-point increase in chest CT severity score was associated with a 0.035 increase in HRT onset value.
Linear regression showed that each 1-point increase in chest CT severity score was associated with a 0.122 decrease in HRT slope value.

Hypertension and smoking status were identified as additional independent predictors of abnormal HRT onset and slope, alongside COVID-19 severity, though no subgroup differences in these factors were observed.

In a study of 138 ME/CFS patients versus 53 healthy controls, key mitochondrial respiration parameters including basal respiration, ATP production, and maximal respiration were significantly diminished in neutrophils of patients.
Spare respiratory capacity, reflecting mitochondria's ability to meet increased energy demands, is particularly impaired in severe cases of ME/CFS.
Vermeulen et al. reported normal OXPHOS capacity in PBMCs from ME/CFS patients despite worse performance on exercise testing, contradicting other reports of OXPHOS impairment.
Tomas et al. observed consistently reduced OXPHOS parameters, particularly maximal respiration, in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients.

Jammes et al. classified ME/CFS patients into two subgroups based on oxidative stress markers: one with higher oxidative stress and reduced antioxidant defences, and another with less pronounced oxidative stress but still differing significantly from healthy controls.

Proteomic (SWATH-MS) studies of PBMCs from ME/CFS patients revealed differentially expressed proteins pointing to impairments in oxidative phosphorylation, redox regulation, and mitochondrial function.
Lymphoblastoid cell lines from ME/CFS patients show striking inefficiency in ATP synthesis via Complex V, accompanied by compensatory upregulation of glycolysis.
Lymphoblasts from ME/CFS patients show elevated TORC1 (mTORC1) activity, driving upregulation of Complex I and Complex V mitochondrial protein subunits.
Multiple studies report significantly lower plasma Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) levels in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls, implicating CoQ10 deficiency in ME/CFS pathophysiology.
ME/CFS patients show increased post-exercise metabolic activity (a hypermetabolic state), reduced acetylation, and dysregulated purine metabolism, contributing to post-exertional malaise.
ME/CFS patients show abnormal blood lactate responses and impaired recovery after exertion, with an earlier shift to anaerobic metabolism even at low-to-moderate exercise intensities.

Elevated levels of exosome-associated mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) have been detected in ME/CFS patients and correlate with symptom severity, though no disease-causing mtDNA mutations have been identified.
Two studies identified alterations in DNA methylation patterns in PBMCs of ME/CFS patients, mainly affecting genes related to cellular metabolism and immune signalling.
Curriu et al. found no differences in CD57, CD27, or CD28 expression between ME/CFS patients and controls, suggesting T cell senescence may not be a dominant feature of ME/CFS.
Research on NK cells in ME/CFS has not revealed significant changes in potential senescence markers such as CD57 and NKG2A.

A transcriptomic study by Eaton-Fitch et al. found abnormalities in T and NK cells consistent with exhaustion, including downregulation of both type 1 and type 2 IFN signalling and reduced IFN-γ production, alongside upregulated PD-1 and CTLA-4 signalling pathways.

Iu et al. found reduced chromatin accessibility in genes associated with NF-κB/TNF-α signalling and upregulation of T-bet, EOMES, and TCF-1 in ME/CFS T cells, epigenetic features supporting T cell exhaustion.

Walitt et al. reported differential expression of genes within the IL-10 and NF-κB pathways in male ME/CFS patients, with a trend toward IL-10 upregulation and NF-κB downregulation, consistent with an exhausted T cell phenotype.

Walitt et al. reported increased PD-1 expression on CD8+ T cells in the cerebrospinal fluid of ME/CFS patients, while PD-1 on CD4+ T cells was unchanged in both blood and CSF, and TIGIT/CD244 showed no significant alterations; CD266 was decreased.
Steiner et al. demonstrated an association between ME/CFS and an autoimmune risk allele variant of CTLA-4, suggesting a genetic predisposition to immune exhaustion in these patients.

Saito et al. found that patients with Long COVID and ME/CFS symptoms have elevated expression of PD-1, TIM-3, TIGIT, and Gal-9, with TIM-3+ cells associated with impaired TNF-α/IFN-γ expression and PD-1+ cells correlated with elevated cytokine expression.
ME/CFS patients exhibit reduced glycolysis in both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets, consistent with a state of hypometabolism, with CD8+ T cells also showing reduced mitochondrial membrane potential.

Mandarano et al. reported negative correlations between resting glycolysis and cytokines such as IL-2 and TNF-α, uniquely observed in ME/CFS patients, linking proinflammatory cytokines to reduced immune cell metabolic activity.

NK cells in ME/CFS show decreased glycolytic reserve and reduced CD36 fatty acid transporter levels combined with increased fatty acid oxidation, suggesting a compensatory mechanism against lipid overload that may impair NK cell function.
B cells of ME/CFS patients show reduced mitochondrial mass and increased reliance on amino acids upon stimulation, indicating a shift to alternative substrates for ATP production.

In vitro, mtDNA from ME/CFS patients stimulated human microglia to release proinflammatory cytokines, particularly IL-1β, suggesting a mechanism by which peripheral mitochondrial stress signals to the central nervous system to drive neuroinflammation.
A PBMC study measuring OXPHOS without distinguishing immune cell types noted normal glycolysis but reduced mitochondrial respiration, a feature potentially linked to immune exhaustion.

IL-6 has been reported as both elevated and decreased across different ME/CFS cohorts, and cytokine dysregulation overall remains inconsistent, limiting its use as a reliable senescence or exhaustion biomarker.
EBV was detected more frequently in sputum of ME/CFS patients (85%, 11/13) than in healthy donors (50%, 5/10).
EBV viral load in sputum (copies/mL) was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than in age-matched healthy controls.
EBV copies/mL in the elderly SENIOR control group showed a non-significant elevated trend compared to age-matched healthy donors.
HHV6 was detected at similar frequency in ME/CFS patients (6/13) and healthy donors (5/10), with no significant difference in viral load between groups.
HCMV was not detected in sputum of any ME/CFS patient or healthy control, only in the glucocorticoid-immunosuppressed control donor.

HAdV was detected in sputum of one severely affected, wheelchair-bound ME/CFS patient (Id12) and in the immunosuppressed glucocorticoid-treated control donor, but in no other ME/CFS patients or healthy/SENIOR controls.
On a group level, autoantibodies to type I interferon were only slightly, non-significantly elevated in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy donor controls.
The one severely affected, HAdV-positive ME/CFS patient (Id12) showed somewhat elevated autoantibodies to type I interferon compared to other ME/CFS and healthy donor participants.
The eldest SENIOR healthy control participant (age 77) showed elevated anti-type I IFN autoantibodies compared to other participants.
SARS-CoV-2 was detected in sputum from only one participant, the B-cell-depleted (Rituximab-treated) negative control donor, despite no active infection symptoms at sampling.

The highest EBV load observed in the whole cohort (526 million copies/mL) was found in the glucocorticoid-immunosuppressed asthmatic control donor, who also released all other tested viruses except SARS-CoV-2.
Only a small minority of ME/CFS-diagnosed respondents rated their NHS experience as good or excellent, with the majority reporting very poor, poor or mixed experiences.

Long COVID respondents most commonly reported mixed feelings about their NHS experience, with substantial proportions reporting very poor or poor experiences and fewer reporting good/excellent experiences.
Time from symptom onset to ME/CFS diagnosis varied widely, with most diagnosed within the first two years but a notable proportion (12.9%) taking over 10 years.
A greater number of comorbidities was significantly associated with a longer time to diagnosis in people with ME/CFS, but not in people with long COVID.
Age, ethnicity and gender were not significantly related to time to diagnosis in either ME/CFS or long COVID.
Time to diagnosis for ME/CFS was similar before and after publication of the 2021 NICE guideline, indicating no measurable improvement.
Only a small proportion of respondents felt the 2021 NICE guideline had made a positive difference to the healthcare they received.
The majority of diagnosed ME/CFS patients used self-management pacing strategies, including reorganising their life, resting more, and reducing activities.
Diagnosed long COVID patients used similar self-management strategies to ME/CFS patients, including reorganising life, resting more, and reducing activities.
More than half of diagnosed ME/CFS patients reported receiving no help from the NHS in the previous two years.
Most diagnosed long COVID patients received an assessment from a long COVID clinic within the last two years, more than reported for ME/CFS specialist services.
Most diagnosed ME/CFS patients reported a moderate impact of the condition on their lives, with substantial proportions reporting severe impact.
Most diagnosed long COVID patients reported a moderate impact of the condition on their lives, with fewer reporting severe impact than in ME/CFS.

The ten most prevalent ME/CFS symptoms were unrefreshing sleep, debilitating fatigue, brain fog, musculoskeletal/nerve pain, PEM, light/noise sensitivity, headache, IBS-type symptoms, temperature sensitivity, and dizziness.
The most prevalent long COVID symptoms were fatigue, brain fog, musculoskeletal/nerve pain, unrefreshing sleep, breathlessness, headache, PEM, IBS-type symptoms, dizziness, tinnitus and sleep sweats.

Eight of the ten most prevalent symptoms overlapped between ME/CFS and long COVID (brain fog, dizziness, fatigue, headache, IBS, musculoskeletal/nerve pain, PEM, sleep disturbance), while light/noise and temperature sensitivity were unique to ME/CFS and breathlessness, tinnitus and sleep sweats were unique to long COVID.
Hierarchical clustering identified three symptom co-occurrence clusters in ME/CFS: a fatigue/sleep/brain-fog cluster, a PEM/pain cluster, and a headache/sensory-sensitivity/dizziness/IBS cluster.

Hierarchical clustering identified three symptom co-occurrence clusters in long COVID: a fatigue/brain-fog/pain/sleep cluster, a tinnitus/sleep-sweats cluster, and a breathlessness/headache/PEM/IBS/dizziness cluster.
For both ME/CFS and long COVID, less prevalent symptoms were associated with a higher proportion of respondents reporting severe or very severe impact of the condition.
A small but notable proportion of individuals reporting a diagnosis of ME/CFS did not experience postexertional malaise (PEM), despite PEM being a key required diagnostic criterion.

Broad autoantibody profiling using Luminex and REAP platforms found no significant differences in autoantibody reactivity, including against GPCRs such as beta-adrenergic receptors, between ME/CFS patients and controls.
Subtle trends in autoantibody reactivity ratios were observed between male and female ME/CFS subgroups, suggesting possible sex-related differences warranting further study.
Patterns of autoantibody reactivity suggestive of herpesvirus reactivation were noted in ME/CFS patients, indicating a potential area for further investigation.
Sphingolipid metabolism is consistently reduced in people with ME/CFS compared to unaffected metabolites.
Common metabolites such as isoleucine, valine, and glucose remain unchanged in ME/CFS despite reduced sphingolipid metabolism.
Abnormal sphingolipid metabolism has also been observed in other chronic fatigue-driven diseases such as Q-fever fatigue syndrome.
Oxidant-mediated skeletal muscle fatigue is associated with abnormal sphingolipid metabolism, similarly to ME/CFS.
At least half of people with ME/CFS, both males and females, showed a widespread decrease in plasma sphingolipids and glycosphingolipids.
Twenty to thirty molecular species of sphingolipids were decreased in people with ME/CFS, with ceramide species being the majority.
Sphingosine-1-phosphate inhibits inflammation, enhances neuroprotection, protects against fatigue development, and regulates skeletal muscle metabolism.
Treating skeletal muscle with sphingomyelinase, which hydrolyzes membrane sphingomyelin into ceramide, results in muscle weakness and promotes muscle fatigue.

The authors propose that inhibiting sphingosine-1-phosphate lyase (SPL), the terminal enzyme controlling S1P degradation, could restore reduced sphingolipid metabolites and represents a potential new approach for managing ME/CFS, though this warrants future investigation.
Supplementary treatments targeting oxidative stress have failed to achieve the desired outcome in ME/CFS.
Cognitive behavioral therapy and graded exercise provide only modest benefit for some ME/CFS patients, and many sufferers report worsening fatigue symptoms with exercise.
The prevalence of ME/CFS is estimated to exceed 2 million people in the United States, likely underestimated due to underdiagnosis.
ME/CFS is comparable to autoimmune diseases, particularly multiple sclerosis, in prevalence (0.2% to 1%), sex ratio, and long-term disability.
The extent of inflammation is closely associated with disease severity in people with ME/CFS.

Across 639 included ME/CFS studies, diagnostic criteria use was highly heterogeneous: 44% used multiple criteria, 16% did not specify criteria, 24% used a single criterion not requiring postexertional malaise, and only 10% used a single criterion requiring postexertional malaise.
Reporting of participant demographic and clinical detail was poor across the ME/CFS literature, with most studies failing to report ethnicity or disease severity.
Most systematic reviews on ME/CFS published 2018-2023 were of low methodological quality as assessed by AMSTAR 2.
Reanalysis of public single-cell RNA-seq data (GSE14577) identified 1373 differentially expressed genes between CFS patients and controls, including 638 upregulated and 735 downregulated genes.
GO enrichment of the CFS-associated DEGs showed significant enrichment in neuron projection guidance, axon guidance, and muscle contraction biological processes.
KEGG pathway analysis of CFS-associated DEGs showed significant enrichment in TGF-beta signaling, protein digestion and absorption, and neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction pathways.
In a mouse CFS model, PKM2 overexpression and knockdown produced discrepant reported effects on Morris water maze cognitive performance relative to the Model group, as stated in the text.
Physical/motor ability (open field, grip strength, rotarod) did not differ significantly between Model, Model+PKM2-OE, and Model+PKM2-KD groups, though the control group had normal physical ability.

Hippocampal CA1 histopathology (HE and Nissl staining) showed neuronal karyopyknosis, karyolysis, cytoplasmic degeneration, inflammation, and astrocyte proliferation in Model mice; this damage was more pronounced with PKM2 overexpression and improved with PKM2 knockdown.
Immunohistochemistry showed PKM2 protein was significantly increased in hippocampal tissue of Model mice versus controls, further elevated by PKM2 overexpression, and reduced by PKM2 knockdown.
Western blot showed H4K12la and total H4 were increased in hippocampal tissue of Model mice versus controls, further increased by PKM2 overexpression, and decreased by PKM2 knockdown.

Mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 was upregulated while fusion/biogenesis proteins MFN1 and PGC1α were downregulated in hippocampal tissue of Model mice, and these changes were exacerbated by PKM2 overexpression and reversed by PKM2 knockdown, indicating mitochondrial dynamic imbalance.
Serum lactate levels were elevated in Model mice compared to controls, with no significant difference in serum lactate between the Model+PKM2-OE and Model+PKM2-KD groups.
Brain tissue lactate was higher in Model mice than controls, further increased by PKM2 overexpression, and decreased by PKM2 knockdown.
Brain tissue IL-1β and TNF-α were elevated in Model mice versus controls, further increased by PKM2 overexpression, and reduced by PKM2 knockdown.
In ReNcell VM human hippocampal neurons, lactate stimulation increased PKM2, LDHB, H4K12la, phospho-P65, IL-1β, and TNF-α, and PKM2 overexpression further increased these markers.

Glycolysis inhibitor 3-BP reduced LDHB, H4K12la, phospho-P65, IL-1β, and TNF-α expression in PKM2-overexpressing hippocampal cells without changing PKM2 protein itself, indicating these downstream effects depend on glycolytic flux rather than PKM2 abundance.
NF-κB inhibitor SN-50 reduced phospho-P65, IL-1β, and TNF-α without affecting PKM2, LDHB, or H4K12la, indicating NF-κB acts downstream of PKM2/H4K12la lactylation in mediating neuroinflammation.

NF-κB activator (activator-1) increased phospho-P65, IL-1β, and TNF-α expression compared to the PKM2-OE+3-BP group without changing PKM2, LDHB, or H4K12la, confirming that NF-κB activation drives the downstream inflammatory response.

Glycolysis and lactate levels were increased by lactate stimulation and further by PKM2 overexpression in hippocampal cells, reduced by 3-BP, with no additional differences among the 3-BP, 3-BP+SN-50, and 3-BP+activator-1 groups, indicating NF-κB modulation acts downstream of the glycolytic/lactate node.

JC-1 staining showed lactate stimulation and PKM2 overexpression reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in hippocampal cells; this was partially reversed by 3-BP and further by SN-50, while the NF-κB activator worsened the loss of membrane potential.
A support vector classifier built on whole-brain structural gray matter voxel patterns (MVPA) significantly distinguished patients with CFS from healthy controls in a held-out test set.

Twelve cortical regions (six per hemisphere, including superior frontal gyrus, central sulcus, superior temporal sulcus, paracentral lobule/sulcus, precentral/postcentral gyrus, intraparietal sulcus, supramarginal gyrus, orbital gyri) drove classifier discrimination of CFS from controls, together accounting for 0.85 of the model's probabilistic confidence.

Cortical thickness of five regions (left paracentral lobule/sulcus, left precentral gyrus, left central sulcus, right intraparietal sulcus/transverse parietal sulci, right superior temporal sulcus) was significantly associated with SF-36 health status scores, robust to multiple-comparison correction.
The same five cortical regions were significantly associated with fatigue severity (FS-14), though this association did not remain significant after multiple-comparison correction.
The same five cortical regions were significantly associated with pain intensity (MPQ-PRI), though this association did not remain significant after multiple-comparison correction.
The association between cortical thickness of the five regions and SF-36 scores was significant only within the CFS group and not within the healthy control group.

Average cortical thickness of the five CFS-associated brain regions was significantly reduced in patients with CFS compared to healthy controls, and this remained significant after adjusting for age, gender, and BMI.
Cortical thickness of the five CFS-associated regions showed a marginal, non-significant inverse correlation with duration of illness in the CFS group.
Patients with CFS had significantly different (worse) clinical questionnaire profiles compared with healthy controls, including scores for health status, pain, and disease duration.
The paper cites literature indicating that CFS and depression frequently co-occur and may share pathological pathways, with about 30% of CFS patients reporting depressive symptoms.
The paper cites prior work characterizing CFS as a metabolic and immune inflammatory disease with elevated blood lactate and urea nitrogen levels.

The paper cites fMRI literature reporting that patients with CFS show declines in static and dynamic functional connectivity of the default mode network, which could identify CFS and change with symptom improvement.
The paper cites data indicating a high prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome among individuals who have recovered from COVID-19.

In the authors' prior case-control study, fibromyalgia patients showed significantly higher DTR amplitude, sagittal acceleration, and angular velocity, along with a shorter electromechanical delay compared to controls.
Normoactive or hypoactive DTR responses were found to rule out fibromyalgia with 94.1% sensitivity and 61.3% specificity, suggesting utility as a rule-out criterion.
Tahabit et al. reported that maximum Hmax/Mmax amplitudes were significantly increased in fibromyalgia patients compared to controls, supporting spinal cord hyperexcitability.
Prior research cited in this review indicates elevated levels of IL-6, IL-1β, IL-8, and/or TNF-α in fibromyalgia patients.

80% of pediatric hEDS patients had a clinical diagnosis of anxiety, a rate the authors describe as markedly higher than in the general pediatric population.
43% of pediatric hEDS patients had a diagnosis of depression, higher than general pediatric population rates but lower than reported adult hEDS/HSD rates.
ADHD was present in 17% of pediatric hEDS patients, higher than the ~5% general population rate.
Autism spectrum disorder was diagnosed in 5% of pediatric hEDS patients, higher than the ~1% general population rate.

Despite 86% of patients having at least one psychiatric diagnosis, only 47% had ever had a psychology evaluation and only 51% were on psychiatric medication, indicating a gap between mental health need and care received.
44% of pediatric hEDS patients reported a sleep problem and 42% reported poor sleep, with 25% having a formal sleep diagnosis.

The observed rate of sleep apnea (4%) in this pediatric hEDS cohort was lower than expected and lower than rates reported in adult EDS (32%) and other pediatric hEDS studies (7-26%), possibly due to inadequate screening.

Higher PROMIS Pain scores independently predicted worse HRQoL on the PEDS-QL Rheum Pain and Hurt and Daily Activities subscales in multiple regression.

PROMIS Depression and ASWS sleep score were not significant independent predictors of any PEDS-QL Rheum HRQoL subscale in multivariable regression, despite being individually correlated with HRQoL measures.
Ethnicity was a significant predictor of the PEDS-QL Rheum Treatment subscale, potentially reflecting underlying health inequities in treatment-related quality of life.
When anxiety, depression, sleep, and pain were considered simultaneously, anxiety (GAD-7) and pain (PROMIS Pain) emerged as the most predictive variables of HRQoL in pediatric hEDS patients.

Male mice with Enpp1 gene deletion spontaneously develop heterotopic ossification in the posterior longitudinal ligament, providing a genetic mouse model of OPLL.

Spinal hypermobility (repeated neck flexion/extension via drip stimulation) progressively increased ossification of the PLL and spinal canal starting at 8 weeks, with the fast hypermobility (FH) group showing the greatest ossified area versus controls and the slow hypermobility (SH) group.
Spinal hypermobility stimulation had no statistically significant effect on mouse body weight across control, SH, and FH groups.

Histological (H&E) analysis confirmed significantly increased PLL ossification area in the hypermobility groups compared to controls after 8 and 12 weeks, with no significant difference between SH and FH groups at these timepoints.
After 24 weeks of hypermobility stimulation, mobility groups displayed spinal cord compression, most pronounced in the FH group.

After 16 weeks of stimulation, motor function (BMS score and maximum inclined-plane angle tolerated for 5 s) was significantly reduced in hypermobility groups compared to controls, with the greatest reduction in the FH group.

Cervicothoracic ossification severity, scored using the Mata scale, increased over time in all groups and was significantly higher in hypermobility groups than controls starting at 8 weeks, with the FH group showing the highest scores.

After 8 weeks of stimulation, cervicothoracic spinal range of motion (θ1) was lower in the FH group than controls, while thoracolumbar range of motion (θ2) showed no significant difference at this timepoint.
After 12 weeks of stimulation, thoracolumbar spinal range of motion was significantly lower in the FH group than in controls.

In a case-control study of 74 female TMD patients and 73 healthy controls, 83% of patients with a Beighton score ≥3 had TMJ involvement compared to 41% of those with scores 0-2, a statistically significant difference.

In an epidemiological study of 193 adolescents, higher joint mobility (Beighton score ≥5) correlated with higher prevalence of TMJ sounds, particularly reciprocal clicking, and more severe TMD symptoms including difficulty opening the mouth and jaw pain, especially in girls.

A case-control study of 42 patients with reciprocal clicking or chronic closed lock versus 20 controls found reciprocal clicking strongly associated with both GJH and TMJ hypermobility, and chronic closed lock significantly associated with GJH, while trauma was not a significant contributor.

A cross-sectional study of 895 adults found subjects with four or more hypermobile joints had higher risk of reproducible TMJ reciprocal clicking, lower risk of limited mouth opening, and no significant association with myalgia/arthralgia, suggesting GJH predisposes to mechanical but not painful TMD.

A cross-sectional study of 193 adolescents found 22% of girls versus 3% of boys were extremely hypermobile (Beighton >5), girls reported significantly more TMD symptoms than boys, and GJH appeared to play a key role in TMD development when combined with oral parafunctions.
A cross-sectional study of 120 individuals (60 symptomatic, 60 nonsymptomatic) found no significant association between GJH and intra-articular TMJ disorders, nor between GJH and TMJ hypermobility.

A cross-sectional study of 43 women (17 hypermobile, 26 non-hypermobile) found higher but non-significant frequencies of joint noise and deviation during mouth opening in the hypermobility group, with no significant differences in dental occlusion (Angle Class).

A cross-sectional study of 162 subjects found no statistically significant relationship between GJH and the amount of condylar displacement or TMD, though other associations (e.g., skeletal pattern and malocclusion, gender and TMJ function impairment) were significant.

A clinical study of 69 patients with TMJ hypermobility (mild, moderate, severe) versus 20 healthy controls found masticatory muscle activity frequency, duration and resting periods differed significantly across all severity groups, with muscle activity decreasing as hypermobility severity increased.

A literature review and meta-analysis reported an odds ratio of 5.4 for hypermobility in TMD cases, but sensitivity analysis showed the association shifted from significant to non-significant in two out of five scenarios, concluding the GJH-TMD relation remains unclear.

In 51 healthy patients without TMJ dysfunction, average interincisal distance was 50.7 mm with condyle movement beyond the eminence in most individuals (n=41), and no significant correlation was found between maximal vertical movement and distance covered beyond the eminence crest.

A study comparing gender differences in mandibular movements found significant morphological differences in opening/closing pathway shapes between men and women, but no significant correlations between condylar translation and incisor opening/closing movements, limiting the use of incisor opening as a diagnostic proxy for condylar function.

A study found no significant association between imaging-based variables (disc position, condylar position, condylar excursion) and outcomes (maximum mouth opening, pain, maximum lateral movement), concluding dysfunction type and imaging severity were not correlated with pain intensity or mandibular motion range.

A biomechanical model study found that agreement between clinical diagnosis of hypermobility disorders and patient-specific biomechanical predictions was coincidental, and the model overestimated susceptibility to hypermobility disorders, indicating morphology alone is insufficient to distinguish patients from controls.

Pullinger (2013) found TMJ osseous anatomical and orthopedic organization (fossa shape/size, condyle-fossa position, joint space ratios) held predictive value for distinguishing disc derangement subdiagnoses from non-affected individuals, but osseous models accounted for only about one-third of variance, so the association should not be overstated.

In the absence of randomized studies on surgical techniques, autologous blood injection into the superior joint space and pericapsular tissues combined with intermaxillary fixation is described as the most scientifically supported treatment for recurrent TMJ luxation currently available.
Exercises to strengthen masticatory muscles are suggested to help reduce repercussions of TMJ hypertranslation-related hypermobility, though supporting evidence lacks randomized clinical studies.

GJH is described as being associated with chronic pain syndromes and fibromyalgia, as well as musculoskeletal injuries such as ankle sprains, shoulder instability, ACL injuries and hand osteoarthritis.

Non-painful symptoms such as muscle fatigue, joint instability, and kinesiophobia are noted to be common in patients with GJH, and recent findings suggest non-painful symptoms may precede TMD pain, warranting greater research focus.
Generalized joint hypermobility is described as a risk factor for acute and chronic musculoskeletal injuries and is also linked to chronic pain syndromes and fibromyalgia.

Generalized joint hypermobility may occur as an isolated finding or as a feature of inherited connective tissue disorders such as hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), the most common hereditary connective tissue disorder.

In the original 1964 study by Carter and Wilkinson, about half of children with congenital hip dislocation had joint laxity compared with only 7% of control children, forming the basis of early joint hypermobility criteria.

Kalaykova et al. (2006) found that although participants with symptomatic TMJ hypertranslation showed large condylar angles, nearly half of healthy controls also exhibited this feature, suggesting condylar position alone is insufficient to predict functional hypermobility signs.

Obwegeser et al. (1987) found condyle movement beyond the articular eminence in most of 51 healthy individuals without TMJ dysfunction, with no significant correlation between maximal vertical movement and distance covered by the condyle beyond the eminence crest.

Lewis, Buschang and Throckmorton (2001) found significant gender differences in the shape of condylar and incisal opening/closing pathways but no significant correlation between condylar translation and incisor opening or closing movements, limiting the use of incisor opening as a diagnostic proxy for condylar function.

One study found no significant association between imaging-based variables (disc position, condylar position, condylar excursion) and clinical variables (maximum mouth opening, pain, maximum lateral movement), indicating that imaging severity does not correlate with pain intensity or range of mandibular motion.

A patient-specific biomechanical model incorporating articular eminence angle and jaw-closing muscle line predicted vulnerability to TMJ open-locks, but agreement with clinical diagnosis of hypermobility disorders was coincidental and the model overestimated susceptible participants, indicating morphology alone cannot distinguish patients from controls.

Pullinger (2013) found that TMJ osseous anatomical and orthopedic organization (fossa shape/size, condyle-fossa position, joint space ratios) has predictive value for distinguishing non-affected individuals from those with disc derangement subdiagnoses, but accounts for only about one-third of the variance.
A 2014 study found a positive correlation between higher mouth opening capacity and more anterior positioning of the condyle relative to the articular eminence, especially during wide mouth opening.

In the absence of randomized studies on surgical techniques for recurrent TMJ luxation, autologous blood injection into the superior joint space and pericapsular tissues combined with intermaxillary fixation is currently the most scientifically supported treatment.

Exercises to strengthen the masticatory muscles are recommended as first-line conservative self-management for TMJ hypertranslation to reduce the repercussions of hypermobility, despite a lack of randomized clinical trials supporting this approach.

Recent findings cited in the review suggest that non-painful musculoskeletal symptoms (muscle fatigue, joint instability, kinesiophobia) may precede the onset of TMD pain, highlighting a need for greater research focus on these non-painful symptoms.

Idiopathic gastroparesis, including cases attributable to Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, was the underlying indication for jejunal tube placement in 63.8% of the surgical cohort and 42.7% of the endoscopic cohort.
Patients receiving endoscopic jejunal tube placement had a significantly higher rate of needing re-intervention (62.8%) compared to those with surgical placement (32.4%).
Jejunal tube dislodgement occurred significantly more often with endoscopic placement (25.5%) than with surgical placement (8.8%).
Jejunal tube occlusion rates were numerically higher with endoscopic (27.7%) versus surgical (14.7%) placement, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Among individual techniques, re-intervention rates were lowest for surgical flange (31.1%) and surgical Witzel (38.9%) tubes, and highest for endoscopic PEG-J (61%) and DPEJ (64.3%) tubes.
Fibroblast-derived 3D ring tissues synthesized a circumferentially aligned, collagen-rich fibrous ECM network positive for collagen type I, collagen type III and fibronectin.
Low-dose treatment with incyclinide, an MMP inhibitor, increased the strength and stiffness of the fibroblast-derived ECM rings.
High-dose incyclinide decreased tensile properties of the ECM rings, likely reflecting a toxic effect on the fibroblasts.
Treatment with TGF-β1 increased collagen levels and tensile properties of the ECM rings, mimicking a fibrotic environment in vitro.
Treatment with PAT-1251, a LOXL2 inhibitor, had no effect on collagen levels in the ECM rings.
PAT-1251 significantly reduced the strength and stiffness of ECM rings, including in rings where these properties were elevated by TGF-β1 treatment, despite unchanged collagen levels.

The infant presented with a novel manifestation of ATS: congenital right-sided cervical lung herniation, evidenced by an intermittent reducible neck swelling that appeared with crying/straining and disappeared with quiet breathing.

Chest CTA revealed herniation of the right upper lobe into the neck, mosaic attenuation with air-trapping in multiple lobes, a tortuous airway, and small anterior-posterior tracheal/main bronchial dimensions, along with markedly elongated and tortuous ascending aorta and aortic arch branches.

The patient also had posterior eventration of the right hemi-diaphragm with herniation of a portion of the liver, and small anterior hernias of both hemi-diaphragms, consistent with the known predisposition to diaphragmatic and other hernias in ATS.

Conservative management (no surgical intervention) of the cervical lung hernia over 4 years of follow-up resulted in spontaneous resolution of the cervical hernia, with persistence of diaphragmatic eventration/hernia at 43 months.

The authors describe hypermobility of the first ray at the tarso-metatarsal joint (TMTJ) as the principal biomechanical determinant underlying the development of hallux valgus, particularly in juvenile cases associated with flat foot.

Following the combined minimally invasive Lapidus arthrodesis and distal Austin-Chevron osteotomy, mean AOFAS functional scores improved significantly from a pre-operative average of 62 to a post-operative average of 86.
The hallux valgus angle improved from a mean pre-operative value of 23° to a mean post-operative value of 9°, and the intermetatarsal angle improved from 17° pre-operatively to 8° post-operatively.
Unlike traditional Lapidus procedures, the minimally invasive technique used in this study resulted in no detectable shortening of the first or second metatarsal bones at radiographic follow-up.

Non-union of the proximal TMTJ arthrodesis occurred in 7 of 278 cases (2%) at 6 months, of which 5 were symptomatic and 3 required surgical revision, and distal osteotomy non-union occurred in 3 of 278 cases (1%).

Hardware-related pain or screw protrusion was reported in 36 of 278 cases (13%), with proximal screws implicated in 17 cases (6%) and distal screws in 19 cases (7%); patients treated with headless screws for the Lapidus arthrodesis (used from 2015 onward) were all asymptomatic.

Patient-reported satisfaction with the combined surgical technique was high, with 69% very satisfied, 24% moderately satisfied, 3% satisfied, and 4% dissatisfied; recurrence of deformity occurred in 5 of 278 cases (2%).
In young patients with LSTV (sacralised L5), segmental lordosis at the L4-S1 level was significantly lower than theoretical PI-based values by almost 10 degrees.
The upper lumbar arc (L1-L4) lordosis was significantly greater than theoretical values, consistent with a compensatory hyperextension mechanism above the transitional level.
Overall L1-S1 lumbar lordosis in LSTV patients matched the theoretical value predicted from pelvic incidence, showing no significant difference despite abnormal internal distribution.

The L5-S1 disc showed near-parallel endplates with a mean lordotic angle of only 1°, more than 10° lower than literature values for asymptomatic subjects without LSTV, consistent with disc hypoplasia at the transitional level.
LSTV patients had a high mean pelvic incidence of 67°, concordant with prior reports showing elevated PI in subjects with LSTV.
Radiological evaluation of the Castellvi classification showed that 58% of subjects had type IIA and 42% had type IIB lumbosacral transitional vertebrae.
MRI showed adjacent-level abnormalities in most subjects, with mild L4-L5 retrolisthesis observed in 63% of patients, supporting hyperextension-related mechanical stress at that level.
Discopathy, predominantly at the L4-L5 level, was present in 81% of subjects with available MRI, consistent with early adjacent-level degeneration in young LSTV patients.

The L4-L5 disc contributed a greater proportion of overall lumbar lordosis (32%) compared to literature values in asymptomatic subjects without LSTV (27%), while the L5-S1 disc contributed less (23% vs. 35%), reflecting redistribution of lordosis away from the hypoplastic transitional disc.

Sagittal spine morphotype analysis (Roussouly classification) showed 37% of subjects had type III and 63% had type IV morphology, indicating recreation of large lordotic curves to match pelvic incidence.

In an illustrative case of a young LSTV patient with advanced L4-L5 and L3-L4 discopathy, ALIF at L4-L5 combined with a disc prosthesis at L3-L4 restored theoretical lumbar lordosis distribution and markedly improved pain and functional disability at 2-year follow-up.

Whole-exome sequencing in the child with isolated spherophakia and short stature identified a COL11A1 variant classified as of unknown significance, typically associated with Stickler syndrome type 2, but the patient showed none of the hallmark STL2 features.
The same COL11A1 variant was found in the asymptomatic father of normal height, indicating the variant was inherited rather than de novo and unlikely to explain the phenotype.
Zonular fibers are primarily composed of FBN1 (64%) and LTBP2 proteins, forming the structural basis for zonular integrity relevant to spherophakia.
Autosomal dominant FBN1 mutations are linked to Weill-Marchesani syndrome and Marfan syndrome, both associated with syndromic spherophakia.
Autosomal recessive mutations in ADAMTS10, ADAMTS17, and LTBP2 have been implicated in Weill-Marchesani-like syndromes with spherophakia.

Syndromic bilateral spherophakia is associated with several systemic connective-tissue and genetic conditions, including homocystinuria, Alport syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome, and Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome.

Khan et al. identified three distinct recessive ADAMTS17 mutations in children with isolated spherophakia and proportionate short stature (Weill-Marchesani-like syndrome), without brachydactyly, high-arched palate, or joint stiffness.
Sporadic LTBP2 variants have been linked to zonular fiber weakness causing isolated spherophakia without systemic manifestations.
Lens thickness in spherophakia frequently exceeds the normal range (3.89-4.26 mm), reaching up to 5.84 mm in reported cases.
In a study of 165 spherophakic eyes, lens power was a strong diagnostic indicator (IQR 34.54-46.51 D) with 94.3% sensitivity and 91.9% specificity for spherophakia.
The crystalline lens in spherophakia has an increased wet weight, approximately 53% greater than that of a normal lens.

Bilateral amblyopia is a common presentation in spherophakia due to delayed diagnosis of lenticular myopia in early childhood, consistent across multiple case series (26 eyes BCVA 6/12-1/60; 32 eyes BCVA 6/18-6/60).
In this patient, Grade 1 (mild) phacodonesis was detected on careful slit-lamp examination, indicating early zonular fiber instability without iridodonesis or zonular dialysis.

Pentacam biometry showed normal axial lengths (21.186 mm OD, 21.206 mm OS) and normal keratometry values in the patient, confirming that the progressive high myopia was lenticular rather than axial or corneal in origin.

The patient had bilaterally shallow anterior chamber depths (2.00 mm OD, 1.83 mm OS) and narrowed anterior chamber angles (16.3° OD, 17.4° OS) compared to normal ranges, consistent with anterior lens displacement in spherophakia and raising angle-closure glaucoma risk.

Calculated crystalline lens power using the SRK-T formula was +29.00 D (OD) and +32.00 D (OS), higher than values typical for high axial myopia (18.00-25.50 D) though below the reported spherophakia range.
Sturge-Weber syndrome has recently been reported in association with isolated spherophakia, a previously unrecognized connection.

Endocrine assessment of growth hormone levels for the patient's short stature was within normal limits, and after genetic evaluation ruled out syndromic associations, the short stature was attributed to familial traits, supporting a diagnosis of isolated (non-syndromic) spherophakia.

A newly designed sutureless scleral-fixated IOL (CM T Flex), similar to the Carlevale SFIOL, was evaluated in 57 eyes and showed fewer cases of haptic exposure, IOL dislocation, and cystoid macular edema compared to prior designs, though the study was small.
Refractive laser surgery was deemed contraindicated in this patient because ongoing spherical changes in the crystalline lens make myopia progression unpredictable.
Serum asprosin levels were significantly lower in women with fibromyalgia compared to healthy female controls.
Serum asprosin levels showed moderate diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing fibromyalgia patients from healthy controls, with an AUC of 0.708 at a cut-off of 17.72 ng/mL.

MYC was selected as one of three hub genes linked to mast cell activation during renal IRI via PPI network and machine learning analysis.

In the elevated plus maze, BK40196-treated TgAPP mice spent significantly less time in closed arms and more time in open arms than DMSO-treated mice, indicating anti-anxiety effects.
BK40196 treatment significantly reduced phosphorylated tau (ptau396) levels in brain lysates of both young and old rTg4510 mice compared to vehicle, with no effect on total tau levels.

Cupric silver staining showed that BK40196-treated rTg4510 mice had significantly fewer degenerating/stained cells in the cortex compared to DMSO-treated mice, suggesting reduced neurodegeneration and cell loss.
ELISA confirmed significantly reduced phosphorylated tau (ptau199 and ptau396) levels in BK40196-treated rTg4510 mice compared to vehicle-treated mice.
Serum miR-4497 was significantly downregulated by about 2.66-fold in children with atopic dermatitis compared to healthy controls.
Serum miR-4497 was downregulated in allergic rhinitis patients compared to controls, but this lost strict significance after FDR correction.
Serum miR-4497 was markedly downregulated (about 27.9-fold) in children with bronchial asthma compared to controls.

Transfection of miR-4497 into PMA/ionomycin-activated HMC-1 mast cells reduced secretion of the Th2 chemokine MDC compared to activated positive control and miR-control cells.

Prior evidence cited in the study indicates that both stress and CRH increase small bowel permeability through a mast-cell-dependent mechanism.
Eosinophil-derived CRH has been implicated in mast cell activation, per prior literature cited in the introduction.

Multiple peripheral nervous system complications, including inflammatory polyneuropathy, small fiber neuropathy, Parsonage-Turner syndrome, cranial mononeuropathies, and myasthenia gravis, have been reported after COVID-19 vaccination.
Small fiber neuropathy following COVID-19 vaccination should be suspected in patients presenting with dysesthesia, dysautonomia, and lower extremity paresthesia.
A skin biopsy of the proximal or distal lower limb is generally recommended for diagnosing small fiber neuropathy following COVID-19 vaccination.
Shoulder pain persisting more than 3 weeks after COVID-19 vaccination should raise suspicion for Parsonage-Turner syndrome rather than typical injection-site pain.
Needle electromyography can help support the diagnosis of Parsonage-Turner syndrome following COVID-19 vaccination, in addition to physical examination.
Inflammatory polyneuropathy after COVID-19 vaccination should be diagnosed early and treated with supportive care and immunoglobulin or plasmapheresis to prevent respiratory distress.

DIO mice exhibited significantly increased capsaicin-evoked forelimb wiping (pain) behavior compared to control mice at 22 weeks of age, but this enhancement was no longer statistically significant by 30 weeks of age.
DIO mice developed significantly increased body weight from 18 weeks of age and elevated blood glucose and serum insulin levels from 22 weeks of age onward compared to control mice.

Ex vivo Pirt-GCaMP3 Ca2+ imaging showed that capsaicin-evoked sensory axon Ca2+ responses in DIO ear skin were higher than controls at 22 weeks (both 2 μM and 10 μM capsaicin) and partly at 18 weeks (10 μM only), but were attenuated relative to controls at 30 weeks, while KCl-evoked responses did not differ between groups.

No significant changes were observed in sensory nerve-blood vessel branching patterns, vascular smooth muscle cell coverage of large vessels, or myelination of sensory nerves between control and DIO ear skin at 22 and 30 weeks.
Expression of the vascular hyperpermeability marker PLVAP was increased in DIO skin capillaries near the epidermal-dermal boundary at 22 and 30 weeks of age but not at 18 weeks.
The number of CD45+ immune cells in the epidermis did not differ significantly between control and DIO ear skin, despite the presence of sensory hypersensitivity.
Ngf mRNA expression was significantly increased in the epidermis of DIO ear skin compared to control at 22 weeks of age, whereas Bdnf and Ntf3 expression levels were unchanged.
Pirt-GCaMP3-positive sensory nerves in the epidermis express the NGF receptor TrkA, but not TrkB or TrkC.

Dermal NGF expression, primarily localized to vascular smooth muscle cells, did not differ significantly between control and DIO ear skin at any age examined.
In primary cultured mouse keratinocytes, high insulin treatment significantly increased Ngf mRNA expression, whereas high glucose had no inductive effect.
Pre-treatment of DIO ear skin explants with an anti-NGF neutralizing antibody significantly suppressed capsaicin-mediated sensory hypersensitivity compared to untreated DIO explants.

DIO also increased NGF expression in the epidermis of footpad skin at 22 weeks of age, similar to ear skin, with no observable differences in innervation or vascularization patterns between ear and footpad skin.
Cultured NIH/3T3 mouse fibroblasts express Gli1 at baseline.
TGF-β treatment induced collagen 1A1 and α-SMA expression in 3T3 fibroblasts in a dose-dependent manner, indicating fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition (FMT).

Verteporfin inhibited TGF-β-induced fibroblast-to-myofibroblast transition by suppressing α-SMA and collagen 1A1 expression in 3T3 cells.
Verteporfin decreased TGF-β-induced phosphorylation of smad3 in 3T3 fibroblasts.
Intraperitoneal PDF (4.25% glucose plus methylglyoxal) for 21 days significantly increased peritoneal thickness and collagen 1 accumulation compared to PBS-treated control mice.
YAP and α-SMA expression were upregulated in the peritoneum of mice following induction of peritoneal fibrosis.

Collagen 1 accumulation and α-SMA-marked myofibroblast activation were significantly reduced in the peritoneum of YAP conditional knockout mice compared to controls.
YAP conditional knockout suppressed peritoneal expression of TGF-β, CTGF, and phosphorylated smad2/3 compared to controls.
YAP conditional knockout reduced CD31-positive blood vessel density in the peritoneum, indicating decreased angiogenesis.
Peritoneal solute transfer rate (D/D0 glucose) did not significantly differ between YAP conditional knockout and control mice, despite reduced fibrosis and angiogenesis.
Intraperitoneal verteporfin treatment attenuated peritoneal thickening and collagen 1A1 accumulation induced by PDF, compared to control mice.
Verteporfin treatment ameliorated the PDF-induced increase in peritoneal α-SMA expression.
Verteporfin treatment suppressed peritoneal expression of TGF-β, CTGF, phosphorylated smad2/3, and CD31, indicating reduced fibrogenic signalling and angiogenesis.
Peritoneal solute transfer rate (D/D0 glucose) did not significantly differ between verteporfin-treated and control mice, mirroring the YAP CKO result.
Delayed gastric emptying (DGE) occurred in the majority of patients after retroperitoneal sarcoma surgery, with over a quarter classified as clinically relevant.

Univariate analysis showed that complete celiac ganglion resection during retroperitoneal sarcoma surgery was associated with a 22.5-fold increased risk of clinically relevant delayed gastric emptying.
Multivariate analysis confirmed complete celiac ganglion resection as an independent risk factor for clinically relevant delayed gastric emptying after retroperitoneal sarcoma surgery.
In non-adjusted analyses, exposure to a greater number of childhood maltreatment types was associated with progressively higher odds of probable depression in adulthood.
Non-adjusted odds of PTSD symptoms increased steeply with number of childhood maltreatment types, reaching over 10-fold for those with three or more types.
Adding severe violence exposure in adulthood to childhood maltreatment substantially amplified the odds of PTSD symptoms compared with childhood maltreatment alone.
Odds of self-harm (including suicidal ideation/attempts) were markedly higher in those with combined exposure to childhood maltreatment and adult severe violence than childhood maltreatment alone.
Exposure to three or more types of childhood maltreatment was associated with more than double the odds of self-reported IBS in adjusted analysis.
IBS odds were further increased, though not dramatically, when adult severe violence exposure was combined with childhood maltreatment compared with childhood maltreatment alone.
Exposure to three or more childhood maltreatment types was associated with roughly double the adjusted odds of self-reported fibromyalgia.
Combined exposure to childhood maltreatment and adult severe violence was associated with higher odds of fibromyalgia than childhood maltreatment alone.
Childhood maltreatment exposure at any level was not significantly associated with self-reported cancer or type 2 diabetes.
Associations between childhood maltreatment and ischemic heart disease, COPD, and obesity were inconsistent, without a clear dose-response relationship.
Childhood maltreatment exposure was associated with all health-related risk behaviors studied, including a dose-dependent increase in heavy smoking.

Odds of drug abuse were substantially higher among individuals with combined severe childhood maltreatment and adult violence exposure than those with high childhood maltreatment but no adult violence.

Household dysfunction during childhood (parental mental illness, substance abuse, criminality, or divorce) was significantly, though modestly, associated with PTSD, self-harm, heavy smoking, and hazardous drinking, independent of childhood maltreatment.

Overall, exposure to severe violence in adulthood (revictimization) amplified the odds of mental health problems and health-related risk behaviors associated with childhood maltreatment, but did not similarly amplify odds of the physical health conditions studied, aside from cancer in the most exposed group.

Although childhood maltreatment alone was not associated with cancer, the most exposed group (three or more maltreatment types combined with adult violence) showed significantly higher odds of cancer.

Women reported significantly higher rates of mental health problems, IBS, fibromyalgia and cancer, while men reported significantly higher rates of ischemic heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and all three health-related risk behaviors.

Women were victimized by severe violence in a dose-dependent manner to a greater extent than men across the lifespan, and childhood violence exposure was very often combined with adulthood violence exposure.
Hazardous drinking odds increased further when severe adult violence exposure was added to childhood maltreatment, showing a clear amplification effect.

Presence of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) was one of the clinical variables incorporated into a diagnostic score (contributing 3 of 7 points) used to identify masked hypertension among office-normotensive patients.

Absence of IBS was one of the variables (contributing 2 of 6 points) in a score used to identify sustained hypertension versus white coat hypertension among office-hypertensive patients, implying IBS presence is more associated with white coat hypertension.

A composite clinical BP phenotype score (threshold of 7, combining dyslipidemia, IBS, orthostatic SBP increase, and 6-minute walk test BP responses) identified masked hypertension with 90% sensitivity and 86% specificity when using 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring paired with office BP as the reference standard.

A composite clinical BP phenotype score (threshold of 6, combining male sex, absence of IBS, metabolic syndrome criteria, obesity, and standing/6MWT BP responses) identified sustained hypertension versus white coat hypertension with 82% sensitivity and 78% specificity.
Among office-normotensive participants, a systolic BP increase of more than 10 mmHg after the 6-minute walk test contributed 1 point to the masked hypertension prediction score.

A post-6-minute-walk-test blood pressure of at least 130/80 mmHg contributed 3 points to the masked hypertension prediction score, the highest weight among that score's variables alongside dyslipidemia and IBS.

Among office-hypertensive participants, a composite clinical score of 6 points (male sex, absence of IBS, ≥3 metabolic syndrome criteria, obesity, standing BP ≥140/90, and BP ≥140/90 after 6MWT) identified sustained hypertension with 82% sensitivity, 78% specificity, 90% PPV, and 64% NPV.
Male sex contributed 2 points to the sustained hypertension prediction score among office-hypertensive participants.

Absence of irritable bowel syndrome (rather than its presence) contributed 2 points toward predicting sustained hypertension among office-hypertensive participants, in contrast to IBS presence being predictive of masked hypertension among normotensives.
Having 3 or more metabolic syndrome criteria contributed 3 points to the sustained hypertension prediction score among office-hypertensive participants.
Obesity was included as a 3-point component of the diagnostic score used to distinguish sustained hypertension (SH) from white coat hypertension (WCH) among office-hypertensive patients.
A standing BP of 140/90 mmHg or higher contributed 3 points to the score predicting sustained hypertension over white coat hypertension in office-hypertensive patients.
A post-6-minute walk test BP of 140/90 mmHg or higher contributed 1 point to the score predicting sustained hypertension over white coat hypertension among office-hypertensive patients.
Gastroparesis prevalence is markedly higher in type 1 and type 2 diabetes than in the general population.
Obesity, especially combined with neuropathy, increases the likelihood of gastroparesis in type 2 diabetes, alongside elevated HbA1c, disease duration over 10 years, and vascular complications.
Autonomic neuropathy disrupts sympathetic and parasympathetic balance to the GI tract, producing motility abnormalities that underlie diabetic gastroparesis.
GLP-1 receptor agonists such as exenatide and liraglutide have been linked to the onset or worsening of gastroparesis.

In a 65-year-old man with refractory postoperative diabetic gastroparesis unresponsive to metoclopramide and ondansetron, clonidine 100 mcg twice daily resolved nausea within two days, restored oral intake, and was associated with improved renal function and blood pressure control.
Metoclopramide can alleviate nausea and vomiting but may not normalize gastric emptying, suggesting persistent vomiting in diabetic patients is not solely due to motility defects.
Relamorelin, a ghrelin receptor agonist, has shown promise in improving gastric motility and reducing nausea and vomiting in diabetic gastroparesis.
A single oral dose of clonidine 0.3 mg may reduce nausea and vomiting by acting on sensory or central neural pathways rather than through direct prokinetic effects.
Approximately one-third of gastroparesis cases show persistent symptoms with intermittent exacerbations, while another third follow a progressively worsening course.
Intravesical LL-37 administration induced chronic pelvic pain (allodynia) in mice compared to vehicle-treated controls, establishing a model of IC/BPS-like disease.
LL-37 exposure caused acute bladder inflammatory pathology, including severe edema and PMN infiltration in the lamina propria.
LL-37-induced bladder inflammation produced bladder motor dysfunction, evidenced by increased urinary urgency behavior.
EMG recordings showed enhanced visceromotor responses to graded urinary bladder distension in LL-37-treated mice, indicative of bladder hypersensitivity.
Despite robust bladder inflammation, LL-37-treated mice showed no evidence of colonic inflammatory pathology.
No change in colonic mucosal permeability was observed despite bladder inflammation.
Despite absence of colon inflammation, IC/BPS-like bladder disease produced a constipation phenotype evidenced by prolonged colonic glass bead expulsion time.
Mice with IC/BPS-like bladder disease exhibited increased visceromotor responses to colorectal distension, showing colonic irritability without primary colon inflammation.

Retrograde tracing showed the bladder is innervated by sensory neurons from T13-L1/L5-S1 DRG segments with no vagal (nodose) input, while the colon is innervated by overlapping DRG segments plus sparse nodose ganglion input.
Approximately 15.5% of L6 DRG neurons showed dual CTB fluorophore labeling from both bladder and colon injections, revealing a shared 'polyorganic' sensory neuron population innervating both organs.

Bladder and colon are innervated by two non-overlapping autonomic neuron populations in the major pelvic ganglia, indicating that shared innervation across organs is mediated by spinal sensory rather than autonomic neurons.
In vivo calcium imaging revealed that 7.8% of sensory neurons responding to bladder distension were also activated by colon distension alone, functionally confirming polyorganic sensory neurons.

Chemogenetic inhibition of polyorganic sensory neurons co-innervating bladder and colon (via intersectional dual-Gi DREADD/DCZ) attenuated colonic hypersensitivity and dysmotility upon bladder inflammation, without altering bladder hypersensitivity.

Whole-mount imaging showed that lamina propria mast cells, unlike muscularis mast cells, form close physical contact with TRPV1+ sensory neurons (nociceptors) in the bladder, in the region where inflammation occurs.

Conditional depletion of mast cells in Mas-TRECK mice attenuated bladder inflammation, urinary urgency, and bladder hypersensitivity, and also alleviated colon irritability and dysmotility, showing mast cells are necessary for interorgan sensitization.
Pharmacological inhibition of CysLTR2 using the antagonist HAMI3379 decreased both bladder hypersensitivity and colon hypersensitivity in the IC/BPS-like disease model.
Conditional deletion of Cysltr2 specifically in bladder-innervating sensory neurons attenuated both bladder and colon hypersensitivity, mirroring pharmacological CysLTR2 blockade.
Approximately 96.3% of bladder mast cells were MrgprB2-positive, with MrgprB2+ cells spatially enriched in the lamina propria.
MrgprB2-deficient mice showed attenuated bladder inflammation, urinary urgency, and bladder hypersensitivity, and a significant reduction in comorbid colon irritability and dysmotility.
According to GTEx data, the human urinary bladder shows the second-highest MRGPRX2 expression among all surveyed tissues.
Reanalysis of human bladder single-cell RNA-seq data showed MRGPRX2 expression was restricted exclusively to the mast cell cluster identified by canonical markers CPA3, FCER1A, KIT, and TPSB2.

The MRGPRX2 antagonist EP-001 blocked calcium influx induced by the MRGPRX2 ligand Compound 48/80 in peritoneal mast cells from humanized MRGPRX2 knock-in mice, confirming its antagonist activity in vitro.

In vivo oral administration of EP-001 to huMRGPRX2KI mice with IC/BPS-like disease attenuated bladder inflammation, urinary urgency, and bladder hypersensitivity, and also reduced comorbid colonic irritability and dysmotility.

Clinically, 30-75% of patients with interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome (IC/BPS) report symptoms resembling irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), suggesting a unifying pathophysiology between the two conditions.

Conditional deletion of Cysltr2 specifically in bladder-innervating neurons (via AAV9-Cre in Cysltr2flox/flox mice) mirrored pharmacological CysLTR2 blockade, significantly attenuating both bladder and colon hypersensitivity in the IC/BPS model.
Approximately 96.3% of bladder mast cells were found to be MrgprB2-positive in reporter mice.
MrgprB2+ mast cells were spatially enriched in the lamina propria of the bladder relative to the muscularis layer.
MrgprB2-deficient mice showed attenuated bladder inflammation in the IC/BPS model compared to wild-type.
MrgprB2-deficient mice showed reduced urinary urgency and bladder hypersensitivity in the IC/BPS model.
Deletion of MrgprB2 alone significantly reduced comorbid colon irritability and dysmotility, despite the manipulation being restricted to the bladder-inflammation model.

Flow cytometry of huMRGPRX2 knock-in mice confirmed uniform MRGPRX2 expression on c-Kit+CD200R3+ mast cells with no expression in other bladder immune cell lineages.
