TVSymp from mid-chest, upper abdomen, and lower back all showed consistently high correlation with finger TVSymp across the protocol.

Mean skin conductance level and NS.SCR measures from the mid-back showed relatively low correlation with finger EDA, possibly due to noise, motion artifacts, or sweat pooling in moisture-retentive regions.

Unlike finger EDA, torso-derived EDA signals were unable to reflect the decrease in sympathetic tone (NS.SCR, TVSymp) following the Cold Pressor task and after the Stroop task, suggesting reduced sensitivity to relaxation/deactivation periods.
Five of twenty subjects were excluded from analysis due to skin conductance values exceeding acquisition system cutoffs, most often caused by lower-back electrode detachment during the protocol.
The 6-month self-paced aquatic exercise intervention significantly decreased resting diastolic blood pressure in the intervention group.
The intervention group showed a significant post-intervention increase in peak expiratory flow.
No significant differences in heart rate or blood pressure during the orthostatic hypotension test were found between groups or pre-to-post within either group.
The intervention group showed a significantly greater 6-Minute Walk Test distance post-intervention compared to baseline.
The intervention group significantly improved 60-second Sit-to-Stand scores, reflecting increased lower limb strength.
The control group showed greater Sit-Reach (hamstring flexibility) scores than the intervention group, despite the intervention including stretching at every session.
The intervention group had a significant decrease in platelet concentration from pre- to post-intervention, while the control group showed no change.
Prior to the intervention, the exercise group had significantly lower monocyte concentration than the control group, with no significant pre-to-post changes in either group.
The intervention group significantly improved (reduced) FACIT-scored fatigue pre- to post-intervention and had significantly lower fatigue than controls post-intervention.
The intervention group's total HADS score (combined depression and anxiety) significantly decreased pre- to post-intervention.

The intervention group's HADS depression subscale score significantly decreased pre- to post-intervention, with nearly all intervention participants on anti-depressants also reducing depression scores.
No adverse events or worsening of ME/CFS symptoms (including post-exertional malaise) were reported during the 6-month aquatic exercise trial.
Average intervention attendance over the 6-month program was 75%, lower than shorter-duration aquatic studies (86.9-88%), attributed to the longer trial duration.
Unlike the earlier 5-week pilot study, the 6-month RCT found no significant change in hand grip strength, possibly due to lack of specific hand/forearm exercises and larger sample variance.
Viral infections were reported as the most common contributing factor to the development of ME/CFS among study participants, with multiple co-conditions common in all participants.
A substantial proportion of the ME/CFS cohort had comorbid mental health conditions, with 40.6% diagnosed with clinical depression (on anti-depressants) and 28.1% with an anxiety disorder.
A broad panel of cytokines including CXCL10, IFN-γ, IL-4, IL-5 and IL-7 has been reported elevated in ME/CFS patients and correlated with disease severity.
An estimated 60% of individuals with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) fulfill diagnostic criteria for ME/CFS.
In mice, prior resolution of influenza infection followed one month later by S. pneumoniae reinfection resulted in increased IL-6 production, demonstrating trained innate immune memory.
BCG vaccination of mice lacking an adaptive immune system conferred cross-protection against subsequent Candida albicans infection, evidencing trained innate immunity in vivo.
Human PBMCs showed increased cytokine production after BCG vaccination when subsequently exposed to S. aureus and C. albicans, suggesting cross-protective trained immunity occurs in humans.
Endogenous ligands such as lipoprotein(a), oxidized LDL, aldosterone, catecholamines, cytokines, and uric acid can induce trained immunity in innate immune cells.
Studies investigating epigenetic changes in ME/CFS found alterations in immune cells and evidence of metabolic reprogramming, though not specific to trained immunity.

Following training with Candida albicans cell wall components, monocytes showed increased glucose consumption/glycolysis and upregulation of mTOR and mTOR-related genes compared with untrained monocytes.
The mTOR inhibitors rapamycin and metformin interrupted development of trained immunity when administered during training with various stimuli including BCG.
Intravenous BCG vaccination of mice led to enhanced expansion of bone marrow hematopoietic and mesenchymal stem cells with increased myelopoiesis relative to lymphopoiesis.

Bone marrow transferred from BCG-vaccinated mice into T-cell depleted mice improved control of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, showing that trained immunity is inherited by descendant immune cells.
Hematopoietic stem cells from BCG-vaccinated humans showed distinct transcriptomic profiles that persisted in peripheral blood monocytes for at least 3 months after vaccination.
Long-term trained immunity was observed in monocytes of BCG-vaccinated children for over a year after vaccination.
Recovered hospitalized COVID-19 patients showed increased monocyte counts and proinflammatory transcriptomic profiles months after discharge compared with healthy controls.

Monocytes from convalescent COVID-19 patients had increased chromatin accessibility at genes involved in cell migration and production of inflammatory mediators, indicating a pro-inflammatory epigenetic skew.
PBMCs from convalescing COVID-19 patients produced more IL-1β and IL-6 when stimulated with spike-nCoV pseudovirus, consistent with a trained immune phenotype.

Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPC) from COVID-19 convalescents up to a year after recovery showed increased epigenetic/transcriptomic activation of genes driving myeloid differentiation and a significantly higher prevalence of granulocyte-monocyte progenitors.

Transcriptional dysregulation of monocytes and heightened serum cytokines correlating with disease severity have been described in ME/CFS, though trained-immunity-specific studies have not yet been performed in this condition.

Approximately 40% of individuals infected with Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) develop symptomatic flu-like illness, and about 20% of acute Q fever patients develop a long-lasting post-infectious fatigue syndrome resembling ME/CFS.

Monocytes from acute Q fever patients showed increased production of IL-1β, IL-1Ra, IL-6 and IL-10 up to 27 days after the last sick day, with IL-10 remaining elevated at six months, suggesting long-term monocyte/macrophage alterations consistent with a trained phenotype.
Activation of the type I interferon (IFN-I) pathway in monocytes of primary Sjögren's disease patients was associated with higher clinical disease activity scores.

In THP-1 monocytes, training with type I interferon (IFN-I) induced elevated production of IL-6, TNFα and CCL2 and increased glucose consumption upon LPS restimulation, demonstrating that IFN-I acts as a potent trainer of monocytes.
Outpatient metformin treatment reduced the incidence of post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC) by 41%.
An observational clinical trial (NCT06257420) is investigating the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin for reducing overall symptom burden and improving quality of life in ME/CFS.

Using computable phenotype (CP) labels rather than diagnostic codes, 60.1% of PASC CP-positive patients were also ME/CFS CP-positive, and 47.1% of ME/CFS CP-positive patients were also PASC CP-positive, indicating substantial EHR overlap between the two conditions.

Using ICD-10-CM diagnostic codes (index dates from October 1, 2022 onward), only 6.9% of PASC diagnostic patients also had an ME/CFS diagnosis, while 33.0% of ME/CFS diagnostic patients also had a PASC diagnosis, a much lower overlap than seen using CP labels.

Machine-learning computable phenotype models found dyspnea, fatigue, and 'finding related to attentiveness' (cognitive impairment) as the strongest shared predictive conditions distinguishing both PASC and ME/CFS patients from matched controls.
Conditions specifically most-predictive for the PASC computable phenotype (beyond the shared three) included another respiratory condition, cardiac conditions, and sensory (smell/taste) disorders.

Conditions specifically most-predictive for the ME/CFS computable phenotype (12 additional beyond the three shared) included vitamin deficiencies, immune dysfunction, neuropsychiatric conditions, pain conditions, hypothyroidism, and sleep conditions.

The cardiopulmonary condition cluster (including palpitations, chronic cough, dyspnea) was substantially more common in patients with a PASC diagnosis or PASC CP label than in ME/CFS patients, representing the largest distinguishing feature between the two conditions.

The neurological and comorbidity condition clusters showed some specificity (though less pronounced than the cardiopulmonary cluster for PASC) for patients labeled with the ME/CFS computable phenotype.

A supporting model trained to directly distinguish EHR records of patients diagnosed only with PASC versus only with ME/CFS performed poorly (AUC 0.63), indicating condition-record profiles of the two illnesses are only moderately separable.
The independently trained PASC and ME/CFS computable phenotype models achieved similar and strong discriminatory performance versus matched controls (AUC 0.841 and 0.842, respectively).

The ME/CFS computable phenotype labeled 71.6% of ME/CFS-diagnosed patients, 52.5% of PASC-diagnosed patients, 56.7% of R53.82 (unspecified chronic fatigue) patients, and only 16.9% of controls, demonstrating strong differentiation from controls with partial cross-labeling.
The PASC computable phenotype labeled 68.0% of PASC-diagnosed patients, 53.0% of ME/CFS-diagnosed patients, 38.2% of R53.82 patients, and only 13.0% of controls.

The proportion of patients identifying as female was higher in the PASC, ME/CFS, and R53.82 diagnostic groups compared with controls, with this female predominance especially pronounced in the ME/CFS group.

The proportion of patients identifying as Black or African American was lower, and White higher, in the PASC and ME/CFS diagnostic groups relative to controls, with this racial disparity being larger in the ME/CFS group; the ME/CFS group also had a higher proportion identifying as not Hispanic/Latino.

Vitamin deficiencies (B vitamins, vitamin D, and iron) were identified as most-predictive conditions specific to the ME/CFS computable phenotype, possibly reflecting immune activation from initial infection characterized as anemia of inflammation or chronic disease.
Post-exertional malaise, considered the hallmark symptom of ME/CFS, could not be directly captured in this EHR-based analysis because no ICD-10-CM code exists for it.

Orthostatic intolerance is recognized as an important symptom pattern in PASC and ME/CFS, and although POTS now has an ICD-10-CM code (too recent for inclusion in modeling), tachycardia and palpitations emerged more generally as relevant conditions in this study.

In this pilot user-testing case series, 8 of 9 Long COVID testers who completed feedback surveys (89%) reported that the wearable device and educational materials were helpful for their symptom management.
Among testers who experienced a symptom relapse (postexertional malaise) during the study, most reported that the device and educational materials reduced the severity or duration of that relapse.

Nearly half of testers had never used a wearable device before, and none of the testers had difficulty setting up the device, suggesting feasibility of wearable adoption in Long COVID patients regardless of prior experience.
At 12-month follow-up, all responding testers reported that they were still consistently using their wearable device and continued to derive benefit for symptom and health management.
In a separate cited survey of 3762 Long COVID patients, pacing and energy monitoring were rated as the most helpful treatments for managing symptoms and avoiding functional peaks and valleys.

A cited 2022 survey of 488 individuals with ME/CFS found that heart rate monitoring via wearable devices helped most respondents better understand their postexertional malaise triggers and improved self-care ability for a subset.

The cited DETECT study found that combining wearable-derived physiological data with self-reported symptoms detected COVID-19 infection more accurately than symptoms alone and could track patient status beyond the acute infection phase.

The cited Warrior Watch Study (Mount Sinai) found that changes in heart rate variability were directly correlated with COVID-19 infection, supporting wearables as tools to monitor and manage the disease.

The authors note that a higher proportion of user testers reported benefit from wearable-supported pacing than Long COVID patients who tried pacing alone in a separately cited study, suggesting an added benefit from device-supported pacing.
The prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) among post-COVID-19 patients was 21.4%, based on a validated CFS severity score.
Participants aged 45-59 years had markedly higher adjusted odds of CFS compared to those under 18 years.
Participants aged 60 years and above had the highest adjusted odds of CFS compared to those under 18 years.
Female participants were nearly twice as likely as males to develop CFS after adjustment for covariates.
Path analysis showed that presence of comorbidities was significantly associated with higher CFS scores.
In path analysis, male gender was significantly associated with lower CFS scores compared to female gender.
COVID-19 vaccination status did not significantly predict CFS scores in the path analysis model.
Comorbidities significantly increased the likelihood of developing chronic fatigue syndrome.
Joint pain, muscle pain, fatigue after mild exertion, and headache were the most frequently reported new-onset symptoms among post-COVID-19 participants.
Sore throat, reduced memory, and reduced sleep were among the least frequently reported post-COVID-19 symptoms.
Participants who had been infected with SARS-CoV-2 more than once were more likely to report fatigue.
Vaccinated participants showed a slightly higher descriptive fatigue prevalence than unvaccinated participants, though this was confounded by vaccinated individuals being generally older.

Cited literature indicates immune irregularities in long COVID including elevated non-classical monocytes, activated and double-negative B cells, and IL-4/IL-6-secreting CD4+ T cells, alongside reduced conventional dendritic cells, exhausted T cells, and cortisol levels.
Recent studies suggest EDS prevalence is much higher than the historical estimate of 1 in 5,000, potentially between 0.75% and 2% of the population.
Hypermobile EDS (hEDS) is reported to account for 80-90% of all EDS cases, making it the most common subtype and the only one diagnosed clinically rather than genetically.
The average time to receive an hEDS diagnosis is reported to exceed ten years, contributing to underdiagnosis and delayed access to care.
Functional digestive disorders occur in between one-third and three-quarters of EDS patients.
Fatigue and dysautonomia are very common among EDS patients but remain under-recognized in clinical practice.

The 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria are more restrictive than prior Villefranche and Brighton criteria, so some patients who previously met older diagnostic criteria no longer qualify for an hEDS diagnosis.

Despite their high prevalence in EDS patients, dysautonomia, fatigue, and digestive problems are not included in the hEDS diagnostic checklist even when they exceed levels unusual for the general population.
Chronic fatigue in EDS patients often results from comorbid POTS and dysautonomia.
Mild dilatation of the aortic root is reported as a cardiovascular symptom associated with EDS.
EDS patients commonly experience gastrointestinal comorbidities including food allergies/intolerances, IBS, hiatus hernia, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and constipation.
Neurologic and psychiatric comorbidities, including depression, anxiety, and phobias, are reported in EDS patients.
Although only some EDS forms are lethal, most cases are associated with poor quality of life.
Genetic testing for the most common EDS-associated gene variants was negative in this patient despite a strong clinical and family phenotype of hypermobility.
Postural Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS) was diagnosed in the patient via tilt table testing.
The authors conclude that small fibre neuropathy (SFN) was responsible for the patient's habitual/recurrent syncope, while dramatic joint dislocations explained her insomnia.
Recurrent painful joint dislocations and subluxations occurring even during sleep led to severe sleep disturbance, limiting sleep to 4-5 hours per night.
Echocardiography revealed a hypermobile atrial septum and a 5 mm patent foramen ovale in the patient.
The patient had a positive medical history for ADHD, an intra-articular ankle ganglion, and allergic asthma, occurring alongside her hypermobile EDS.
The patient's family history was strongly positive for joint hypermobility across multiple maternal and paternal relatives, suggestive of a hereditary hypermobility disorder.
A meta-analysis of 13 studies found that obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) prevalence was almost 50% among patients with EDS or Marfan syndrome.
Within the meta-analysis, OSAS prevalence was higher among Marfan syndrome patients than among EDS patients.
In a study of 24 pediatric EDS patients, OSAS was found in 42%.
Pediatric EDS patients had lower Child Health Questionnaire scores and higher Sleep-Related Breathing Disorder and Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores than healthy controls.
In a study of 56 hypermobile EDS patients, insomnia occurred in 22%, OSAS in 26%, periodic limb movement disorder in 17%, and hypersomnia in 15%.

In the same cohort of 56 hypermobile EDS patients, 65% required pharmacologic treatment for their sleep disorder, 29% were referred to behavioral sleep medicine, and 2 patients with OSAS required CPAP.
Sleep and quality-of-life scores (PSQ, ESS, PedsQl) significantly improved with treatment in the 56-patient hypermobile EDS cohort.

In a prospective parallel study of 100 EDS patients, OSAS prevalence was 32%, with frequent daytime sleepiness and impaired quality of life; OSAS was associated with fatigue and excessive daytime sleepiness.
Despite not having OSAS, the index patient still reported chronic fatigue and daytime sleepiness.

The authors speculate that the wake-night rhythm depends strongly on the balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous system activity, potentially explaining a contribution of SFN to the patient's sleep disturbance.
The authors judge that ADHD alone was unlikely to have caused the patient's sleep disorder, since she never required pharmacologic ADHD treatment.
Nerve conduction studies in the patient were non-informative despite clinical hypoesthesia and reduced tendon reflexes.

A homozygous non-canonical splice site variant c.1756-13C>A in PLOD1 was identified by exome sequencing in a boy with kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome features and had previously been annotated with conflicting pathogenicity classifications.

Whole blood RNA sequencing showed that the PLOD1 c.1756-13C>A variant caused aberrant splicing with incorporation of 11 intronic nucleotides, generating a premature stop codon, demonstrating a deleterious loss-of-function effect.

Unlike other EDS subtype genes that are not expressed in peripheral lymphocytes, PLOD1 is expressed in whole blood, enabling RNA-based functional splicing analysis directly from a blood draw rather than requiring skin fibroblasts.
The Beighton score was significantly higher in the hypermobile group than in the normal group, confirming successful group stratification.
Sagittal radiocapitellar joint congruence increased significantly when the forearm was pronated compared with supinated, but did not change between flexion and extension.
Coronal ulnohumeral congruence increased significantly with pronation and with combined flexion and pronation compared with extension and supination.
Sagittal and axial ulnohumeral joint congruence did not change significantly with elbow flexion or forearm rotation.
In full extension and supination, coronal ulnohumeral joint congruence was significantly higher (i.e., less incongruent) in the normal group than in the hypermobile group.
In 30° of flexion and supination, sagittal radiocapitellar congruence was significantly higher in the hypermobile group than in the normal group.
In 30° of flexion and supination, sagittal ulnohumeral congruence was significantly lower in the hypermobile group than in the normal group.
In 30° of flexion and pronation, coronal ulnohumeral joint congruence was significantly higher in the normal group than in the hypermobile group.

Only in full extension and pronation did elbow joint congruence not differ significantly between the normal and hypermobile groups, suggesting this position could reduce false-positive PLRI diagnoses.
Intrarater reliability of the MRI joint congruence measurements was excellent, whereas interrater reliability was only moderate.

The median sagittal radiocapitellar incongruence measured in healthy elbows exceeded the 2.0 mm threshold previously proposed by Hackl et al to identify posterolateral rotatory instability (PLRI), suggesting this diagnostic threshold may need upward adjustment.
Arthrochalasia-type EDS results from alterations in type I collagen, underlying the connective tissue fragility seen in this condition.

The diagnostic criteria for arthrochalasia-type EDS include congenital bilateral hip dislocation, skin hyperextensibility and fragility, and severe generalized joint hypermobility, confirmable with genetic testing.

Traditional growing rods (low-profile Mesa screws and rods) were implanted from T4 to L1 at age 5 with tranexamic acid/desmopressin prophylaxis, resulting in only 150 ml blood loss and no major complications.
An intraoperative area of skin breakdown occurred when a disinfectant wipe was used to prep skin for spinal cord monitoring electrode placement, reflecting extreme skin fragility.
After the first lengthening of the traditional growing rods (20 months post-implantation), spinal T1-S1 height increased by 25 mm.
Replacement of traditional growing rods with dual MAGEC magnetically-controlled growth rods (T2 to L4) at age 10 resulted in 1000 cc of blood loss, attributed to vascular fragility from aEDS.
A superficial rash occurred around the surgical wound after MAGEC rod implantation, diagnosed by a dermatologist as allergic contact dermatitis, which healed within 3 weeks.
The MAGEC rods were subsequently lengthened non-surgically 13 times at 3-4 month intervals, an average of 3 mm each time, with no wound or metalwork complications.
At 17-year follow-up, the patient's Cobb angle remained stable at 100 degrees with good correction of the kyphosis after growth-rod management without definitive spinal fusion.
The patient developed a chronic hip dislocation at age 9 and continues to ambulate via wheelchair, though he maintains good sitting balance.

Histological examination of the proband's arterial tissue revealed a dissecting hematoma in the media layer, myocyte loss, sclerosis, and destruction of the elastic laminae, consistent with structural vascular wall degeneration.

Fibroblast metabolic labeling showed that the proband secreted significantly less type III collagen into the culture medium and accumulated less in the cell layer than an age-matched control, with evidence of intracellular degradation products.
The signal ratio of type III to type I collagen was lower in the proband compared to normal reference values, suggesting a qualitative defect in stable type III collagen.

Exome sequencing identified a novel heterozygous 18-bp in-frame duplication in COL3A1 (c.2868_2885dup) causing insertion of six amino acids (Leu-Ala-Gly-Pro-Pro-Gly) into the collagen III alpha-1 chain, not previously reported in gnomAD, LOVD, or HGMD, and classified as pathogenic per ACMG criteria (PVS1, PM2).
The same COL3A1 duplication was detected in the proband's asymptomatic 22-year-old brother but was absent in the father, indicating likely maternal transmission and variable/incomplete penetrance.

Molecular dynamics simulations of wild-type versus mutant collagen trimers showed comparable overall conformation and thermodynamic stability, with similar RMSD/RMSF and only small differences in interchain binding free energy.

Compared to wild type, the mutated homotrimer exhibited greater mean curvature and flexibility during molecular dynamics simulations, suggesting local structural destabilization at the duplication site.

The duplicated sequence lies near the canonical MMP-1 collagenase cleavage site and hemopexin-domain-binding exosite of collagen III, potentially generating a new cleavable Gly|Leu triplet and introducing a hydrophobic Leu residue that could enhance MMP-mediated collagen turnover.
Most of the eleven patients with 2q32 microdeletions encompassing COL3A1 showed minor features of vascular EDS, supporting COL3A1 haploinsufficiency as a disease mechanism.

Although COL5A2 was included in the deleted region in these patients, skin biopsies showed no features of classical EDS, suggesting COL5A2 haploinsufficiency alone does not produce the classical EDS phenotype.
One patient with a 2q32 microdeletion encompassing COL3A1 experienced a vessel rupture at a young age, indicative of a severe vascular EDS-related complication.
Female patients had a consistently higher recorded prevalence of EDS diagnosis than males across all age cohorts and racial/ethnic groups.
Recorded prevalence of EDS diagnosis declined markedly with age, with a steep drop after age 61.
Patients with an EDS diagnosis had significantly increased odds of a recorded myopia diagnosis compared to the general population.
Degenerative myopia was recorded at significantly increased odds in EDS patients compared to the general population.
Dry eye syndrome diagnosis was significantly more prevalent and had increased odds in EDS patients across nearly all age groups.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) diagnosis showed the strongest and most consistent increased odds of any ocular-relevant condition in EDS patients across all age strata.
Angioid streaks showed the highest prevalence odds ratio of all ocular conditions studied in EDS, though based on only 11 records, limiting reliability.
Carotid cavernous fistula was significantly more prevalent and at increased odds in EDS records, most markedly in the 0-30 age cohort.
Diabetic retinopathy secondary to type 2 diabetes was significantly less prevalent and had decreased odds in EDS patients compared to the general population.
Both neovascular and non-neovascular age-related macular degeneration were significantly less prevalent in EDS records compared to the general population.
Retinopathy of prematurity had significantly decreased odds in EDS patients aged 0-30, an unexpected finding given the higher preterm birth rate reported in EDS pregnancies.
Glaucoma diagnosis was significantly more prevalent in EDS patients than the general population overall and in the 0-30 and 31-60 age cohorts.
Hypertensive retinopathy was significantly less prevalent overall in EDS patients compared to the general population.
A prior case series found ophthalmologic signs, including dry eye, blue sclera, and high myopia, in 90% of a small EDS cohort.

A prior case study found that nearly a quarter of a large EDS cohort required ophthalmic surgery, with about half experiencing a complication, and most were undiagnosed with EDS at the time of surgery.
The authors recommend that ophthalmological referral/workup be considered for newly diagnosed EDS patients given the frequency of associated ocular findings.

Prime editing successfully introduced a heterozygous C1R c.902G>C (p.Arg301Pro) mutation into hTERT-immortalized gingival fibroblasts, confirmed by Sanger sequencing and ddPCR showing ~50% mutant allele burden in three clones.
mhGFBs and hGFBs showed no significant differences in fibroblast-like morphology or expression of filamentous actin, vimentin, CD90, and PDGFRα markers.
MTT proliferation assays showed no significant difference in cell proliferation between mhGFBs and hGFBs, and no significant variation among three mhGFB clones.
mhGFBs and hGFBs displayed comparable cell growth and cell size up to 120 hours, and no significant difference in population doubling time at 72 hours.
C1R and C1S mRNA expression did not significantly differ between mhGFBs and hGFBs, indicating the mutation does not alter transcription of these complement genes.
Despite unchanged C1R mRNA, mhGFBs secreted significantly lower levels of C1r protein into culture medium than hGFBs, indicating a post-transcriptional defect.
mhGFBs showed significantly higher procollagen α1(V) mRNA expression compared to hGFBs.
mhGFBs showed significantly higher MMP-1 mRNA expression compared to hGFBs, at baseline without cytokine treatment.
mhGFBs showed significantly higher TIMP-1 mRNA expression compared to hGFBs at baseline.
Vimentin, procollagen α1(I), and procollagen α1(III) mRNA expression did not differ significantly between mhGFBs and hGFBs.
Immunocytochemical staining showed no significant difference in the amount/intensity of type I collagen between mhGFBs and hGFBs.
F-CHP staining showed a non-significant trend toward increased unfolded/denatured collagen in mhGFBs compared to hGFBs.
Sirius Red collagen deposition assay showed significantly lower collagen deposition in mhGFBs compared to hGFBs under baseline culture conditions.

TNF-α or IL-1β treatment further reduced collagen deposition in mhGFBs relative to untreated mhGFBs, an effect not observed in hGFBs, indicating heightened sensitivity of mutant cells to inflammatory cytokines.
In wild-type hGFBs, TNF-α and/or IL-1β stimulation significantly increased mRNA expression of C1R, C1S, procollagen α1(III), procollagen α1(V), MMP-1, TIMP-1, and IL-6 compared to untreated controls.

Unlike hGFBs, cytokine-stimulated mhGFBs showed significant upregulation of only MMP-1 and IL-6 mRNA (not C1R, C1S, or procollagens), and the magnitude of MMP-1/IL-6 induction was much greater in mhGFBs than in hGFBs, indicating a dysregulated inflammatory response to the C1R mutation.
Musculoskeletal anomalies of some kind were identified in 86.6% of children with Down syndrome evaluated in this hospital-based study.
Hypotonia was present in 77.3% of the children with Down syndrome, one of the most common findings in the whole group.
Joint laxity was present in 77.3% of children with Down syndrome, assessed via Beighton Hypermobility Score in those aged 6 years or more.
Pes planus (flat feet) was found in 82% of ambulatory children with Down syndrome.
Orthopedic abnormalities (other than pes planus) were prevalent in 69.3% of ambulatory children with Down syndrome.
The occurrence of genu valgum (knock knees) increased with increasing body mass index in children with Down syndrome.
Reserpine administration induced allodynia and hyperalgesia in rats, shown by reduced tail withdrawal latency, paw withdrawal latency, and paw withdrawal threshold compared to normal rats.
Modafinil reversed reserpine-induced allodynia and hyperalgesia, increasing withdrawal latencies/threshold across all three pain tests.
Haloperidol (D2 antagonist) co-administration attenuated modafinil's analgesic benefit, reducing withdrawal latencies/threshold compared to modafinil alone.
Reserpine increased depressive-like immobility in the forced swim test and impaired rotarod motor coordination compared to normal rats.
Modafinil reduced immobility time and improved rotarod performance relative to the reserpine group.
Haloperidol reversed modafinil's antidepressant and motor-coordination benefits.
Reserpine caused significant depletion of thalamic dopamine relative to normal rats.
Modafinil boosted thalamic dopamine concentration relative to the reserpine group.
Haloperidol blocked modafinil's dopaminergic effect, reducing thalamic dopamine concentration.
Reserpine-induced dopamine depletion led to elevated thalamic substance P (SP), driving mast cell activation.
MRGPRX2 (mast cell receptor for SP) expression was markedly increased in the thalamus of reserpine-treated rats.
Thalamic histamine, released upon mast cell degranulation, was substantially elevated in reserpine-treated rats.
Modafinil reduced thalamic SP, MRGPRX2, and histamine levels compared to the fibromyalgia (reserpine) group, indicating mast cell stabilization.
Haloperidol reversed modafinil's suppression of SP, MRGPRX2, and histamine, increasing all three relative to the modafinil group.
Reserpine activated the PI3K pathway in the thalamus, increasing PI3K levels versus normal rats.
Reserpine increased the p-Akt/T-Akt ratio in the thalamus compared to normal rats, indicating Akt pathway activation.
Modafinil down-regulated thalamic PI3K and p-Akt/T-Akt levels compared to the reserpine group.
Reserpine-induced DA depletion increased thalamic IL-17, contributing to mast cell-microglial activation.
Reserpine caused upregulation of thalamic NF-κB, TNF-α, and IL-6 relative to normal rats.
Modafinil's immunomodulatory activity down-regulated IL-17, NF-κB, TNF-α, and IL-6 in the thalamus compared to the reserpine group.
Haloperidol reversed modafinil's anti-inflammatory effect, raising thalamic inflammatory mediator concentrations again (no exact percentages given).
Reserpine caused thalamic histopathological damage including congested blood vessels, degenerating neurons with neuronophagia, focal astrocytosis, and diffuse gliosis.
Modafinil treatment markedly improved thalamic histopathology, restoring more organized neuronal morphology and intact vasculature; haloperidol reversed this benefit.
Toluidine blue staining showed numerous dark-stained (degranulated) mast cell-associated neurons in the reserpine group compared to faint staining in normal rats, confirming mast cell degranulation.
Modafinil normalized mast cell staining (fewer dark-stained neurons) versus the reserpine group, while haloperidol treatment restored numerous dark-stained neurons.
Reserpine and haloperidol both increased thalamic microglial Iba-1 immunohistochemical expression compared to the normal group, indicating microglial activation.
Modafinil treatment significantly reduced thalamic PI3K levels by 76.9% and p-Akt/T-Akt ratio by 47.6% compared to the reserpine-only FMS group.
Co-administration of haloperidol blocked modafinil's inhibitory effect on thalamic PI3K and p-Akt/T-Akt levels, reversing the treatment benefit.
Reserpine administration increased thalamic IL-17 levels by 3.8-fold compared to normal rats, implicating IL-17 in mast cell-microglial activation.
Reserpine increased thalamic NF-κB levels by 0.9-fold compared to normal rats as part of the inflammatory cascade.
Reserpine increased thalamic TNF-α levels by 0.8-fold compared to normal rats.
Reserpine increased thalamic IL-6 levels by 11.2-fold compared to normal rats.
Modafinil reduced thalamic IL-17 by 56.7% compared to the reserpine group, indicating impaired mast cell-microglial activation.
Modafinil reduced thalamic NF-κB levels by 31.7% compared to the reserpine group.
Modafinil reduced thalamic TNF-α levels by 41% compared to the reserpine group.
Modafinil reduced thalamic IL-6 levels by 55.5% compared to the reserpine group.
Haloperidol co-administration reversed modafinil's anti-inflammatory effect, raising thalamic concentrations of inflammatory mediators relative to the modafinil group.

Reserpine-treated rats exhibited severely congested thalamic blood vessels, numerous dark degenerating neurons with neuronophagia, and focal astrocytosis with diffuse gliosis, whereas normal rats showed no histopathological changes.

Modafinil treatment normalized thalamic histopathology with organized neuronal morphology, minimal degeneration, and intact vasculature, but this benefit was reversed by haloperidol co-administration which reintroduced dark neurons, gliosis, and thickened blood vessel walls.

Toluidine blue staining showed increased dark-stained (degranulated) thalamic mast cells in reserpine-treated rats compared to faintly stained mast cells in normal rats; modafinil normalized staining, while haloperidol caused reappearance of dark-stained mast cells.

Immunohistochemistry showed increased thalamic Iba-1 (microglial marker) expression by 2.5-fold after reserpine and 1.3-fold after haloperidol co-treatment compared to normal rats, while modafinil decreased Iba-1 expression by 54.6% relative to the reserpine group, indicating controlled microglial activation.

Serum neurotensin levels were significantly higher in women with fibromyalgia compared with healthy controls.

Serum neurotensin levels were negatively correlated with the FIQR 'tenderness to touch' subscale score in FM patients.

HFD-fed mice showed impaired glucose tolerance compared with chow-fed mice.
Immunohistochemical staining showed increased microglia in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus of HFD-fed mice compared with chow-fed mice.

Intracerebroventricular cromolyn sodium (mast cell stabilizer) reduced body weight and fat mass compared with saline in HFD-fed mice.
Cromolyn sodium treatment reduced adipocyte size and hepatic lipid droplet content compared with control.
Cromolyn sodium-treated mice showed improved glucose tolerance compared with controls.
Cromolyn sodium-treated mice showed reduced food intake and increased energy expenditure in metabolic cage experiments.

Cromolyn sodium treatment similarly reduced microglial (Iba1+) number in the hypothalamic ARC compared with control.

Cromolyn sodium increased the number of activated (c-Fos+) neurons in the ARC, DMH, and PVH but not in the VMH.
Pharmacological inhibition of mast cells with cromolyn sodium increased the number of activated (POMC+c-Fos+) POMC neurons in the ARC.
Cromolyn sodium-treated mice had more STAT3-activated cells in the ARC than controls, indicating increased leptin sensitivity.
Exogenous leptin significantly reduced food intake in cromolyn sodium-treated HFD mice but failed to suppress appetite in control mice, indicating cromolyn ameliorated leptin resistance.
Cromolyn sodium-treated mice showed increased α-MSH immunostaining in the hypothalamic PVN and DMH nuclei compared with controls.

Gain-of-function mutations in the SCN9A gene encoding Nav1.7 have been linked to chronic spontaneous pain conditions including inherited erythromelalgia, paroxysmal extreme pain disorder, and small fiber neuropathy.
Loss-of-function mutations in Nav1.7 result in congenital insensitivity to pain, with patients unable to perceive pain despite normal sensitivity to touch and pressure, often accompanied by anosmia.
Functional mutations in the SCN10A gene encoding Nav1.8 have been found in patients with chronic pain due to small fiber neuropathy.
Mutations in SCN11A, encoding Nav1.9, are associated with several hereditary pain disorders including familial episodic pain, congenital insensitivity to pain, and inherited small fiber neuropathy.

In acute inflammatory pain states, gene expression of voltage-gated sodium channels, particularly Nav1.7 and Nav1.8, is significantly increased, lowering the threshold for C-fibers and Aδ-fibers and contributing to hyperalgesia.
Nav1.8 expression is significantly increased in chronic inflammatory pain.

In Nav1.9 knockout mice, inflammatory responses were diminished and mechanical hypersensitivity induced by CFA and formalin was significantly reduced, indicating a role for Nav1.9 in pathological pain.
Nav1.9 acts as a subthreshold amplifier of cold sensory signals, and disruption of Nav1.9 expression in rodents increases the threshold for cold-induced pain, supporting its role in cold nociception.

Vixotrigine, a Nav1.7 inhibitor that stabilizes the inactivated channel state, was FDA-approved as an orphan drug for trigeminal neuralgia in 2013, but its phase II clinical trial was later terminated for failing to meet primary or secondary efficacy endpoints.

PF-05089771, a highly selective Nav1.7 inhibitor that stabilizes the channel's inactivated conformation, failed to significantly improve pain scores in a randomized double-blind clinical study for diabetic neuropathic pain, leading Pfizer to discontinue its development.

Peripheral deletion of Nav1.7 produces extreme pain insensitivity in mice and humans, yet nociceptor activity in the dorsal root ganglia itself is not affected; central opioid receptor blockade can reverse the analgesia, implicating opioid-dependent central mechanisms rather than peripheral nociceptor firing.

VX-150, an early Nav1.8-targeted compound, showed promising therapeutic effects in multiple proof-of-concept Phase II trials but its development was halted due to high required dosage and adverse effects such as dizziness and headaches.

VX-548 (suzetrigine), a selective Nav1.8 inhibitor designed for moderate to severe acute pain, showed favorable pharmacokinetics and safety with reduced dosing, and was under FDA review as a potential first new pain medication in decades.

In a Phase II study for sciatica (lumbosacral radicular pain), VX-548 significantly reduced pain, but similar pain relief was also observed in the placebo group, raising concerns about the drug's true efficacy.

Nav1.9 has relatively low sequence homology (approximately 50%) with other Nav channel subtypes, making it comparatively straightforward to design selective inhibitors with theoretically fewer off-target side effects.
Fluoroquinolone antibiotics are associated with peripheral neuropathy, including small fiber neuropathy.

Unlike most other antibiotics, some fluoroquinolone-associated adverse effects such as tendinopathy or neuropathy can begin after drug discontinuation and may subsequently progress into a chronic disability.
Fluoroquinolones are associated with tendon disorders, particularly tendinopathy and tendon rupture.
Fluoroquinolones are associated with CNS toxicity, including seizure and encephalopathy.
Fluoroquinolones are associated with cardiovascular toxicity, including QT interval prolongation, aortic dissection, and aneurysm rupture.
Fluoroquinolones are associated with phototoxicity as a serious adverse effect.
Fluoroquinolone use is associated with C. difficile infections as a serious adverse effect.
Ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin can cause acute renal failure specifically via crystallization, distinguishing this AE mechanism from other fluoroquinolones.
Fluoroquinolones are associated with hepatic toxicity as a serious adverse effect.
Unlike AEs from most other antibiotics, some fluoroquinolone AEs such as tendinopathy or neuropathy may occur after drug discontinuation and can subsequently progress into FQ-associated disability.
The risk of serious fluoroquinolone-related adverse events is increased by patient age, comorbidities, treatment dose/duration, and concomitant drug intake (drug-drug interactions).
Overall, fluoroquinolones appear to carry a higher risk of serious adverse events than most other antibiotics used for the same indications.
78% of patients undergoing autonomic testing for autonomic symptoms satisfied criteria for central sensitization syndrome (CSS).
Patients with CSS were younger, more frequently female, and had longer symptom duration and more comorbidities than non-CSS patients.
Patients with CSS scored higher on the Compass-31 autonomic symptom questionnaire than non-CSS patients.
Patients with CSS scored higher on the Neuropathy Total Symptom Score-6 (sensory symptom) scale than non-CSS patients.
Orthostatic end-tidal CO2 was lower in patients with CSS compared with non-CSS patients on capnography testing.
Orthostatic decline in cerebral blood flow velocity (CBFv) was greater in patients with CSS compared with non-CSS patients.
Peripheral nervous system markers, including sudomotor testing and skin biopsy findings for small fiber neuropathy, did not differ between patients with and without central sensitization syndrome.
The frequency of moderate autonomic failure was similar between patients with and without central sensitization syndrome.
Patients with central sensitization syndrome had a lower autonomic failure severity score than patients without central sensitization syndrome, despite similar AF frequency.
A cluster of five brain-enriched miRNAs was consistently downregulated in both MSA-C and MSA-P plasma compared to healthy controls, iPD, and PSP patients.
iPD plasma samples showed distinctly higher expression of miR-154-5p, miR-382-5p, and miR-495-3p compared to MSA variants, suggesting opposing molecular patterns between iPD and MSA.
PSP samples showed intermediate miRNA expression levels overall, with miR-154-5p specifically reduced compared to iPD.
In the MSA-C subgroup, miR-29a-3p plasma levels positively correlated with levodopa equivalent daily dose.

Several brain-enriched plasma miRNAs showed significant negative correlations with SCOPA-AUT autonomic subscale scores (urinary, sexual, total), suggesting a role in autonomic homeostasis and dysfunction across parkinsonian syndromes.
MSA patients (both subtypes) exhibited more prominent autonomic nervous system symptoms—particularly gastrointestinal, urinary, and cardiovascular—compared to iPD and PSP patients on SCOPA-AUT.
A two-miRNA panel (miR-153-3p, miR-598-3p) discriminated iPD from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.73.
A three-miRNA panel (miR-154-5p, miR-409-3p, miR-411-5p) discriminated MSA-C from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.88.
A four-miRNA panel (miR-136-3p, miR-154-5p, miR-329-5p, miR-487b-3p) discriminated MSA-P from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.91.
A three-miRNA panel (miR-22-3p, miR-382-5p, miR-654-3p) discriminated PSP from healthy controls with an AUC of 0.88.
miR-154-5p and miR-409-3p together distinguished iPD from MSA-C with an AUC of 0.93.
miR-153-3p and miR-154-5p together discriminated iPD from MSA-P with an AUC of 0.95.
miR-410-3p alone distinguished PSP from iPD with an AUC of 0.76, and together with miR-330-3p differentiated MSA-C from MSA-P with an AUC of 0.76.
miR-411-5p and miR-487b-3p distinguished MSA-C from PSP with an AUC of 0.83, and miR-153-3p and miR-329-5p discriminated MSA-P from PSP with an AUC of 0.86.
Over half of the differentially expressed miRNAs mapped to a shared genomic cluster on chromosome 14q32, suggesting coordinated regulation by transcription factors or methylation events.

In silico transcription factor binding site analysis identified enrichment of CEBPB, MAZ, and CREB1 binding sites in the promoters of half of the dysregulated miRNAs, including 8 of 9 Chr14-located miRNAs.

KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of dysregulated miRNA targets showed significant enrichment in Prion diseases, Hippo signaling, Mucin type O-Glycan biosynthesis, Adherens junction, Wnt signaling, TGF-beta signaling, Ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, and FoxO signaling pathways.
Hierarchical cluster analysis of five inflammatory/immune markers (NLR, ESR, CRP, C3, C4) identified three distinct clinical phenotypes among 184 CTD-PAH patients.

Cluster 1 (vasculopathic phenotype, n=92) had normal-range inflammatory markers (low ESR/CRP, higher C3/C4) but the poorest hemodynamic profile, including elevated PVR/mPAP and reduced CI and TAPSE/PASP.

Cluster 2 (vasculitic phenotype, n=63) showed elevated ESR and IgG with decreased complement C3 and C4, but more favorable hemodynamics (lower PVR/mPAP, higher CI and TAPSE/PASP) than the other clusters.

Cluster 3 (mixed phenotype, n=29) had the highest NLR, CRP, and ESR levels combined with the worst hemodynamic parameters (higher PVR, lower CI), representing combined vasculopathic and vasculitic features.

Patients with the vasculitic phenotype achieved treat-to-target (low-risk) status within one year significantly more often (71.4%) than those with vasculopathic (39.1%) or mixed (37.9%) phenotypes, remaining significant after adjustment for PAH and CTD therapy.
The vasculitic phenotype had significantly higher survival than the vasculopathic and mixed phenotypes, while the mixed phenotype had the lowest survival among the three.

The vasculitic phenotype (Cluster 2) had significantly higher positivity rates for anti-Ro52, anti-Ro60, anti-U1-snRNP, anti-dsDNA, and anti-Sm antibodies compared to the other clusters, and was predominantly composed of SLE-PAH patients (63.5%).

CTD subtype distribution varied by cluster: Cluster 2 (vasculitic) had a significantly higher proportion of SLE and lower proportion of SSc and UCTD than Clusters 1 and 3, while mixed phenotype (Cluster 3) was particularly common in SSc-PAH and MCTD-PAH.

A higher proportion of patients in the vasculitic and mixed phenotype clusters received medium-to-high dose glucocorticoids (≥0.5 mg/kg/day prednisone equivalent) than in the vasculopathic cluster, with no significant difference in immunosuppressant use across clusters.

Overall cohort outcomes: over a median follow-up of 28 months, 22 of 184 patients (20.0%) died and 52 (28.3%) experienced clinical worsening (all-cause mortality, transplant, PAH-related hospitalization, unsatisfactory clinical response, or need for parenteral prostacyclin analogues).
FTL mRNA and protein levels were reduced in TAO orbital adipose tissue compared to healthy controls, consistent with abnormal ferroptosis activation.
NQO1 mRNA and protein were downregulated in TAO orbital adipose tissue, supporting reduced antioxidant/ferroptosis-inhibitory capacity.
MGST1 mRNA and protein levels were reduced in TAO orbital adipose tissue, consistent with loss of a lipid-peroxidation-protective, ferroptosis-inhibitory factor.
Ceruloplasmin (CP1) mRNA and protein were downregulated in TAO orbital adipose tissue, implicating reduced antioxidant iron-efflux capacity.
LGMN (Legumain) mRNA and protein were upregulated in TAO orbital adipose tissue, consistent with its role as a ferroptosis-driver gene.
AQP3 mRNA was upregulated in TAO orbital adipose tissue, but protein-level increase did not reach statistical significance.
Total SMAD2/3 protein was decreased while phosphorylated SMAD2/3 (P-SMAD2/3) was increased in TAO orbital adipose tissue, indicating activation of the TGF-β/Smad2/3 pathway.
TGF-β mRNA expression was elevated in TAO orbital adipose tissue compared to healthy controls.

Single-cell RNA-seq of orbital tissue identified 18 cell types across 16,364 cells, with neutrophils and a venous endothelial cell subset (VEC2) present exclusively in TAO patients, indicating inflammatory cell infiltration during disease progression.
The proportion of macrophages was increased in TAO disease-group orbital tissue relative to healthy controls in single-cell data.
AUCell scoring of seven ferroptosis-related genes across all annotated cell types showed macrophages and fibroblasts had the strongest association with ferroptosis signal activation.

The macrophage C2 subgroup, characterized by high CD163 and CCL18 expression, showed significantly higher ferroptosis activation signals than the other three macrophage subgroups (C1, C3, C4) and was enriched for cell death and oxidative stress pathways.
CCL18 expression correlated with multiple ferroptosis-related genes, supporting a link between CCL18-high macrophage C2 cells and ferroptosis signaling in TAO.

Cell-cell communication analysis (CellphoneDB) showed increased TNF signaling interactions between macrophage C2 and other orbital cell types during TAO progression, potentially linked to ferroptosis activation.
Cell-cell communication analysis showed downregulated TGF-β pathway interactions between macrophage C2 and other cells during TAO progression, linked to loss of ferroptosis suppression.

Protein-protein interaction network analysis of macrophage C2 marker genes revealed tight interactions with JUN, FOS, HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, and HSPA8, suggesting these as candidate genes for intervening in TAO progression.
Tissue immunofluorescence confirmed higher infiltration of CD163+ macrophages in orbital adipose tissue of TAO patients compared to normal controls.
In vitro, polarized CD163+ macrophages showed significantly elevated TGF-β mRNA expression compared to M0 macrophages.

Transwell co-culture of orbital fibroblasts with CD163+ macrophages for 48h reduced FTL, NQO1, and MGST1 (transcription and translation), decreased LGMN transcription but increased LGMN translation, and reduced SMAD2/3 protein, indicating macrophage-driven ferroptosis-related gene changes via TGF-β/Smad2/3 signaling.

Direct TGF-β1 (5 ng/mL, 24-48h) treatment of orbital fibroblasts decreased most ferroptosis-inhibitory gene mRNA and protein (FTL, NQO1, MGST1) while increasing TMSB4X and LGMN mRNA and LGMN/AQP3 protein, and shifted SMAD2/3 toward its phosphorylated form, replicating the pattern seen in TAO tissue.
Restart random-walk network analysis using macrophage C2 marker genes as seeds identified CD163 and LGMN as hub genes, consistent with prior single-cell and validation findings.
Drug-gene interaction analysis via DGIdb identified HSP90AA1, HSP90AB1, and CSF1R among the top hub genes as interacting with multiple drugs, proposing them as potential therapeutic targets for TAO.

Myosin Va expression was significantly reduced in the colon longitudinal muscle myenteric plexus of chronic restraint stress-induced IBS-D rats.

PA treatment significantly increased/restored Myosin Va expression in the IBS-D rat model.

Molecular docking analyses predicted strong binding affinity between patchouli alcohol and neurotransmitter-related targets identified via network pharmacology.

Chemogenetic activation of Gi-DREADD (hM4Di) with DCZ in enteric neurons significantly decreased fecal quantity, mass, and water content compared with saline and AAV-Cre control groups.
DCZ-activated Gi-DREADD mice showed prolonged gastrointestinal transit time (GITT) and colonic bead expulsion time compared with control groups.

Ex vivo isometric muscle tension recordings showed dose-dependent decreases in frequency and amplitude of colonic contractions with 10 and 20 nmol/L DCZ in Gi-DREADD-transduced colonic tissue compared with control groups.

Immunostaining showed that mCherry-labeled AAV9-hM4Di transduced cells strongly co-localized with PGP9.5-positive enteric neurons in the myenteric plexus, confirming efficient and neuron-specific viral transfection.

No significant difference was found in the percentage of transduced neurons positive for nNOS versus ChAT, indicating unbiased viral transfection across excitatory and inhibitory enteric neuron subtypes.

ACh-induced calcium transients (ΔF/F0) in isolated enteric neurons were markedly suppressed in Gi-DREADD-treated colonic tissue compared with saline, saline+DCZ, and AAV-Cre+DCZ groups.

After cessation of DCZ administration (recovery period), fecal quantity, mass, and water content in Gi-DREADD-treated mice returned to pre-DCZ baseline levels, demonstrating reversibility of the chemogenetically induced constipation phenotype.

Reserpine injection markedly increased immobility time in the forced swim test compared to controls, indicating depressive-like behavior.

Reserpine-injected rats exhibited histopathological damage in DRG spinal cord tissue including chromatolysis, shrunken pyknotic neurons, mononuclear/macrophage infiltrates, and loss of satellite ganglionic cells, which was ameliorated by semaglutide (especially intermediate and high doses).
The first MFS patient carried a missense FBN1 mutation in exon 28 (c.C3442G, p.P1148A), confirmed by Sanger sequencing and predicted deleterious by structural modeling.
The second MFS patient carried a stop-gain FBN1 mutation in exon 37 (c.C4567T, p.R1523X), confirmed by Sanger sequencing and predicted deleterious by structural modeling.

MFS-iECs showed a significantly increased percentage of SA-β-gal positive (senescent) cells compared with wild-type iECs.
MFS-iECs exhibited upregulation of the senescence markers p53 and p21 at both protein and mRNA levels compared with wild-type iECs.

SB-431542 treatment reduced the percentage of SA-β-gal positive senescent cells in MFS-iECs, demonstrating reversal of the endothelial senescence phenotype.

Disruptions in the gastrointestinal microbiome in ME/CFS are associated with an increase in pro-inflammatory species and a reduction in anti-inflammatory species.

Cytokines such as CCL11 may damage white-matter microglia responsible for neural pruning, potentially reducing new nerve cell generation, affecting memory, and contributing to neurological symptoms of long COVID/ME/CFS.

Resting-state qEEG analysis of the cortical autonomic network in ME/CFS patients versus healthy controls showed evidence of reduced higher-order homeostatic regulation and adaptability of autonomic nervous system function.

Individuals with severe ME/CFS showed distinctive saliva biomarkers of fatigue compared to controls.

NICE's 2021 guideline concluded that CBT and GET do not lead to improvement or recovery in ME/CFS, and GET is harmful and should not be offered.

The PACE trial's own primary outcome scores (fatigue and physical functioning) at the end of treatment and at 6-month follow-up showed patients remained ill enough to qualify for re-entry into the same trial, indicating no meaningful improvement from CBT/GET.

Analysis of PACE and FINE trial individual participant data revealed a significant ceiling effect in the Chalder Fatigue Scale, with 65-75% of participants scoring maximum on the bimodal scale at baseline, undermining the scale's ability to detect deterioration.

Reanalysis of objective outcomes from three CBT/GET trials showed discrepancies between subjective improvement and objective measures: subjective physical functioning improved while objective 6-minute walk test or CPET measures showed no improvement or deterioration.
Multiple patient surveys report high rates of symptom worsening (harm) following GET, including a 60% harm rate in an Action for ME survey and 81.1% worsening in the Oxford Brookes University survey.

The MAGENTA trial in children found no evidence GET was more effective than activity management, and accelerometer data showed GET participants had a reduction in moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, indicating a negative effect.

Post-exertional malaise (PEM), an abnormally delayed and disproportionate worsening of symptoms after exertion, is the defining characteristic of ME/CFS, historically documented since the 1955 Royal Free Hospital outbreak, but was removed as a mandatory diagnostic criterion by the 1991 Oxford and 1994 Fukuda (CDC) criteria, both of which were co-authored by proponents of the cognitive-behavioural model.

Handgrip strength (HGS) is impaired in ME/CFS and provides objective evidence for PEM and abnormally delayed muscular recovery, distinguishing ME/CFS patients from cancer-related fatigue patients and healthy controls.

The PACE trial's 6-minute walk test differences between treatment groups (8.17m at end of treatment, 16.70m at follow-up) were trivial compared to the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 156-167m established in a related condition (fibromyalgia), suggesting no real improvement.

A systematic review by Ahmed et al. concluded that CBT and GET are not supported as effective treatments for ME/CFS due to methodological flaws and biases, including in the PACE trial, which scored high risk of bias.

The PACE trial's GET therapist manual explicitly states that planned physical activity, not symptoms, determines what participants are asked to do, and that GET involves gradual, planned, incremental increases in exercise, confirming NICE's characterization of GET as fixed-increment therapy contrary to White et al.'s claims.
CBT for ME/CFS as delivered in the PACE trial also incorporates fixed, planned incremental increases in activity irrespective of symptoms, not merely symptom management, per PACE trial CBT manuals.

PACE trial quality-of-life (EQ-5D) scores after CBT/GET treatment were similar to or worse than scores for people with five or more chronic health conditions, cerebral thrombosis, and worse than angina, rheumatoid arthritis, MS, lung cancer, stroke, or ischaemic heart disease.
An extensive literature review found that CBT and GET have a negative rather than positive effect on employment and illness/disability benefit status in ME/CFS patients.
Approximately 51% of long COVID patients meet ME/CFS diagnostic criteria, and ME/CFS and long COVID share many symptoms and underlying biological abnormalities across multiple laboratories.

The amended Cochrane exercise review concluded that the impact of exercise therapy on serious adverse reactions in ME/CFS is uncertain because certainty of evidence is very low and most studies did not report on safety.

The global prevalence of Long COVID is currently estimated at approximately 6%.
Long COVID prevalence is higher among individuals of female gender, certain racial and ethnic groups, and those living in nonurban areas, though anyone can develop it after SARS-CoV-2 infection.

The most common Long COVID symptom clusters include exaggerated fatigue, postexertional malaise (PEM)/postexertional symptom exacerbation (PESE), cognitive impairment (brain fog), dysautonomia, pain/myalgias, and smell/taste alterations.
There is currently no single laboratory finding that definitively confirms or rules out a diagnosis of Long COVID, and a prior positive COVID-19 test is not required for diagnosis.
Physical activity recommendations must be carefully tailored to the patient's current tolerance because overly intense activity can trigger PEM/PESE and worsen muscle damage.

There are limited data to guide medication management specifically for Long COVID, so treatment generally follows standard practice with attention to shared decision-making and avoiding medications that improve one symptom while worsening others (eg, PEM/PESE).
Long COVID often manifests as an 'invisible disability' with fluctuating, multi-domain symptoms and is recognized as a potential disability under the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The Attention Network Test has been shown to have clinical value for assessing cognitive function in patients with CFS.
Some researchers have proposed using continuous attention assessment as a reliable biomarker for diagnosing CFS.

Prior fMRI studies found brain functional or metabolic abnormalities in the prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, parieto-occipital cortex, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and precuneus in patients with CFS, which may underlie fatigue and cognitive impairment.

In EDS, the dermal extracellular matrix contains an abnormal amount of denatured or fragmented collagen, severely impairing formation of a stable, properly organized collagen structure.

The patient's wound healing appeared inhibited while she was concurrently taking three psychotropic medications (Trittico, Pramolan, Pregabalin), with clear improvement observed after these medications were discontinued in the ICU.

Electron microscopy comparison showed that collagen fibers were circular and regularly arranged in a control patient sample, whereas in an EDS patient sample the fibers were irregularly arranged, thinner, and angled.

Laser speckle contrast analysis (LASCA) with a near-infrared laser was used throughout hospitalization to visualize microperfusion and distinguish wound areas that had re-opened from those that had healed.

A multi-stage burn treatment protocol combining acellular dermal matrix grafting, autologous in vitro cultured keratinocytes/fibroblasts suspended in platelet-rich plasma, collagen injections, and MEEK-technique split-thickness skin grafting successfully healed a 60% TBSA II/III degree burn in an EDS patient, who was discharged home after 182 days.

A cited case (Bourji et al.) reported sulfonamide-induced leukocytoclastic vasculitis confined to the skin in a patient with EDS, underscoring the need for careful diagnostic workup of drug reactions in this population.
The EDS patient had comorbid depression (since 2020) and hypothyroidism secondary to Hashimoto's disease alongside her connective tissue disorder and burn injury.
EDS involves defective collagen synthesis and processing due to gene alterations, which is hypothesized to underlie connective tissue and vascular fragility contributing to pancreatic damage.
Multiple EDS subtypes have been linked to mutations in genes controlling collagen cross-linking, including TNXB and AEBP1, resulting in unstable collagen fibrils.
The patient, diagnosed with EDS, presented with acute-on-chronic pancreatitis following a complicated history of gallstone pancreatitis, necrotizing pancreatitis, and pseudocyst formation.
The patient's C-reactive protein rose from 16.6 g/dL to 40.8 g/dL on admission, indicating a new inflammatory process during the acute-on-chronic pancreatitis episode.

Despite meeting clinical and imaging criteria for acute pancreatitis, the patient's lipase level was normal, consistent with reports that chronic or acute-on-chronic pancreatitis patients often lack significant lipase/amylase elevation due to pancreatic atrophy.

Treatment with high-volume IV fluids, pain management, and gradual dietary reintroduction to a low-fat diet resulted in pain control and symptomatic improvement, with continued improvement noted on a pancreatitis-friendly diet after discharge.

The authors hypothesize that EDS-related connective tissue fragility causes pancreatic capillary vessel leaks/damage, driving a chronic inflammatory state that leads to pancreatic atrophy, fibrosis, and recurrent/chronic pancreatitis without identifiable classic triggers.

This case closely mirrors a previously published case report of EDS-associated chronic pancreatitis in a female patient of similar age, both presenting with recurrent severe abdominal pain, no alcohol/drug use disorder, no identifiable trigger medications, normal calcium/triglycerides, and imaging showing atrophic, fibrotic pancreas with ductal dilation.

Genetic risk factors for chronic pancreatitis, unrelated to this patient's confirmed status, include mutations in PRSS1, CFTR, SPINK1, and chymotrypsin C, which act as modifier genes increasing susceptibility.
In silico variant effect prediction classified both the G189S and G906R COL3A1 glycine substitutions as deleterious, supporting their causality in vEDS.
The G189S variant is absent from gnomAD and ClinVar, but the related G189R substitution at the same codon (rs587779507) has been previously reported in dbSNP and ClinVar.
Both COL3A1 mutant fibroblast lines (G189S and G906R) showed reduced cell proliferation compared with wild-type fibroblasts.
Both COL3A1 mutant fibroblast lines showed increased apoptosis (Annexin V/PI positivity) compared to wild-type cells.
COL3A1+/G189S cells displayed enlarged, irregular 'pancake'-shaped morphology and increased p21 mRNA levels, consistent with induction of cellular senescence.

Both mutant lines showed increased intracellular collagen III, with reduced extracellular collagen III in G189S but similar extracellular levels in G906R, indicating a shift toward intracellular retention.
Immunostaining confirmed collagen III retention in the ER (increased colocalization with PDI) and ER enlargement in mutant cells, more pronounced in G906R than G189S.
Secreted collagen III from both mutant lines was digested more rapidly by trypsin than wild-type, showing that mutant misfolded collagen III is secreted extracellularly.
Decellularized matrix from mutant fibroblasts showed a less developed, punctate collagen III network with apparently fewer fibrils compared with wild-type.
COL3A1 mutant cells showed increased levels of the ER chaperone BIP, with more prominent activation of the IRE1 arm of the UPR, particularly in COL3A1+/G906R.
Both mutations caused EIF2α phosphorylation, but only COL3A1+/G906R showed a significant increase in ATF4 levels (a trend was seen in G189S), indicating allele-specific PERK arm activation.
COL3A1 mutations did not activate the ATF6 arm of the UPR, indicating that not all three canonical UPR arms are engaged by these mutations.
CHOP levels were increased in COL3A1+/G906R cells but not COL3A1+/G189S cells, supporting ER-stress-associated apoptosis specific to the C-terminal mutation.
COL3A1 mutant cells showed activation of proteasomal degradation (increased poly-ubiquitinated proteins) but no change in autophagy (LC3I to LC3II conversion or autophagic flux).
5 mM PBA for 24 hours reduced BIP protein levels in COL3A1+/G189S cells but not in COL3A1+/G906R cells, showing allele-specific efficacy of the chemical chaperone.
500 µM TUDCA also reduced BIP protein levels in COL3A1+/G189S cells, supporting a shared chemical-chaperone effect on protein folding.

Carbamazepine did not alter BIP protein levels or the phospho-eIF2α:total eIF2α ratio in vEDS fibroblasts, indicating no reduction of ER stress via protein degradation promotion, unlike its reported effect in COL10A1 mutations.

Dose-response testing showed PBA reduced BIP and PERK pathway markers across all tested concentrations in COL3A1+/G189S cells, whereas only lower PBA concentrations reduced ER stress markers in COL3A1+/G906R cells.
5 mM PBA significantly reduced spliced XBP1 levels, with a trend toward lower CHOP mRNA, in COL3A1+/G189S cells, suggesting higher efficacy of 5 mM versus 500 µM PBA.
500 µM PBA, despite improving BIP and EIF2α phosphorylation, had no effect on CHOP or spliced XBP1 levels in COL3A1+/G906R cells.

PBA reduced intracellular collagen III retention in COL3A1+/G189S cells at 24 hours, but only a longer 72-hour PBA incubation reduced intracellular collagen III in COL3A1+/G906R cells, indicating treatment duration is an important parameter for the C-terminal mutation.

PBA had genotype-dependent effects on COL3A1 mRNA: 24-hour 500 µM PBA increased COL3A1 mRNA in G906R cells (but not at 72 hours), while PBA reduced COL3A1 mRNA in G189S cells, possibly reflecting PBA's HDAC-inhibitor activity.

Combined treatment of 500 µM PBA with 20 µM CBZ for 24 hours did not reduce intracellular collagen III levels in COL3A1+/G906R cells, indicating no added benefit of combining folding and degradation-targeting drugs.

PBA did not significantly increase the amount of collagen III secreted into conditioned media over 24 hours, but secreted collagen III was more resistant to trypsin digestion after PBA treatment, indicating improved folding quality rather than increased quantity.
PBA treatment increased collagen III incorporation into the deposited extracellular matrix, producing a better-formed collagen network in mutant fibroblasts.
PBA treatment reduced apoptosis levels in COL3A1 mutant patient fibroblasts as measured by Annexin V/PI FACS.

The AEBP1 gene encodes two protein isoforms, AEBP1 and ACLP, which have distinct but often conflated roles in inflammation, fibrosis, and connective tissue biology.

Overexpressing PRL2 in PRL2-KO BMMCs attenuated the increased degranulation rate and cytokine expression seen in KO cells, restoring a phenotype closer to WT.
Proteomic analysis of activated BMMCs identified the phospholipase D signaling pathway as the most enriched pathway among proteins differentially expressed in PRL2-KO versus WT BMMCs.
PRL2-KO BMMCs exhibited increased and sustained cytosolic calcium influx after antigen stimulation compared with WT BMMCs, confirmed by both confocal microscopy and flow cytometry.
PRL2-KO BMMCs displayed earlier detection of the first exteriorized granule and a shortened lag time between calcium rise and granule exteriorization compared with WT BMMCs.
3D analysis showed that exteriorized granule structures released from PRL2-KO BMMCs were larger and had more heterogeneous (less spherical) shapes than those from WT BMMCs.
Co-immunoprecipitation showed increased VAMP-8/SNAP-23 SNARE complex formation upon antigen stimulation in PRL2-KO mast cells compared to the resting state.
Phosphorylation of PI3K and PLCγ1 was increased in PRL2-KO BMMCs following IgE/DNP-BSA stimulation compared with WT BMMCs, implicating the PI3K/PLCγ1 axis in PRL2's inhibitory role.

Pre-treatment of WT and PRL2-KO BMMCs with wortmannin (PI3K inhibitor) reduced PI3K/PLCγ1 phosphorylation, calcium influx, and β-hexosaminidase release, confirming the PI3K/PLCγ1 axis mediates the enhanced activation in PRL2 deficiency.
PRL2 protein was decreased in BMMCs following IgE-mediated stimulation and in mast cells of IgE-treated mouse lung tissue, consistent with reported inflammation-induced PRL2 degradation.
Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) pre-treatment blocked PRL2 protein degradation in IgE-stimulated BMMCs in a dose-dependent manner.

Oral HCQ (80 mg/kg/d for 7 days) alleviated passive systemic anaphylaxis severity in WT mice, reducing hypothermia, pulmonary perivascular edema, and serum MCPT-1, LTC4, PGD2, and histamine, while reversing PRL2 degradation in lung tissue.
PRL2 knockout did not affect the in vitro proliferation/differentiation of bone marrow-derived mast cells; WT and KO BMMCs reached comparable maturity and purity.

Peripheral blood proportions of lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils were comparable between WT and PRL2 CKO mice, suggesting the PSA phenotype is not due to altered baseline myeloid/immune cell composition.
Plasma IL-6 increased up to 85-fold above baseline during the mast cell activation event that followed mRNA-1273 booster vaccination.
IL-1 receptor antagonist rose 54-fold above baseline during the post-vaccination MCA event, remaining elevated longer than most other cytokines.
IL-10 concentrations rose 54-fold above baseline during the post-vaccination MCA event.
IL-5 concentrations increased approximately 5-fold above baseline during the post-vaccination MCA event.
IL-11 concentrations rose 6.1-fold above baseline during the post-vaccination MCA event.
The Th1-associated chemokine CXCL10 showed the largest and most persistent increase, peaking at 19-fold above baseline and remaining ≥4-fold elevated for 48 hours.
GM-CSF concentrations increased up to 6.4-fold above baseline during the post-vaccination MCA event.
CCL2 (MCP-1) showed a modest but statistically significant elevation (up to 3.1-fold) at early time points of the post-vaccination MCA event.
Th1-biased cytokines IFN-α, IFN-γ and TNF-α changed less than 4-fold and were not statistically significant during the post-vaccination MCA event, contrasting with the strong Th2 cytokine response.
Serum tryptase peaked concurrently with DAO and IL-6 during both the vaccination-triggered and infection-triggered MCA events, confirming mast cell activation.

Plasma histamine reached life-threatening concentrations of 15-18 ng/ml at 5-8 hours post-admission during the post-vaccination MCA event, then rapidly declined by 14-18 hours coinciding with symptom improvement.

DAO antigen concentrations were moderately elevated during the MCA event and correlated 99% with DAO activity, indicating that DAO enzymatic function was not compromised despite prior reports of DAO inactivation during severe MCA in other mastocytosis patients.

Plasma arginine concentrations decreased significantly at all seven measured time points during the post-vaccination MCA event, consistent with endothelial cell distress and nitric oxide pathway consumption.
Plasma lysine was significantly reduced at 5, 8 and 14 hours after admission during the post-vaccination MCA event.
Ornithine, a precursor of citrulline, was significantly reduced 8 and 14 hours after admission during the post-vaccination MCA event.

Citrulline-based functional small bowel length showed a peak 4.3-fold (77%) reduction during the first 14 hours of the post-vaccination MCA event, indicating significant small bowel enterocyte dysfunction that recovered rapidly with clinical improvement.

Plasma LPC lipid species were markedly reduced (5.6-8.1 fold, up to 12.3-fold for LPC 18:2) during the post-vaccination MCA event, with 87% of baseline LPC consumed by 18 hours, likely via autotaxin-mediated conversion to lysophosphatidic acid.
Plasma LPE lipid species decreased 2.9-4.5 fold (up to 7.7-fold for LPE 18:2) during the post-vaccination MCA event, paralleling LPC degradation.
Platelet count dropped 26% from 186 G/L at admission to 137 G/L after 14 hours during the post-vaccination MCA event.

The anti-IL-6 receptor antibody tocilizumab (80mg) was administered approximately 3-6 hours after admission in both MCA events, coinciding with rapid clinical improvement and normalization of fever, though causality could not be established.
The patient's indolent systemic mastocytosis was driven by the KIT D816V mutation, the underlying clonal driver of the mast cell disorder in which both MCA events occurred.

A second, less severe MCA event occurred 442 days later, following a PCR-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.4/BA.5 infection, again with highly elevated IL-6 and tryptase, supporting infection as the trigger.

In vitro challenge of HMC1.1 and LAD2 mast cell lines with the BNT162b2 and mRNA-1273 vaccines produced only a non-significant, dose-dependent trend toward degranulation, and interpretation was confounded because both vaccines also decreased mast cell viability in a dose-dependent manner.

Arginine-to-ADMA and arginine-to-SDMA ratios decreased 2.3-2.4 fold at 5 and 8 hours post-admission during the post-vaccination MCA event, consistent with endothelial cell distress, before recovering by 22 hours.
tIK transgenic mice showed significantly reduced scratching behavior by day 14 compared to DNCB-treated BALB/c controls.
tIK transgenic mice exhibited a notable reduction in ear thickness compared to DNCB-treated BALB/c controls.
DNCB caused weight loss in both BALB/c and tIK Tg mice, but tIK Tg mice exhibited less weight reduction, suggesting protection against DNCB-induced physical stress.
tIK Tg mice displayed thinner epidermis with a 12 μm reduction in ear and 19 μm reduction in dorsal skin compared to DNCB-treated BALB/c mice.
Mast cell numbers were reduced by over 50% in both ear and dorsal skin of tIK Tg mice, along with significantly lower degranulation, compared to DNCB-treated BALB/c mice.
DNCB-treated BALB/c mice showed a threefold increase in serum IgE levels compared to untreated controls.
tIK Tg mice showed significantly lower serum IgE than DNCB-treated BALB/c mice, suggesting tIK modulates IgE production.
DNCB significantly upregulated TSLP mRNA in ear tissue, while tIK Tg mice showed a marked reduction in TSLP expression.
DNCB significantly upregulated c-Kit mRNA in ear tissue, while tIK Tg mice showed a marked reduction.
DNCB significantly upregulated GATA1 mRNA in ear tissue, while tIK Tg mice showed a marked reduction.
DNCB significantly upregulated GATA2 mRNA in ear tissue, while tIK Tg mice showed a marked reduction.
DNCB significantly upregulated MCCPA mRNA in ear tissue, while tIK Tg mice showed a marked reduction.
DNCB significantly upregulated MCP5 mRNA in ear tissue, while tIK Tg mice showed a marked reduction.
TSLP protein was markedly upregulated by DNCB treatment, but tIK Tg mice exhibited lower TSLP protein levels than DNCB-treated BALB/c mice, as shown by western blot.
