In tIK Tg mice, IL-4+ (Th2) CD4+ T cell frequency in draining lymph nodes was significantly decreased compared to DNCB-treated BALB/c mice, while the decrease in IL-17+ (Th17) cells was not statistically significant.
DNCB exposure increased Th1 (IFN-γ+), Th2 (IL-4+), and Th17 (IL-17+) CD4+ T cell populations in draining lymph nodes and spleen of BALB/c mice, while Treg (Foxp3+) frequencies were unchanged.
Treg (Foxp3+) cell frequencies remained unchanged with DNCB treatment and were not significantly affected by tIK overexpression.

DNCB-treated BALB/c mice showed significantly elevated Th1 (IFN-γ, TNF-α), Th2 (IL-4, IL-6, IL-13), and Th17 (IL-17) cytokine mRNA in ear skin lesions, while tIK Tg mice showed reduced expression of all these cytokines.
In an IgE-mediated passive systemic anaphylaxis model, tIK Tg mice exhibited significantly less hypothermia following antigen challenge compared to BALB/c controls.

In the passive systemic anaphylaxis model, DNCB-treated BALB/c mice had significantly higher serum mMCP-1 (80.3 ng/ml) than tIK Tg mice (49.9 ng/ml), indicating reduced mast cell degranulation with tIK overexpression.
The authors note, citing prior work, that tIK inhibits STAT3 signaling, a pathway essential for Th17 differentiation, consistent with the observed reduction in Th17 responses.
The authors cite prior work showing tIK suppresses macrophage activation and reduces pro-inflammatory cytokine release, contributing to its broader anti-inflammatory effects.
Mast cell lineage numbers are increased in the lungs during COVID-19, contributing to inflammation via release of preformed and de novo synthesized mediators.
The authors previously showed that serum carboxypeptidase A3 (CPA3) predicts COVID-19 severity.
Combining serum levels of total tryptase, CPA3, chymase, and PGD2 improved the predictive ability for mast cell activation and severe COVID-19 outcomes compared to using CPA3 alone.

The authors propose a serum mast cell activation profile (combining tryptase, CPA3, chymase, and PGD2) as a potential biomarker for SARS-CoV-2 infection with implications for targeted therapy development.
HDM-sensitised subjects showed the highest levels of total and HDM/Der p 1-specific serum IgE compared with non-HDM atopic and healthy controls.
T-cell proliferative responses to synthetic peptide D were significantly higher and more frequent in HDM-sensitised subjects than in the combined non-HDM-sensitised group.
T-cell responses to peptide B showed only a non-significant trend towards being higher in HDM-sensitised subjects compared with non-HDM sensitised controls.
Fine mapping in HLA-DR4 transgenic mouse splenocytes localised the minimal naturally processed T-cell epitope within peptide D to the 7-mer core sequence IGIKDLD.

Analogues D111B and D121B, unlike the parent peptide D or intact Der p 1, activated a Der p 1-specific T-cell hybridoma when presented by fixed (paraformaldehyde-treated) antigen presenting cells, showing they function as antigen-processing-independent apitopes.

A single subcutaneous injection of peptide D121B bound directly to CD11c+ dendritic cells in vivo in HLA-DR4 mice, as shown by ex vivo activation of a Der p 1-specific T-cell hybridoma, confirming steady-state DC targeting required for tolerance induction.

Dose-escalation pretreatment with apitope D121B prior to Der p 1 peptide D immunisation suppressed splenocyte IFN-γ responses to D121B, D111B, peptide D and Der p 1 antigen compared with PBS-treated control mice.

In silico analysis predicted that D121B binds multiple HLA-DR alleles (DRB1*0301, *0404, *0701, *1401) as well as specific HLA-DQ molecules, broadening its potential population coverage as a tolerogen.

Peptide D121B, containing the minimal T-cell epitope, induced a positive T-cell proliferative response in PBMC from a Der p 1-sensitised, HLA-DR4 positive human subject, confirming relevance of the epitope in humans.
Some subjects across all three study groups (HDM-sensitised, atopic controls, and healthy controls) showed T-cell proliferative responses to Der p 1 despite lacking detectable Der p 1-specific IgE.

Unlike peptide D, no minimal T-cell epitope could be identified within peptide B, as none of its shorter overlapping 15-mer analogues activated splenocytes in the mouse recall assay, suggesting a cryptic epitope dependent on the full-length peptide.
Body weight did not change in either the vehicle control or RMFE-treated groups following oral administration, indicating no treatment-related stress.
CADESI-04 clinical dermatitis scores markedly increased after ovalbumin sensitization compared to pre-treatment baseline in both vehicle and RMFE groups.
By Day 42, CADESI-04 scores were lower in the RMFE-treated group than the vehicle control group, indicating clinical improvement in skin lesions.
Epidermal thickness was more than 3-fold greater at ovalbumin-induced atopic skin sites than at non-induced control sites.
RMFE treatment significantly reduced ovalbumin-induced epidermal thickening compared to vehicle control.
Infiltrating immune cells (neutrophils/monocytes) were approximately 9-fold higher at ovalbumin-modeled skin sites than at non-atopic control sites.
RMFE treatment significantly diminished immune cell infiltration at the AD lesion site relative to vehicle control.
CD4+ T cell expression in the epidermis and dermis was increased at ovalbumin-treated skin sites compared to non-treated control areas.
RMFE treatment decreased the number of CD4+ T cells in atopic skin lesions.
Activated (toluidine blue-stained) mast cell numbers in the dermis were significantly increased at ovalbumin-induced atopic sites compared to non-treated control sites.
Oral RMFE treatment reversed the ovalbumin-induced increase in activated dermal mast cells, restoring counts to near control levels.
Ovalbumin-specific IgE expression in the skin was significantly increased in both the vehicle and RMFE ovalbumin-exposed groups compared to the untreated control site.
RMFE treatment significantly reduced ovalbumin-specific IgE expression compared to vehicle control, despite similar mean levels reported.
Dorsal skin IL-4 protein levels were significantly higher in ovalbumin-exposed vehicle control dogs than in unexposed control skin.
RMFE treatment significantly decreased IL-4 protein levels in AD skin compared to vehicle control.
IL-4 mRNA levels in dorsal-ventral skin were increased in both ovalbumin-treated groups relative to control, with only a slight, non-conclusive decrease with RMFE treatment.
Th2-related cytokines IL-5, IL-13, IL-31 and the skin barrier gene filaggrin were significantly increased in ovalbumin-exposed vehicle skin compared to control skin.
Unexpectedly, IL-13 mRNA was further significantly increased, rather than decreased, upon RMFE treatment.
Pro-inflammatory cytokine (TNF-α, IL-1β) and chemokine (CCL17) mRNA transcripts were significantly increased in ovalbumin-exposed skin compared to control skin.
RMFE treatment significantly reduced TNF-α, IL-1β, and CCL17 mRNA transcript levels in AD skin compared to vehicle control, suggesting improved inflammatory response.
Over half of the 117 Parkinson's disease patients studied (55.56%) exhibited peripheral neuropathy (PD-PN) based on large and small fiber nerve function assessments.
Nearly a quarter (24.79%) of PD patients exhibited small fiber nerve damage on peripheral nerve function testing.
18.8% of PD patients exhibited large fiber nerve damage on peripheral nerve function testing.
11.97% of PD patients exhibited combined large and small fiber nerve damage.
Higher motor severity (UPDRS Part III) scores were an independent risk factor for peripheral neuropathy in PD patients.
Advanced age was an independent risk factor for peripheral neuropathy in PD patients.

After using Propensity Score Matching to control for confounders like age and disease duration, there was no significant difference in peripheral neuropathy incidence between PD patients treated with oral levodopa and those not treated.

Quantitative sensory testing in the pediatric cohort showed patterns consistent with Aδ- and C-fiber damage, including increased cold, warmth, and mechanical detection thresholds, higher thermal sensory limen, and allodynia.
Skin biopsy analysis showed low intraepidermal nerve fiber density in 9 of 18 tested children, indicating small fiber neuropathy.
The neuropathic pain phenotype substantially impacted physical quality of life and pain scales but did not significantly affect social life domains.
Two children carried heterozygous variants of unknown significance in SCN9A, a voltage-gated sodium channel gene implicated in small fiber neuropathy.
Three children carried heterozygous variants of unknown significance in SCN10A, a voltage-gated sodium channel gene implicated in small fiber neuropathy.
One patient carried a likely disease-associated variant in HUWE1, a gene outside the VGSC family, as a potential monogenic cause of the pain phenotype.
One patient carried a likely disease-associated variant in TRIO, a gene outside the VGSC family, as a potential monogenic cause of the pain phenotype.
One patient carried a likely disease-associated variant in PYGM, a gene outside the VGSC family, as a potential monogenic cause of the pain phenotype.
Two children with abnormal pain sensation carried heterozygous variants of unknown significance in SCN9A.
Three children with abnormal pain sensation carried heterozygous variants of unknown significance in SCN10A.
One patient carried a likely disease-associated variant in HUWE1, a gene not encoding a VGSC, implicated as an additional monogenic cause of pain symptoms.
One patient carried a likely disease-associated variant in TRIO, identified as an additional monogenic cause of pain symptoms outside VGSC genes.
One patient carried a likely disease-associated variant in PYGM, identified as an additional monogenic cause of pain symptoms outside VGSC genes.
The authors conclude that genetic testing in children with neuropathic pain should be comprehensive rather than restricted to VGSC genes, and supplemented by detailed clinical workup.

Adolescents with T1D who had abnormal autonomic function tests and more severe autonomic symptoms (COMPASS-31 ≥24) had significantly lower WHO-5 well-being scores than those with fewer autonomic symptoms.
Confirmed large or small fiber neuropathy in T1D adolescents was not associated with a difference in WHO-5 well-being scores compared to those without confirmed neuropathy.
Confirmed LFN/SFN in T1D adolescents showed no difference in WHO-5 well-being scores compared to healthy controls.
T1D adolescents with abnormal autonomic tests and COMPASS-31 ≥24 had significantly lower WHO-5 well-being scores than the remaining adolescents with T1D.
T1D adolescents with abnormal autonomic tests and COMPASS-31 ≥24 had significantly lower WHO-5 well-being scores than healthy control adolescents.
Female adolescents with T1D reported significantly lower WHO-5 well-being scores than male adolescents with T1D.
Just over a quarter of T1D adolescents (28%) scored below 50 on the WHO-5, a threshold indicating need for depression screening.
Ten percent of T1D adolescents (all female) scored ≤28 on the WHO-5, a level equivalent to depression.
Total DISABKIDS HRQoL score did not differ significantly between the different neuropathy subgroups.
The social inclusion subdomain of DISABKIDS was lower in adolescents with abnormal autonomic tests and more autonomic symptoms compared to those with fewer symptoms.
Confirmed LFN/SFN was not associated with lower DISABKIDS scores compared to remaining T1D adolescents.
Abnormal autonomic tests with COMPASS-31 ≥24 were not associated with lower DISABKIDS scores compared to remaining T1D adolescents.
Female adolescents with T1D had lower DISABKIDS HRQoL scores compared to males across all subdomains tested.
Ten percent of T1D adolescents scored below 50% of the maximum DISABKIDS total score, with most (5/6) being female and showing low physical limitation and social inclusion subscores.
Lower gastric motility index was positively associated with lower total HRQoL scores (DISABKIDS) in T1D adolescents, suggesting reduced GI motility correlates with reduced quality of life.
Lower uroflow acceleration, an early sign of detrusor/autonomic dysfunction, was positively associated with lower total HRQoL scores (DISABKIDS) in T1D adolescents.
No associations were found between other neurological/autonomic test results (nerve conduction velocity, IENFD, QSART, CARTs, GI transit times) and questionnaire-based well-being/HRQoL measures.
Patchouli alcohol improved gastrointestinal motor function and effectively inhibited diarrhea and increased visceral sensitivity in an IBS-D rat model.
Patchouli alcohol treatment increased BMPRII-expressing neuronal subsets in the intestinal myenteric plexus of IBS-D rats.
Patchouli alcohol increased the phosphorylation level of BMP-SMAD pathway-related proteins in intestinal neurons of IBS-D rats.
IBS-D functional bowel disease is characterized by abnormal colonic contraction, as confirmed in this study.
The genetic correlation between fibromyalgia and irritable bowel syndrome was modest (rg=+0.38), arguing against a robust shared genetic factor underlying these two functional somatic disorders.
Fibromyalgia showed a considerably stronger genetic correlation with major depression (+0.54) than with anxiety disorder (+0.28), though CIs overlapped.
The genetic correlations of IBS with major depression and with anxiety disorder were identical (+0.62 each).
Major depression and anxiety disorder showed a very high genetic correlation of +0.91, supporting a shared pool of genetic risk variants for internalizing psychiatric disorders.
IBS had the lowest total heritability (35%, mostly disorder-specific) among the four disorders studied and the highest unique-environmental contribution (72%).
Fibromyalgia heritability was estimated at 43% (95% CI 39-47%), consistent with prior twin studies of FM and chronic widespread pain.
A latent common factor underlying MD, AD, FM, and IBS was moderately heritable (a2=0.49), with a small shared-environment contribution (c2=0.04) and larger unique-environment contribution (e2=0.47).

Common factor loadings were roughly twice as strong for the internalizing psychiatric disorders (MD, AD: +0.82 to +0.84) as for the functional somatic disorders (FM, IBS: +0.36 to +0.41), suggesting the common factor largely reflects IPD liability.

For fibromyalgia and IBS, only about 20% (18-19%) of genetic risk derived from the common factor shared with internalizing psychiatric disorders, with 81-82% of genetic variance being disorder-specific.

IBS showed a negative shared-environment variance estimate, consistent with non-additive genetic variance or gene-by-environment interaction, since the DZ twin correlation was less than half the MZ correlation.
Lifetime prevalences in intact families were approximately 20% for MD, 19% for AD, 6% for IBS, and 1% for FM, with somewhat higher rates in half-sibling samples.

Within-person cross-disorder phenotypic correlation between MD and AD was around +0.69 across all relative groups, substantially higher than other cross-disorder correlations (+0.25 to +0.35), indicating strong comorbidity.

Shared environmental effects were evidenced by higher correlations in half-siblings reared together compared to half-siblings reared apart for MD, AD, and FM, but this pattern was not clearly seen for IBS.

A prior Swedish twin study (Kato et al., 2009) identified a two-factor common pathway model with an affective factor shared between IPDs and FSDs (more genetic) and a second factor specific to FSDs (more environmental); the current study's findings, with only 4 variables, are broadly congruent with that two-factor structure.
The ratio of enteric glial cells to neurons differs markedly between species, being approximately 7:1 in humans compared to about 1:1 in mice.
The human enteric nervous system contains far more neurons (168 million) than the mouse ENS (2.5 million), reflecting substantial interspecies differences in ENS size and complexity.
Human ENS expression and functional influence of the H3 histamine receptor on GI motility is lower than in mice, indicating species-specific differences in histaminergic modulation of gut motility.

Supernatants from colonic biopsy specimens of IBS patients activated human enteric neurons in voltage-dye recordings, with distinct response patterns between IBS-D and IBS-C subtypes, suggesting subtype-specific soluble mediators driving ENS dysfunction.

Dysregulation of mast cell-enteric nervous system interactions, including release of histamine, tryptase and cytokines, is implicated in IBS, IBD and functional dyspepsia via effects on neuronal signaling.

Myenteric S neurons from colon specimens of chemotherapy-treated colorectal cancer patients were hyperexcitable, showing lower rheobase and threshold for action potential generation compared to neurons from non-treated patients.

In murine and human enteric glial cells, ATP activation of a p38-dependent MAPK pathway via P2X2 receptors triggers cytokine release and a gliosis phenotype, and the drug Ambroxol acts as a P2X2 antagonist that prevents ATP-induced enteric gliosis and abrogates gliosis in human intestinal organotypic culture exposed to surgical trauma.
Studies in human enteric glial cell cultures implicated macrophage colony-stimulating factor in glial-immune communication contributing to visceral hypersensitivity in human Crohn's disease.

Human serosal visceral nociceptor mechanosensitivity was attenuated by the TRPV4 antagonist HC067047 or the 5-HT4 agonist tecaserod, both used therapeutically for IBS pain, supporting the use of this in vitro model for analgesic drug testing.
Loss-of-function mutations in Piezo2 channels result in GI symptoms in patients, a phenotype partially recapitulated by Piezo2 deletion in DRG neurons in animal models.

In duodenal biopsies from Parkinson's disease patients, submucosal enteric neuronal calcium responses, mitochondrial membrane potential, and neuron/ganglia numbers did not differ significantly from controls, suggesting GI symptoms in PD may instead stem from myenteric rather than submucosal dysfunction.

A single-cell transcriptomic atlas of the human and mouse ENS identified diverse neuronal (>20 subtypes) and glial (3-7 subtypes) populations, with conserved gene expression patterns across species for neurotransmitter synthesis/signaling genes and developmental genes such as RET and Sox10, alongside species-specific differences in cell abundance and types.

Extrinsic rectal afferents exhibit spontaneous multiunit activity and lower mechanosensitive thresholds than colonic afferents, and their firing rates increase after exposure to capsaicin and inflammatory soup, indicating heightened sensitivity under inflammatory conditions.

Human pluripotent stem cell-derived ENS progenitors differentiated into functional enteric neurons expressing 5HT, GABA and NOS phenotypes, formed connections that induced smooth muscle contraction upon optogenetic stimulation, and engrafted precursors rescued disease-related mortality in a Hirschsprung disease (Ednrb) mouse model.

Human primary neurons obtained from intestinal biopsies can be cryopreserved using a cryoprotective agent and controlled cooling and remain viable and functional after thawing, as confirmed by calcium imaging.

Retrograde tracing of human colon motor neurons showed cholinergic (ChAT-immunoreactive) excitatory neurons clustered aborally, while nitric oxide synthase-immunoreactive inhibitory neurons projected both orally and anally, with VIP immunoreactivity almost always co-localized with NOS.

Human submucosal neurons show notable species differences in P2X purinergic receptor subtypes compared to mice, involving endogenous purines as regulators of neurotransmission in the human ENS relevant to secretomotor function.

The enteric nervous system is responsible for at least 60% of the gut secretory response, mediating secretion in response to enterotoxins, noxious agents, invasive organisms, inflammatory mediators, and postoperative ileus.
A study of ME/CFS patients found gut microbiome dysbiosis classified patients with 83% accuracy and was accompanied by elevated inflammatory blood markers attributed to microbial translocation.
16S rRNA stool analysis in ME/CFS patients revealed reduced bacterial diversity and richness, fewer anti-inflammatory species, and higher pro-inflammatory Enterobacteriaceae.
ME/CFS patients show higher levels of Enterococcus, Streptococcus, and Enterobacteriaceae, while beneficial Bifidobacteria and anti-inflammatory Firmicutes are decreased.
Metagenomic analysis found increased Alistipes and reduced butyrate-producing Faecalibacterium emerging as potential diagnostic biomarkers for ME/CFS.
In a discordant identical-twin case study, the affected twin showed reduced Bifidobacterium and Faecalibacterium abundance and decreased gut alpha diversity compared to the unaffected twin.

A case-control study of 48 ME/CFS patients and 52 controls identified 26 distinct bacterial markers, with Coprobacillus, Eggerthella, and Blautia as key differentiators, decreased Faecalibacterium and increased Coprobacillus.

A study of 35 ME/CFS patients and 70 controls found a distinct microbial pattern with decreased anti-inflammatory Firmicutes, and internal vs. external control comparisons showed overlaps between patients and relatives.
ME/CFS patients show markedly elevated IgA and IgM antibodies against bacterial LPS compared to controls, consistent with bacterial translocation across a leaky gut.

The 'metabolic trap hypothesis' proposes ME/CFS patients carry multiple IDO2 gene mutations correlating with symptom severity, leading to insufficient kynurenine production, elevated tryptophan, and disrupted serotonin/melatonin pathways.

A pilot study by Jackson et al. found that antibiotics improved sleep quality in ME/CFS patients by reducing lactic acid-producing bacteria and Gram-positive bacteria, lowering proinflammatory cytokines.
A four-week combined antibiotic and probiotic treatment enhanced neurological symptoms and sleep quality in ME/CFS patients but did not alleviate fatigue.
An 8-week course of various probiotics improved well-being and reduced inflammation in ME/CFS patients in an uncontrolled Italian pilot study.

A study of Lactobacillus paracasei F19, Lactobacillus acidophilus NCFB 1748, and Bifidobacterium lactis Bb12 in 15 ME/CFS patients found improved neurocognitive function but no significant reduction in fatigue or physical activity.
A systematic review by Corbitt et al. found a lack of evidence for probiotics as a treatment for gastrointestinal symptoms in ME/CFS, largely due to poor study quality.
Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 supplementation in 48 ME/CFS patients lowered systemic inflammatory markers CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6.

A randomized controlled crossover study of high-polyphenol cocoa vs. low-polyphenol chocolate in ME/CFS patients (n=10) showed promising reduction in fatigue and enhanced residual function on the London Handicap Scale, though limited by small sample and short duration.
A systematic review found no supportive evidence that elimination or modified diets benefit patients with ME/CFS.
A systematic review including 68 patients and a subsequent open-label pilot trial of HRG80 red ginseng (n=188) both indicated potential benefit of ginseng therapy for ME/CFS.
CoQ10 levels have been shown to be lower in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy individuals.
A randomized controlled trial of 12-week Ubiquinol-10 supplementation in ME/CFS patients showed no significant improvement in fatigue via Chandler's Fatigue Scale, but improved night-time awakenings.
A meta-analysis concluded that CoQ10 is an effective and safe supplement for reducing fatigue symptoms, though more controlled studies are needed.
A 16-week randomized placebo-controlled trial of oral melatonin (1 mg) and zinc (10 mg) in 50 ME/CFS patients showed significant reductions in physical fatigue and improved quality of life.

A meta-analysis was unable to establish a significant connection between overall vitamin and mineral deficiencies and fatigue in ME/CFS patients, and found no clear advantage of nutritional interventions.

A retrospective study of 60 ME/CFS patients (many with comorbid IBS) receiving colon infusion of 13 common fecal bacteria found 70% responded positively at four weeks, with 58% of contactable patients maintaining symptom resolution for 15-20 years.

A retrospective study comparing FMT to oral treatment (diet/lifestyle, pre/probiotics, natural remedies) found 17 of 21 patients receiving FMT from ten different donors achieved at least 60% improvement.
An 8-week course of multi-strain probiotics improved subjective well-being and reduced inflammation in ME/CFS patients in a small uncontrolled Italian pilot study.

A probiotic combination (L. paracasei F19, L. acidophilus NCFB 1748, B. lactis Bb12) in 15 ME/CFS patients improved neurocognitive function but showed no significant reduction in fatigue or physical activity in a subgroup of nine patients.
A systematic review by Corbitt et al. found insufficient evidence that probiotics treat gastrointestinal symptoms in ME/CFS patients, largely attributable to poor study quality.
Bifidobacterium infantis 35624 supplementation in 48 ME/CFS patients lowered systemic inflammatory markers CRP, TNF-α, and IL-6.
Daily Lactobacillus casei strain Shirota for two months may significantly lessen anxiety and restore eubiosis in ME/CFS patients.
A systematic review of 68 patients and a separate open-label pilot trial of HRG80 red ginseng in 188 patients both indicated potential benefit of ginseng therapy for ME/CFS.
CoQ10 levels have been found to be lower in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy individuals.

A 12-week RCT of Ubiquinol-10 supplementation in ME/CFS patients found no significant improvement in fatigue by Chandler's Fatigue Scale, though secondary symptoms like night-time awakenings improved.

In an animal model, 21-day CoQ10 administration altered the gut environment, increasing fecal hydrogen and butyrate, reducing trimethylamine and Helicobacter, and boosting Ruminococcus and Lachnospiraceae abundance.
A meta-analysis concluded that CoQ10 is an effective and safe supplement for reducing fatigue symptoms.
A 16-week RCT of oral melatonin (1 mg) and zinc (10 mg) in 50 ME/CFS patients showed significant reductions in physical fatigue and improved quality of life.

Thiamine, partially produced by gut bacteria such as Bacteroides (reduced in ME/CFS), and required for growth of Faecalibacterium (also diminished in ME/CFS), may be reduced in availability in ME/CFS gut ecosystems.
A meta-analysis was unable to establish a significant connection between overall vitamin and mineral deficiencies and fatigue in ME/CFS patients, though vitamin E deficiency's role remains uncertain.
A systematic review indicated some potential benefit of d-ribose supplementation for symptom management in ME/CFS.

A retrospective study of 60 ME/CFS patients (many with comorbid IBS) receiving colon infusion of 13 common fecal bacteria found 70% responded positively after four weeks, with 58% of contactable patients maintaining symptom resolution for 15-20 years.

In a retrospective comparison, 17 of 21 ME/CFS patients receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from ten different donors achieved at least 60% improvement, versus an oral treatment comparator group.

A randomized, placebo-controlled pilot study of fecal microbiota transplantation in 11 ME/CFS patients found no notable differences in health-related quality of life between treatment and placebo/autologous groups at 1 and 6 months.
Antibiotic treatment prior to fecal microbiota transplantation significantly enhances donor microbiota engraftment.

FMT engraftment success is most strongly linked to combined upper and lower gastrointestinal administration, with Bacteroidetes and Actinobacteria showing better engraftment than Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, and gram-positive bacteria engrafting less well than gram-negative bacteria.
Neomycin treatment in ME/CFS patients with small intestinal bacterial overgrowth resulted in reported improvements in pain, depression, and cognitive function.
Moclobemide enhanced vitality and energy in ME/CFS patients without notably alleviating depression.

Thiamine, which is partially produced by gut bacteria such as Bacteroides that are often reduced in ME/CFS patients, may be diminished, potentially affecting the competitive gut microbial ecosystem including thiamine-dependent Faecalibacterium.

A meta-analysis found no significant association between overall vitamin and mineral deficiencies and fatigue severity in ME/CFS patients, though some uncertainty about vitamin E deficiency persisted.
A systematic review indicated potential benefits of D-ribose supplementation for symptom management in ME/CFS patients.

In a retrospective study of 60 ME/CFS patients (many with comorbid IBS) treated with colonic infusion of a 13-strain fecal bacteria culture, 70% responded positively after four weeks, and 58% of contactable patients maintained symptom resolution for 15-20 years.

In a retrospective comparison, 17 of 21 ME/CFS patients receiving fecal microbiota transplantation from ten different donors achieved at least a 60% symptom improvement, compared to an oral treatment regimen.

In the only randomized placebo-controlled pilot trial of fecal microbiota transplantation in ME/CFS (n=11), there were no significant differences in health-related quality of life between transplant and placebo (autologous) groups at 1 and 6 months.
Antibiotic pre-treatment prior to fecal microbiota transplantation significantly enhances donor microbiota engraftment.

FMT success is most strongly linked to administration method, especially combining upper and lower gastrointestinal delivery, with Bacteroidetes and Actinobacteria showing better engraftment than Firmicutes and Proteobacteria, and gram-negative bacteria engrafting better than gram-positive.
In ME/CFS patients with high stool Streptococcus counts, antibiotic treatment that reduced these counts was associated with improved sleep quality.
Neomycin treatment in ME/CFS patients with small intestinal bacterial overgrowth was associated with reported improvements in pain, depression, and cognitive function.

Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs commonly used for pain management in ME/CFS have been associated with gastrointestinal disturbances, raising concern for their long-term use given high baseline gut-related symptoms.
Moclobemide was found to enhance vitality and energy in ME/CFS patients without notably alleviating depression.
Phenelzine showed no significant benefits for ME/CFS symptoms.
A small trial of escitalopram in ME/CFS patients with comorbid major depressive disorder showed substantial reductions in both ME/CFS and depression symptoms.

Fluoxetine generally did not show significant symptom improvement in depressed or non-depressed ME/CFS patients, except in one study where it improved depressive symptoms without significantly affecting fatigue levels.
Duloxetine did not reduce general fatigue but produced notable improvements in mental fatigue, pain relief, and overall symptom perception compared to placebo.
Antidepressants posed a risk of altering gut flora in several animal models via inhibition of efflux pumps and/or amino acid transporters, potentially exacerbating inflammation and immune responses.

In ME/CFS, salivary glands undergo pathological changes including mast cell accumulation and autoantibody targeting of muscarinic receptors, affecting saliva production and thus nutrition and oral health.
Genome-wide microarray profiling identified 489 HERV loci (502 probesets) differentially expressed between at least two of the ME/CFS, FM, co-diagnosed, and healthy control groups.
ME/CFS patients showed markedly greater HERV dysregulation than FM, co-diagnosed, or healthy control groups.

The co-diagnosed (ME/CFS+FM) group showed a HERV expression profile minimally different from healthy controls, defining it as a distinct low-epigenetic-impact nosologic entity rather than a simple combination of ME/CFS and FM.
Cluster 1, comprising 251 HERV loci (293 probesets), was specifically overexpressed in ME/CFS patients compared to all other study groups.
Cluster 2, comprising 119 HERV loci (163 probesets), was specifically underexpressed in ME/CFS patients compared to all other study groups.
Cluster 3, comprising 68 HERV loci (74 probesets) including the HERV-T, LTR84, and PRIMA41 families, was specifically overexpressed in fibromyalgia patients.
Cluster 4, comprising 54 HERV loci (64 probesets), was underexpressed across all three patient groups (ME/CFS, FM, co-diagnosed) relative to controls.

ME/CFS patients could be subdivided into two subgroups by HERV expression magnitude; subgroup 2 showed more pronounced dysregulation (especially downregulated Cluster 2) and correlated with greater fatigue and reduced motivation than subgroup 1 and the co-diagnosed group.
The MLT1 HERV family was the only family significantly downregulated across all three patient groups, accounting for more than a third of DE HERV in each cluster.
The HERV-W family was found downregulated in all patient groups (more accentuated in FM and co-diagnosed than ME/CFS), contradicting a prior report of HERV-W upregulation in fibromyalgia.

Differential gene expression analysis of the same samples identified 368 genes (1037 probesets) differentially expressed between at least two study groups, with ME/CFS showing the most pronounced gene dysregulation.
In ME/CFS, 258 upregulated HERV loci (Module 3) correlated with 34 genes involved in alpha-beta T cell activation and T-helper 17 cell commitment.
In ME/CFS, 78 downregulated HERV loci correlated with pathogen-detection-related genes, suggesting immune-pathogen sensing pathway involvement.
HERV downregulated across all three disease groups (Modules 1 and 6) correlated with genes involved in immune cell differentiation and cell-cell adhesion regulation.

HERV and genes upregulated in FM but downregulated in ME/CFS (Modules 2, 5, 7, 8) implicated telomere structure maintenance, cellular response to glucocorticoids, and NF-κB signaling regulation, indicating divergent inflammatory states between the two diseases.

HERV loci upregulated in ME/CFS (Module 3) were markedly enriched for binding sites of the chromatin remodeling/epigenetic repressor factors SETDB1 and TRIM28, and for CTCF, implicating impairment of the TRIM28/SETDB1 HERV-silencing axis in ME/CFS.
CIBERSORTx digital cytometry showed a decrease in γδ T cells in the ME/CFS subgroup 2 relative to other study groups.
CIBERSORTx digital cytometry showed an increase in resting CD4 memory T cells and plasma cells in the ME/CFS subgroup 2 relative to other study groups.
Module 3 HERV loci correlated with immune cell fractions, e.g., LTR65_20p11.21 correlated with γδ T cell abundance and MER49_11q13.1 correlated with resting CD4 memory T cell/plasma cell abundance.
Module 3 (immune-response HERV/genes upregulated in ME/CFS subgroup 2) showed a strong association with ME/CFS diagnosis.
Expression of MER31_3p26.1 and HERV16_3p21.31, both members of Module 3, correlated with physical and mental fatigue scores in ME/CFS patients, as assessed by the MFI and SF-36 instruments.
The HERV loci MLT1_5q32 (near CD74) and MLT1_4q24 (within NFKB1 first intron) were both downregulated in ME/CFS, FM, and co-diagnosed groups along with their co-localized genes.

The HERV elements MLT1_8q12.1 (within LYN's tenth intron) and MLT1_Xp22.3 (within TLR8's long isoform second exon) showed lower expression specifically in ME/CFS subgroup 2, likely reflecting co-transcription with their host genes.
Intergenic solo LTR elements were found underexpressed specifically in ME/CFS, pointing to epigenetic regulatory involvement.

Among symptom questionnaires (FIQ, MFI, SF-36), only MFI Physical Fatigue and Reduced Motivation subdomains differed significantly between patient groups, specifically between ME/CFS and co-diagnosed patients.
ME/CFS showed the greatest heterogeneity of HERV family involvement with 66 dysregulated families, versus 22 families in FM and 16 shared across all three patient groups.

Genomic context analysis showed that HERV loci repressed in ME/CFS (Cluster 2) and overexpressed in FM (Cluster 3) were significantly associated with gene 3' ends, while HERV loci silenced across all three pathologies (Cluster 4) were significantly associated with intronic regions.
The great majority of differentially expressed HERV loci across all clusters were solitary LTR elements rather than full proviral HERV, mirroring their overall abundance in the human genome.

Genomic context analysis showed that HERV loci repressed in ME/CFS (Cluster 2) and overexpressed in FM (Cluster 3) were significantly associated with gene 3' endings, while loci silenced across all three patient groups (Cluster 4) were significantly associated with intronic regions.
Intergenic solo LTR elements were found to be underexpressed specifically in ME/CFS, pointing to epigenetic regulatory involvement.
HERV-W family expression was downregulated in all patient groups relative to healthy controls, directly contradicting a prior report of HERV-W upregulation in fibromyalgia.

Genomic mapping of co-clustered HERV and gene modules revealed no major overlaps, with most DE HERV loci separated from their correlated DE genes by at least 100 kbp, suggesting largely independent transcription.
An MLT1 family HERV element (MLT1_5q32) located 18,114 bp upstream of CD74 was co-downregulated with CD74 across ME/CFS, FM, and co-diagnosed groups, suggesting cis-regulatory coupling.
An MLT1 element (MLT1_4q24) located within the first intron of NFκB1 was co-downregulated with NFκB1 across ME/CFS, FM, and co-diagnosed patient groups.
MLT1 elements located within LYN's tenth intron and TLR8's second exon showed lower expression specifically in ME/CFS subgroup 2, likely reflecting co-transcription with these immune genes.

Transcription factor binding site enrichment analysis found that HERV loci in Modules 1 through 7 were enriched for binding sites of immune-response transcription factors, while Module 8 showed no significant TFBS enrichment.
HERV downregulated across all three patient groups (Modules 1 and 6) were enriched in transcription factor binding sites involved in angiogenesis regulation.
HERV loci upregulated in FM but downregulated in ME/CFS (Modules 2, 5, 7) were enriched in transcription factor binding sites for miRNA transcription and glucocorticoid signaling.

HERV loci upregulated in ME/CFS (Module 3) were markedly enriched for binding sites of the chromatin remodeling repressors SETDB1 and TRIM28 and the chromatin organizer CTCF, suggesting impairment of the TRIM28/SETDB1 HERV-silencing axis as an underlying mechanism.
LTR65_20p11.21 expression negatively correlated with γδ T cell abundance and positively correlated with resting CD4 memory T cell and plasma cell abundance in ME/CFS subgroup 2.
MER49_11q13.1 expression showed a strong negative correlation with resting CD4 memory T cell abundance in the ME/CFS cohort.
MER72_4q34.3 expression correlated with plasma cell abundance across the study cohort.
Module 3 HERV/gene eigengene expression strongly associated with diagnosis of ME/CFS subgroup 2, the strongest disease-trait correlation found in the study.

Expression of MER31_3p26.1 and HERV16_3p21.31, both upregulated in ME/CFS subgroup 2, correlated positively with MFI fatigue subdomain scores and negatively with SF-36 subdomain scores, indicating association with worse physical and mental fatigue.
Using the FIQ severity cutoffs, approximately 88% of cases in the studied cohort were classified as severely affected while 12% were moderately affected.

Across FIQ, MFI, and SF-36 questionnaires, no statistically significant differences were found between patient groups except for MFI Physical Fatigue and Reduced Motivation subdomains, both differing only between the ME/CFS and co-diagnosed groups.

Unlike HERV expression profiles, hierarchical clustering and PCA of differentially expressed genes did not cluster all samples by study group, with the notable exception of ME/CFS subgroup 2, which showed a distinctly different gene expression profile.
Familiality of ME/CFS, i.e. the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to familial (genetic + shared environmental) effects, was estimated at 42%.
IBS showed the lowest familiality estimate among the studied disorders, at 22%.
Having a first-degree relative with ME/CFS was associated with a 2.23-fold increased recurrence risk of ME/CFS.
Having a first-degree relative with agoraphobia (AGPH) was associated with the smallest observed increase in IBS risk among all disorder pairs studied.
Familial correlation between ME/CFS and fibromyalgia (FM) was very high, nearly at the ceiling value.
The familial correlation between major depressive disorder (MDD) and ME/CFS was the strongest observed between an internalizing disorder and a functional disorder.
The familial correlation between agoraphobia and fibromyalgia was the weakest among all disorder pairs studied, though still moderate.
Among the three functional disorders, ME/CFS showed the strongest familial coaggregation with internalizing disorders, while IBS showed the weakest.

Significant spousal resemblance (familial coaggregation among cohabiting partners) was observed within ME/CFS and fibromyalgia, as well as within MDD, dysthymia, GAD, and agoraphobia, and each disorder also showed spousal coaggregation with at least one other disorder.

Excluding participants with somatic disorders with symptoms overlapping ME/CFS, IBS, and FM had little to no impact on familial coaggregation estimates, supporting specificity of the coaggregation findings to the functional disorders themselves.

When IBS and FM diagnostic criteria were made as strict as ME/CFS (requiring 6-month duration and interference with daily activities), severity-aligned IBS coaggregated more strongly with internalizing disorders than under the original looser criteria, and the gap between ME/CFS and FM coaggregation with IDs narrowed, indicating diagnostic criteria strictness partly explains observed differences.

Unlike λR based on all first-degree relatives combined, tetrachoric correlations calculated between individual sibling pairs and parent-offspring pairs/trios did not consistently reach statistical significance, though the pattern of relative strength of coaggregation (e.g., IBS being less strongly associated with IDs than ME/CFS and FM) was consistent.
Two-thirds of the Long COVID Questionnaire Cohort self-reported having PEM based on DSQ-derived severity groupings, with over a third reporting severe PEM.
Objective assessment via qualitative interviews after CPET found that only 2 of 34 (5.9%) Long COVID Exercise Cohort patients met PEM criteria, far lower than self-reported estimates.
All nine ME/CFS patients met objective PEM criteria following CPET, a far higher rate than in Long COVID (5.9%) or healthy volunteers (0%).

In six patients enrolled in both questionnaire and exercise cohorts, four self-reported PEM via DSQ but none met objective PEM criteria by qualitative interview after CPET, showing discordance between self-report and objective assessment.
ME/CFS patients showed markedly reduced exercise capacity, with only 11.1% reaching at least 84% of predicted peak VO2, compared to 55.6% of HV and 73.5% of Long COVID EC patients.
A lower proportion of ME/CFS patients reached 90% of age-predicted maximal heart rate at peak exercise compared to healthy volunteers and Long COVID EC patients.
ME/CFS patients had significantly lower physical functioning than either Long COVID QC or EC cohorts, and QC had significantly lower physical functioning than EC.
ME/CFS patients self-reported the highest pain interference, followed by the Long COVID questionnaire cohort, with both significantly higher than the Long COVID exercise cohort.

The Long COVID questionnaire cohort reported significantly higher levels of depression and sleep disturbance compared to the exercise cohort, with no difference between the exercise cohort and ME/CFS.
ME/CFS patients showed sustained worsening of physical and mental fatigue over 72 hours after CPET compared to minimal change in healthy volunteers.
Long COVID exercise cohort patients reported lower mental fatigue and minimal change in physical fatigue relative to pre-CPET baseline over the following 72 hours.

At the individual level, about half of Long COVID exercise cohort patients showed improvement in physical and mental fatigue VAS across post-CPET timepoints, compared to about a third of healthy volunteers and none of the ME/CFS patients.

The majority of healthy volunteers and Long COVID exercise cohort patients expressed positive themes (e.g., feeling invigorated, restored, empowered) following CPET, while this was rare among ME/CFS patients.

Word cloud analysis revealed that respiratory and neurological symptoms such as lung tightness, lung burning, tachycardia, shakiness, and tingling were unique bothersome symptoms in the Long COVID exercise cohort and were not reported by ME/CFS patients, while over a quarter of EC patients reported no bothersome symptom at all versus all ME/CFS patients reporting one.

Symptom onset and peak timing after CPET differed between groups, with Long COVID exercise cohort patients generally having immediate onset peaking within 4 to 24 hours, compared to symptom peaks at 48 to 72 hours in ME/CFS patients.

Pain symptom ratings did not significantly change across morning, afternoon and evening, but there was large individual variation, with some participants reporting pain 100% of the time and others 0%, and this variation did not appear to affect time spent resting.
Fatigue levels did not significantly differ across the day, with most participants (8 of 9) reporting consistently high fatigue 90–100% of the time.

Activities requiring greater energy expenditure, such as showering, meal preparation, shopping, household activities and socialising, produced the greatest activity-related fatigue and difficulty, though no significant diurnal pattern was found.

Participants' perceived performance (activities done well or poorly) did not significantly change across the day, though two participants reported completing activities poorly more than 88% of the time, driving evening variation.

Time spent on meaningful versus non-meaningful activities did not significantly differ across the day; meaningful activities (self-care, work, household) occupied 50–65% of time while non-meaningful activities (rest, recreation, leisure, planning) occupied 25–50%.

Across two 24-hour recording periods, participants averaged 58% of time awake, distributed as 37% recreation/leisure, 22% resting, 19% self-care, 10% household activities, 8% working, and 2% each for planning, transport and treatment.

Within recreation and leisure time, seated sedentary activities (e.g. TV, reading, social media) comprised 12–65% of activities while active recreation (shopping, baking, walking) accounted for only 0–11%.

Participants spent an average of 42% of the recorded time asleep, with most (7 of 9) beginning sleep between 8:00pm-10:00pm and all waking between 7:00am-9:00am; sleep duration per night could not be captured due to non-consecutive recording days.

Participants reported that ME/CFS substantially reduced their ability to participate in meaningful activities such as work, study, volunteering, exercise and socialising, leading to occupational deprivation.
Qualitative data showed ME/CFS-related changes in time-use adversely affected participants' relationships, including loss of friendships and family members assuming caregiving roles.

Most participants found completing the NIH ACTRE insightful for understanding their time-use and the meaning of their activities, but described it as time-consuming, intensive and cognitively demanding.
Participants felt the NIH ACTRE's two-day recording period and 1-4 Likert scale failed to capture the fluctuating, nuanced nature of ME/CFS symptoms.
The NIH ACTRE is cited in prior literature as a highly reliable self-administered time diary for chronic health conditions, with reported ICC 0.88-1.00 and Cronbach's alpha 0.77.
ME/CFS is cited in the literature as reducing a person's quality of life by 50%.
Participants with ME/CFS showed decreased occupational participation across all domains measured by the Occupational Self-Assessment.
Qualitative themes of loneliness, feeling confined, feeling like a burden, and loss of previous life/roles were reported, indicating an adverse impact of ME/CFS on occupational identity.
A lack of independence and control among participants indicated a reduction in occupational competence.
The article argues that ME/CFS, Lyme disease, and fibromyalgia have been historically misclassified as psychosomatic or psychogenic conditions, leading to stigmatization and delayed care.
The authors contend that reliance on population-based clinical guidelines, without integration of individualized patient needs, contributes to diagnostic errors at the medicine-psychiatry interface.
The paper critiques terms such as 'medically unexplained symptoms' and 'functional disorders' as having limitations and potential for misuse in clinical practice.
The prevalence of any long-COVID symptom among children declined over time but remained substantial, from 44.9% at 1 month to 37.8% at 3 months and 22.8% at 6 months after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Multivariable logistic regression found that age, sex, severity of acute COVID-19, and vaccination against SARS-CoV-2 were not significantly associated with development of long-COVID in children.
In analyses restricted to ME/CFS-type symptoms, increasing age was significantly associated with higher odds of developing these symptoms at each follow-up.
Sleep disturbance was significantly associated with a decline in quality-of-life score from admission at all three follow-up points (1, 3, and 6 months).
Presence of any long-COVID symptom at the 3-month follow-up was significantly associated with a decline in quality-of-life score.
Cough at the 6-month follow-up was significantly associated with a decline in quality-of-life score.
ME/CFS-type symptoms at 6 months were significantly more prevalent among older children (7–17 years) and parents than among younger children (0–6 years).
Fatigue was significantly more prevalent among parents than among children at all three follow-up time points.
Cough, fatigue, and sleep disturbance were the most consistently prevalent long-COVID symptoms among children across the 1-, 3-, and 6-month follow-ups.
At 6 months, parents had a substantially higher rate of any persisting symptom than their children.
None of the children in this cohort reported olfactory or gustatory disorders at any follow-up, whereas some parents did.
No child in the cohort exhibited ME/CFS symptoms at the time of hospital admission for acute COVID-19, indicating these symptoms emerged only during the post-acute follow-up period.
Adults with ME/CFS reported systemic changes to previous physical, cognitive, and affective functioning that led to significant disruption of occupational participation and poor well-being.
Participants described a pattern of occupational prioritisation in which leisure occupations were lost first, followed by productivity occupations, and eventually self-care occupations.

Environmental barriers to occupational participation identified included stigma and misunderstanding of ME/CFS, financial hardship, lack of appropriate health services, and strain on personal support networks and relationships.
The authors conclude there is a clear role for occupational therapy to intervene early in ME/CFS to prevent significant negative impacts on occupational participation.
Combined IgG and IgM antibody responses to HHV-6-dUTPase accounted for 63.7% of the variance in a latent construct combining disability, fatigue, depression, and anxiety scores in RRMS patients.

Total scores on the Fibro-Fatigue, Hamilton Anxiety, and Hamilton Depression scales were substantially associated with IgG and IgM responses to HHV-6-dUTPase, explaining approximately 38.7% to 51.0% of the variance.
The three neuropsychiatric rating scale scores (fatigue, anxiety, depression) were significantly correlated with IgA reactivity to both HHV-6/EBV dUTPases and with IgG/IgA/IgM reactivity to EBV EBNA.
The authors conclude that reactivation and replication of HHV-6 and EBV significantly contributes to chronic fatigue syndrome, depression, and anxiety symptoms due to RRMS.
Combined acupuncture at both Zusanli (ST36) and Guanyuan (CV4) points was more effective than acupuncture at either single point, with differing effects on sympathetic and parasympathetic activity.
Acupuncture was superior for regulating immediate (short-term) HRV changes, whereas moxibustion was superior for regulating long-term HRV changes in CFS patients.
The therapeutic mechanism of acupuncture at the Zusanli (ST36) point may act through the parasympathetic nervous system.
The therapeutic mechanism of acupuncture at the Guanyuan (CV4) point may act through the sympathetic nervous system.
Both acupuncture and moxibustion effectively alleviated fatigue symptoms in CFS patients, with combined acupuncture and moxibustion showing greater effectiveness than either alone.
Participants with Class III obesity had substantially higher odds of self-reporting fair/poor overall health compared with normal-weight participants (9.6% vs 3.2%).
Class III obesity was associated with markedly higher odds of self-reported severe pain compared with normal weight (28.3% vs 13.2%).
Class III obesity was associated with substantially higher odds of severely limited physical activity relative to normal weight.
Class III obesity was associated with an increased risk of incident fibromyalgia compared with normal weight in a longitudinal Cox proportional-hazards analysis.
Class III obesity was associated with nearly four-fold higher odds of severe pain compared with normal weight.
Class III obesity was associated with over three-fold higher odds of severely limited physical activity compared with normal weight.
Class III obesity was associated with an increased hazard of incident fibromyalgia compared with normal weight.
Class III obesity was associated with an increased hazard of incident insomnia compared with normal weight.

Participants with hEDS/HSD identified physical, mind-body, instruction/instructor, and accessibility factors as key facilitators and barriers to participating in an 8-week online Pilates program designed for hypermobility.
Participants reported both physical and psychological (mind-body) benefits as outcomes of completing the online Pilates program, alongside drawbacks such as pain, fatigue, and discouragement.
Direct carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF) is described as a common neurovascular complication associated with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS).
Mutations in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III procollagen essential to blood vessel and hollow organ wall structure, are stated to be the primary cause of vascular EDS.

Selective transvenous embolization (TVE) using coils combined with 20% n-butyl-2-cyanoacrylate (NBCA) achieved complete, durable occlusion of a right CCF in a patient with EDS after two treatment sessions, with symptom resolution maintained at 2-year follow-up.

The first embolization session significantly reduced shunt flow but did not achieve natural occlusion due to vascular fragility, and shunt flow rapidly increased within a short period, requiring a second treatment.
Arterial dissection and rupture are reported to occur in 65% of patients with vascular EDS.
CCF occurs in 2.4%-9.8% of EDS cases, with about half of these resulting in aneurysm rupture.

EDS has an estimated prevalence of approximately 1 in 150,000 individuals across all subtypes, and vEDS carries a poor prognosis with 80% of affected individuals experiencing vascular issues or organ rupture by age 40 and a median lifespan of 48 years.

In the 1990s, interventional radiology was considered contraindicated for EDS patients due to substantial complication rates of 22%-35% and mortality rates of 6%-12%, though more recent case series report successful endovascular treatments alongside some procedure-related deaths.
A published case series by Adham et al. of 13 patients with CCF caused by vascular EDS reported successful endovascular treatment in all patients with no perioperative or in-hospital complications.

Hemorrhagic occurrences in distant vessels such as the splenic and iliac arteries have been noted in 22%-35% of individuals with vascular EDS, possibly due to decreased intima and media vessel thickness increasing circumferential wall stress.

A transvenous rather than transarterial approach is preferred for embolization in EDS patients because veins have lower pressure than arteries, reducing risk of ectopic injury and allowing a reduced arterial puncture profile.

A woman with FKBP14-related kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome experienced sigmoid colon perforation due to diverticular rupture, indicating that severe intestinal fragility can occur in this EDS subtype.

A 17-year-old woman with EDS and recurrent right elbow subluxations/dislocations and coronoid deformity underwent soft tissue reconstruction (capsular plication, LCL reconstruction with local autograft, hinged external fixation) with marked improvement in stability and function sustained over 10 years.
Prior nonsurgical management with rehabilitation and muscle strengthening exercises over approximately seven years produced no clinical benefit for the patient's recurrent elbow instability.

The patient's coronoid process became deformed and smoothed and the sigmoid notch became shallow due to repetitive shear trauma from recurrent elbow dislocations, with subluxation of the radial head and a degenerated, detached lateral collateral ligament.

In a cited cohort of 60 EDS patients, joint pain occurred in 88%, swelling in 51%, and dislocation in 72%, with 64% having impaired upper extremity function and 73% having less than normal upper limb function, and EDS types II and III being most common.
A cited study of 50 EDS patients found reduced bone mineral density and bone quality along with increased prevalence of fragility fractures compared with controls.

A cited case series found that 92.3% of EDS patients had a history of recurrent dislocation (15.4% elbow, 46.2% radial head), with shallow trochlear notch in 70% and elbow osteoarthritis in 30.8%, and no clear varus-valgus instability, suggesting congenital joint capsule laxity and coronoid height loss as causes of posterior/posterolateral elbow dislocation.
A cited series of 320 orthopedic procedures in EDS patients reported a 91% complication rate, underscoring the surgical risk in this population.

A cited study reported an 80% success rate of glenohumeral joint stabilization using capsulorrhaphy with a tendon allograft in EDS-related shoulder instability, an approach suggested as potentially applicable to elbow reconstruction.

A cited case series (Cole et al, n=3) used bone graft to the olecranon fossa for EDS-related elbow instability, achieving functional stability and patient satisfaction despite loss of full extension, though with only short follow-up.

A cited case report (Schneider et al) described medial and lateral ligament reconstruction combined with a temporary hinged internal fixator in an EDS patient with recurrent elbow instability, showing excellent stability and ROM at 1-year follow-up.
Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is caused by heterozygous deleterious variants in the COL3A1 gene, which encodes type III collagen.

Transcriptomic profiling of vEDS fibroblasts/spheroids showed upregulation of genes involved in mitochondrial function, organellar ribosomal subunits, and biosynthesis, suggesting an augmented adaptive metabolic response.

Genes involved in cell migration, differentiation, and stress response were downregulated in vEDS fibroblasts/spheroids, indicating abnormalities in cellular signaling and extracellular matrix maintenance.

Proteomic analysis of vEDS samples found induced proteins significantly enriched for the mitochondrial matrix, minichromosome maintenance (MCM) complex, low-density lipoprotein particle biology, and cellular responses to catabolic processes and DNA damage stimuli.

Ultrastructural and high-content imaging of vEDS cells revealed endoplasmic reticulum dilation along with increased autophagosomes and lipofuscin deposits, indicating organellar stress and altered autophagic/catabolic activity.
3D fibroblast spheroids integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data are proposed as a suitable experimental model to dissect vEDS pathogenesis and identify new therapeutic targets.
DS disaccharides were completely absent from colon tissue of Chst14-/- mice, confirming loss of dermatan sulfate biosynthesis.
A specific CS-only disaccharide (ΔHexUA-GalNAc(6S)) was significantly increased in the colon of Chst14-/- mice compared with wild-type.
CS disaccharide ΔHexUA-GalNAc(4S) levels were significantly higher in the colon of Chst14-/- mice compared with wild-type mice.
Total CS/DS disaccharide content in the colon was significantly lower in Chst14-/- mice compared with wild-type mice despite compensatory CS increases.
Decorin, the major CS/DS proteoglycan core protein in colon, is normally modified predominantly with DS in wild-type mice, but in Chst14-/- mice this DS modification is lost and replaced by CS.
Expression of other genes involved in CS/DS synthesis besides Chst14 did not differ significantly between Chst14-/- and wild-type mouse colon.
Colons of Chst14-/- mice were significantly shorter than wild-type colons at 10 weeks of age, without diverticula or gross anatomical abnormality.
Chst14-/- mice weighed significantly less than wild-type mice.

Treatment with the calcium channel blocker nifedipine, a smooth muscle relaxant, suppressed intestinal contraction and eliminated the colon length difference between Chst14-/- and wild-type mice, indicating that increased smooth muscle contraction underlies colon shortening in Chst14-/- mice.
No differences were observed between Chst14-/- and wild-type mice in daily defecation amount, food intake, or gastrointestinal transit time.
Colon extensibility and rupture strength did not differ significantly between Chst14-/- and wild-type mice despite collagen structural abnormalities.

Submucosal collagen fibrils in Chst14-/- colon were sparse, disorganized, of lower density, and had significantly smaller diameters compared with wild-type, despite unchanged collagen gene expression.

Gene expression of collagen components (Col1a1, Col3a1) and CS/DS-proteoglycan core proteins (Dcn, Bgn, Vcan) in the colon did not differ between Chst14-/- and wild-type mice, indicating collagen fibril structural changes are not due to quantitative changes in these genes.

In the DSS-induced colitis model, no significant differences were found between Chst14-/- and wild-type mice in DAI scores, body weight change, or histological/immune markers of inflammation severity, indicating DS deficiency does not aggravate colitis.
During DSS-colitis recovery (day 15), Chst14-/- mice showed significantly lower histological (H&E) injury scores than wild-type mice, indicating faster tissue repair.
Unlike wild-type mice, which showed significant DSS-induced colon shortening at day 8, Chst14-/- mice did not show this DSS-induced colon shortening.
After discontinuation of DSS (day 15), colonic Tgfb gene expression decreased in Chst14-/- mice but continued to rise in wild-type mice.
Colonic Il1b gene expression significantly increased on day 8 of DSS administration only in wild-type mice, not in Chst14-/- mice.
Female Chst14-/- mice showed reduced body weight and colon shortening similar to male Chst14-/- mice, and nifedipine similarly eliminated colon length differences in females.
Colonic Dcn gene expression was significantly lower in female Chst14-/- mice compared with male mice of both genotypes, suggesting a sex-specific difference not seen in males.
More pronated foot posture (higher FPI) was positively correlated with greater foot and ankle hypermobility (FAFI) in children.
More everted/pronated resting calcaneal stance position was associated with greater foot and ankle hypermobility.
Greater ankle dorsiflexion range measured by the Lunge test was correlated with greater foot and ankle hypermobility.
Increasing age was inversely correlated with foot and ankle hypermobility, consistent with prior findings using the Beighton and LLAS tests.
BMI showed no statistically significant relationship with 6-minute walk test distance.
BMI showed no statistically significant relationship with foot and ankle hypermobility (FAFI).
Children with greater foot and ankle joint hypermobility walked shorter distances on the 6-minute walk test, consistent with prior findings of reduced physical capacity in hypermobile young dancers.

A multivariable linear regression using age, Lunge test, RCSP, FPI, and 6MWT as predictors explained only 24.9% of the variance in foot and ankle hypermobility (FAFI), indicating additional unexamined factors are relevant.
There was no significant difference in FAFI scores between left and right feet, supporting use of either side for subsequent analyses.
A FAFI score of 4 out of 6 was used as the diagnostic cut-off point for defining foot and ankle hypermobility positivity in this validated paediatric tool.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome clustered significantly among relatives within families affected by Chiari malformation type 1, suggesting a shared genetic basis.
Headache as a symptom showed significant intrafamilial clustering among relatives with Chiari malformation type 1.
Neck pain showed significant intrafamilial clustering among relatives with Chiari malformation type 1.
Syringomyelia as a neurological comorbidity showed significant intrafamilial clustering among relatives with Chiari malformation type 1.
Hydrocephalus as a neurological comorbidity showed significant intrafamilial clustering among relatives with Chiari malformation type 1.
Dyslexia as a neurodevelopmental condition showed significant intrafamilial clustering among relatives with Chiari malformation type 1.
Age of onset of Chiari malformation type 1 showed significant intrafamilial similarity among affected relatives.
The paper notes that recent studies have highlighted first ray hypermobility and intrinsic metatarsal rotation as important factors in hallux valgus deformity, affecting surgical planning.

Patients with Down syndrome commonly exhibit connective tissue and musculoskeletal features, including muscle hypotonia, ligament laxity, and joint hypermobility, alongside characteristic craniofacial features.
The authors note that certain Down syndrome craniofacial characteristics, such as midfacial hypoplasia, can contribute to obstructive sleep apnea.

The authors performed Le Fort II distraction osteogenesis using a halo-type external distraction device in a 2-year-old boy with Down syndrome and reported successful outcomes for midfacial hypoplasia-related respiratory compromise.
A de novo heterozygous frameshift variant in FMR1 was identified by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing as the cause of Fragile X syndrome in a female patient.
Standard FMR1 CGG repeat expansion analysis was normal in this patient, meaning the classical trinucleotide repeat test would have missed the causative point variant.

By age 28, the patient presented with mild joint hypermobility along with macrocephaly, coarse facial features, left talo-valgus deformity, a port-wine stain, a café-au-lait spot, and a piezogenic papule.
This case represents only the second reported female patient with Fragile X syndrome caused by a heterozygous point variant rather than the classical CGG repeat expansion.

Reserpine-induced fibromyalgia model (RIFM) rats developed pronounced mechanical and thermal allodynia/hyperalgesia and increased spontaneous pain behavior, shown by reduced Von Frey withdrawal threshold, cold allodynia and tail-immersion latencies, reduced Randall-Selitto and hot-plate thresholds, and elevated Rat Grimace Scale scores versus healthy controls.

A single intraperitoneal dose of suramin (100 mg/kg) reversed reserpine-induced mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity, increasing Von Frey threshold, cold allodynia and tail-immersion latencies, and Randall-Selitto and hot-plate thresholds, and reducing Grimace Scale scores relative to untreated RIFM rats.
RIFM rats displayed depressive-like behavior, shown by markedly prolonged immobility time in the forced swim test compared to normal control rats.
Suramin treatment increased mobility (reduced immobility) in the forced swim test relative to untreated RIFM rats, indicating an antidepressant-like effect.

RIFM rats exhibited locomotor and motor coordination deficits, including reduced open-field distance traveled, speed, and central-zone entries, increased latency and immobility time, and reduced rotarod residence time, compared to healthy controls.
Suramin treatment ameliorated reserpine-induced motor impairments, increasing open-field activity metrics and rotarod residence time compared to untreated RIFM rats.

Histopathological examination revealed neuronal loss/necrosis, vacuolization of the intercellular brain matrix, and increased reactive microglial infiltration in the thalamus of RIFM rats compared to intact neuronal architecture in control rats.

Suramin-treated RIFM rats showed neuroprotective histological improvement in the thalamus, with abundant intact neurons resembling normal controls and minimal glial infiltration compared to untreated RIFM rats.
Thalamic P2X7 receptor protein levels were significantly overexpressed in RIFM rats compared to normal controls.
Suramin administration significantly reduced thalamic P2X7 receptor expression compared to untreated RIFM rats.
Thalamic P2X4 receptor protein levels were significantly overexpressed in RIFM rats compared to normal controls.
Suramin administration significantly reduced thalamic P2X4 receptor expression compared to untreated RIFM rats.

RIFM rats showed upregulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome components NLRP3, NEK7, and active caspase-1, with a corresponding decrease in pro-caspase-1, in the thalamus compared to normal rats; this was confirmed by immunohistochemistry.
Suramin treatment downregulated NLRP3, NEK7, and active caspase-1 while restoring pro-caspase-1, and reduced NLRP3/caspase-1 immunoreactivity in the thalamus, compared to untreated RIFM rats.
Thalamic GSDMD, the pyroptosis executioner protein, was elevated in RIFM rats relative to healthy controls.
Suramin treatment reduced the reserpine-induced elevation of thalamic GSDMD compared to untreated RIFM rats.
RIFM rats exhibited elevated thalamic levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-18, IL-6, and TNF-α compared to normal rats.
Thalamic NLRP3 protein was upregulated twofold in reserpine-induced fibromyalgia (RIFM) rats compared to controls, and suramin treatment downregulated NLRP3 by 58.7% relative to untreated RIFM rats.
Thalamic NEK7 was upregulated 3.2-fold in RIFM rats relative to controls, and suramin reduced NEK7 by 64.2% compared to untreated RIFM rats.
Active caspase-1 was upregulated fourfold in the thalamus of RIFM rats via western blot, and suramin decreased caspase-1 by 52% compared to untreated RIFM rats.

Pro-caspase-1 expression decreased by 73.6% in the thalamus of RIFM rats compared to normal rats, and suramin treatment increased pro-caspase-1 to 2.4-fold relative to untreated RIFM rats, consistent with enhanced cleavage into active caspase-1.
Immunohistochemistry showed a 2.8-fold increase in thalamic NLRP3 expression in RIFM rats compared to healthy rats, which was reduced by 53.7% with suramin treatment.
Immunohistochemistry showed a 2.4-fold increase in thalamic caspase-1 expression in RIFM rats compared to healthy rats, which was reduced by 51% with suramin treatment.
Thalamic gasdermin D (GSDMD), a pyroptosis executioner protein, was elevated 1.5-fold in RIFM rats compared to controls, and suramin treatment reduced this increase by 50%.
Thalamic IL-1β was elevated 1.7-fold in RIFM rats compared to normal rats, and suramin countered this elevation to 55% relative to untreated rats.
Thalamic IL-18 was elevated by 97% in RIFM rats compared to normal rats, and suramin countered this elevation to 43% relative to untreated rats.
Thalamic IL-6 was elevated 2.9-fold in RIFM rats compared to normal rats, and suramin countered this elevation to 65% relative to untreated rats.
Thalamic TNF-α was elevated fourfold in RIFM rats compared to normal rats, and suramin countered this elevation to 66.7% relative to untreated rats.
Phosphorylated p38 MAPK protein was increased 4.7-fold in the thalamus of RIFM rats compared to controls, and suramin suppressed this rise to 57.4% relative to untreated rats.
Thalamic NF-κB was elevated 1.2-fold in RIFM rats compared to normal rats, and suramin reversed this effect by 98% relative to untreated rats.

Thalamic expression of the M1 microglia marker CD86 increased 14.7-fold in RIFM rats compared to normal rats, indicating M1 polarization, while suramin downregulated CD86 by 79.9% compared to RIFM rats, shifting microglia toward the M2 phenotype.

Thalamic expression of the M2 microglia marker CD163 decreased by 95% in RIFM rats compared to normal rats, while suramin treatment upregulated CD163 by 10.5-fold compared to untreated RIFM rats, indicating restoration of the M2 microglial phenotype.
In young women with fibromyalgia, reduced functional connectivity between the left anterior insula and ACC correlated negatively with pain catastrophizing and pain intensity.
In depression patients, decreased left insula-ACC connectivity showed a negative correlation with Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) scores.
A second MDD study similarly found decreased insula-ACC connectivity negatively correlated with depressive symptom severity assessed by HDRS.
Both FM and MDD patients showed increased functional connectivity between the DLPFC seed and the ACC compared with healthy controls, representing a shared neurosignature.

Functional connectivity between the thalamus and precuneus was increased in both FM and MDD patients compared to healthy controls, possibly reflecting rumination and pain catastrophizing via default mode network hyperconnectivity.
Both FM and MDD patients showed reduced functional connectivity between the insula seed and the MFG, SFG, ACC, and putamen relative to controls.

In FM patients, the PAG seed showed reduced functional connectivity to pain perception/modulation regions (insula, amygdala, thalamus, SMA, DLPFC, dmPFC), and this reduction correlated with pain intensity, quality of life, catastrophizing, and disease duration.
FM patients showed increased functional connectivity in all central executive network seeds (IPL, DLPFC, MFG) with the PCC, ACC, hippocampus, and mPFC compared to controls.

In FM patients, most seeds from the central autonomic network (reduced connectivity with SMA, amygdala, thalamus, insula, PCC, PFC) and salience network (reduced connectivity with SI/M1, MFG, SFG, putamen, ACC) demonstrated reduced functional connectivity versus controls.
Greater connectivity between the insula and cingulate cortex was associated with decreased pressure-pain thresholds in FM, indicating a neural basis for pain hypersensitivity.
In FM patients, altered functional connectivity between the insula and the default mode network was linked to reduced clinical pain.

Studies of the cognitive control network in FM found increased functional connectivity between the DLPFC and ACC/mPFC, regions involved in top-down modulation of pain, and hyperconnectivity in these areas correlated with pain catastrophizing.
A cited meta-analysis of rs-FC in MDD found reduced connectivity in the frontoparietal network and increased connectivity in the default mode network compared to controls.

A study of 1,300 participants observed reduced default mode network functional connectivity only in individuals with recurrent MDD, suggesting prolonged disease burden contributes to these alterations.

In MDD patients, the left insula showed decreased resting-state functional connectivity with the contralateral middle frontal gyrus, superior frontal gyrus, and middle occipital gyrus, and with the right ACC, indicating diminished interhemispheric communication.
The bilateral ACC seed showed decreased connectivity with the hippocampus, PCC, angular gyrus, thalamus, striatum, insula, STG, MTG, SFG, and cerebellum in MDD patients versus controls.
In MDD patients, the amygdala seed showed increased functional connectivity with the IFG, right MFG, right MCC, and paracingulate gyrus compared to controls.

In MDD patients, the precuneus seed showed reduced connectivity with motor areas (bilateral fusiform gyrus, right SMA, left precentral/postcentral gyrus) but increased connectivity with executive function regions (right superior/middle frontal gyrus, left middle/inferior frontal gyrus).

Resting-state functional connectivity between descending pain modulatory system structures, particularly M1 and the ventral lateral thalamus, correlates with pain modulation capacity and response to transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) in FM.

A resting-state EEG study in women with FM reported heightened beta-3 frequency band connectivity between the left DLPFC and right ACC compared to controls, corroborating the fMRI-based DLPFC-ACC hyperconnectivity finding.
Major depressive disorder affects more than half of fibromyalgia patients, with a weighted prevalence of up to 63%.
Reactive oxygen species accumulate in differentiating beige adipocytes and drive UCP1-dependent thermogenesis.
ROS elevation activates mast cells, and serotonin synthesized and released by mast cells inhibits proliferation of beige progenitor cells and adipocyte browning.
Hydrogen peroxide-activated mouse bone marrow-derived mast cells (BMMCs) inhibited brown differentiation of SVF cells and thermogenesis of beige adipocytes.
Unlike the synthetic antioxidant N-acetylcysteine (NAC), luteolin elevated expression of thermogenic and beige-selective marker genes along with intracellular ROS generation in beige adipocytes.
Luteolin inhibited hydrogen peroxide-induced mast cell activation and ROS generation in bone marrow-derived mast cells.
Luteolin partially reversed the inhibitory effects of H2O2-activated BMMCs on the brown differentiation of SVF cells and beige adipocyte thermogenesis.
Luteolin activates the Nrf2/Catalase pathway in beige adipocytes to regulate intracellular ROS levels and promote thermogenic gene expression.
In mast cells, luteolin modulates the Nrf2/Catalase pathway to suppress H2O2-induced ROS generation and mast cell activation.
Serotonin synthesized and released by mast cells inhibits beige progenitor cell proliferation and adipocyte browning.
Unlike luteolin, the synthetic antioxidant NAC does not elevate expression of thermogenic and beige-selective marker genes in beige adipocytes despite also affecting ROS levels.
H. pylori-infected patients showed significantly greater gastric mast cell infiltration than uninfected individuals.
