Mast cell infiltration significantly correlated with severity of gastric inflammation in H. pylori-positive individuals.
H. pylori infection increased release of β-hexosaminidase, a degranulation marker, from RBL-2H3 mast cells, similar to the compound 48/80 positive control.
RNA-seq of H. pylori-infected RBL-2H3 mast cells identified 1032 upregulated and 538 downregulated genes compared to uninfected cells.
H. pylori infection upregulated multiple cytokines in mast cells including IL-4, IL-13, CCL1, CCL2, CCL7, and IL-3, with CCL2 (MCP-1) showing the highest fold change/gene amplification.
Twelve receptor genes showed at least a 4-fold increase upon H. pylori infection, and GPR171 was selected for further study due to its high expression.
H. pylori infection increased GPR171 mRNA and protein expression in RBL-2H3 and HMC-1 mast cell lines, peaking at 6 hours post-infection.
GPR171-positive mast cells were increased in gastric mucosa of H. pylori-infected patients compared to uninfected controls.
KEGG and GSEA analyses showed significant enrichment of the HIF-1α signaling pathway in H. pylori-infected mast cells, with increased HIF-1α mRNA and protein levels.
H. pylori infection significantly increased intracellular ROS levels in RBL-2H3 mast cells.
CoCl2, a chemical HIF-1α stabilizer, increased GPR171 expression in mast cells in a concentration-dependent manner, with 200 μM producing maximal upregulation in RBL-2H3 cells.
Pretreatment with the HIF-1α inhibitor PX-478 reduced CoCl2- and H. pylori-induced upregulation of GPR171 in RBL-2H3 and HMC-1 cells.
ChIP assay showed HIF-1α robustly binds the HRE2 region (but not HRE1) of the GPR171 promoter in HMC-1 cells treated with H. pylori or CoCl2.

Luciferase reporter assays showed H. pylori and CoCl2 increased GPR171 promoter activity via the wild-type HRE2 construct but not via HRE2-mutant or empty vector constructs, confirming direct HIF-1α-mediated transactivation of GPR171.
Knockdown of GPR171 in RBL-2H3 cells had no effect on H. pylori-induced mast cell degranulation (β-hexosaminidase release).
GPR171 knockdown markedly reduced CCL2 and CCL7 mRNA and CCL2 protein levels induced by H. pylori infection in mast cells.
BigLEN, the endogenous ligand of GPR171, induced upregulation of CCL2 expression in RBL-2H3 mast cells, supporting a direct role for GPR171 signaling in CCL2 production.
ERK1/2 phosphorylation was significantly increased in H. pylori-infected RBL-2H3 and HMC-1 mast cells.
Pretreatment with the ERK1/2 inhibitor U0126 partially reduced H. pylori-induced CCL2 mRNA and protein expression in mast cells.
GPR171 knockdown impaired H. pylori-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation in mast cells, placing GPR171 upstream of ERK signaling.
The GPR171 antagonist MS21570 dose-dependently downregulated H. pylori-induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation and CCL2 expression in mast cells.
CCL2 expression by immunohistochemistry was increased in H. pylori-infected gastric tissue and positively associated with severity of gastric inflammation.
Linear regression analysis showed a positive correlation between CCL2 IHC score and mast cell infiltration in H. pylori-infected patients.

In a mouse model of H. pylori PMSS1 infection, the GPR171 antagonist MS21570 partially reduced gastric CCL2 mRNA/IHC expression and alleviated gastric inflammation scores, without affecting bacterial colonization levels.
Quercetin treatment reduced wheal formation and scratching behavior in an ovalbumin-induced chronic urticaria mouse model.
Quercetin reduced eosinophilic infiltration and mast cell degranulation in the skin lesions of CU mice.
Quercetin treatment lowered serum levels of IgE, histamine, TNF-α, MCP-1, and IL-13 in the OVA-induced chronic urticaria mouse model.
Bioinformatic and multi-database analyses indicated that quercetin exerts therapeutic effects on chronic urticaria through the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway.
Quercetin upregulated CD300f expression in the skin of chronic urticaria mice and activated CD300f signaling.
Quercetin-induced CD300f activation led to downstream phosphorylation of SHP-1.

Quercetin bound to CD300f on LAD2 mast cells to inhibit IgE-mediated β-hexosaminidase release, histamine release, calcium influx, mast cell degranulation, and F-actin cytoskeleton remodeling by suppressing the AKT/IKK/NF-κB inflammatory pathway.
Overall, the study concludes quercetin alleviates chronic urticaria by activating the CD300f/SHP-1 signaling pathway to negatively regulate IgE-mediated mast cell activation.

Casein and whey protein hydrolysates reduced diarrhea, anxiety-like behavior, and visceral hypersensitivity in a mouse model of IBS induced by Citrobacter rodentium infection and water avoidance stress.
Casein and whey protein hydrolysates increased abundance of short-chain fatty acid-producing gut bacteria, including Alloprevotella and Alistipes, in IBS mice.
Whey protein hydrolysate significantly increased colonic mRNA levels of the tight junction protein zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) in IBS mice.
Whey protein hydrolysate significantly increased colonic mRNA levels of claudin-1 in IBS mice.
Casein hydrolysate significantly improved colonic mRNA levels of occludin in IBS mice.
Casein and whey protein hydrolysates decreased levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α in IBS mice.
The casein-derived peptide RGPF was identified as a COX2-inhibitory peptide with an IC50 of 0.36 mM, predicted to bind the COX2 active site via hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
The casein-derived peptide FPK was identified as a COX2-inhibitory peptide with an IC50 of 0.64 mM, predicted to bind the COX2 active site via hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
The casein-derived peptide NPW was identified as a COX2-inhibitory peptide with an IC50 of 1.10 mM, predicted to bind the COX2 active site via hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions.
A single-cell atlas of human peripheral nerves revealed cell type-specific transcriptional changes in diabetic peripheral neuropathy along with abnormal expansion of mast cells.
GLUT3-mediated glucose uptake under high-glucose diabetic conditions upregulates ERK1/2 phosphorylation in mouse mast cells.
Sustained high-glucose stimulation induces aberrant mTOR hyperactivity, causing endoplasmic reticulum stress and mitochondrial oxidative stress that impair mast cell mitochondrial function.
Dysregulated mast cells degranulate and release histamine, tryptase, and other inflammatory factors into the neural microenvironment, driving neuropathy in diabetic mice.
Mast cell-deficient mice were protected from nerve immune imbalance and progression of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, supporting a causal role for mast cells in disease progression.
Diclofenac etalhyaluronate (DEH) treatment had no effect on complement activation as measured by downstream complement cascade products in human plasma.
DEH showed no agonist activity at MRGPRX2, as measured by calcium influx in CHO-K1 cells stably expressing the receptor.
DEH did not induce direct mast cell degranulation in the human mast cell line LAD2.
DEH did not induce direct basophil activation, as assessed by expression of activation markers in the KU812 human basophil leukemia cell line.

The authors propose that DEH-induced anaphylaxis in non-IgE-mediated cases might instead result from non-immunological hypersensitivity due to cyclooxygenase-1 inhibition by the NSAID component of the drug, though this was not directly tested.
Female mice fed the MCD diet showed pronounced hepatic oxidative DNA damage (8-OHdG) compared to minimal expression in control diet-fed mice.
Both low- and high-dose CBG treatment significantly reduced hepatic 8-OHdG levels in MCD-diet-induced MASH mice.
MCD-diet-induced MASH mice showed increased leukocyte accumulation near hepatic arteries, portal veins, and bile ducts compared with control diet mice.
Both low- and high-dose CBG treatment decreased leukocyte infiltration in MASH mouse livers.
Low- and high-dose CBG treatment showed little to no improvement in hepatocellular ballooning in MASH mouse livers.
CBG treatment did not recover the MCD-diet-induced drop in liver-to-body weight ratio in female MASH mice, unlike the effect previously seen in male mice.
MCD-diet-fed mice exhibited enhanced hepatic fibrosis (collagen deposition) compared to control diet mice.
Both low- and high-dose CBG administration reduced fibrotic collagen deposition in MCD-diet-fed mouse livers.
CBG treatment (both doses) significantly reduced the number of hypertrophied, desmin-positive activated hepatic stellate cells compared to vehicle-treated MASH mice.
MCD-diet-fed mice showed increased CK19-positive cholangiocyte proliferation (ductular reaction) compared to control diet mice.
CBG treatment significantly reduced cholangiocyte proliferation (CK19+ ductular reaction) compared to the MCD diet group.
CD45+ leukocyte infiltration was significantly increased in MCD-diet-fed mouse livers compared to control diet mice, and significantly reduced by both CBG doses.
Hepatic monocyte-derived macrophage populations (CD11b+, Ly6C+, CD115+) were markedly increased in MCD-diet MASH mice compared to controls, by 5.4-, 13-, and 14-fold respectively.

Low-dose CBG reduced CD11b+, Ly6C+, and CD115+ cells by approximately 1.47-, 1.67-, and 2.2-fold, and high-dose CBG reduced these populations by 1.1-, 1.3-, and 1.5-fold respectively, compared to MCD-diet-fed mice.
Hepatic CD4+, CD8a+, and CD4+/CD8a+ T cell populations were increased 5.7-, 6.79-, and 9.36-fold respectively in MCD-diet MASH mice compared to controls.
CBG treatment reduced total CD3+ cells (low dose 1.84-fold, high dose ~1.36-fold) and CD4+, CD8a+, CD4+/CD8a+ subsets (low dose 1.96x/1.77x/2.02x; high dose 1.35x/1.53x/1.5x) in MASH mouse livers.
Hepatic mast cell tryptase-positive cells accumulated near the portal triad in MCD-diet MASH mice, with none observed in control mice.

Both low and high doses of CBG treatment decreased the activation and accumulation of hepatic mast cells (tryptase expression) in MCD-diet-fed mice, establishing CBG as a candidate mast cell stabilizer.

Co-localization of the mast cell IgE receptor FcεRI and TGF-β1 was increased in MCD-diet MASH mice, indicating TGF-β1 secretion from activated mast cells, and this was significantly reduced by CBG treatment.
CBG treatment significantly reduced mast-cell-associated FcεRI/TGF-β1 co-localization, supporting inhibition of TGF-β1 secretion from mast cells as a mechanism of CBG's antifibrotic effect.
Co-localized TGF-β1 and desmin (marking TGF-β1-driven HSC activation) was increased in MCD-diet-fed MASH mice and decreased with both low and high dosages of CBG treatment.
CBG treatment showed little or no change in hepatic lipid accumulation (steatosis) in female MASH mice, consistent with prior findings in male mice.

High-dose CBG worsened liver inflammation and fibrosis in male MASH and control mice in a prior study, whereas the same high dose showed anti-inflammatory and anti-fibrotic effects in female MASH mice, indicating male mice are more sensitive to CBG dosage than females.
Neuropathy of any type was detected in 89% of patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis.
Small fiber neuropathy (SFN), assessed via QST and skin biopsy, was present in 65% of patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis.
Combined small and large fiber neuropathy was seen in 48.1% of patients.
Pure large fiber neuropathy without small fiber involvement was found in 20% of patients.
Pure small fiber neuropathy without large fiber involvement was found in 10% of patients.
Older age was identified as a significant risk factor for developing small fiber neuropathy in AL amyloidosis.
Patients with SFN were significantly more likely to have soft tissue involvement compared to those without SFN.
SFN was associated with poorer overall survival after a median follow-up of 37.5 months.
SFN emerged as an independent prognostic factor for early mortality (within 12 months) in multivariate analysis.
In a cohort of 606 IBD patients followed over 18 years, 4 had myasthenia gravis, a prevalence of 0.66%, which was 8.56 times higher than the proportion of MG among all patients seen at the center.
Using the lowest and highest reported worldwide MG prevalence estimates, the prevalence ratio of MG in IBD patients versus the general population was even higher, ranging from 26.40 to 44.00.
A prior Swedish MG registry study found a 2.3-fold increased risk of Crohn's disease among MG patients.
The same Swedish MG registry study found a 2.1-fold increased risk of ulcerative colitis among MG patients.
A systematic literature review identified 23 papers describing 30 individual patients with concurrent IBD and myasthenia gravis.

Among the 30 literature-reviewed patients, MG most often preceded IBD diagnosis, by 3–15 years for Crohn's disease and 0.2–13 years for ulcerative colitis, though in a subset MG followed IBD diagnosis by 1–4 years.
Among the 30 literature-reviewed IBD-MG patients, 16 (5 CD, 11 UC) had a third additional autoimmune disease.

Among literature-reviewed IBD-MG patients tested for antibodies, 86.9% (20/23) were AChR-antibody positive while only one of very few tested was MUSK-antibody negative, and none were tested for LRP4 or agrin antibodies.
In the literature-reviewed IBD-MG patients, thymectomy improved MG in 54.5% (6/11) of those with reported outcomes, though one patient developed SLE and UC after thymectomy.

Across seven MG registries reporting associated autoimmune diseases, the prevalence of co-occurring IBD ranged from 0.35% in a cohort of 565 MG patients up to 2.56% among 39 MG patients older than 70 years.

Case Patient 1 (male, UC/CD with gastrocolonic fistula) had elevated AChR antibodies (10.7), positive P-ANCA (1:640), decreased TSH (0.2), and RNS decrement up to 22% at baseline that worsened to 31% after forced contraction; he was also diagnosed with small fiber neuropathy based on distal paresthesia and abnormal skin wrinkling test.

Case Patient 2 (female, UC with primary sclerosing cholangitis) had AChR antibodies above 20, positive ANA, normal IgG4, and abnormal skin wrinkling (mean score 0.5) consistent with small fiber neuropathy; her MG later required rituximab and IVIG, and she died of multiple complications.

Case Patient 3 (female, CD with prior fibromyalgia and later MS) was AChR-antibody negative with normal EMG/NCS and RNS, but had small fiber neuropathy confirmed by abnormal skin wrinkling (mean score 1.75) and borderline low vitamin B12 (227).

Case Patient 4 (female, CD with orbital pseudotumor) was the first reported anti-MUSK-antibody-positive MG case in IBD, with elevated anti-MUSK antibodies (0.09 NMOL/L), negative AChR antibodies, RNS facial nerve decrement >10%, low vitamin B12 (173), and small fiber neuropathy confirmed by abnormal skin wrinkling (mean score 0.5).

All four index IBD-MG patients had subtle small fiber neuropathy and low-borderline vitamin B12 levels, which may be partially explained by B12 deficiency (often autoimmune) though immune-mediated small fiber neuropathy could not be excluded.

Immunosuppressive treatment for IBD (prednisone, azathioprine, infliximab) may mask or delay MG diagnosis by partially or completely controlling myasthenic symptoms, a pattern also reported in prior literature.

The authors propose that shared HLA genotypes, common abnormalities in innate/adaptive immunity, a pro-inflammatory environment with Treg/Th17 imbalance, increased CXCL13 production, and gut-brain axis/vagal innervation of the thymus may explain the MG-IBD association, though this was not directly tested.

The authors propose that Type II autoimmune pancreatitis (an IBD extraintestinal manifestation) may share pathomechanisms with anti-AChR MG via overexpression of the cell adhesion molecule Mad-1, while Type I autoimmune pancreatitis, part of the IgG4-related disease spectrum, may parallel anti-MUSK MG; up to 4% of IBD patients have elevated IgG4 levels.
Pyridostigmine treatment did not exacerbate gastrointestinal symptoms in the index patients, consistent with most other published reports.
In the literature review, colectomy was associated with variable MG outcomes: two patients experienced total regression of MG after colectomy, while three others developed MG after colectomy.
IENFD below the 5th percentile, consistent with small-fiber neuropathy, was found in 80% of patients with Tarlov cysts using the Collongues et al normative reference data.
IENFD below the 5th percentile was found in 72% of patients with Tarlov cysts using the Lauria et al worldwide normative dataset.
80% of surveyed Tarlov cyst patients reported neuropathic pain.
76% of surveyed Tarlov cyst patients reported allodynia.
93% of surveyed Tarlov cyst patients reported pain while sitting.
11% of surveyed Tarlov cyst patients reported anal sphincter problems.
66% of surveyed Tarlov cyst patients reported urinary sphincter problems.
27% of patients with Tarlov cysts reported persistent genital arousal, a symptom potentially linked to small-fiber neuropathy or elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure.
54% of patients with Tarlov cysts reported restless legs symptoms.
41% of patients with Tarlov cysts reported early satiety, consistent with autonomic dysfunction.
93% of patients with Tarlov cysts reported bladder dysfunction, consistent with autonomic dysfunction.
88% of patients with Tarlov cysts reported bowel dysfunction, consistent with autonomic dysfunction.
51% of patients with Tarlov cysts reported increased sweating, consistent with autonomic dysfunction.
45% of patients with Tarlov cysts reported Raynaud's phenomenon, consistent with autonomic/vascular dysfunction.
Headache was reported by 57% of patients with Tarlov cysts, a symptom potentially linked to elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure.
Fatigue was reported by 86% of patients with Tarlov cysts, a symptom potentially linked to elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure.
Cognitive issues were reported by 86% of patients with Tarlov cysts, a symptom potentially linked to elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure.
Pulsatile tinnitus was reported by 59% of patients with Tarlov cysts, a symptom potentially linked to elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure.

The authors propose that elevated pulsatile cerebrospinal fluid pressure within the nerve root sheath drives Tarlov cyst formation at the dorsal root ganglion and may progressively damage small nerve fibers there, contributing to small-fiber dysfunction.
Serum TGFβ1 levels did not differ significantly among PSP, PD, MSA, and healthy control groups.
Serum LAP-TGFβ1 levels did not differ significantly among PSP, PD, MSA, and healthy control groups.
TGFβ1 levels in the total extracellular vesicle (EV) population did not differ significantly across PSP, PD, MSA, and HC.
LAP-TGFβ1 levels in the total extracellular vesicle (EV) population did not differ significantly across PSP, PD, MSA, and HC.
TGFβ1 levels in neuronally-derived extracellular vesicles (NDEVs) were markedly increased in PSP patients compared with PD, MSA, and healthy controls.
LAP-TGFβ1 levels in neuronally-derived extracellular vesicles (NDEVs) were markedly increased in PSP patients compared with PD, MSA, and healthy controls.
TGFβ1/LAP-TGFβ1 were detectable in NDEVs of all PSP patients, but were below detection limit in 25.0% of MSA, 71.8% of PD, and 100% of HC.
NDEV TGFβ1 showed excellent diagnostic performance distinguishing PSP from other parkinsonian syndromes and from healthy controls.
NDEV LAP-TGFβ1 showed perfect diagnostic performance distinguishing PSP from other parkinsonian syndromes and from healthy controls with no overlap.
Within the PSP cohort, NDEV TGFβ1 and LAP-TGFβ1 levels did not differ between PSP-Richardson's syndrome and other PSP variant subtypes.
NDEV TGFβ1 and LAP-TGFβ1 levels were not associated with age, sex, disease severity, or presence of inflammatory/autoimmune comorbidities.

In midbrain organoids derived from iPSCs of four PSP-RS patients, TGFβ1 and LAP-TGFβ1 levels were higher than in organoids derived from healthy control iPSCs, validating the NDEV findings in a preclinical disease model.

Serum LAP-TGFβ1 results measured by ELISA in this study contradicted a prior preliminary study by the same group that found increased serum LAP-TGFβ1 in PSP vs HC using proximity extension assay (PEA) technology.

About one third of older COVID-19 hospitalization survivors experienced persistent symptoms continuously through 12 months post-discharge.
Fatigue was the most common persistent symptom, reported in 28% of the cohort.
Myalgia was a common persistent symptom, reported in 19% of the cohort.
Dyspnea was a common persistent symptom, reported in 13% of the cohort.

Having two or more persistent symptoms doubled the risk of decline in instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) over one year.
Having two or more persistent symptoms was associated with a more than doubled risk of falls over one year.

Among women, having at least one persistent post-COVID symptom was associated with roughly twice the risk of decline in basic activities of daily living.

Approximately 76% of adult All of Us participants with EHR data had multiple chronic conditions (MCC), and over 40% had six or more chronic conditions.

The proportion of participants diagnosed with six or more chronic conditions rose substantially with age, from about a third in early adulthood to over two-thirds in advanced old age.

Participants with MCC differed significantly from those with 0-1 conditions across demographic characteristics, being older and more likely to be male, White, non-Hispanic/Latino, insured, ever married, and not currently employed (including higher retirement rates).
In early adulthood, the most frequently occurring multiple-chronic-condition combination involved anxiety disorders together with depression, bipolar disorder, or other depressive mood disorders.
In late adulthood and advanced old age, the most frequently occurring multiple-chronic-condition combination was hyperlipidemia together with hypertension.

A significantly higher proportion of ME/CFS participants had evidence of prior Dengue virus exposure than controls, though based on very few individuals.

Correlations between eotaxin/CCL11 and other plasma factors were present in healthy controls but absent in the ME/CFS group.

Cytokine differences observed locally in CSF between ME/CFS subgroups were not mirrored by differences in plasma cytokine levels.
Plasma IL-7 was significantly elevated in CSF Cluster 1 patients compared to both Cluster 2 patients and healthy controls.

Analysis of ME/CFS-related tweets found the majority conveyed neutral or negative sentiment, with only 12% classified as positive.

The proportion of negative ME/CFS-related tweets increased from 36.7% to 49.9% and positive tweets increased from 11.1% to 14.3% across the pre-COVID-19, post-COVID-19, and post-NICE-guideline periods, with statistically significant differences across all comparisons.
LDA topic modeling of ME/CFS-related tweets identified distinct topics corresponding to fibromyalgia and post-COVID-19 condition (PCC), reflecting these as prominent comorbid discussion topics.
Thematic frequency analysis found 8.9% of ME/CFS tweets discussed PCC, 4.18% discussed research, 2.59% discussed fibromyalgia, 1.78% discussed treatment, and 0.3% discussed the UK NICE guideline.

Thematic analysis found that patients with ME/CFS and fibromyalgia frequently expressed frustration with categorization of their illness as psychological or psychosomatic and with dismissal by physicians, friends, and family.
Tweets discussing ME/CFS research funding highlighted severe underfunding relative to other diseases, citing NIH figures of $13 million in active ME/CFS awards versus $3294 million for HIV/AIDS.

The PACE trial randomized 641 ME/CFS patients to pacing, CBT, GET, or specialist medical care and found CBT and GET more effective than pacing or specialist care for reducing fatigue and improving physical functioning.
Only 5% of ME/CFS patients experience full recovery without targeted intervention, whereas observational studies report an 18% recovery rate following cognitive behavioral therapy.
The global prevalence of ME/CFS has been estimated at 0.89%, with higher prevalence among women aged 40 to 50 years.
Female sex and psychological factors have been identified as risk factors for developing post-COVID-19 condition (PCC).

A tweet quoted a study reporting that individuals with both ME/CFS and long COVID had significantly impaired endothelial function.
A systematic review found that stigma is associated with increased pain intensity, disability, and depression among people living with chronic pain.

Tweets reflected patient belief that the 2021 NICE guideline update reclassified ME/CFS as a physiological/neurological condition rather than a psychological one, placing it under the Neurological Conditions section.

Prospective studies controlling for ascertainment bias failed to show an association between acute infection and development of ME/CFS, while other studies found associations between ME/CFS onset and elevated premorbid stress, psychopathology, or severe life events.

Tweets proposing a shared biological etiology between ME/CFS and PCC cited variable hypotheses including immunopathology, microclots, brainstem malfunction, chronic inflammation, respiratory muscle dysfunction, and mitochondrial aberrations.

ME/CFS patients exhibit altered antibody responses, including production of IgG reactive with gut microbial antigens, though whether these antibodies are pathogenic or protective is unclear.

Post-exertional malaise is described as a cardinal symptom present in 95% of individuals with ME/CFS.

An ultrasound-measured increase in plantar gapping of ≥1.1 mm at the first metatarsocuneiform joint diagnosed first ray hypermobility with good sensitivity and high specificity.

Ultrasound-measured dorsal translation, plantar gapping, and medial gapping did not significantly differ between symptomatic and asymptomatic hallux valgus feet.
Prolotherapy significantly reduced pain and crepitus VAS scores from a mean of 7 at baseline to 1.85 by the end of six months.
Tenderness of the muscles of mastication significantly decreased from baseline to the end of the sixth month following prolotherapy.
Maximum inter-incisal mouth opening increased numerically from baseline to 34.98 mm by six months but did not reach statistical significance.
The association between pain score and mouth opening before versus after prolotherapy was borderline significant.
The first-needle success rate for the prolotherapy injection protocol was 91.3%.
The only notable adverse effects were mild, transient paresthesia in 3 patients and a transient eyelid spasm/ptosis in 1 patient, with no permanent facial nerve damage or bruising.
Most enrolled patients (72%) declined to undergo the prolotherapy procedure, largely due to fear and anxiety about the injection technique.
At baseline, preauricular pain and restricted mouth opening were the most common signs (64%), followed by intra-auricular pain (40%), muscle tenderness (36%), and crepitus (32%).
Symptom variables differed between patients who opted for prolotherapy and those who declined, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.
Peripheral plasma C5a concentration was significantly higher in female fibromyalgia patients than in female healthy controls.
In healthy controls, higher C5a levels correlated with a higher (more sensitive) cold pain threshold, but this correlation was absent in fibromyalgia patients.
In healthy controls, higher C5a levels correlated with a lower warm pain threshold, but this correlation was absent in fibromyalgia patients.
No correlation was found between C5a level and self-reported pain intensity (VAS) in either the healthy control or fibromyalgia groups.
After propensity score matching on age, WBC, CRP, C3 and C4 to control for background inflammation, C5a remained significantly higher in the fibromyalgia group than in matched healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients reported significantly higher average pain intensity over one week compared to healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients had a significantly higher (more sensitive) cold pain threshold than healthy controls, while warm pain threshold did not differ significantly between groups.
White blood cell count was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Levels of CRP, C3, and C4 did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
No correlation was found between C5a and its upstream complement proteins C3 and C4.
Serum prealbumin levels were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Platelet counts were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
CRP levels were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
The CRP/prealbumin ratio was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
Lymphocyte counts were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients compared to healthy controls.
CRP levels showed a weak positive correlation with Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores, suggesting a link with disease severity.
Fibromyalgia patients with Type D personality had significantly higher depression scores (BDI) than fibromyalgia patients without Type D personality and healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients with Type D personality had significantly higher anxiety scores (BAI) than fibromyalgia patients without Type D personality and healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients with Type D personality had significantly higher somatosensory amplification scores (SAS) than fibromyalgia patients without Type D personality and healthy controls.
Widespread Pain Index (WPI) scores were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients with Type D personality than in those without it.
Symptom Severity (SS) scale scores (fatigue, cognitive complaints, sleep disturbance) were significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients with Type D personality than in those without it.
Type D personality scale scores (total and subtypes) showed a strong positive correlation with depression scores in fibromyalgia patients.
Type D personality scale scores (total and subtypes) showed a strong positive correlation with anxiety scores in fibromyalgia patients.
Type D personality scale scores (total and subtypes) showed a strong positive correlation with somatosensory amplification scores in fibromyalgia patients.
The total effect of Type D personality severity on fibromyalgia symptom severity was not statistically significant in the mediation model.
The direct effect of Type D personality severity on fibromyalgia symptom severity, independent of somatosensory amplification, was not statistically significant.

Somatosensory amplification significantly mediated the relationship between Type D personality severity and fibromyalgia symptom severity, with the indirect effect being statistically significant while total/direct effects were not, indicating a moderate mediation effect explaining ~15% of variance in FM severity.
The frequency of personal history of psychiatric illness was significantly higher in fibromyalgia patients with Type D personality compared to other groups.

Familial history of psychiatric illness and familial fibromyalgia was significantly more frequent in fibromyalgia patients with Type D personality compared to other groups, suggesting a possible familial/genetic predisposition component.
Up to 50% of patients with chronic urticaria are reported to be resistant to antihistamine treatment.
Many patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis continue to suffer severe symptoms even when treated with antihistamine doses four times the approved dose.
After mast cell activation, extracellular local histamine concentrations can reach 10-1000 µM, vastly exceeding the <100 nM local tissue free drug concentrations achieved by many antihistamines.

Careful analysis of human clinical studies using exogenous histamine challenge and endogenous mast cell activation with prophylactic antihistamine pretreatment shows the assumed efficacy of antihistamines rapidly diminishes.

The review proposes that prostaglandin E2 normally suppresses mast cell activation and maintains immune homeostasis, and that its reduction may link NSAID use and menstrual cycle hormonal fluctuations as cofactors in food-dependent anaphylaxis.

NSAIDs are described as disrupting gastrointestinal integrity, reducing PGE2 synthesis via COX inhibition, and promoting mast cell activation, thereby exacerbating food allergy symptoms as a known cofactor.

The review states that hormonal fluctuations during the menstrual cycle affect the COX pathway, modulating mast cell activation and allergic sensitivities, positioning menstruation as an under-recognized cofactor in food allergy.
FcεRI aggregation triggers p38α signaling that stimulates Ets-1 transcription via recruitment of the SWI-SNF chromatin-remodeling complex in IgE-stimulated mast cells.
Pcyt1a expression and downstream glycerophospholipid metabolism are induced in IgE-stimulated mast cells as a consequence of the p38α-Ets-1-SWI/SNF signaling axis.
Pcyt1a-driven glycerophospholipid metabolism promotes mast cell degranulation by enabling limited macropinocytosis of FcεRI.
Glycerophospholipid metabolism alters H3K9me3 histone deposition at the Prkcd gene promoter, linking lipid metabolism to epigenetic regulation of FcεRI-mediated signaling in mast cells.

Glycerophospholipid metabolism acts as a driver of allergic diseases such as atopic dermatitis, supported by murine model data, in silico analysis of human disease datasets, and examination of clinical samples.
In a murine model of allergic rhinitis, administration of IL-21 significantly reduced symptoms and serum concentrations of ovalbumin-specific IgE.
IL-21 inhibits IgE secretion from B cells stimulated by the combination of CD40 ligand and IL-4.
IL-21 treatment suppressed IgE class switch recombination in splenic B cells of anaphylactic mice, significantly decreasing total and allergen-specific serum IgE.
IL-21 receptor signaling was shown to influence Th2 immune responses, which are closely tied to allergic reactions and IgE production.

Binding of IgE to FcεRI induces a transition from low- to high-affinity state accompanied by conformational (bending/straightening) changes in IgE, mechanically stabilizing the complex and priming mast cells for activation.
Mast cell activation induces rapid actin filament polymerization forming membrane protrusions/lamellipodia that drive secretory granule movement toward the plasma membrane during degranulation.
Microtubule reorganization creates tracks that guide secretory granule transport toward the plasma membrane, essential for efficient mast cell degranulation.
Increased extracellular matrix/substrate stiffness has been associated with heightened mast cell activation and enhanced release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine.
Increased ECM stiffness has been associated with enhanced T cell activation and proliferation, potentially amplifying immune responses in allergic reactions.
Stiffer extracellular matrices can induce a pro-inflammatory phenotype in macrophages, altering their cytokine secretion and tissue remodeling activity in allergic disease.

Mechanosensitive receptor activation (e.g., integrins) triggers MAPK signaling (ERK, JNK, p38), which can amplify mast cell degranulation and release of pro-inflammatory mediators in Type 1 hypersensitivity.

Rho GTPases regulate actin cytoskeleton organization and cytoskeletal remodeling required for granule exocytosis, thereby modulating mast cell activation and degranulation and immune cell migration to allergen exposure sites.

Allergen-induced IgE cross-linking activates integrin-mediated focal adhesion signaling, recruiting focal adhesion kinase (FAK) which contributes to cytoskeletal rearrangement, MAPK activation, mast cell degranulation, and immune cell migration/cytokine release.
Recent findings suggest that, similar to mast cells, basophils may possess mechanosensitive channels contributing to their activation and degranulation during allergic responses.
Eosinophils can respond to mechanical cues within tissue extracellular matrix, which may influence their migratory behavior during allergic responses.
Among 16 patients with suspected small fiber neuropathy following COVID-19 vaccination, 9 fulfilled diagnostic criteria for SFN based on clinical and electrophysiological data.

The authors argue that establishing causality between COVID-19 vaccination and small fiber neuropathy is difficult, but temporal association and analogies with other vaccinations and infections support a possible causal hypothesis.

A 75-year-old woman with idiopathic small-fiber neuropathy undergoing cardiac CTA for exertional fatigue and dyspnea was incidentally found to have a 16-mm wide-neck Windsock aneurysm of the interventricular septum along with a patent foramen ovale and left-to-right shunting.
Among 17 SFN patients with ongoing spontaneous pain, microneurography identified pathological (hyperactive or hypoactive) C-nociceptors.
A significantly greater proportion of hyperactive nociceptors was found in patients whenever ongoing spontaneous pain was present in the examined foot area (OSPF).
At the individual patient level, there was no significant correlation between the rating of ongoing spontaneous pain and the proportion of hyperactive nociceptor fibers.
Pain ratings to electrical sinusoidal stimulation (eSS) were higher in patients with ongoing spontaneous pain in the foot (OSPF group) compared to those without.
Ratings of pain to electrical sinusoidal stimulation correlated with the proportion of hyperactive nerve fibers observed via microneurography.

Spontaneous activity and mechanical sensitization of predominantly mechano-insensitive C-fibers (CMi) are proposed as potential biomarkers for ongoing pain in SFN, and CMi dysfunction is not captured by IENFD or QST.
Microneurography detects C-nociceptor dysfunction relevant to ongoing pain that is not revealed by conventional quantitative sensory testing (QST) or intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD).
A heterozygous FBN1 missense variant (c.701G>A, p.Gly234Asp) in the first hybrid domain was identified in a family with nonsyndromic isolated aortic dissection across two generations.
Homozygous Fbn1G234D/G234D mice die suddenly starting at 3 weeks of age with 50% mortality by 5 weeks, while heterozygous mutants are healthy with a normal lifespan.
Aortic root and ascending aorta diameters progressively increased in mutant mice starting at 3 weeks of age, measured by echocardiography.

Elastic laminae in mutant ascending aortas showed breaks and fragmentation evident as early as 1 week of age, with disrupted contact between elastic fibers and smooth muscle cells, culminating in multiple intimomedial tears by 5 weeks.

FBN1 immunostaining was substantially decreased in the aortic media of mutant mice as early as postnatal day 3, persisting to 3 weeks, though FBN1 was upregulated in the subendothelial layer by 5 weeks as lesions expanded.

Primary smooth muscle cells from mutant mice showed delayed elastogenesis in vitro, forming far fewer elastin fibers by day 10 and requiring an additional 6 days to form fibers compared with wild-type SMCs.
Endothelial cells in mutant aortas failed to align with blood flow, showed reduced surface area and increased roundness, and upregulated VCAM-1 expression from 1 week of age.
CD45-positive immune cell infiltration increased over time in mutant aortas, initially in the adventitia at 1 week, then spreading into the intima and infiltrating the media by 3-5 weeks.

Single-cell RNA sequencing identified three monocyte/macrophage subclusters in AD aortas: MHCII+ resident inflammatory macrophages present by 3 weeks, CD206+Lyve1+ protective adventitial resident macrophages, and a CCR2+ bone marrow-derived monocyte/macrophage population that markedly expanded by 5 weeks with plasticity toward M1/M2-like states.

Differential expression analysis of smooth muscle cells showed upregulation of ECM genes Tnc, Acan, and Col18a1, and downregulation of elastic/collagen fiber genes Mfap4, Mfap5, and Pcolce2 in AD aortas compared with WT.
Higher levels of ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 were observed at intimomedial tear sites in AD aortas at 5 weeks, with no significant difference between inner and outer curvature.

Phosphorylated NF-κB was significantly upregulated in the ascending aorta of 3-week-old AD mice before dissection onset, along with significantly higher pStat1 and pStat3 levels, colocalizing with CD45-positive cells.
In situ gelatin zymography revealed high matrix metalloproteinase activity localized to intimomedial tears in AD aortas.

Macrophage depletion with clodronate liposomes reduced adventitial macrophages but did not improve survival or elastic lamina quality, and did not affect CD45+ intimal cells, CCR2+ or MHCII+ macrophages, or pNF-κB/pStat3 levels.

In vitro binding assays showed that mutant FBN1 fragment rF23-G234D had markedly reduced secretion and significantly impaired binding to LTBP-1, -2, and -4, while binding to FBLN4 and FBLN5 was unaffected.

Contrary to the canonical increased TGFβ signaling seen in Marfan syndrome models, pSmad2 and pERK1/2 were not upregulated (pSmad2 was decreased) in AD aortas compared with WT, indicating failed activation of TGFβ signaling due to the G234D mutation.

A related FBN1 variant, Gly234Val, was previously reported in a large Danish Marfan family with high penetrance of fatal aortic dissection and is listed in ClinVar with conflicting pathogenicity classifications.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT) was identified in 9 of 153 subjects (6.4%), all of whom had celiac disease with ongoing symptoms.
Among patients with persisting symptoms on a gluten-free diet, the prevalence of HαT was 12.3%.
Excluding HαT-positive subjects, basal serum tryptase levels were significantly higher in celiac disease patients compared with those with non-celiac gluten sensitivity.
Duodenal mast cell counts were significantly higher in celiac disease patients compared with controls.
Duodenal mast cell counts were 24% higher in HαT-positive celiac disease patients than in HαT-negative celiac disease patients.
Mast cell counts did not differ based on the presence of villous atrophy or clinical presentation among celiac disease patients.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia is caused by increased copy number of the TPSAB1 gene encoding alpha-tryptase, leading to elevated basal serum tryptase.
The prevalence of hereditary alpha-tryptasemia among celiac disease patients (6.4%) was similar to that reported in the general population.
The authors recommend that evaluation for hereditary alpha-tryptasemia be considered in managing celiac disease patients with persisting gastrointestinal symptoms despite a gluten-free diet.

Acute ingestion of 3 g L-arginine did not significantly alter heart rate variability or cardiovascular (heart rate, blood pressure) recovery compared to placebo after submaximal exercise in healthy young men.
A trend toward faster vagal reactivation, measured by rMSSD, was observed with L-arginine intake, but the effect size was small and not clinically meaningful.
Both L-arginine and placebo protocols showed significant time-based changes in HRV and cardiovascular variables during the 20-minute post-exercise period, reflecting normal physiological recovery.
Baseline serum ADMA levels were significantly higher in type 2 diabetic patients with neuropathy compared to diabetic control subjects without neuropathy.
Six months of α-lipoic acid (ALA) treatment significantly decreased serum ADMA levels in diabetic neuropathy patients.
Plasma nitrite (NO) concentration significantly increased after 6 months of ALA treatment in diabetic neuropathy patients.
Serum TNF-α levels significantly decreased after 6-month ALA treatment in diabetic neuropathy patients.
Current perception threshold (CPT), a measure of peripheral small- and large-fibre sensory nerve function, significantly improved after 6 months of ALA treatment.
Composite Autonomic Score (CAS), reflecting cardiac autonomic neuropathy severity, significantly decreased (improved) after ALA treatment.
Current perception threshold (CPT) values were higher in diabetic neuropathy patients before ALA treatment compared to diabetic control subjects.
Composite Autonomic Score (CAS) was higher in diabetic neuropathy patients before ALA treatment compared to diabetic control subjects.
VCAM-1 levels were significantly higher in diabetic neuropathy patients compared to control subjects both before and after ALA treatment.
No significant changes were observed in BMI, glucose, creatinine, uric acid, HbA1c, VCAM-1, ICAM-1, or lipid parameters after ALA treatment in the patient group.
Improvement in current perception threshold (CPT) after ALA treatment correlated positively with the decrease in ADMA levels.
Change in TNF-α levels was positively correlated with change in ADMA levels after ALA treatment.
Changes in ICAM-1 concentrations correlated positively with changes in VCAM-1 levels after ALA treatment.
Changes in ICAM-1 concentrations correlated positively with changes in TNF-α levels after ALA treatment.
Improvement in peripheral sensory nerve function (CPT) was significantly correlated with the decrease in cardiac autonomic neuropathy severity (CAS) after ALA treatment.
Patients classified as CPT-defined responders to ALA treatment showed significantly greater decreases in ADMA levels than non-responders.
Patients classified as CAS-defined responders to ALA treatment showed significantly greater decreases in ADMA levels than non-responders.
In IBS-D patients sensitised to grass, the mean GSRS score significantly increased from T0 (outside pollination season) to T1 (during pollination season).
The lower gastrointestinal component of the GSRS score significantly increased across seasons in grass-sensitised IBS-D patients, while the upper GI component remained unchanged.
VAS scores for abdominal pain/distension significantly increased during pollination season only in grass-sensitised IBS-D patients.
In IBS-D patients sensitised to house dust mite (a perennial allergen used as positive control), no significant seasonal variation in GSRS or VAS scores was observed.
Unsensitised IBS-D patients showed no significant change in GSRS or VAS scores between pollination and non-pollination periods, serving as a negative control.
In the overall IBS cohort (all subtypes), a non-significant trend towards increased lower-GI GSRS scores was observed in grass-sensitised patients during the pollen season.

In a bivariate regression model of IBS-D symptom variability (GSRS), male sex was the only covariate significantly associated with greater symptom variation among sex, age, atopy history, allergic comorbidities, and total/specific IgE levels.
Nearly 50% of both the overall IBS cohort and the IBS-D subgroup were sensitised to either grass or house dust mite aeroallergens.

The authors cite prior evidence that atopic disorders (seasonal allergic rhinitis, eczema) are associated with a higher likelihood of developing IBS, and that in mouse models allergic airway disease triggers colonic mucosal immune activation with elevated tryptase, a marker of mast cell degranulation.

The IBS cohort had frequent atopic comorbidities, most commonly respiratory manifestations (allergic rhinitis and asthma), while eczema and nasal polyposis were not observed in the IBS-D subgroup; serum IgE and eosinophil counts were similar across groups.

K-prototypes clustering of UK Biobank chronic pain participants based on age, sex, and number of pain sites identified five optimal clusters, reducing total dissimilarity cost from 131,738.3 to 53,833.8.
The 'Fibromyalgia-like pain' (FP) cluster (11.2% of cohort) comprised mostly individuals reporting pain all over the body (90.4%) across all ages, with females predominating (71.7%).
The 'Multisite pain' (MP) cluster (17.9% of cohort) consisted of individuals aged over 60 who all reported pain at multiple sites, with females predominating (77.5%).
The 'Elderly with regional pain' (ERP) cluster (23.5% of cohort) predominantly comprised males (67.1%) over 65 years with fewer pain sites and the least socioeconomic deprivation.
Depression over the past six months was reported by 38% of the FP (fibromyalgia-like pain) cluster compared to under 10% of the ERP cluster, with FP median PHQ-9 score of 6 (IQR 3–11).
Fatigue lasting six months or more was reported by 63.9% of the FP cluster, decreasing to about one-third in MP and YRP, and about 20% in MRP and ERP.
Unrefreshing sleep as a moderate to severe problem was reported by 58.9% of the FP cluster compared to over 70% of other clusters experiencing only mild or no issues.

Cognitive symptoms (memory, thinking skills, concentration problems) were reported by more than half of individuals in the FP and MP clusters, versus about one-third in other clusters, with over 20% of FP reporting moderate-to-severe issues.
Overall health was rated lowest in the FP cluster (median EQ-VAS score 61, IQR 40–77.2), followed by MP (median 75, IQR 60–86), with all other clusters scoring above 80.

Multinomial logistic regression showed that membership in the MP, YRP, MRP, and ERP clusters was significantly associated with a decreased relative risk of adverse health outcomes (depression, sleep, cognition, fatigue, mobility, overall health) compared to the FP reference cluster, with MRP and ERP showing the lowest risk.
Membership in the Younger with regional pain (YRP) cluster was associated with the lowest relative risk of mobility problems among all clusters.

Osteoarthritis was the most common pain-associated condition overall (30.2%), followed by migraine (16.1%) and non-diabetic neuropathy/nerve damage (9.9%), with over 60% of FP and MP cluster members reporting osteoarthritis and about one-third reporting migraine.
A higher proportion of rheumatoid arthritis and gout was observed in the Middle age with regional pain (MRP) and Elderly with regional pain (ERP) clusters compared to other clusters.
Widespread pain clusters (FP, MP) reported longer pain durations than regional pain clusters, with 62.5% of FP and 44.1% of MP living with pain for more than five years.

Nearly half (45.6%) of individuals in the FP cluster reported living with three or more pain-associated conditions, compared to over 60% in most other clusters having only one or no pain-associated conditions.

In contrast to a prior middle-aged osteoarthritis cohort study finding younger participants (50-64 years) had more pain sites, this study found that younger UK Biobank participants (under 60 years) experienced fewer pain sites.
More than 88% of chronic overlapping pain condition (COPC) progression trajectories identified in the All of Us cohort were reproducible in the independent Mayo Data Warehouse cohort.
Female COPC/mental-condition trajectories encompassed more than 96% of the trajectories seen in males, indicating a substantially broader disease progression pattern in women.
Chronic low back pain generally emerges earlier in the disease course than other chronic overlapping pain conditions.
Fibromyalgia tends to develop later in the trajectory, typically following the onset of other chronic overlapping pain conditions.
Endometriosis appears to be associated with an increased prevalence of chronic overlapping pain conditions in women.

Longer chronic overlapping pain condition progression trajectories (i.e., a greater number of prior conditions) are associated with a greater risk of developing an additional COPC or mental health condition.

Passive transfer of IgG purified from a fibromyalgia patient caused mechanical hyperalgesia (reduced paw withdrawal threshold) in mice by day 4, which normalised by day 14, compared with healthy control IgG.
FMS-IgG passive transfer also induced cold hyperalgesia (reduced withdrawal latency) in mice by day 4, resolving by day 14, relative to HC-IgG.
FMS-IgG injection reduced forelimb grip strength in mice at day 7 compared with HC-IgG, consistent with reduced muscular power previously reported.
FMS-IgG did not alter hind paw pinch pain threshold in mice compared with HC-IgG.
FMS-IgG injected male mice showed no difference from HC-IgG mice in zero-maze anxiety/locomotion testing at day 14.

Pooled IgG from 18 PACS patients with high pain/fatigue burden failed to induce mechanical hyperalgesia, cold hyperalgesia, reduced grip strength, or pinch hypersensitivity in mice compared with pooled IgG from 18 recovered COVID-19 individuals.
Mice injected with pooled PACS-IgG showed no difference in Y-maze spatial working memory compared with recovered-IgG injected mice, indicating no transfer of cognitive symptoms.

IgG from UK fibromyalgia patients showed significantly increased binding to satellite glial cells in vitro compared with healthy control IgG, cross-validating previous Swedish and Canadian FMS cohort findings.

Human IgG binding on satellite glial cells co-localised more closely with the surface marker MHC class I than with the intracellular marker glutamine synthetase, suggesting the autoantibody target is a cell-surface antigen.

In vivo exposure to FMS- or HC-IgG prior to DRG harvest reduced subsequent in vitro SGC surface IgG binding in both groups, with a larger reduction in the FMS group, abolishing the FMS>HC staining difference seen with in vitro-only incubation.

Pooled serum IgG from both high-symptom-burden PACS groups (G1, G2) and a recovered COVID-19 group (RC2) showed very high and indistinguishable SGC staining, all stronger than the FMS positive control.

Recovered COVID-19 individuals reporting no pain or fatigue showed equally strong anti-SGC IgG staining as the high-symptom-burden PACS groups, indicating that anti-SGC titre alone does not explain PACS pain symptoms.
A single vaccinated healthy control with a prior COVID-19 infection showed low anti-SGC antibody titres, suggesting vaccination may reduce off-target autoantibody responses after infection.

Both PACS and FMS are associated with anti-SGC IgG serum autoantibodies, but only FMS-IgG, not PACS-IgG, was pronociceptive on passive transfer, indicating anti-SGC autoreactivity occurs after COVID-19 infection irrespective of pain symptoms.
1.1% of UK Biobank participants (5,354 individuals) were linked to at least one piece of evidence for ME/CFS, a higher proportion than most prevalence estimates.
Only about a third (36%, n=1,922) of individuals with any ME/CFS evidence had two or more independent pieces of supporting evidence, partly due to missing data.
ME/CFS status defined by ICD-10 code G93.3 (post-viral fatigue syndrome) was the data type most likely to be corroborated by another line of evidence (72%).
ME/CFS status defined by Pain Questionnaire responses was the least likely to be corroborated by another data type (43%), partly due to data missingness.
The authors conclude that ME/CFS status in UK Biobank, and potentially other biobanks, is best defined using multiple concordant lines of evidence rather than a single data source.

Using the most consistent evidence and accounting for bed- or house-bound individuals unable to participate in UK Biobank, the authors revised the estimated UK ME/CFS prevalence upward to 410,000 people.
Genetically predicted higher circulating TNF levels were associated with a decreased risk of ME/CFS in the IVW MR analysis.
Genetically predicted increased CXCL5 levels were associated with elevated risk of ME/CFS.
Genetically predicted increased CCL20 levels were associated with elevated risk of ME/CFS.
Higher genetically predicted levels of CD8+ natural killer T cells as a percentage of T cells and lymphocytes were significantly linked to increased ME/CFS risk.
Higher genetically predicted CD19 expression on IgD+ CD38- B cells was significantly linked to an increased risk of ME/CFS.
A genetically predicted higher absolute monocyte count was significantly linked to an increased risk of ME/CFS.
Higher genetically predicted CD80 expression on CD62L+ myeloid dendritic cells was significantly linked to increased ME/CFS risk.
A higher genetically predicted percentage of activated and secreting CD4 regulatory T cells among CD4 Tregs was significantly linked to increased ME/CFS risk.
Higher genetically predicted CD80 expression on myeloid dendritic cells was significantly linked to increased ME/CFS risk.
Higher genetically predicted CD3 expression on naive CD8+ T cells was significantly linked to a decreased risk of ME/CFS.
Higher genetically predicted CD3 expression on CD28+ CD45RA- CD8+ T cells was significantly linked to a decreased risk of ME/CFS.
Higher genetically predicted FSC-A (cell size marker) on CD8+ T cells was significantly linked to a decreased risk of ME/CFS.
A higher genetically predicted percentage of TCRγδ T cells among lymphocytes was significantly linked to a decreased risk of ME/CFS.
Higher genetically predicted CD19 expression on memory B cells was significantly linked to a decreased risk of ME/CFS.
A higher genetically predicted percentage of TCRγδ T cells among T cells was significantly linked to a decreased risk of ME/CFS.
CD80 expression on CD62L+ myeloid dendritic cells was causally associated with reduced CXCL5 levels in follow-up MR analysis exploring upstream relationships.
CD3 expression on naive CD8+ T cells was causally associated with lower CCL20 levels in follow-up MR analysis.
CD3 expression on CD28+ CD45RA- CD8+ T cells was causally associated with lower CCL20 levels in follow-up MR analysis.
Mediation analysis found that inflammatory cytokines (CXCL5, CCL20) did not significantly mediate the causal relationship between immune cell traits and ME/CFS risk.

Healthy male controls showed a significant 1.9-fold increase in circulating EV concentration 24h after maximal exercise compared to baseline, whereas ME/CFS patients' EV concentration returned to near-baseline levels, indicating failure to mount an exercise-induced EV response.

PRKAR2A protein levels in EVs were consistently decreased in ME/CFS patients compared with controls at baseline, 15 min, and 24h postexercise, indicating persistent dysregulation independent of exercise.
DARS1 (Aspartyl-tRNA synthetase 1) protein levels in EVs were consistently decreased in ME/CFS patients compared with controls across all three time points.

ANXA3, VIM, GGCT, and SYNCRIP were differentially abundant in EVs of ME/CFS patients at both 0h and 24h but not 15 min, suggesting exercise-related perturbations stabilize by 24h and reflect persistent cellular stress.

Eight proteins involved in detoxification, protein folding, mRNA processing, inflammation, cell adhesion, and cell structure were differentially abundant between ME/CFS and controls at both baseline and 15 min postexercise, suggesting chronic baseline dysregulation unaffected by acute exercise response.

VBP1 was the sole protein differentially abundant at both postexercise time points (15 min and 24h), showing decreased levels in ME/CFS patients, indicating exercise-induced dysregulation without recovery by 24h.

At baseline, EV proteins differentially abundant between ME/CFS and controls were enriched for metabolism, neutrophil degranulation, and biological oxidations pathways, indicating disruptions in metabolic and innate immune processes even at rest.

At 15 min postexercise, DAPs between ME/CFS and controls were enriched for immune system/disease pathways, vesicle-mediated transport and biogenesis pathways, and cellular response to stress pathways, suggesting failure of EV-mediated immune response and impaired EV biogenesis.

GSEA revealed complement and coagulation cascade pathways were significantly upregulated in male ME/CFS patients relative to controls at 15 min postexercise, consistently identified across three pathway databases, driven by complement (C3, CFH, C4BPA, C1qA/B/C) and coagulation (FGA, FGB, FGG, factor XI, factor V, plasminogen) proteins.

GSEA showed strong downregulation of numerous energy metabolism pathways (TCA cycle/respiratory electron transport, BCAA degradation, tryptophan metabolism, fatty acid and lipid metabolism) in male ME/CFS patients versus controls at 15 min postexercise, suggesting an energy production deficit underlying fatigue and exercise intolerance.

Three mitochondrial-function pathways (mitochondrial biogenesis, cristae formation, mitochondrial calcium ion transport) showed significantly reduced EV protein levels in ME/CFS versus controls, implicating mitochondrial dysfunction in impaired recovery and PEM.

The complement system pathway was the only pathway significantly enriched at baseline (0h) and remained elevated at 15 min postexercise, suggesting the complement system is primed for overactivation prior to exercise and exacerbated in the immediate postexercise phase in ME/CFS.

The O2/CO2 exchange in erythrocytes pathway (HBB, HBA1, CA2, SLC4A1, CA1) was significantly enriched in ME/CFS versus controls at both 15 min and 24h postexercise, indicating a prolonged disruption in gas-exchange processes that did not return to baseline by 24h.

Citrate synthase (CS), the first TCA cycle enzyme, showed the largest reduction in EV levels from baseline to 15 min postexercise among ME/CFS patients, while it was unchanged in controls, indicating impaired energy metabolism.

SERPINF1, an antiangiogenic neurotrophic protein, was significantly upregulated in ME/CFS EVs for both the 15min/0h and 24h/0h within-subject ratios, remaining elevated 24h postexercise unlike controls, possibly reflecting a compensatory stress response.

GSEA of the 15min/0h within-subject fold-change ratios identified 96 significantly dysregulated pathways between ME/CFS and controls, with complement/coagulation pathways strongly upregulated (NES 2.3-3.1), TCA cycle/respiratory electron transport strongly downregulated (NES -2.5), and the innate immune system pathway (112 proteins) upregulated during the rapid exercise response.

Desmoglein 1 (DSG1) levels in EVs (0-24h change) were negatively correlated with Bell Activity Scale scores in ME/CFS patients, meaning higher postexercise DSG1 levels were associated with more severe functional disability.

ERP29 15min/0h ratio was strongly positively correlated (R=.93) with Bell Activity Scale scores, such that more disabled ME/CFS patients showed decreased ERP29 postexercise while more functional patients showed an increase, suggesting failure of the ER stress response chaperone in more severe patients.

The 24h/0h ratio of LCP1 (lymphocyte cytosolic protein 1) positively correlated with SF-36 Physical Component Summary scores in ME/CFS patients, with increased LCP1 associated with better physical function.

The 24h/0h ratio of ANXA2 was positively correlated with proportion of waking time spent reclined (worse disease severity), while the 24h/0h ratio of TUBB6 was negatively correlated with reclined time, in ME/CFS patients.

Ten EV proteins whose 24h/15min ratio positively correlated with PEM severity at 24h formed a highly interconnected PPI network (enrichment p<1e-16) centered on ER stress and protein folding, with DNAJB11, HSPA5, PPIB, and PDIA4 as central hubs.
The 24h/15min ratio of NME1 was strongly negatively correlated with the change in myalgia after exercise in ME/CFS patients: decreasing NME1 was associated with worsening muscle pain.

The change in FCN2 (ficolin-2, a lectin complement pathway protein) levels from 0h to 15min positively correlated with baseline myalgia severity, linking complement/immune overactivation to muscle pain in ME/CFS.

The 24h/15min ratio of KTN1 (kinectin, involved in intracellular transport) showed a strong significant positive correlation with arthralgia (joint pain) severity at 24h postexercise in ME/CFS patients.

68 EV proteins showed significant positive correlations between their 24h/15min ratio and worsening unrefreshing sleep in ME/CFS patients; a 12-protein carbon metabolism cluster including GPI, IDH1, LDHA, DLST, ACLY, and TALDO1 (glycolysis, TCA cycle, pentose phosphate pathway) was highly interconnected in PPI analysis.

In contrast to the current male cohort where complement was overactivated, the authors' prior study of female ME/CFS patients found the complement system to be inhibited 15 minutes postexercise, suggesting a sex difference in complement activation in ME/CFS.
A prior study by Castro-Marrero et al. found that baseline plasma C3 levels were elevated in severe and moderate female ME/CFS cases compared with mild cases.
In the same prior cohort, 42.8% (107/250) of female ME/CFS patients exhibited increased circulating levels of C1q.
Nunes et al. found no significant difference in baseline plasma C1q between ME/CFS and controls but reported downregulation of C1s and upregulation of C6 in the ME/CFS group.
A metabolomic analysis of baseline plasma from a Japanese cohort found significantly decreased citrate levels in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.

Prior muscle biopsy studies found significant reductions in citrate synthase, succinate reductase, and cytochrome-c oxidase in anterior tibialis and quadriceps muscle of ME/CFS patients compared with controls.

In the same cohort's prior plasma metabolomics study, male ME/CFS patients showed a significant decrease in the TCA cycle metabolite alpha-ketoglutarate 15 minutes postexercise that was not seen in sedentary controls.

A prior muscle tissue study found decreased HSPA5 (BiP/GRP78) and increased ER stress marker EIF2AK3/PERK in skeletal muscle from ME/CFS patients, alongside increased WASF3, and showed transgenic mice overexpressing WASF3 exhibited impaired exercise tolerance.
The authors previously found plasma tubulin proteins TUBA1B/A/C to be part of a protein group able to classify ME/CFS patients versus controls with 86% accuracy.

The identified EV protein dataset overlapped substantially with established EV proteome databases, with 88% and 93% of proteins matching entries in Exocarta and Vesiclepedia pre- and postfiltering, respectively, and known EV markers CD9, CD63, TSG101, and FLOT1 were detected.

A carbon-metabolism protein cluster (including GPI, IDH1, LDHA, TALDO1, DLST, and ACLY) within the unrefreshing-sleep-associated PPI network showed changes in EV levels during exercise recovery that were strongly and positively correlated with worse unrefreshing sleep in ME/CFS patients.

A protein cluster involved in the RHO GTPase cycle and prefoldin-mediated transfer of substrate to CCT/TriC (CCT7, CCT4, STIP1, PFDN6) correlated with changes in unrefreshing sleep severity postexercise in ME/CFS patients.

In healthy controls only, 14 EV proteins (including CA1, COX2, PCSK6, EMILIN1, GPD2, and SELP) showed significant correlations between their 24h/15min ratios and VO2peak, correlations that were absent in ME/CFS patients, indicating disrupted EV-mediated exercise adaptation in ME/CFS.
In healthy controls only, six EV proteins including CA1, PCSK6, and UTRN correlated significantly with ventilatory anaerobic threshold (VAT), with these associations absent in ME/CFS patients.

In the authors' prior female ME/CFS EV proteomics study, EMILIN1 levels were significantly higher in ME/CFS patients compared with controls 24 hours postexercise, consistent with a prolonged vascular stress response.

In sedentary male controls, mean EV concentration significantly increased 1.9-fold at 24 hours postexercise compared with baseline, an increase that was not observed in male ME/CFS patients whose concentration returned close to baseline.

Eight proteins involved in detoxification, protein folding, immunoregulation, mRNA processing, inflammation, cell adhesion, and cell structure (ADH5, BLMH, FKBP3, HNRNPK, PTGES3, RAP1A, RDX, TXNDC5) were differentially abundant in EVs between ME/CFS and controls at both baseline and 15 min postexercise, with BLMH showing increased levels in ME/CFS.

The patient's plasma HERV-W ENV (MSRV envelope) protein level was below the positivity cutoff established from control samples, unlike the frequent overexpression reported in MS and some ME/CFS/post-COVID patients.
Genome-wide microarray analysis identified 502 differentially expressed HERV probe sets between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
Hierarchical clustering showed the male patient's PBMC HERV expression profile grouped together with other ME/CFS patient samples rather than healthy controls, despite being the only male sample.

Principal component analysis showed the patient's HERV profile was closer to ME/CFS patients than to controls along PC1 (29.1% variance), while not perfectly aligning with female ME/CFS cases along PC2 (9.3% variance).
Among the 29 most highly overexpressed HERV loci in the patient's sample, one mapped near QKI, a gene involved in myelination and oligodendrocyte differentiation.
Another top overexpressed HERV locus in the patient's sample mapped near LINGO2, a gene implicated in the glutamatergic synapse.

Screening of 1559 immune/inflammation/CNS-related genes and 289 exogenous virus probes on the microarray showed no values exceeding the reference female ME/CFS group, indicating absence of marked inflammation, active exogenous infection, or viral reactivation in this patient.
The patient tested moderately positive for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies, typically associated with myasthenia gravis, though of unknown clinical significance given his normal EMG.

A 9-month rituximab treatment regimen (1 g doses targeting CD20+ B cells) produced significant improvement in fatigue starting after the third dose, doubling the patient's Bell functional score from 10 to 20 and sustaining remission for at least 3 years.

A range of supplements (magnesium, NADH, D-ribose, L-carnitine, ubiquinol, melatonin, vitamin B1, alpha-lipoic acid, vitamin D, and low-dose naltrexone) failed to improve the patient's ME/CFS symptoms.
Oral teriflunomide, a low-efficacy MS disease-modifying therapy, was discontinued due to adverse effects including tachycardia and tiredness.
Subcutaneous glatiramer acetate stabilized MS disease activity over 3 years but produced no symptomatic (fatigue) improvement, leading to discontinuation.
Amantadine, modafinil, and fampridine, trialed to address the patient's fatigue, proved ineffective.
The patient tested positive for EBV IgG in 2015, consistent with EBV infection being a known risk factor for developing MS.
Overexpression of TTMV9 transcripts, previously reported as elevated in the female ME/CFS reference group (potentially indicating a weakened immune system), was absent in this patient.
A cited meta-analysis reports that rituximab treatment reduces relapse frequency in MS.
Clinical trials of rituximab for ME/CFS showed an initial partial reduction in symptoms, but a subsequent continuation trial failed to demonstrate benefit.

The authors note that their findings align with prior reports of EBV infection causing endogenous retroviral repression in CD19+ B cells, and observed an overall downregulation of HERV expression in the patient's PBMCs alongside a subset of overexpressed loci.
Pooled analysis of 7 studies found that acupuncture significantly reduced fatigue severity scale (FSS) scores at 5 weeks compared to control interventions, with high heterogeneity.
Pooled analysis of 7 studies found that acupuncture significantly reduced long-term fatigue (FSS) at 13 weeks compared to control interventions, with high heterogeneity.
Pooled analysis of 4 studies assessing SPHERE (somatic and psychological health) scores showed a nonsignificant trend toward improvement with acupuncture, as the confidence interval crossed zero.

Pooled analysis of 2 studies assessing the Self-rating Depression Scale (SDS) showed a nonsignificant trend toward reduced depressive symptoms with acupuncture, as the confidence interval crossed zero.
Funnel plot analysis across the four outcome measures showed substantial asymmetry, suggesting possible publication bias that may overestimate acupuncture's effectiveness for CFS.
Methodological quality of the 9 included studies was generally low, with a Jadad score of 3, reflecting inadequate reporting of allocation concealment, blinding, and withdrawals/dropouts.

Fibrinaloid microclots differ from normal blood clots in electron microscopic appearance, amyloid dye staining, secondary structure (β-sheet vs α-helix), resistance to fibrinolysis, and proteome composition.
Anomalous amyloid fibrin clotting can be induced by extremely small amounts of bacterial lipopolysaccharide, on the order of one LPS molecule per 100 million fibrinogen molecules.
Certain small molecules such as specific estrogens or unliganded iron can cause fibrinogen to form highly anomalous amyloid clots, originally termed 'dense matted deposits'.

Amyloid microclot proteomes differ markedly from normal clot proteomes: they are enriched in low-abundance, highly amyloidogenic plasma proteins and lack many high-abundance plasma proteins, whereas normal clot proteomes roughly mirror the soluble plasma proteome.

Fibrinaloid microclots resist fibrinolysis because their cross-β amyloid structure confers protease resistance and because anti-fibrinolytic proteins become trapped within the clot, explaining their persistence and contribution to blood stasis.
Both long COVID and ME/CFS are strongly associated with fatigue, a symptom the authors link (as with other diseases discussed) to fibrinaloid microclot burden.
Cancer, particularly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), is strongly linked to thromboembolic states, with thrombotic events often leading to worse outcomes.
Use of Xue Fu Zhu Yu decoction has been associated with more than a four-fold decrease in mortality from ischemic heart disease.
In a traumatic brain injury model, XFZYD reversed the TBI-induced reduction of BDNF and TrkB in the hippocampus and increased synaptic connections and expression of PSD95, GAP43, and TUBB3.
In an alopecia model, XFZYD significantly inhibited serum and skin tissue levels of IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α.
Using a PTK787-induced segmental vascular injury zebrafish model, seven active components of XFZYD, including ferulic acid, paeoniflorin, and hesperidin, were identified as promoting angiogenesis.
Hydroxysafflor yellow A (HSYA), a main active ingredient of Xuebijing, showed outstanding performance in promoting endothelial cell proliferation.
Triterpenoid saponins such as platycodins, saikosaponins, and glycyrrhizin, found in the herbs of Xue Fu Zhu Yu, may inhibit toxic amyloidogenesis.
Saikosaponins, components of Xue Fu Zhu Yu, have been found to have efficacy as anti-cancer agents.
Insoluble fibrinaloid microclots can block blood flow through microcapillaries, leading to loss of oxygen transfer, hypoxia, and other pathological consequences.
Chronotropic incompetence (CRI < 80%) was detected in 81.5% of subjects with moderate-severe long-term post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Abnormal heart rate recovery, indicating parasympathetic dysfunction, was found in 33% of subjects with moderate-severe long-term post-COVID-19 syndrome.
Overall autonomic dysfunction (chronotropic incompetence and/or abnormal heart rate recovery) was present in 88.9% of moderate-severe long-term post-COVID-19 subjects.
In mildly symptomatic long-term post-COVID-19 subjects, chronotropic incompetence was found in 35% and abnormal heart rate recovery in 20%, giving an overall AD prevalence of 35%.
Even asymptomatic post-COVID subjects showed measurable autonomic dysfunction, with chronotropic incompetence in 12.5% and abnormal heart rate recovery in 8%.
Peak VO2 was numerically lower in moderate-severe versus mild and asymptomatic long-term post-COVID subjects but the difference was not statistically significant.
37% of moderate-severe long-term post-COVID-19 subjects had mildly diminished functional capacity (peak VO2 ~78% predicted), with none showing moderate or severe limitation.

Failure to achieve the anaerobic threshold during exercise testing was more common with increasing symptom severity: 51.8% of moderate-severe, 25% of mild, and 12.5% of asymptomatic subjects failed to reach AT.
Neither chronotropic incompetence nor abnormal heart rate recovery correlated with cardio-respiratory fitness (peak VO2) in any of the studied groups.
No dynamic hyperinflation, exhausted ventilatory reserve, or exercise-induced oxygen desaturation was detected in either the mild or moderate-severe long-term PCS groups.
Dyspnoea was the predominant exercise-limiting symptom, reported by 77.8% of moderate-severe and 75% of mildly symptomatic long-term PCS subjects.
Only 47 of 192 subjects (about a quarter) had long-term (>12 months) post-COVID complaints, indicating that most working-age subjects recover without persistent symptoms.
24% of post-COVID subjects (47 of 192) exhibited long-term post-COVID-19 syndrome (PCS) based on CFSQ score, even up to 30 months after acute infection.
Peak VO2 was numerically lower in moderate-severe long-term PCS patients compared to mild and asymptomatic subjects, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
Only 37% of moderate-severe and 35% of mildly symptomatic long-term PCS patients had objectively reduced physical capacity (VO2 <80% predicted), similar to 29% of asymptomatic controls.
A statistically significant proportion of moderate-severe long-term PCS patients failed to reach the anaerobic threshold during CPET, compared to mild and asymptomatic groups.
Moderate-severe long-term PCS patients reported substantially higher symptom burden during CPET than mildly symptomatic and asymptomatic groups.
Among symptomatic long-term PCS patients, dyspnea was the predominant symptom limiting exercise (77.8%), followed by leg fatigue (22.2%), with no chest pain reported.
BMI did not significantly differ across fatigue severity groups nor compared to asymptomatic individuals, contrasting with prior studies implicating obesity as a risk factor for post-COVID illness.

None of the CPET parameters could be considered predictors for long-term post-COVID syndrome in univariate analysis, and severity of acute illness was not associated with development of long-term sequelae.

Moderate-severe long-term PCS patients showed a lower threshold of perception for exertion, with self-reported exertion on the BORG scale not corresponding to the actual intensity of load, heart rate, breathing rate, or metabolic equivalent.

Autonomic nervous system dysfunction, characterized by parasympathetic excess and sympathetic withdrawal, is proposed as an underlying but understudied mechanism contributing to exercise intolerance and low cardio-respiratory fitness in PCS, drawing an analogy to its role in chronic fatigue syndrome.

No dynamic hyperinflation, exercise-induced bronchospasm, exercise-induced desaturation, or exhausted ventilatory reserve was found during CPET, and no patient showed a restrictive pattern on baseline spirometry, suggesting no specific pulmonary limitation.
Among 178 patients who met the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria, 47 (26.4%) were found via genetic testing to have additional or alternative diagnoses requiring distinct management strategies.
Only 178 of 907 patients (19.62%) referred for suspected hEDS actually fulfilled the 2017 hEDS diagnostic criteria on clinical evaluation.
A cited study proposed a 52-kDa fibronectin fragment as a potential exploratory biomarker for hEDS, though it remains clinically unvalidated.
