Hereditary alpha tryptasemia, caused by extra germline copies of TPSAB1, has an estimated population prevalence of 5.5-8% and produces multisystem symptoms that overlap with hEDS, including GI dysmotility, autonomic dysfunction, and joint laxity.

Within the HCTD registry cohort, a notable number of patients meeting hEDS criteria had underlying inflammatory or immunological disorders, specifically common variable immunodeficiency type 2 (CVID2) and hereditary alpha tryptasemia.
Pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 have been shown in inflammatory conditions to compromise ligament integrity, suggesting a possible mechanistic contributor to joint laxity.

Extra-articular manifestations of hEDS commonly include functional gastrointestinal disorders, POTS, chronic pelvic pain, and psychological dysfunction, which often constitute the primary reason patients seek hEDS evaluation.
Joint hypermobility is a recognized feature of several chromosomal abnormalities, including triple X syndrome, 1q21.1 deletion syndrome, and 16p13.11 microduplication syndrome.
Joint laxity has been reported as a primary or secondary manifestation in RYR1- and SEPN1-related myopathies, highlighting overlap between neuromuscular disorders and hypermobility phenotypes.
Participants with hEDS recalled significantly fewer words on a delayed free-recall verbal memory test compared to matched controls.

Across all other objective cognitive domains (attention, executive functioning, language, visuospatial functioning, and other memory measures), there was no significant difference between hEDS participants and matched controls.
The hEDS group reported significantly more depressive symptoms than matched controls.
The hEDS group reported significantly more fatigue than matched controls.
The hEDS group reported significantly more pain than matched controls.
The hEDS group reported significantly more subjective cognitive difficulties than matched controls.
The hEDS group reported significantly more difficulty participating in social roles and activities than matched controls.
In a larger hEDS sample, worse subjective cognitive ability was moderately correlated with worse performance on a working memory task (digit span backward).
Worse subjective cognitive ability was moderately correlated with worse visuospatial construction performance (Rey Complex Figure copy) in hEDS participants.
Worse subjective cognitive ability was moderately correlated with worse executive functioning performance (D-KEFS verbal fluency switching) in hEDS participants.
Worse subjective cognitive ability was moderately correlated with higher depression symptoms in hEDS participants.
Worse subjective cognitive ability was moderately correlated with higher anxiety symptoms in hEDS participants.
Worse subjective cognitive ability was moderately correlated with higher fatigue in hEDS participants.
Worse subjective cognitive ability was moderately correlated with higher pain levels in hEDS participants.
Worse subjective cognitive ability was strongly correlated with greater difficulty participating in social roles in hEDS participants.
The paper cites prior literature that generalized hypermobility is linked to higher rates of musculoskeletal injury, including in volleyball players, as the rationale for the study.
Higher Beighton scores were significantly correlated with reduced medio-lateral centre of pressure range of motion during single-leg dynamic balance on the non-dominant leg.

Beighton score showed no significant association with most other lower limb injury risk factors assessed (Landing Error Scoring System, most dynamic balance measures, and most Limb Symmetry Index measures).
Asymptomatic hypermobile volleyball players showed significantly greater limb symmetry on the single-leg hop for distance test compared to non-hypermobile players.
All 69 pediatric hEDS patients presenting for physical therapy listed pain as their chief complaint, and 92% also cited joint hypermobility as a reason for presentation.
Among pediatric hEDS patients with reported pain locations, the knee was the most commonly affected joint (68%), followed by shoulder (46%), hip (41%), and back (39%).
Pediatric hEDS patients reported moderate average pain intensity (5.0 out of 10) in the week prior to their initial PT evaluation.
Despite normal joint strength, pediatric hEDS patients reported poor perceived physical mobility, with low subscores for participating in sports and performing daily activities.
PT-assessed joint strength (ankle, knee, shoulder, hip) was near-normal in pediatric hEDS patients despite significant pain and poor perceived mobility.
Within the hip joint, strength varied by movement direction, with extension notably lower than flexion.
No correlation was found between PT-assessed joint strength and self-reported pain intensity in pediatric hEDS patients.
Joint strength at the hip, knee, and shoulder were positively correlated with each other, while shoulder and ankle strength showed a weak negative correlation.
Joint pain showed a weak negative correlation with joint strength at the ankle, knee, shoulder, and hip, with the strongest relationship at the shoulder.
There was an incongruence in pediatric hEDS patients between near-normal objective joint strength, significant self-reported pain, and poor perceived physical mobility.
There was an average delay of 17 months between formal hEDS diagnosis and initial physical therapy evaluation.

A single-arm meta-analysis of nine studies (303 patients, 364 knees) found a pooled mean post-operative redislocation rate of 9% following surgical management of patellar instability in hypermobile patients, similar to reported redislocation rates in non-hypermobile surgical patients.
Redislocation rates after MPFL reconstruction (MPFLR) in six studies of hypermobile patients ranged widely from 7.3% to 28.5%, and pooling was not possible due to high heterogeneity.

Non-MPFLR surgical procedures (e.g., lateral release, Roux-Goldthwait, semitendinosus tenodesis) in hypermobile patients showed a pooled redislocation rate of 17%, higher than but not significantly different from MPFLR-associated rates.
Allograft-based surgical reconstruction in hypermobile patients showed a pooled redislocation rate of 9%, similar to autograft-based redislocation rates.
Autograft-based surgical management in hypermobile patients showed redislocation rates ranging widely from 2% to 23% across five studies, with no pooling performed due to high heterogeneity.
Post-operative Kujala Anterior Knee Pain Scale scores in hypermobile patients improved significantly compared to preoperative scores in the three studies that reported both timepoints.

A higher Beighton score was significantly associated with younger age, female sex, and presence of knee hyperextension, but was not significantly associated with post-operative outcomes or functional testing scores.
Generalized joint hypermobility (GJH) did not correlate with post-operative functional testing scores and did not impact quality-of-life measures in patients undergoing patellar instability surgery.

One study found no significant difference in post-operative complication rates between patients with syndromic (e.g., EDS, Down syndrome) versus non-syndromic causes of hypermobility undergoing patellar instability surgery.

Across four studies comprising 104 patients, 17 (16.3%) had post-operative complications, all classified as Clavien-Dindo Grade III-b, with pain requiring revision surgery being the most common (41.2% of complications).

The redislocation rate in hypermobile patients following surgery (0%-22%) was similar to reported redislocation rates in non-hypermobile patients undergoing surgery (7%-25%), but markedly lower than redislocation rates in non-hypermobile patients undergoing conservative/non-operative treatment (35%-71%), suggesting operative treatment in hypermobile patients may be superior to non-operative management of non-hypermobile patients.

One case-control study reported that hypermobile patients undergoing isolated MPFLR achieved zero redislocations and significant improvements in Kujala, Oxford knee, Lysholm, Tegner, and SF-12MCS scores, but functional improvements were significantly inferior compared to non-hypermobile patients undergoing the same procedure.

The review notes that capsular laxity as a cause of hip microinstability, including in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, can be assessed with dynamic imaging techniques such as leg traction MRI and dynamic ultrasound to reveal increased femoral head distraction or translation relative to the acetabulum.
Approximately one in five children with generalised joint hypermobility experience symptoms such as joint instability, poor coordination, proprioceptive deficits, and musculoskeletal pain.

The working diagnostic threshold for generalised joint hypermobility in children was concluded to be a Beighton score of 6 or more out of 9, with 7 or more considered more appropriate during childhood.
A longitudinal study of musculoskeletal pain in school children found that children with hypermobility-associated disorders were more likely to develop chronic pain than non-hypermobile peers.

A prior systematic review found no consensus on outcome measures for children with hypermobility-associated conditions and lower limb symptoms, identifying 20 different instruments used as primary outcome measures across pain, function, fatigue and quality of life.

In round one, 52 of 85 invited experts (61.2%) completed the survey; of the original 20 outcome measures, 8 did not reach the 70% consensus threshold and were excluded, while participants suggested 42 additional outcome measures that met the survey scope.

In round two, 46 of 52 round-one participants (88.5%) responded; of 54 outcome measures presented, 45 were excluded for not reaching consensus, leaving nine outcome measures across four domains (three pain, two function, three fatigue, one quality of life).
In round three, 44 of 46 round-two participants (95.6%) responded and ranked the outcome measures in order of importance in the three domains with multiple consensus measures.

The PedsQL Pediatric Pain Questionnaire (child-reported) was ranked as the most important outcome measure in the pain domain for assessing children with hypermobility-associated conditions and chronic lower limb pain.
School absenteeism (number of school days missed within the last fortnight) was ranked as the most important outcome measure in the function domain.
The PedsQL Multidimensional Fatigue Scale (child-reported) was ranked as the most important outcome measure in the fatigue domain.
The PedsQL Generic Core Scales (child-reported) was the only outcome measure to reach consensus in the quality-of-life domain, so no ranking was required.
Child-reported outcome measures were ranked above parent-reported outcome measures in both the pain and fatigue domains where both reached consensus.

No paediatric hypermobility condition-specific outcome measure was identified through the literature search or suggested by participants, meaning all consensus measures were generic tools validated in other paediatric populations rather than hypermobility-specific instruments.
Parents have typically underreported their child's pain, supporting the recommendation to prioritise child self-report over proxy reporting in this population.

Among genodermatoses diagnosed via whole genome sequencing, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome was the second largest diagnostic group, including three individuals with classic/type 1, one with vascular, and one with kyphoscoliotic EDS.
Three individuals with clinically diagnosed hypermobility-type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome all had negative whole genome sequencing results, i.e., no causative variant was identified.

Of 376 probands recruited for the BRGP, 79 (21%) were included due to cutaneous or neurocutaneous manifestations, with neurofibromatosis type 1 being the largest single diagnostic group (38% of those undergoing WGS).
Seventeen novel variants (mostly SNVs, two CNVs) were identified across 14 genes in the genodermatoses cohort studied by WGS.
Double molecular diagnoses were found in 7 of 30 (23%) positive WGS tests in this cohort, a higher frequency than the 2-7.5% typically reported in the literature for comprehensive genomic testing.
After reverse phenotyping excluded incidental second findings, three of 30 (10%) cases retained a true additive double diagnosis, still above the literature-expected rate.
A homozygous SDR9C7 variant previously reported only in Chihuahua dogs was confirmed for the first time as causative for ichthyosis in a human patient.
An ALDH3A2 variant causing Sjögren-Larsson syndrome, initially classified as VUS, was reclassified as likely pathogenic after being independently reported in the Brazilian population in 2022.

All three individuals with incontinentia pigmenti had the common IKBKG exon 4-10 deletion, confirmed by long-read sequencing, the genomic mechanism responsible for nearly 65% of incontinentia pigmenti cases.
A pathogenic TSC2 deletion (exons 6-7) causing tuberous sclerosis was missed by prior gene panel sequencing and only identified when the patient underwent whole genome sequencing.

A patient with Cockayne syndrome type B (10q11.22q11.23 deletion plus ERCC6 variant) developed a previously undescribed acute neurological presentation of migraine progressing to hemiplegia and total retrograde amnesia at age 26.

Runs of homozygosity (ROH) analysis confirmed unrecognized consanguinity in a patient with a rare homozygous variant despite denial of consanguinity, showing a high inbreeding coefficient (FROH = 20.8%).
A patient with albinism and Angelman syndrome had a heterozygous OCA2 duplication rendered homozygous through paternal isodisomy of chromosome 15, explaining the dual phenotype.
A patient with Ellis-van Creveld syndrome also carried a second molecular diagnosis of 22q11.2 microduplication syndrome, with overlapping clinical features complicating phenotypic attribution.

A patient with clinical features suggestive of Rothmund-Thomson syndrome had a negative WGS result, consistent with the genetic heterogeneity of this condition where known genes (ANAPC1, RECQL4, CRIPT, DNA2) explain only about 70% of cases.
Two patients with Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome manifestations had negative WGS results, consistent with the typical genetic findings (or lack thereof) in this condition.
Shoulder pain over 16 weeks decreased by 0.89 NRS points in the high-load exercise group and 0.33 NRS points in the low-load exercise group, with no significant difference between groups.
Pain trajectories over the 16-week intervention period did not significantly differ between the high-load and low-load exercise groups.
Acute exercise-induced pain remained low (below 0.5 NRS) throughout the 16 weeks and did not differ significantly between high-load and low-load exercise groups.
Arthroscopic IGHL reconstruction with gracilis tendon graft significantly improved Subjective Shoulder Value from 50.0 to 89.6 postoperatively.
QuickDASH scores significantly improved from 76.5 preoperatively to 42.7 postoperatively following IGHL reconstruction.
WOSI scores significantly improved from 1,355.9 preoperatively to 491.5 postoperatively following IGHL reconstruction.
No postoperative instability events or perioperative complications occurred after arthroscopic IGHL reconstruction in this cohort.
A minority of patients developed early instability arthropathy or persistent subluxation after IGHL reconstruction, with one patient having an inferior clinical result.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly larger sural nerve cross-sectional area than healthy controls both at baseline and after 24 months of follow-up.
Fibromyalgia patients had significantly larger vagus nerve cross-sectional area than healthy controls both at baseline and after 24 months.
Sural nerve enlargement in FM patients remained stable rather than progressing over the 24-month follow-up period.
Vagus nerve enlargement in FM patients remained stable rather than progressing over the 24-month follow-up period.
Baseline autonomic symptom severity (COMPASS-31) correlated with final sural nerve cross-sectional area at 24 months.
Higher neuropathic pain scores (DN4) at baseline and at 24 months were associated with a greater increase in vagus nerve size and higher final vagus nerve CSA values.
A meta-analysis cited in the introduction found that approximately 49% of fibromyalgia patients show objective signs of small fiber neuropathy.
A prior cross-sectional study by the same group found significantly increased CSA at the vagus nerve, sural nerve, and C6 nerve root in FM patients compared with healthy controls.
Inflammatory markers including IgG, TNF-alpha, and IL-6 have been identified in skin biopsies of fibromyalgia patients, supporting a neurogenic inflammation mechanism involving C-fibers.
Heart rate variability studies in fibromyalgia have reported attenuated HRV and an increased low-to-high frequency ratio, indicating heightened sympathetic tone and reduced parasympathetic activity.

Quitadamo et al. observed stable IENFD and clinical features over an 18-month follow-up in FM patients, though reduced IENFD was linked to greater disability progression, particularly in motor performance.

Another study exploring autonomic dysfunction reported reduced (rather than increased) vagus nerve CSA in both fibromyalgia and generalized anxiety disorder, contrasting with the present study's finding of vagus nerve enlargement.
In Sjögren's syndrome-associated peripheral neuropathy, a sural nerve CSA cutoff of 2.6 mm2 effectively differentiated small fiber neuropathy patients from controls, including some with normal IENFD.
Ebadi et al. reported that patients with small fiber neuropathy had enlarged sural nerve CSA compared to healthy controls, without significant differences in nerve echogenicity.

The genuine neurofeedback (NFT) group showed a significant reduction in overall fibromyalgia symptom severity (SSS) both immediately after treatment and at 10-12 month follow-up, whereas sham and treatment-as-usual groups showed no improvement.
At long-term follow-up, the NFT group showed significantly greater reduction in symptom severity than both the sham-NF (NFS) and treatment-as-usual (TAU) control groups.

NFT patients showed a 17% reduction in FIQ-final score immediately post-intervention and a further 22% reduction at follow-up, with significantly greater improvement than TAU but not significantly different from sham NF.

Widespread pain index (WPI) improved significantly within both NFT (23% reduction) and NFS (28% reduction) groups at follow-up, but there was no significant between-group difference, indicating pain relief was not specific to genuine neurofeedback.
The NFT group showed a significant 19% long-term reduction in fatigue (FIQ-fatigue), with significantly greater improvement than both NFS and TAU groups, while neither control group improved.

The NFT group showed significant immediate and long-term reduction in anxiety symptoms (14% at follow-up), but this improvement was not significantly greater than sham or TAU groups in the between-group comparison.

The NFT group showed a 26% reduction in cognitive symptoms (SSS-Cog) at follow-up, with significantly greater long-term improvement than both NFS and TAU groups, while neither control group changed significantly.
In the NFT group, immediate reduction in anxiety significantly predicted long-term reduction in overall symptom severity, while immediate improvements in fatigue or widespread pain did not.
In the sham (NFS) group, immediate improvement in widespread pain (WPI) negatively predicted long-term reduction in overall symptom severity, contrary to expectation.

Both real (NFT) and sham (NFS) neurofeedback groups successfully downregulated the Amyg-EFP signal during active regulation compared to passive watching within sessions, with no significant difference between groups.
Both NFT and NFS groups generalized the ability to downregulate the Amyg-EFP signal independently of feedback (transfer runs), with no significant group difference in this generalization ability.
A positive correlation between average transfer score and average Amyg-EFP downregulation was found only in the NFT group, not in the NFS group.

Only the NFT group showed a significant linear learning trend across sessions in Amyg-EFP downregulation ability, while the NFS group showed no such trend, indicating genuine neurofeedback-specific skill acquisition.

Greater Amyg-EFP downregulation capacity during training was positively correlated with long-term improvement in overall symptom severity (SSS), cognitive dysfunction, and anxiety, specifically in the NFT group and not in the NFS group.

Prior neuroimaging literature cited in this study links fibromyalgia pathology to amygdala abnormalities, including reduced gray matter volume and altered amygdala activity and connectivity, supporting the amygdala as a therapeutic target.
At the 2-year follow-up (T1), the percentage of B cells expressing Mu-opioid receptor (MLM) was significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients than in pain-free controls.
MLM on B cells did not significantly change between the prepandemic baseline (T0) and the 2-year follow-up during the pandemic (T1), indicating stability of the biomarker over time.

Confocal microscopy showed that Mu-opioid receptor was localized in the cytoplasm (internalized) in B cells of fibromyalgia patients, whereas it remained at the cytoplasmic membrane in pain-free controls.
Pain intensity (NRS) in fibromyalgia patients did not significantly change between the prepandemic baseline and the 2-year pandemic-era follow-up.

Psychological questionnaire scores (FIQ, Illness Perception Questionnaire-Revised, Coping Strategies Questionnaire, DASS-21, Chronic Pain Acceptance Questionnaire) did not significantly change from prepandemic baseline to pandemic-era follow-up in fibromyalgia patients.
No significant correlation was found between MLM expression on B cells at T1 and psychological questionnaire results at either T0 or T1.

Citing prior literature, the authors note that patients with chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia have previously been shown to have lower PBMC β-endorphin concentrations than pain-free individuals, supporting the hypothesis that low endogenous opioid availability could drive Mu-opioid receptor internalization.
Women with vestibulodynia plus co-occurring chronic primary pain conditions (VBD+) showed higher local vulvovaginal pain intensity than women with vestibulodynia alone (VBD).
VBD+ patients demonstrated increased pain sensitivity at remote (non-genital) body sites via quantitative sensory testing compared to VBD-only patients.
Women with VBD+ reported taking more pain-related medications than women with VBD alone.
VBD+ women reported greater adverse mood states and somatic/psychological symptoms than VBD-only women.
VBD+ women reported greater pain catastrophizing compared to VBD-only women.
GWAS analysis identified genetic variants associated with vestibulodynia (VBD) alone that are located in genes regulating reproductive and nervous system development.
GWAS analysis identified genetic variants associated with VBD+ subtype located in genes implicated in synaptic transmission and related chronic primary pain condition (CPPC) pathophysiology.
Up to three in four women with vestibulodynia may have co-occurring chronic primary pain conditions such as episodic migraine, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, and temporomandibular disorder.
Fibromyalgia is described as the musculoskeletal syndrome most commonly linked to central sensitization, with an estimated prevalence of 5% in the general population.
Although fibromyalgia is typically considered a condition of middle-aged women, the paper notes it affects both sexes at any age.
In fibromyalgia, central sensitization signs commonly manifest as abdominal pain, anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, and poor cognitive functioning.
Structural and functional brain changes have been reported in fibromyalgia patients, but the findings remain somewhat inconclusive.
Central sensitization in osteoarthritis is indicated to cause disabling symptoms including physical and psychological dysfunction.
Rheumatoid arthritis patients show a generalized increase in pain sensitivity even in the absence of joint inflammation, suggesting a central rather than purely peripheral mechanism.
The Central Sensitization Inventory (CSI) has demonstrated high sensitivity (81%) and specificity (79%) as a screening tool for central sensitization.

A pronociceptive conditioned pain modulation (CPM) profile, common in musculoskeletal disorders, is linked to higher risk of developing chronic pain, greater prevalence of pain conditions, and higher injury-related pain.
Thermal and mechanical pain threshold testing in patients with hand osteoarthritis showed that central mechanisms contribute to movement-related hyperalgesia.
In osteoarthritis, lower CPM was associated with constant intermittent pain, whereas higher CPM was linked with a greater likelihood of unpredictable pain.
Bilateral involvement and primary hyperalgesia in rheumatoid arthritis patients are proposed as evidence of impaired central pain processing.
Exercise therapy, manual therapy, and pharmacological therapy have been shown to desensitize the central nervous system in patients with chronic pain.
Exercise therapy effects on central sensitization are robust in patients with mild to moderate pain but inconsistent in those with more complex pain conditions.
Randomized trials suggest psychological treatments help reduce pain levels in people with chronic conditions, potentially mediated by improved self-efficacy and reduced catastrophizing.

A meta-analysis suggests dietary patterns and nutrient intake may improve analgesic properties for certain pain types, but there is insufficient evidence they positively affect central sensitization specifically.
Duloxetine reduced pain levels in knee osteoarthritis patients with multiple painful sites but was not effective in those with fewer than three painful sites.

Central sensitization-related CNS dysfunction is linked to fatigue, sleep difficulties, swollen tissue sensations, paresthesia, cognitive dysfunction, dizziness, and overlapping conditions such as IBS, headache, and restless legs syndrome.

Increased muscle sensitivity from central sensitization manifests as allodynia (pain from normally non-painful stimuli), hyperalgesia (increased pain from nociceptive stimuli), or expanded referred pain areas with somatosensory changes.
Serum and urinary SDF-1 levels were significantly increased in type 2 diabetes patients compared to healthy controls, including in the normoalbuminuric subgroup.
Serum and urinary P-selectin were significantly elevated in type 2 diabetes patients compared to controls, consistent with its role in endothelial activation.
Plasma and urinary AOPPs were significantly increased in type 2 diabetes patients versus controls, with an ascending trend from normo- to micro- to macroalbuminuria.
Serum and urinary mtDNA copy number were altered in diabetic patients, decreasing with worsening renal function and correlating with inflammatory and oxidative biomarkers.
KIM-1, a marker of proximal tubule dysfunction, was significantly elevated in diabetic patients versus controls.
Synaptopodin, a podocyte injury marker, was significantly elevated in diabetic patients compared to controls.
Podocalyxin, a podocyte injury marker, was significantly elevated in diabetic patients compared to controls.
Neurosonologic parameters (IMT-CCAs, PI-ICAs, RI-ICAs, PI-MCAs, RI-MCAs) were significantly increased in type 2 diabetes patients compared to controls, indicating cerebral vessel remodeling.
The breath-holding index, a measure of cerebrovascular reactivity, was decreased in diabetic patients compared to controls, reflecting reduced cerebral vasodilatory capacity.
Serum SDF-1 correlated negatively with eGFR and serum mtDNA and positively with UACR, KIM-1, NAG, synaptopodin, and podocalyxin in univariable analysis.
Serum P-selectin correlated negatively with eGFR and serum mtDNA and positively with UACR, KIM-1, NAG, synaptopodin, and podocalyxin, independent of albuminuria level.
AOPP levels correlated negatively with eGFR and serum mtDNA and positively with UACR, KIM-1, NAG, synaptopodin, podocalyxin, and urinary mtDNA in an ascending pattern across albuminuria stages.
In multivariable regression, serum mtDNA correlated directly with eGFR and negatively with serum P-selectin and serum SDF-1, explaining 65.6% of variance.
In multivariable regression, urinary mtDNA correlated directly with podocalyxin, urinary P-selectin, and urinary SDF-1, explaining 62.8% of variance.
IMT-CCAs correlated negatively with eGFR and positively with UACR, synaptopodin, serum P-selectin, and serum AOPPs in a multivariable model explaining 70.2% of variance.
PI-ICAs correlated negatively with eGFR and positively with serum P-selectin and serum SDF-1 in a multivariable model explaining 51.1% of variance.
PI-MCAs correlated negatively with eGFR and positively with serum P-selectin and serum SDF-1 in a multivariable model explaining 58.9% of variance.
RI-ICAs correlated negatively with eGFR and positively with NAG, serum P-selectin, serum SDF-1, and UACR in a multivariable model explaining 76.3% of variance.

RI-MCAs correlated negatively with eGFR and positively with NAG, KIM-1, synaptopodin, podocalyxin, serum P-selectin, and serum SDF-1 in the strongest multivariable model, explaining 84.8% of variance.

In multivariable analysis, BHI correlated directly with eGFR and negatively with podocalyxin, serum P-selectin, and serum SDF-1, explaining 79.0% of variance, reflecting impaired cerebrovascular reactivity linked to renal and inflammatory biomarkers.
Preformed and newly synthesized mediators released by IgE/antigen-activated mast cells drive macrophages toward a phenotype distinct from the classical M1/M2 polarization paradigm.
Exposure of macrophages to supernatant from activated mast cells induces epigenetic reprogramming of the macrophages.
Mast cell-mediator priming strongly alters macrophage phagocytosis, cytokine production, and transcriptomic responses upon secondary exposure to bacteria or bacterial products.
Adoptive transfer of mast cell-primed macrophages significantly affects the outcome of sterile inflammation and bacterial peritonitis in vivo.
The number of infiltrated activated mast cells was positively correlated with the mesenchymal marker CDH2 (N-cadherin) expression in human endometriotic lesions.
The number of infiltrated activated mast cells was negatively correlated with the epithelial marker CDH1 (E-cadherin) expression in human endometriotic lesions.
Mast cells co-cultured with primary endometrial epithelial cells promoted cell migration and EMT via the MRGPRX2/CCL2/CCR4 signalling pathway in vitro.
In a wild-type/c-kit^sh mouse model of endometriosis, deficiency of mast cell activation suppressed the development of endometriotic lesions via restriction of EMT.
Sacco et al. (2014) found significantly higher fasting glucose levels in migraine with aura patients compared to migraine without aura and healthy controls.
Elevated fasting glucose was associated with increased odds of migraine with aura compared to migraine without aura, but not compared to controls.
In an OGTT-based case-control study, migraine patients specifically showed a pronounced hyperinsulinemic response compared to other headache sufferers and healthy controls.

Bhoi et al. (2012) reported that among migraine patients, 31.9% met metabolic syndrome criteria and 11.1% had insulin resistance, with insulin resistance significantly associated with migraine attack duration but not frequency, severity, or aura.

Wang et al. (2017) found that migraineurs with prediabetes had significantly higher fasting insulin and HOMA-IR and lower QUICKI compared to prediabetic controls, though no overall differences were seen between migraineurs and controls.
A systematic review by Hosseinpour et al. (2021) reported a reduced incidence of migraine among diabetic patients, possibly due to altered central pain processing in chronic hyperglycemia.
Ali et al. (2022) found higher insulin resistance in migraine patients compared to non-migraine controls, with IR correlating positively with migraine severity and disability.

Gur-Ozmen et al. (2019) reported a synergistic effect of obesity and insulin resistance in worsening migraine, with central obesity, metoclopramide use, family history of diabetes, and frequent NSAID use associated with IR development.
Rosta et al. demonstrated that insulin sensitizes TRPV1 receptors in the trigeminovascular pathway, amplifying nociceptive signaling and increasing CGRP release.

Grinberg et al. (2017) showed that hyperinsulinemia and related metabolic disturbances exacerbate neuronal excitability and impair mitochondrial function, thereby lowering the threshold for cortical spreading depression.
Ali et al. (2022) reported significantly elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) in migraine patients with insulin resistance.
An exploratory study by the authors' group in 2017 showed a 53% reduction in migraine frequency after 2 months of alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) supplementation in hyperinsulinemic patients.
Olivito et al. (2024) reported that an 8-week Mediterranean ketogenic diet reduced both migraine frequency and insulin resistance in patients with chronic migraine.
Halloum et al. (2024) highlighted the role of GLP-1 receptor agonists in reducing migraine frequency through dual metabolic and nociceptive modulation.

A meta-analysis by Di Vincenzo et al. (2020) of 10 studies (n=473) found that weight loss produced substantial improvements in monthly headache days, pain intensity, disability, and attack duration in migraine patients.

A meta-analysis of six RCTs (n=407) by García-Pérez-de-Sevilla and González-de-la-Flor (2025) found that omega-3 (EPA/DHA) supplementation, often with omega-6 restriction, significantly reduced pain intensity, attack duration, frequency, and disability in migraine patients.
In twin sisters, migraine attacks ceased within three days of achieving ketosis and recurred after cessation of the ketogenic diet, independent of weight loss.

A systematic review by Caminha et al. (2022) of 10 clinical trials found that the ketogenic diet consistently reduced migraine frequency and severity with minimal side effects, though small sample sizes and design heterogeneity limited conclusions.
The author's group's fractionated low-carbohydrate diet significantly reduced headache severity index in migraine patients with glucose-insulin dysfunction over a 12-month observational study.
A scoping review by Legesse et al. (2025) of 36 studies found a robust association between irregular meal timing/meal skipping and increased migraine frequency and severity.

Albrecht et al. (2019) provided in vivo PET/MRI evidence of increased glial activation in the periaqueductal gray, thalamus, and basal ganglia in migraine with aura, positively correlated with attack frequency.
Eftekhary et al. demonstrated that dural mast cells express CGRP receptor components (tryptase, CLR, RAMP1) in rats, with co-localization of CLR alone confirmed in human dural samples.

Gerring et al. found via GWAS pathway analyses that immune-inflammatory processes, including type I interferon responses, interferon signaling, microglial activity, NK cells, and monocyte-mediated mechanisms, are implicated in migraine, despite no significant single-gene associations.

Hajishizari et al. showed that a higher Dietary Antioxidant Quality Score (DAQS) was significantly associated with lower headache frequency, reduced migraine intensity, and decreased disability.

CCN2 immunoreactivity was markedly higher in stenotic colonic regions of Crohn's disease surgical specimens compared to adjacent non-stenotic tissue.
CCN2 expression intensity in human Crohn's disease intestinal tissue positively correlated with collagen deposition (Masson-positive) area.

Complement C4 plasma levels were significantly lower in HAE-C1INH patients at baseline compared to healthy control plasma, consistent with its established diagnostic use.

HKa levels, measured via SOMAmer 19631-13, were elevated in HAE-C1INH baseline plasma relative to healthy controls and were no longer different from healthy control levels after 26 weeks of lanadelumab treatment.

A2M was elevated in HAE-C1INH baseline plasma relative to healthy controls and returned to approximately healthy control levels after 26 weeks of lanadelumab treatment.

Interleukin-21, a cytokine involved in Th17 cell expansion, was elevated in HAE-C1INH plasma by SomaScan, consistent with a prior report, but this was not confirmed by ELISA in an independent sample set.

Commercial ELISA testing of interleukin-21, A2M, and apolipoprotein B in an independent set of HAE-C1INH and healthy control samples showed no significant differences, contrasting with SomaScan proteomic results, highlighting known discordance between affinity proteomic and immunoassay platforms.
Pathway enrichment analysis (Metacore) of the 120 lanadelumab-normalized proteins identified the kallikrein-kinin system as the most significantly enriched pathway.
Beyond the KKS, pathway enrichment of the 120 altered proteins also identified blood coagulation, cell adhesion, and connective tissue degradation as enriched pathways.

Causal-Associational Network (CASNET) analysis of the 120 altered proteins identified an active subnetwork including proteases (thrombin, tissue kallikreins, cathepsin K, plasminogen), protease inhibitors (inter-alpha trypsin inhibitor heavy chain 4, A2M), apolipoproteins, and complement system proteins.

Elevated levels of the adhesion protein VE-cadherin have previously been reported in plasma from HAE-C1INH patients, consistent with the cell adhesion pathway alterations observed in this proteomic analysis.

Prekallikrein has been reported to bind the low-density lipoprotein receptor and may represent a therapeutic target for cholesterol reduction, supporting a mechanistic link between the kallikrein-kinin system and lipid metabolism.

Several included trials found peppermint oil improved IBS symptoms including stool frequency and consistency, abdominal pain, and distension compared with baseline/placebo.
Two IBS trials found peppermint oil and placebo produced equal outcomes for most patients.
A combination of PO and caraway oil taken twice daily for about four weeks significantly reduced pain intensity, pressure, heaviness, and fullness in functional dyspepsia patients.
M. pulegium treatment reduced stomach pain, upper abdominal dull ache, upper abdominal bloating, and belching in functional dyspepsia patients, though the trial co-administered famotidine.
In healthy volunteers, PO significantly affected duodenal motility and prolonged orocaecal transit time but did not impact gastric emptying.
In pediatric patients with functional abdominal pain, mean pain severity was significantly greater at baseline than during PO treatment, with no adverse events reported.

A single-arm trial of the Nutrition Care Gut Relief Formula (containing peppermint oil) showed improvement in heartburn, indigestion, constipation, and abdominal pain in patients with upper and/or lower GI tract disorders.
In a rat acetic acid-induced colitis model, M. longifolia and its principal constituent eucalyptol decreased NO production in macrophages and downregulated pro-inflammatory cytokines TNF-α and IL-6.

The anti-inflammatory action of peppermint oil, whose main component is menthol, is proposed to occur via activation of TRPM8 channels on immune cells, downregulating chemically-induced colitis in mouse models.

In a mustard oil/ethanol-induced IBS rat model, PO-loaded alginate microbeads downregulated IL-1β expression and increased plasma IL-10 while suppressing IL-6 and TNF-α, indicating anti-inflammatory activity.
MAEO dose-dependently inhibited LPS-induced PGE2 and NO production in RAW 264.7 macrophages via suppression of COX-2 and iNOS mRNA expression, and also inhibited IL-6 and IL-1β mRNA expression.

In a TNBS-induced colitis mouse model, pennyroyal phenolic extract (rosmarinic acid) significantly reduced macroscopic colon injury and reduced COX-2 and iNOS expression compared to untreated colitis mice.

In a TNBS-induced colitis mouse model, spearmint extract-treated colons showed downregulated iNOS expression alongside high COX-2 expression, suggesting reduced inflammation partly via decreased oxidative stress.
M. piperita ethanolic extract reduced LPS-induced NO production and suppressed pro-inflammatory cytokines in RAW 264.7 murine macrophages.
M. piperita essential oil and chloroform extract showed the highest DPPH free-radical scavenging activity, while aqueous extract showed the lowest.
M. pulegium essential oil at 40-60 mg/mL inhibited approximately 80% of free radicals in DPPH scavenging assays, attributed to its pulegone content.
An enteric-coated peppermint oil formulation (Colpermin) showed tolerability and efficacy in treating IBS symptoms after 1 month, with delayed release preventing esophageal reflux and heartburn.
In children with IBS, pH-dependent enteric-coated peppermint oil (Colpermin) reduced the severity of pain associated with IBS.
A fixed combination of caraway and peppermint oil produced statistically and clinically relevant reductions in pain intensity, pressure, heaviness, and fullness versus placebo in FD patients.
In healthy participants, caraway and peppermint oil acted as a gastrointestinal muscle relaxant via menthol's spasmolytic action and as a fundus relaxant.
Intraduodenal application of the combined caraway/peppermint oil formula reduced motility in the gastric corpus and antrum in 24 healthy volunteers.

A trial in healthy volunteers found that a combination of peppermint oil and caraway oil acted as a gastrointestinal muscle relaxant via menthol's spasmolytic action and as a fundus relaxant that may prevent the fullness feeling seen in FD patients.
In 24 healthy volunteers, intraduodenal application of combined caraway and peppermint oil reduced motility (frequency and amplitude of contractions) in the gastric corpus and antrum.

Carmint (a combination of Melissa officinalis, Mentha spicata, and Coriandrum sativum extracts) reduced the frequency and severity of abdominal pain and bloating in IBS patients by the end of the intervention.

A pH-dependent, enteric-coated peppermint oil capsule produced statistically significant improvement in IBS symptoms, with the beneficial effect persisting for 1 month after therapy ended in more than half of treated participants, attributed to menthol's effect on calcium movement across smooth muscle cell membranes.
Enteric-coated, delayed-release peppermint oil capsules taken over an 8-week follow-up effectively improved abdominal pain and discomfort in IBS outpatients.

A novel triple-coated microsphere, highly purified peppermint oil formulation released in the small intestine produced a statistically significant reduction in mean Total IBS Symptom Score and decreased abdominal pain/discomfort compared to baseline in non-constipated IBS patients.

Menthacarin, a fixed combination of peppermint oil and caraway oil, effectively alleviated pain and discomfort and improved quality of life in FD patients with postprandial distress syndrome and epigastric pain syndrome.

In a trial of targeted ileocolonic-release and small-intestinal-release peppermint oil in IBS patients, neither formulation produced a statistically significant reduction in the proportion of abdominal-pain responders versus baseline, though the small-intestinal-release form did improve abdominal pain and discomfort.

Peppermint oil showed no significant difference from placebo in improving IBS-SSS scores, though most participants in both groups achieved clinically meaningful symptom improvement, and the peppermint oil group experienced more side effects.
A cost-effectiveness analysis concluded that small-intestinal release peppermint oil is cost-effective for IBS from both societal and healthcare system perspectives.

In children with functional abdominal pain, enteric-coated peppermint oil improved mean pain severity versus baseline and reduced the entire gut mean peak contraction amplitude, although whole gut transit time was unaffected.

IBS mice (C. rodentium + water avoidance stress model) showed reduced colonic transit time compared to CON mice, and all interventions improved transit time with the synbiotic (L. plantarum ZYC501 + GOS) producing the greatest improvement.

IBS mice exhibited significantly higher abdominal withdrawal reflex (AWR) scores to colorectal distention compared to CON, indicating visceral hypersensitivity, and all interventions lowered AWR scores to CON levels.

IBS mice showed anxiety-like behavior (lower central/peripheral time ratio in open field test, more buried marbles) compared to CON; GOS and the synbiotic were more effective than L. plantarum alone at reversing this behavior.
Colonic histamine levels were significantly elevated in IBS mice versus CON, and only the synbiotic (not L. plantarum or GOS alone) significantly reduced histamine levels.
Colonic mast cell tryptase levels were significantly higher in IBS mice than CON and were reduced by L. plantarum, GOS, and the synbiotic.
Colonic PGE2 levels were significantly elevated in IBS mice compared to CON and were restored by L. plantarum, GOS, and the synbiotic.
Colonic COX-2 expression (by immunofluorescence) was significantly elevated in IBS mice versus CON and was reduced by L. plantarum, GOS, and the synbiotic.

Colonic histological damage scores (decreased muscle thickness, crypt damage, impaired mucosal integrity) were significantly higher in IBS mice than CON, and all interventions improved histological scores.
Goblet cell numbers in colonic tissue were reduced in IBS mice compared to CON, and the synbiotic significantly increased goblet cell numbers above the IBS group.
MUC2 protein and mRNA expression in colon were significantly lower in IBS mice than CON, and all interventions (L. plantarum, GOS, synbiotic) improved MUC2 expression.
Colonic LPS levels were significantly higher in IBS mice than CON; GOS and the synbiotic, but not L. plantarum alone, significantly reduced LPS levels.
Colonic TNF-α mRNA levels were significantly higher in IBS mice than CON, and L. plantarum, GOS, and the synbiotic each reduced TNF-α mRNA levels.
Colonic IL-6 mRNA levels were significantly higher in IBS mice than CON, and L. plantarum, GOS, and the synbiotic each reduced IL-6 mRNA levels.
Colonic TRPV1 mRNA expression was significantly higher in IBS mice than in CON and all intervention groups, consistent with a role in histamine-driven visceral sensitization.

Fecal acetate, propionate, and butyrate were decreased in IBS mice versus CON; all interventions increased SCFA levels, with GOS/synbiotic producing greater propionate increases and the synbiotic producing greater butyrate increases than L. plantarum alone.

Gut microbiota diversity and OTU composition differed significantly among CON, IBS, and IBS+SYN groups, with IBS mice showing reduced diversity compared to CON and the synbiotic group harboring the most unique OTUs.
Genus Akkermansia (along with Allobaculum) was markedly decreased in IBS mice relative to CON, and synbiotic treatment increased Akkermansia abundance.
Genera Helicobacter and Saccharibacteria were significantly increased in IBS mice compared to CON and IBS+SYN groups, and synbiotic treatment decreased their abundance.
Relative abundance of Akkermansia and Lactobacillus positively correlated with colonic transit time discrimination index across the IBS/CON/SYN groups.
Relative abundance of Akkermansia was strongly positively correlated with fecal acetate, propionate, and butyrate levels.

IL-6 was positively correlated with AWR scores, TRPV1 expression, LPS, histamine, and PGE2 levels, and negatively correlated with colonic transit time, anxiety-behavior ratio, SCFAs, and Akkermansia/Lactobacillus abundance.

Histamine, mast cell tryptase, and PGE2 levels were each positively correlated with AWR visceral hypersensitivity scores, supporting a link between mast cell hyperactivation and visceral hypersensitivity.

Genomic CAZy analysis and growth-curve screening showed L. plantarum ZYC501 grew optimally on galacto-oligosaccharides (GOS) compared to FOS, XOS, and inulin, supporting selection of GOS as its companion prebiotic for the synbiotic formulation.

Overall, the synbiotic of L. plantarum ZYC501 and GOS more effectively alleviated colonic transit dysfunction, visceral hypersensitivity, anxiety-like behavior, mucosal barrier disruption, and mast cell hyperactivation than either component alone, via reshaping of gut microbiota (increased Akkermansia/Lactobacillus, decreased Helicobacter/Saccharibacteria) and elevated SCFAs.
Relative abundance of Akkermansia was positively correlated with colonic transit time (discrimination index) in IBS mice.
Relative abundance of Lactobacillus was positively correlated with colonic transit time (discrimination index) in IBS mice.
Relative abundance of Akkermansia positively correlated with fecal levels of acetate, propionate, and butyrate in IBS mice.
Colonic IL-6 mRNA levels positively correlated with visceral hypersensitivity (AWR scores), TRPV1 expression, LPS, histamine, and PGE2 levels.

Colonic IL-6 levels negatively correlated with colonic transit time, anxiety-related central/peripheral time ratio, fecal SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate), and abundance of Akkermansia and Lactobacillus.

Colonic histamine, mast cell tryptase, and PGE2 levels were positively correlated with AWR visceral hypersensitivity scores, indicating a link between mast cell hyperactivation and visceral hypersensitivity.
In vitro growth curve screening identified GOS as the optimal carbon source for L. plantarum ZYC501 growth compared to FOS, XOS, and inulin.
Whole-genome CAZy analysis of L. plantarum ZYC501 identified carbohydrate-active enzymes capable of hydrolyzing GOS and FOS.
16S rRNA sequencing showed increased operational taxonomic unit (OTU) richness in IBS+SYN mice (1000 OTUs, 150 unique) compared to CON (854 OTUs, 27 unique) and IBS (886 OTUs, 33 unique) groups.

Electroacupuncture reduced the loose stool rate and increased the minimum volume threshold for abdominal withdrawal reflex, indicating improved diarrhea and reduced visceral hypersensitivity in IBS-D rats.
Model group colons showed extensive inflammatory infiltration, glandular atrophy and disorganized goblet cells, which were reduced and better organized after EA treatment.
IL-1β, IL-6, and IFN-γ levels were significantly elevated in serum and colon of model rats versus control, and were significantly reduced by EA treatment.
Serum D-lactate and DAO, markers of intestinal mucosal barrier damage, were significantly increased in model rats and significantly reduced after EA treatment.
Tight junction proteins Claudin-1, Occludin, and ZO-1 were significantly reduced in colon of model rats and significantly upregulated by EA treatment.
Transmission electron microscopy showed reduced, disorganized microvilli and fragmented tight junctions with widened gap junctions in model rats, which were restored towards normal by EA.
Comparative transcriptomics identified 1,479 DE lncRNAs, 1,304 DE mRNAs, and 88 DE miRNAs in colon of model versus control rats.

EA treatment reversed transcriptomic dysregulation, altering 1,216 lncRNAs, 1,268 mRNAs and 94 miRNAs compared with the model group, including 429 mRNAs/362 lncRNAs/48 miRNAs down-regulated and 426 mRNAs/342 lncRNAs/10 miRNAs up-regulated by EA.
Genes down-regulated by EA (429 mRNAs) were significantly enriched in the Antigen processing and presentation pathway, linked to mast cell biology.
Genes up-regulated by EA (426 mRNAs) were enriched in Neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, PPAR signaling, and Glutathione metabolism pathways, considered relevant to mast cell activity.
A ceRNA network of 7 DE lncRNAs–miR-139-3p–Bid was identified and implicated in EA's protection of the intestinal mucosal barrier, with Bid elevated in model rats and reduced by EA.
A second ceRNA network of 7 DE lncRNAs–miR-378b–Slc4a5 was identified, with Slc4a5 enriched in the bile secretion pathway and implicated in EA's protective effect on the intestinal barrier.
RT-qPCR validation confirmed that Bid, Ripk3, lncNONRATG013093.2, and miR-223-5p were significantly upregulated in model rats compared to control and significantly downregulated after EA.
RT-qPCR validation showed CD34, lncNONRATG013188.2, lncNONRATG021964.2, miR-139-3p, and miR-200b-3p were significantly downregulated in model rats and increased after EA.
Colonic tryptase and PAR-2 protein levels were significantly elevated in model rats and significantly decreased following EA, indicating EA inhibits mast cell degranulation-related signaling.

Immunofluorescence showed increased numbers of tryptase/PAR-2 co-expressing cells (activated mast cells) in model rat colon, which decreased after EA treatment, indicating EA inhibits mast cell activation.
Carriers of m.3243A>G had significantly prolonged gastric emptying time compared with healthy controls.
Colonic transit time was significantly prolonged in m.3243A>G carriers compared with healthy controls.
Whole gut transit time was significantly prolonged in m.3243A>G carriers compared with healthy controls.
The colonic motility index was significantly decreased in m.3243A>G carriers compared with healthy controls.
No differences were found in segmental pH, transpyloric pH rise, or ileocaecal pH fall between m.3243A>G carriers and healthy controls.
m.3243A>G carriers had fewer high-pressure contraction peaks (10-20 mmHg and >50 mmHg) 30 minutes before the ileocecal junction, and fewer peaks >50 mmHg in the colon, compared with controls.

GI symptom questionnaire scores (Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index and Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale total and most sub-scores, except reflux) were higher in m.3243A>G carriers than in healthy controls.
Whole gut transit time correlated negatively with BMI in m.3243A>G carriers.
No correlation was found between blood heteroplasmy levels and gastric emptying time, colonic transit time, or whole gut transit time in m.3243A>G carriers.
No correlation was found between GI symptom questionnaire scores and gastric emptying, colonic, or whole gut transit times in m.3243A>G carriers.

Differences in gastric emptying time, colonic transit time, whole gut transit time, and colonic motility index versus matched controls were only significant in diabetic m.3243A>G carriers, not in nondiabetic carriers.
m.3243A>G carriers were more likely than healthy controls to have cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy, as measured by cardiac vagal tone.
Forty-five percent of m.3243A>G carriers showed single-, multi-, or pan-segmental delayed GI transit compared with published gender-specific reference values.
Comparative genomic hybridization array analysis identified a heterozygous ~390 kb deletion at chromosome 1q41 encompassing TGFB2, establishing a diagnosis of Loeys-Dietz syndrome type 4.
At baseline, DEXA showed low BMD with a lumbar spine Z-score of -2.1 and a total hip Z-score of -2.6, consistent with skeletal fragility associated with LDS.
Baseline bone resorption marker TRACP-5b was elevated at 502 mU/dL (reference 120-420), suggesting increased bone resorption in this patient with LDS.

Despite normal corrected serum calcium, intact PTH was mildly elevated (72 pg/mL) with a low fractional excretion of calcium (0.3%), raising but not confirming suspicion of normocalcemic primary hyperparathyroidism.
One year of romosozumab therapy increased lumbar spine BMD Z-score from -2.1 to -1.0, with a further increase to -0.5 after one additional year of sequential denosumab.
Femoral neck BMD increased from Z-score -2.6 after one year of romosozumab to -2.0 after subsequent denosumab therapy.
Total hip BMD improved slightly from Z-score -2.6 at baseline to -2.4 after romosozumab and -2.2 after subsequent denosumab therapy.

BMD at the 1/3 radius, a predominantly cortical, non-weight-bearing site, remained relatively stable throughout treatment, in contrast to larger changes at the spine and hip, suggesting site-specific or mechanical-load-dependent skeletal involvement in LDS.
Trabecular bone score improved from 1.314 after one year of romosozumab to 1.412 after one year of subsequent denosumab, suggesting enhanced trabecular microarchitecture.
One year after starting romosozumab, the bone resorption marker TRACP-5b decreased from 502 mU/dL to 200 mU/dL, indicating improved bone metabolism balance.
The bone formation marker BAP increased from 10.7 g/dL to 13.7 g/dL after one year of romosozumab therapy, consistent with increased bone formation.
The patient experienced no fracture events during sequential romosozumab and denosumab therapy over approximately 1.5+ years of follow-up.
In a cited cohort of LDS patients, one-third of adults had bone density Z-scores below -2.0, and approximately 60% experienced at least one lifetime fracture.
In a study of 77 LDS cases (children and adults), low BMD (Z-score <0) was observed at the lumbar spine and total hip, and 61% had experienced at least one fracture event.

Abnormal TGF-β signaling characteristic of LDS reportedly inhibits osteoblast differentiation while promoting osteoclast differentiation and suppresses bone matrix mineralization and mechanical properties.
Studies in TGF-β knockout mice demonstrated cortical bone thinning with limited changes to trabecular bone, supporting a cortical-predominant skeletal mechanism.

Bisphosphonates, previously the only treatment attempted for LDS-related skeletal fragility, have shown inconsistent efficacy, with increased BMD reported in some cases and limited effectiveness in others.

Romosozumab, a monoclonal anti-sclerostin antibody, has a dual effect on bone, increasing trabecular bone density and thickening cortical bone, making sclerostin a potential therapeutic target in LDS-related skeletal fragility.
In a diphenoxylate-induced constipated mouse model, 100 mg/kg lycopene treatment improved gut transit time and intestinal transit rate.
Lycopene treatment alleviated depression- and anxiety-like behaviors in constipated mice.
Lycopene pretreatment enhanced intestinal barrier integrity in the constipated mouse model.
Lycopene pretreatment increased short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production in the gut of constipated mice.
Lycopene rebalanced gut microbiota homeostasis by enriching beneficial bacteria in constipated mice.
Lycopene restored enteric neuronal function, shown by increased expression of the neuronal markers HuC/D and Tuj1.
Lycopene treatment balanced neurotransmitter levels associated with enteric neuronal function in constipated mice.
LYC treatment increased expression of the pan-neuronal marker HuC/D in enteric neurons, indicating restoration of enteric neuronal function.
LYC treatment increased expression of the neuronal marker Tuj1 in enteric neurons, supporting restored enteric neuronal function.
LYC treatment rebalanced enteric neurotransmitter levels in the constipated mouse model.
Brain transcriptomic analysis showed that LYC regulates the cholinergic synapse pathway in association with behavioral improvements.
LYC increased acetylcholine (Ach) content in the brain of treated mice.
The increase in brain acetylcholine and cholinergic pathway regulation by LYC was associated with alleviation of neuroinflammation.
Sucrase-isomaltase deficiency can be diagnosed through disaccharidase enzyme activity testing performed on duodenal mucosal biopsies.

In children with genetic sucrase-isomaltase deficiency, dietary carbohydrate restriction and sacrosidase enzyme supplementation are effective per randomized controlled trials, but these approaches have not yet been rigorously studied in adults.

Gastric emptying breath testing in large pediatric cohorts shows that biological sex, pubertal status, and body size are important determinants when deriving normative reference values for gastric emptying.

Antegrade continence enema therapy is the most common reversible surgical treatment for chronic constipation in children and has high rates of efficacy, but few studies have examined its efficacy in adults.

Auricular neurostimulation via percutaneous electrical nerve field stimulation (PENFS) is FDA-approved for adolescents with irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia, supported by sham-controlled randomized trials, with emerging efficacy data in other pediatric disorders of gut-brain interaction; adult efficacy studies have not been performed.

Auricular neurostimulation via percutaneous electrical nerve field stimulation (PENFS) is FDA-approved for adolescents with irritable bowel syndrome and functional dyspepsia, based on sham-controlled randomized trials showing efficacy.
No efficacy studies of auricular neurostimulation have yet been performed in adults with gastrointestinal disorders, representing a translational research gap.
Microstructural integrity of the central autonomic network white matter tracts showed stronger associations with cardiac and vascular organ damage than white matter in non-CAN brain regions.
In cortical CAN tracts, higher free water compartment values were positively associated with measures of cardiac and vascular organ damage.
In cortical CAN tracts, lower intra-axonal volume was negatively associated with cardiac and vascular organ damage measures.

A 10% increase in the free-water compartment of the left cingulum-insular cortex tract was associated with a substantially increased hazard of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) after imaging.
A 10% increase in the free-water compartment of the right cingulum-insular cortex tract was associated with an even greater hazard of MACE after imaging than the left-sided tract.
Subcortical components of the CAN showed only modest associations with cardiovascular damage, with increased intra-axonal volume particularly linked to cardiac parameters.

Among patients with long COVID, the most frequently worsened symptoms were fatigue and memory impairment (48.4% each), loss of energy (41.9%), visual disturbance (38.7%), and concentration impairment (32.3%).
Patients who required hospitalization during acute COVID-19 (severe group) had higher total long COVID symptom severity scores than those treated at home (mild group).
Serum triglyceride levels showed a significant positive correlation with total long COVID symptom severity.
Fasting blood glucose levels positively correlated with the severity of cardiopulmonary symptoms in long COVID patients.
HDL cholesterol levels showed a negative correlation with the severity of neurological symptoms in long COVID patients.
HDL cholesterol levels showed a strong negative correlation with the severity of psychological symptoms in long COVID patients.
Positive RT-PCR controls without long COVID (PCON) showed reduced gut microbial species richness (Chao1 index) compared with negative controls (NCON).
Beta-diversity analysis showed a significant dissimilarity in gut microbial community composition between long COVID patients and PCON, although neither group differed significantly from NCON.

Random forest analysis identified enrichment of the genera Leuconostoc, Actinomyces, Granulicatella, Weissella, Paludicola, Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1, and Phascolarctobacterium in the gut microbiome of long COVID patients compared with PCON.
ANCOM-BC analysis confirmed enrichment of families Peptostreptococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae and genus Leuconostoc in long COVID patients compared with PCON.
Leuconostoc, Granulicatella, and Actinomyces genera showed strong diagnostic accuracy for distinguishing long COVID from PCON, with AUCs of 0.885, 0.783, and 0.733 respectively.
Compared with NCON, long COVID patients had increased relative abundance of Leuconostoc and Actinomyces and decreased abundance of Lachnospiraceae_UCG_010 and Sutterella.
Systemic symptom severity was inversely correlated with the relative abundance of Family_XIII_AD3011_group in long COVID patients.
Digestive symptom severity showed strong negative correlations with the relative abundance of Barnesiella, Alistipes, and Gordonibacter in long COVID patients.

Otolaryngologic symptom severity was negatively correlated with the relative abundance of seven genera: Subdoligranulum, Clostridium_sensu_stricto_1, Lachnospiraceae_ND3007_group, UCG-002, Ruminococcus, Monoglobus, and Eubacterium coprostanoligenes group.
Blautia and Granulicatella relative abundance positively correlated with the severity of visual symptoms in long COVID patients.
Parabacteroides relative abundance showed a strong negative association with total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol levels in long COVID patients.
Basophil levels directly correlated with Eubacterium ventriosum group abundance and inversely correlated with Rothia abundance in long COVID patients.

The authors interpret enrichment of the opportunistic pathobionts Actinomyces and Granulicatella, together with their negative correlation with basophil levels (a marker of poor COVID-19 prognosis), as suggesting a role in long COVID pathogenesis rather than being purely incidental diagnostic markers.
UK Office for National Statistics estimates that post-COVID-19 condition at 12 weeks after infection ranges from 3.0% (symptom tracking) to 11.7% (self-classification).
Long COVID appears more prevalent in females, and the risk of persistent symptoms increases linearly with age.

In low-risk, non-hospitalised patients with persistent symptoms, at least one organ showed impairment four months after initial COVID-19 infection, and long COVID severity appeared independent of acute infection severity.
Elective surgery patients who developed COVID-19 were 26 times more likely to die in hospital compared to those without COVID-19 infection.
Emergency surgery patients with COVID-19 infection were six times more likely to die in hospital compared to those without COVID-19.
Preoperative COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with higher adjusted odds of 30-day postoperative mortality when surgery occurred 0-2 weeks after diagnosis (OR 4.1).
Surgery performed 3-4 weeks after preoperative COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with an adjusted OR of 3.9 for 30-day mortality.
Surgery performed 5-6 weeks after preoperative COVID-19 diagnosis was associated with an adjusted OR of 3.6 for 30-day mortality.
Patients having surgery more than 7 weeks after COVID-19 diagnosis showed no increased 30-day postoperative mortality compared with those without COVID-19, unless symptoms were ongoing.

Among patients operated on more than 7 weeks after COVID-19 diagnosis, those with ongoing symptoms had higher postoperative mortality (6.0%) than those with resolved symptoms (2.4%) or who were asymptomatic (1.3%).
Postoperative pulmonary complication risk was increased up to 6 weeks after COVID-19 infection, with rates becoming similar to non-COVID patients by 7 weeks.

In a propensity-matched analysis, septic and pulmonary complications were increased beyond 30 days after a positive COVID-19 test, and the rate of ischaemic stroke was increased up to 30 days after a positive test.

Patients with resolved COVID-19 symptoms were found to be at greater risk of 30-day postoperative mortality compared to those with asymptomatic disease, highlighting the importance of both current and past clinical status when timing surgery.
Use of immunosuppressive therapies such as tocilizumab and sarilumab in COVID-19 patients may increase the risk of postoperative infection and delayed wound healing.
CRP levels were significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases compared with controls in both sexes, consistent with chronic low-level inflammation.
Cystatin C was significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases relative to controls, indicating chronic inflammation.
Leucocyte count was significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases relative to controls.
Neutrophil count was significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases relative to controls.
Markers of insulin resistance—triglycerides-to-HDL cholesterol ratio, ALT, ALP and GGT—were significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases.
Low urea levels together with elevated ALT, ALP and GGT were indicative of liver disease/dysfunction in ME/CFS cases.
Erythrocyte distribution width showed a sex-discordant effect, being significantly positive in males and significantly negative in females for ME/CFS status.
Mean corpuscular haemoglobin was the only blood trait showing a significant natural indirect effect (mediated via physical activity, Duration of walk mediator) of ME/CFS status.
Blood phosphatidylcholine and choline levels were lower in ME/CFS cases, replicating prior smaller metabolomic studies.
Higher triglycerides and lower HDL cholesterol were observed in both UKB enzymatic and NMR metabolomic assays for ME/CFS cases.
Of nine amino acids measured, only alanine was significantly elevated, and only in female ME/CFS cases.
Blood pyruvate and lactate, previously proposed as ME/CFS biomarkers, were not significantly different between cases and controls in this large cohort.
Extracellular superoxide dismutase (SOD3) was the only one of 2923 proteins significantly altered in abundance between ME/CFS cases and controls in both sexes.
Seven innate immune complement proteins, including CR2 (the EBV receptor on B and T lymphocytes), were all elevated in ME/CFS cases in the combined-sex total effect analysis.

CDHR2 and CDHR5, which together form the extracellular portion of the intermicrovillar adhesion complex, were significantly up-regulated in ME/CFS cases; disruption of this complex is linked to intestinal dysfunction and inflammatory bowel disease.
Leptin levels were significantly increased in ME/CFS cases, a protein involved in energy homeostasis, and was among the proteins replicated in both sexes for total effect.

Gene Ontology enrichment of proteins with significant total effects highlighted TNF and IL4 production and NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity pathways, although the TNF and IL4 proteins themselves were not significantly altered in abundance.

Blood biomarker differences were substantially stronger in ME/CFS cases with post-exertional malaise (PEM)-like symptoms (26 significant biomarkers) than in those without PEM (9 significant biomarkers).

Five blood traits not significant in the main analysis were significant specifically in the PEM subgroup: albumin, direct bilirubin, eosinophil percentage, haemoglobin concentration and reticulocyte count.
Cystatin C and CRP, biomarkers of chronic inflammation, were significant only in the PEM subgroup and not in the non-PEM subgroup, linking inflammation more specifically to PEM.
In an independent replication using the All of Us cohort, 9 of 14 tested blood traits were significantly associated with ME/CFS with the same direction of effect as in UK Biobank.
Overall, 511 blood-based biomarkers (across blood traits, NMR metabolites and proteins) showed significant total-effect differences between ME/CFS cases and controls.
Blood, metabolite and protein biomarker differences between ME/CFS cases and controls were not explained by reduced physical activity: only 1 of 3237 indirect-effect (NIE) estimates was significant.
166 biomarkers were independently replicated as significant in both female-only and male-only analyses, supporting equivalent ME/CFS pathophysiology between sexes despite known sex-biased prevalence.
Effect sizes for most replicated biomarkers were small-to-medium, with 91% of the 116 female- and male-replicated NDE traits having Cohen's d between 0.2 and 0.5.
Urate was the only blood trait for which the indirect (activity-mediated) effect exceeded the direct effect, for the moderate-activity-days mediator.
BMI was significantly, but only slightly, higher in ME/CFS cases than controls in both sexes.

Despite CRP being highly statistically significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases, only a small minority of cases had clinically moderate CRP elevation (>10 mg/L), illustrating extensive overlap between case and control distributions.
The authors conclude that no single blood trait analysed is an effective standalone biomarker for ME/CFS, despite many showing statistically significant population-level differences.
Among nine amino acids measured by NMR, only alanine was significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases, and this was significant only in females.
Blood pyruvate and lactate, previously proposed as ME/CFS biomarkers, showed no significant difference between cases and controls in this large cohort, failing to replicate earlier reports.
Total effect (TE) analysis, combining direct and mediated pathways, found 39 of 63 blood traits to be significant predictors of ME/CFS case status in the combined male and female cohort.
Beyond blood traits, total-effect analyses identified 251 proteins and 216 metabolites additionally significantly associated with ME/CFS status across the sex-specific or combined analyses.
Urate was the only blood trait for which the activity-mediated indirect effect (NIE) was larger than the direct effect (NDE), using the days/week-of-moderate-activity mediator.

Blood biomarker associations with ME/CFS were stronger among cases reporting post-exertional malaise (PEM)-like symptoms: 26 traits were significant in the PEM subgroup compared with only 9 in the non-PEM subgroup.
Albumin, direct bilirubin, eosinophil percentage, haemoglobin concentration, and reticulocyte count were significant only among ME/CFS cases with PEM-like symptoms, not among cases without PEM.
C-reactive protein and cystatin C, both markers of chronic inflammation, were significantly elevated only among ME/CFS cases reporting PEM-like symptoms, not among those without PEM.

Alanine aminotransferase, apolipoprotein A, HDL cholesterol, TG-to-HDL-C ratio, triglycerides, and the TyG index were significantly associated with ME/CFS in both PEM and non-PEM subgroups, indicating replication independent of PEM status.

In an independent replication using the All of Us cohort (903 cases, 75,943 controls), 9 of 14 tested blood traits were significantly associated with ME/CFS, with the same direction of effect as in UK Biobank.
Across all analyses, 511 blood-based biomarkers (blood traits, NMR metabolites and proteins) differed significantly between ME/CFS cases and controls.

166 biomarkers were independently significant in both female-only and male-only total effect analyses, providing evidence that ME/CFS biological differences are largely equivalent between the sexes despite known sex-biased prevalence.

Of 3237 natural indirect effect (NIE) estimates across all mediator and trait types, only one (mean corpuscular haemoglobin) was significant, indicating that reduced physical activity does not explain the molecular and cellular differences seen in ME/CFS.

A prior UK Biobank study (Huang et al, 2024) identified 168 metabolic biomarkers associated with ME/CFS using individual-level predictive modelling and a different case definition, contrasting with this study's population-average causal mediation approach.

Among 116 blood traits significantly replicated in both sexes (NDE), 91% showed only small-to-medium effect sizes (Cohen's d between 0.2 and 0.5), with no trait showing clear separation between cases and controls.

Although CRP was significantly elevated in ME/CFS cases overall, only 4.8% of female and 2.5% of male cases had CRP above the clinically notable 10 mg/L threshold (versus 2.2% and 1.8% of controls), illustrating why no single blood trait is an effective standalone biomarker.
ME/CFS cases had slightly but statistically significantly higher BMI than controls in both sexes at UK Biobank baseline.

The overall combination of blood marker changes in ME/CFS does not match any other known disease; for example, primary biliary cholangitis shares elevated ALP and GGT with ME/CFS but shows elevated bilirubin, whereas ME/CFS shows lower bilirubin.
In total effect analyses, four proteins—leptin (LEP), CDHR5, alcohol dehydrogenase 4 (ADH4), and RTN4R—were significantly associated with ME/CFS in both male and female cohorts.
About three-quarters (75.6%) of participants reported taking prescription medication, with an average of 4.2 total medications per person.
68.6% of reported medications were used specifically for ME/CFS symptom management, averaging 3.0 ME/CFS-related medications per patient.
Total medication use was significantly higher among US participants (4.9 medications) compared to Canadian participants (3.8 medications).
ME/CFS-related symptom medication use was also greater among US participants (3.7 medications) than Canadian participants (2.6 medications).
Analgesic medications, including NSAIDs and low-dose naltrexone, were the most frequently prescribed medication class for ME/CFS symptoms (31.7%).
Psychotropic medications, including SSRIs and SNRIs, were the second most frequently prescribed medication class for ME/CFS symptoms (26.4%).
Immune-related medications, including corticosteroids, antivirals, and antihistamines, were the third most frequently prescribed medication class overall (10.6%).
No significant correlation was found between disease duration and the number of ME/CFS-related symptom medications used.
No significant correlation was found between participant age and the number of ME/CFS-related symptom medications used.
No significant correlation was found between age at diagnosis and the number of ME/CFS-related symptom medications used.

Analgesic (27.8-34.6%) and psychotropic (22.2-33.3%) medications were consistently the top two most frequently used medication classes across all six symptom categories (cardiovascular, neurological, musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, psychiatric, general).

The third most frequently used medications were immune-related in participants with cardiovascular (12.5%), neurological (10.3%), musculoskeletal (10.9%), and general (11.6%) symptoms, or GI-related in those with neurological (10.3%), GI (19.2%), and psychiatric (16.7%) symptoms.
There were no significant differences in total or ME/CFS-related symptom medication use when stratified by daily step count or total weekly hours of physical movement.

ME/CFS-related symptom medication use showed a U-shaped relationship with weekly physical movement, being lowest (2.9±1.8 medications) at 12-14 hours/week of movement and rising again (4.2±2.3 medications) beyond 15 hours/week.

The most bothersome symptoms reported were post-exertional malaise (84.4%), memory/concentration/focus difficulty (67.4%), unrefreshing sleep (57.8%), decline in social/occupational/educational/personal activities (43.7%), and unexplained muscle/joint pain (36.3%).
Almost three-quarters of participants (71.9%) believed infection was the trigger for their ME/CFS diagnosis, followed by physical and/or emotional trauma (40%).
The authors cite clinical trials reporting that SSRIs are ineffective and may even worsen fatigue in ME/CFS patients.
The authors cite evidence that pain severity increases following exercise in people with ME/CFS, supporting pain as a component of post-exertional malaise.
The authors state that around 70% of people with ME/CFS meet diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia, a primary pain condition.
