Whole-exome association analysis identified significant variants in the Neuroblastoma Breakpoint Family genes NBPF1, NBPF10, and NBPF16, encoding Olduvai (DUF1220) domains, as associated with ME/CFS susceptibility.
The strongest additive MLMM association signal was an intergenic variant near the FAM86B2 gene.
Four additional variants significantly associated with ME/CFS in the additive MLMM were located in intronic regions of ATR, RSPH10B, and ADGRE5-CD97, and the coding region of ACR.
In the additive single-locus mixed model, the strongest association signal for ME/CFS susceptibility was observed at an NBPF10 variant.
A functional stop-retained variant in CD8B was among the genes implicated by the additive single-locus model of ME/CFS susceptibility.
A missense variant in the germ cell alkaline phosphatase gene ALPG was among the genes implicated by the additive single-locus model of ME/CFS susceptibility.
The strongest association signal in the dominant multi-locus mixed model for ME/CFS susceptibility was a variant in PIP4P2-TMEM55A.
A variant in the neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 2 gene NTRK2 showed a significance value similar to the top dominant MLMM signal for ME/CFS susceptibility.
Variants in ATR, SORL1, KRT24, and PIP4P2-TMEM55A were significant under both additive and dominant transmission models of ME/CFS susceptibility.
Additional genes with variants dominantly associated with ME/CFS susceptibility in the multi-locus model included LAMA2, PTPRD, REXO4, SLC38A2, ARSG, ZNF266, and CYP4F8.
A PTPRD genomic region association with ME/CFS susceptibility identified in the Australian cohort was successfully replicated in an independent Nevada, USA ME/CFS cohort.
A cluster of six markers in CSMD3 associated with ME/CFS susceptibility in the Australian cohort was replicated in the Nevada cohort.
Coding-region variants in DCC, ALDH18A1, GALNT16, UNC79, NCOA3, and RAPGEF5 identified in the Australian ME/CFS cohort were replicated in the Nevada cohort, with some novel functional variants noted.

The ALDH18A1 gene association supports prior metabolomic findings of elevated plasma pyrroline-5-carboxylate, an intermediate of proline/ornithine/arginine biosynthesis, in ME/CFS patients, implicating mitochondrial function.
In the Nevada replication cohort, GRIK2 and NPAS2 were significant, echoing earlier GWAS and gene expression results, with GRIK2 linked to schizophrenia/autism and NPAS2 to circadian rhythm control.
Pathway enrichment analysis showed over-representation of the GO biological process 'Regulation of Dendrite Development' among ME/CFS-associated genes DBN1, PTPRD, DCC, and NTRK2.
Prior functional studies on the same ME/CFS patient cohort found mitochondrial Complex V insufficiency combined with increased TORC-1 signalling compared to healthy controls.

An ethnographic study of UK biopsychosocial fibromyalgia services found that 'chronicity rhetoric', reinforced by biomedical research and welfare benefits systems, interrupts practitioners' and patients' efforts to promote healing and recovery.
No treatments have been proven to produce sustainable improvement or recovery for fibromyalgia, and patients are typically dissatisfied with their care.
The authors suggest their findings on chronicity rhetoric likely generalize to other difficult-to-treat conditions such as chronic pain, Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, and Myalgic Encephalomyelitis.

A cited study applied random forest machine-learning algorithms to the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire-Short Form to differentiate patients with myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome, patients with post-COVID-19 condition, and healthy controls, achieving 92.18% accuracy in distinguishing post-COVID-19 sequelae patients from healthy controls.
Genetically predicted higher total cholesterol was causally associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted higher LDL cholesterol was causally associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted higher apolipoprotein B was causally associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted higher apolipoprotein E was causally associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted higher HDL cholesterol was causally associated with reduced risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted higher apolipoprotein A1 was causally associated with reduced risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Triglycerides and lipoprotein(a) were not causally associated with chronic fatigue syndrome risk.
Two-sample MR identified 35 immune cell phenotypes (lymphocytes, monocytes, granulocytes, hematopoietic stem cells) causally associated with chronic fatigue syndrome risk.
CD4+/CD8+ T cell ratio showed the strongest positive causal association with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome among the immune phenotypes tested.
CD28+ CD4- CD8- T cells showed a pronounced negative (protective) causal association with chronic fatigue syndrome risk.
Hematopoietic stem cell absolute count mediated part of the causal effect of HDL-C on chronic fatigue syndrome risk, accounting for 12.6% of the mediated effect.
Percentage of NK CD3- lymphocytes mediated part of the causal effect of HDL-C on chronic fatigue syndrome risk, accounting for 4.9% of the mediated effect.
IgD expression on IgD+ CD38+ B cells mediated part of the causal effect of HDL-C on chronic fatigue syndrome risk, accounting for 6.7% of the mediated effect.
Genetically predicted alcohol consumption was causally associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.

Genetically predicted consumption of champagne/white wine and spirits were both causally associated with substantially increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome, with spirits showing the largest effect.
Genetically predicted cooked vegetable consumption was associated with increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted preference for chili peppers and liking for pizza were each associated with modestly increased risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted cheese consumption was causally associated with reduced risk of chronic fatigue syndrome.
Genetically predicted pork consumption was causally associated with reduced risk of chronic fatigue syndrome, with the strongest protective effect among diet items tested.
Apo A1 and HDL-C mediated the protective effect of cheese consumption on chronic fatigue syndrome risk, accounting for 4.3% and 5% of the total effect respectively.
Sensitivity analyses (Cochran's Q, MR-Egger intercept, MR-PRESSO, leave-one-out) showed no significant heterogeneity or horizontal pleiotropy, supporting robustness of the MR estimates.

Gray matter volume of the right supplementary motor cortex (SMC) was negatively correlated with physical, mental, and total fatigue scores, meaning smaller SMC volume was associated with higher fatigue regardless of fatigue type.
In a follow-up regression, right SMC volume was specifically and significantly correlated with mental fatigue score but not with physical fatigue score.
Right planum temporale volume was negatively correlated with physical fatigue, such that smaller volume was associated with higher physical fatigue scores.
Left putamen volume was significantly positively correlated with physical and total fatigue but not mental fatigue, suggesting larger putamen volume with higher physical/total fatigue.
Left middle temporal gyrus (MTG) volume was significantly positively correlated with physical and total fatigue but not mental fatigue.
Right precentral gyrus volume was significantly positively correlated with physical fatigue scores.
Left parietal operculum volume was significantly positively correlated with physical fatigue scores.
Left orbital part of the inferior frontal gyrus (OIFG) volume was significantly negatively correlated with mental fatigue scores.
Left fusiform gyrus volume showed a significant positive correlation with mental fatigue scores, possibly reflecting a compensatory mechanism.
Both age and sex showed a statistically significant negative correlation with physical, mental, and total fatigue scores across the cohort.
No significant correlations were found between total white matter volume and CFQ fatigue scores.

This integrative review of eight qualitative/mixed-method studies identified structural barriers, societal barriers, and consultation barriers as common issues affecting primary care for HSD/hEDS patients and clinicians.
POTS is reported as the most common form of dysautonomia in EDS/G-HSD, with an 18% prevalence and associated chest pain, palpitations, and dyspnea.
Individuals with EDS/G-HSD show a 2- to 3-fold increase in respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, cough, sputum, wheezing) compared to age- and sex-matched healthy individuals.
hEDS patients reported significantly lower habitual physical activity (Baecke questionnaire) scores than age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
In a study of 20 individuals with classical and vascular EDS, most reported mild dyspnea (70% MRC grade 1), with 15% grade 2 and 10% grade 3.
Morgan et al. observed increased cough, wheezing, and exertional dyspnea in 288 individuals with EDS/G-HSD, associated with limitations in exercise tolerance.
Dynamic hyperinflation, a mechanical ventilatory constraint, was observed to be associated with reduced exercise capacity in 12 hEDS participants during constant load cycling.
In a retrospective evaluation, dysautonomia-associated symptoms such as dyspnea (36% prevalence) and chest pain/tightness (34%) were associated with exercise intolerance in hEDS/G-HSD.

Individuals with dysautonomia had a greater decrease in exercise levels (from moderate/vigorous to light/no exercise: 56% to 15%) after symptom exacerbation compared to non-dysautonomic individuals (68% to 40%).
A 6-week inspiratory muscle training (IMT) program improved exercise capacity by 13% and FEV1 by 10% compared to a non-IMT group in hEDS patients with reduced respiratory muscle strength.

EDS patients with high symptom burden (dyspnea, wheezing, nasal congestion, cough, chest pain) had lower HRQL and greater pain, fatigue, and sleep disturbance than EDS groups with fewer respiratory symptoms.
Pain is reported as a cardinal symptom in over 90% of individuals with EDS/G-HSD and is one of the most frequent and disabling symptoms.
75% of singers with EDS/G-HSD experienced throat pain, functional voice difficulties, and other laryngeal difficulties such as coughing and choking.
More than 80% of individuals with EDS/G-HSD report severe chronic fatigue that limits daily and social activities.
EDS/G-HSD patients with severe fatigue had significantly lower SF-36 physical functioning scores than those with non-severe fatigue.
A systematic review of 13 studies estimated a 39% prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea in individuals with joint hypermobility syndrome.

In a study of 100 EDS patients, excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale) was associated with worse HRQL and lower SF-36 scores across physical, social, and mental health domains compared to healthy controls.
Anxiety is commonly reported in EDS/G-HSD, with an estimated prevalence of 60-75%.
About half of EDS patients with anxiety describe exertional dyspnea.

hEDS individuals with more severe functional respiratory complaints (dyspnea, chest pain, chest tightness) scored higher on depression, anxiety, and central sensitization syndrome (e.g., fibromyalgia) questionnaires.
In a cross-sectional study of 466 adults with joint hypermobility syndrome, 52% modified their work/job duties due to symptoms, and 82% believed their disease impaired their work performance.
hEDS/G-HSD participants had significantly lower Ghent Participation Scale scores (indicating reduced participation in daily and social activities) than age- and sex-matched healthy controls.

A systematic review of 10 studies found that a multi-modal rehabilitation program (aerobic, strength, flexibility, education, cognitive-behavioral elements) of less than 6 weeks significantly improved exercise capacity, muscle strength, daily function, and kinesiophobia in EDS/G-HSD.
MCAS, characterized by abnormal histamine release from mast cells causing inflammation, is a potential contributor to dyspnea and asthma in EDS/G-HSD.

A systematic review of 10 studies found that multi-modal rehabilitation programs (aerobic exercise, strength training, flexibility, education, and cognitive-behavioral elements) lasting less than 6 weeks significantly improved exercise capacity, muscle strength, daily function, and kinesiophobia in the EDS/G-HSD population.
Kinesiophobia (fear of movement) has been associated with greater fatigue severity in individuals with EDS/G-HSD.
EDS patients report significantly lower satisfaction with social activities compared to general population normative values.

Cranio-cervical instability and Chiari malformations may be associated with respiratory symptoms in a subset of individuals with EDS/G-HSD, although their impact on health-related quality of life has not been previously described.
Among 78 eligible websites on EDS/G-HSD exercise training, industry/for-profit organizations (37%) and personal commentary/blogs (24%) were the two most common website categories.
Exercise training content coverage varied substantially across websites, with a mean content score of 13.8 out of 25 predefined items.
Resistance training was the most commonly covered exercise modality, appearing in 88% of websites.
Exercise safety recommendations were addressed by 83% of websites, commonly advising to consult a healthcare provider, exercise under supervision, progress gradually, and prioritize rest.
Sixty-three percent of websites highlighted exercises to avoid, such as high-impact activities and contact sports for individuals with vascular EDS.
Stretching/flexibility exercises, motivational strategies, exercise duration guidance, cardiovascular fitness, and exertional tolerance assessment were less commonly addressed content elements.
The median modified DISCERN quality score across websites was 4 out of 5, indicating overall good quality, though areas of uncertainty were poorly addressed.
The median Global Quality Scale (GQS) score was 3 out of 5 and mean JAMA benchmark score was 3 out of 4, indicating moderate overall website quality.

Only half of websites provided references to support content and just 32% included authorship or proper citations, reducing credibility despite most having ownership disclosures (94%) and updated information (90%).
Total website content scores were moderately-to-strongly correlated with quality metrics, showing a strong correlation with GQS and a moderate correlation with DISCERN.
The mean PEMAT understandability score for websites was 85%, exceeding the 70% reference standard for patient education materials.

The mean PEMAT actionability score was 69%, just below the 70% reference threshold, with most websites identifying at least one actionable step but only 56% breaking actions into explicit, manageable steps.
Only 42% of websites provided visual aids with clear titles or captions, despite the recognized value of captioned diagrams and videos for comprehension and behavior change.

All 78 websites exceeded the recommended grade 6 reading level for patient educational materials, with a mean Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of 11.0 and mean Flesch Reading Ease Score of 43.6, indicating difficult readability.

Muscle strength was the most commonly cited short- and long-term benefit of exercise training on websites (78%), while cardio-metabolic fitness was rarely addressed (18%), despite its relevance to controlling dysautonomia.
Most websites were educational (82%) rather than instructional, representing an opportunity to develop more instructional websites or embedded videos with actionable guidance.
The study population targeted by websites was predominantly EDS (59%), followed by both EDS and G-HSD combined (26%), and G-HSD alone (15%).
Among 429 patients clinically diagnosed with hEDS, 405 (94.4%) had experienced a psychiatric misdiagnosis in at least one of five evaluated categories prior to their hEDS diagnosis.
88% of patients with hEDS reported being told they were fabricating their symptoms before their diagnosis.
76% of patients with hEDS reported being labeled as attention-seeking before diagnosis.
67% of patients with hEDS were misdiagnosed with conversion disorder before their hEDS diagnosis.
60% of patients with hEDS were told that their symptoms were "in their head" before diagnosis.
4% of patients with hEDS were diagnosed with Munchausen syndrome by proxy or a factitious disorder before their hEDS diagnosis, the least common of the five misdiagnosis categories.
There was no statistically significant association between patient age group and the distribution of psychiatric misdiagnosis categories among hEDS patients.
Patients with EDS often have co-diagnoses of POTS, MCAS, gastroparesis, and median arcuate ligament syndrome, adding complexity to correct EDS diagnosis.
Misdiagnosis of EDS in children has been reported to be associated with increased risk of decreased physical activity at school and of developing autism or ADHD.
A patient with type IV (vascular) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome presented with a tibioperoneal trunk aneurysm, posing a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge.

Defective type III collagen resulting from COL3A1 mutations produces thin arterial adventitia and decreased elasticity, increasing susceptibility to dissection, rupture, and arteriovenous fistula in vascular EDS.

Radial artery cannulation, a routine procedure in the general population, can cause an arteriovenous fistula as an iatrogenic complication in patients with vascular EDS, with delayed and unpredictable progression.

The specific type of COL3A1 variant (haploinsufficiency, exon skip, or dominant-negative protein production) may influence procedural risk, with certain variants linked to more severe vascular fragility and earlier onset of complications.
The authors recommend that ultrasound guidance be used for all arterial cannulations in VEDS patients, performed by the most experienced clinician, to enhance accuracy and reduce complications.
For procedures requiring large-bore vascular access in VEDS, the authors recommend surgical exposure over percutaneous approaches to reduce the risk of dissection and rupture.
In the referenced case, the surgical team chose to ligate rather than repair the affected artery, illustrating that conservative management can be preferable in VEDS.
In the Ong et al. (2010) RCT, patients treated with celiprolol had a significantly lower rate of vascular events than controls, corresponding to a 64% relative risk reduction.
Baderkhan et al. (2021) found celiprolol treatment was associated with significant reductions in systolic and diastolic blood pressure.
Hoang et al. (2014) reported that systolic blood pressure and central systolic blood pressure increased over time in celiprolol-treated vEDS patients during 5-year follow-up.

Ong et al. (2010) found that celiprolol treatment increased arterial stiffness markers (reduced carotid distensibility, increased Young's elastic modulus, elevated pulse wave velocity), interpreted as enhanced arterial wall strength via beta2-adrenergic and TGF-beta-mediated collagen synthesis.

Hoang et al. (2014) found that increased arterial stiffness parameters (Young's elastic modulus, reduced distensibility, carotid intima-media thickness growth) occurred similarly in celiprolol-treated and untreated vEDS patients over 5 years, suggesting these changes may reflect aging rather than a celiprolol-specific effect.

Buso et al. (2024) found that 70% (14/20) of vEDS patients experienced one or more major vEDS-related events (12 vascular, 2 gastrointestinal) during a mean follow-up of 72±41 months despite celiprolol treatment.
Baderkhan et al. (2021) reported an annual risk of major vascular event of 4.7% among vEDS patients on celiprolol, with five events, four of which were fatal.

Frank et al. (2019) found no significant difference in overall arterial event incidence or aggregate survival between celiprolol-treated and control groups initially, but a significant reduction in hospitalizations for acute arterial events after celiprolol initiation over median 5.3-year follow-up.
Frank et al. (2019) reported that vEDS patients treated with celiprolol at 400 mg/day had significantly higher survival than those receiving 100-300 mg/day.

Frank et al. (2019) reported a survival curve difference at 11.1 years of follow-up between celiprolol-treated and untreated vEDS patients (19.3% vs 51.5%, p<0.001), described in the text as untreated patients having lower survival than treated patients despite the stated percentages.

Frank et al. (2019) documented that glycine substitutions in COL3A1 were associated with earlier and more severe vascular complications, including arterial dissections and ruptures, compared to splice-site mutations or null alleles which were linked to milder phenotypes.
Across the five pooled studies, 71% of participants (135/189) tolerated the target celiprolol dose of 400 mg/day.

Baderkhan et al. (2021) reported that among 40 patients, fourteen experienced side effects, with six (15%) experiencing severe reactions such as dizziness, hypotension, imbalance, asthma deterioration, and headache, and four patients discontinued celiprolol due to side effects.
Buso et al. (2024) reported that two patients (8%) died during celiprolol dose titration, and 80% of patients reached the recommended dose.
Elevated TGF-beta levels have been observed in vEDS patients, potentially representing a physiological response to impaired collagen synthesis and contributing to vascular fragility.
Preclinical mouse model studies showed that celiprolol significantly improves biomechanical integrity of the thoracic aorta in vEDS, whereas losartan showed no beneficial effect in the same models.

A single 400 mg dose of celiprolol was shown to lower standing diastolic blood pressure by up to 10% without adversely affecting cardiac function, though this BP-lowering effect was not seen in normotensive patients.

Jeunemaitre et al. (2025) explored celiprolol combined with irbesartan, suggesting combination therapy may yield additional protective effects beyond celiprolol monotherapy, though further validation is needed.
Pooled analysis across 12 studies found an overall prevalence of vascular complications in EDS of 30.03%.
Vascular EDS (vEDS) had the highest subtype-specific pooled prevalence of vascular complications at 42.36%.
Unspecified EDS subtype showed a lower pooled prevalence of vascular complications (18.65%) than vEDS, likely due to varied diagnostic criteria.
Hypermobile EDS (hEDS) had a pooled vascular complication prevalence of 19.77%, consistent with a milder vascular phenotype than vEDS.

In a Dutch national cohort of 142 genetically confirmed vEDS patients, 48% experienced arterial aneurysms or dissections, with a median age of 44 years at first vascular event and 41% experiencing multiple vascular events.
A systematic review of 448 EDS patients reported 720 aneurysms overall, predominantly in abdominopelvic and intracranial locations.
A hospitalization-based study found markedly increased odds of carotid artery dissection in EDS patients compared with matched controls (OR 15.02).
The same hospitalization-based study found markedly increased odds of cerebral aneurysm in EDS patients compared with matched controls (OR 5.59).

Vascular complications in vEDS are mechanistically linked to COL3A1 mutations that compromise type III collagen fibril stability, reducing arterial wall strength and increasing risk of rupture, aneurysm, and dissection.
Dysregulated TGF-beta signaling is proposed to exacerbate COL3A1 mutation pathogenicity by promoting extracellular matrix remodeling and contributing to vascular fragility in vEDS.
The authors note that evidence on sex differences in vascular risk among EDS patients remains inconclusive.
The authors suggest genetic variability and adipocytokines may contribute to the observed variability in vascular risk across EDS studies.
Individuals with COL3A1 pathogenic variants had the highest prevalence of arterial events (20.8%) among all genes studied.
TGFBR2 pathogenic variant carriers had a 7.7% prevalence of arterial events, the second highest among the genes studied.
TGFBR1 pathogenic variant carriers had a 7.3% prevalence of arterial events.
TGFB2 pathogenic variant carriers had a 6.4% prevalence of arterial events.
SMAD3 pathogenic variant carriers had a 5.6% prevalence of arterial events.
FBN1 pathogenic variant carriers (Marfan syndrome) had the lowest prevalence of arterial events at 1.5%.
Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that individuals with COL3A1 pathogenic variants had the most numerous and earliest-onset arterial events compared with those with TGF-β pathway gene or FBN1 variants.
In individuals with TGF-β pathway gene variants and in FBN1, aortic events occurred significantly earlier and were more penetrant than arterial events, unlike in COL3A1.
Unlike in the TGF-β genes and FBN1, there was no significant difference between the timing/penetrance of aortic events and arterial events in individuals with COL3A1 variants.
Sex modifies arterial event risk: males with COL3A1 variants had earlier and more frequent arterial events than males with TGF-β pathway gene variants, a difference not observed in females.
Among individuals with FBN1 pathogenic variants (Marfan syndrome), arterial events beyond the aorta occurred primarily in men.
The authors recommend that smoking cessation and hypertension control be emphasized in patients with heritable thoracic aortic disease genes to reduce risk of arterial events.
A young woman with joint hypermobility syndrome and a history of bilateral developmental dysplasia of the hips developed severe bilateral external snapping hip.

Bilateral open iliotibial band fasciectomy, performed five months apart after failed nonoperative management, provided significant relief of active and passive snapping and complete pain relief at 12-month follow-up in this patient with hypermobility syndrome and DDH.

In a retrospective review of 95 AIS patients who underwent vertebral body tethering, the coronal arc of motion at uninstrumented segments distal to the lower instrumented vertebra showed no significant difference between preoperative and 1-year postoperative bending radiographs, indicating no hypermobility developed.

Postoperative patient-reported outcome scores (HOS-ADL, HOS-Sport, mHHS, SF-12 PCS, SF-12 MCS, WOMAC) did not differ significantly between patients with and without joint hypermobility after hip arthroscopy with labral repair.
The non-hypermobility group achieved the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) for HOS-ADL at a significantly higher rate than the hypermobility group.

There was no significant difference between hypermobile and non-hypermobile patients in the patient acceptable symptom state (PASS) attainment for HOS-ADL, or in PASS or MCID attainment for HOS-Sport or mHHS.
Median patient satisfaction after surgery was numerically lower in the hypermobility group compared with the non-hypermobility group.
At minimum 2-year follow-up, reoperation rates and conversion to total hip arthroplasty rates were similar between hypermobile and non-hypermobile patients undergoing hip arthroscopy.
At the sixth-month out-brace evaluation, the reduction in Cobb angle (coronal curvature) was significantly greater in AIS patients with generalised joint hypermobility than in those without it.
During the in-brace evaluation at four weeks, no difference in radiographic measurements was found between AIS patients with and without generalised joint hypermobility.

At the sixth-month out-brace evaluation, apical vertebral rotation, spine height, global coronal balance, and apical translation did not differ between JHM-present and JHM-absent groups, despite the difference seen in Cobb angle change.
Patients with end-stage lesser TMT joint arthritis walked more slowly, with shorter stride length and increased step width, compared to matched healthy controls.
During terminal stance, patients with TMT arthritis showed increased forefoot dorsiflexion and hallux extension relative to controls.
Patients with TMT arthritis had reduced sagittal and transverse plane range of motion in the hindfoot and hallux segments compared to controls.
Coronal plane inter-segmental motion was relatively preserved in TMT arthritis patients compared to controls, suggesting sagittal and transverse plane impairments predominate over coronal changes.

Increased forefoot-to-hindfoot motion observed in TMT arthritis patients may reflect medial column laxity, including potential first ray hypermobility, as a compensatory adaptation for reduced midfoot stability.

Forty-three percent of pediatric celiac disease patients with sustained TTG IgA decline on a gluten-free diet met Rome IV criteria for a disorder of gut-brain interaction, higher than the hypothesized 30% prevalence.
Children who developed DGBI after celiac disease diagnosis had a significantly lower BMI z-score at initial presentation than those who did not develop DGBI.

Functional constipation was the most common DGBI subtype identified among pediatric celiac disease patients with DGBI, followed by functional abdominal pain, functional nausea, IBS, and functional dyspepsia/gastroparesis.
Presence of abdominal pain at initial celiac disease diagnosis visit was associated with a threefold increased likelihood of later developing a DGBI.
Presence of constipation at initial diagnosis visit was associated with increased likelihood of subsequently developing a DGBI.
Presence of vomiting at initial diagnosis visit was associated with increased likelihood of later developing a DGBI.
Nighttime pain awakening at initial diagnosis was strongly associated with increased likelihood of later developing a DGBI, though with a very wide confidence interval.
Complete villous blunting noted on diagnostic biopsy, but not overall Marsh score severity, was associated with increased risk of developing DGBI.
Comorbid joint hypermobility syndrome in pediatric celiac disease patients was associated with over a fivefold increased risk of developing a disorder of gut-brain interaction.
Comorbid headaches were associated with increased risk of developing DGBI in pediatric celiac disease patients.
Comorbid chronic musculoskeletal pain and chronic muscle pain were each associated with increased risk of developing DGBI in pediatric celiac disease patients.

Presence of any comorbid psychiatric diagnosis (including depression, anxiety, ADHD, bipolar disorder, eating disorders, or PTSD) was a significant predictor of developing DGBI, though no single psychiatric condition was independently predictive.
Comorbid type 1 diabetes was associated with a decreased risk of developing DGBI in pediatric celiac disease patients.
Emergency department visits (but not hospitalizations) for gastrointestinal complaints after celiac disease diagnosis were significantly associated with a DGBI diagnosis.

Use of neuromodulation treatments including auricular percutaneous electrical nerve field stimulation (IB-stim) and pyloric botulinum toxin injection with dilation was significantly associated with a DGBI diagnosis.
Patients who were asymptomatic at celiac disease diagnosis rarely went on to develop a DGBI, in contrast to over half of symptomatic patients.
Sex, race, ethnicity, and presence of a family history of DGBI were not significant predictors of DGBI diagnosis in pediatric celiac disease patients.
Mean NLR was significantly higher in Fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Mean NLR was significantly higher in Axial Spondyloarthritis patients than in Fibromyalgia patients.
Mean NLR was significantly higher in Axial Spondyloarthritis patients than in healthy controls.
Regular NSAID consumption was significantly more frequent in Axial Spondyloarthritis patients than in Fibromyalgia patients.
Regular NSAID consumption was significantly more frequent in Axial Spondyloarthritis patients than in healthy controls.
Mean CRP was slightly but significantly higher in Axial Spondyloarthritis patients than in Fibromyalgia patients.
In Fibromyalgia patients, NLR was positively correlated with CRP levels, though the effect size was small.
In Fibromyalgia patients, NLR was positively correlated with FIQR disease-severity scores, though the effect size was small.
In Axial Spondyloarthritis patients, NLR showed a moderate positive correlation with CRP levels.
In Axial Spondyloarthritis patients, NLR was strongly correlated with ASDAS disease-activity scores.
In Axial Spondyloarthritis patients, NLR was strongly correlated with BASDAI disease-activity scores.
NLR was significantly higher in Fibromyalgia patients with severe disease (FIQR ≥59) than in those with non-severe disease.
NLR was significantly higher in Axial Spondyloarthritis patients with high/very high disease activity (ASDAS ≥2.1) than in those with low/inactive disease.
An NLR cut-off of 1.54 discriminated Fibromyalgia patients from healthy controls with moderate diagnostic accuracy.
An NLR cut-off of 1.61 discriminated Axial Spondyloarthritis patients from healthy controls with high diagnostic accuracy.
An NLR cut-off of 1.64 predicted severe Fibromyalgia (FIQR ≥59) with modest diagnostic accuracy.
An NLR cut-off of 1.95 predicted high/very high disease activity in Axial Spondyloarthritis with high diagnostic accuracy.
Reduced resting heart rate variability, reflecting autonomic nervous system dysfunction, has been consistently reported in fibromyalgia patients.
Fibromyalgia patients commonly exhibit elevated anxiety symptoms and comorbid anxiety disorders.
Most reviewed studies support an association between reduced resting HRV and elevated anxiety symptoms in fibromyalgia patients.
Interventions aimed at improving HRV, including exercise, psychotherapy, and mind-body therapies, also appear effective in reducing anxiety symptoms in fibromyalgia patients.

Acid saline injection significantly decreased paw withdrawal thresholds (increased mechanical hyperalgesia) in both untrained and trained acid-saline groups two days after induction, with a large effect size.
Resistance training prior to hyperalgesia induction resulted in a higher paw withdrawal threshold (less pain sensitivity) in the RTA group compared to the untrained acid-saline group at day 73.

Ten days after pain induction, RT continued to prevent the increase in pain sensitivity, with trained acid-saline animals showing higher paw withdrawal thresholds than untrained acid-saline animals, with a large effect size.
Eighteen days after pain induction, the untrained acid-saline group still showed the lowest paw withdrawal threshold compared to the trained acid-saline and untrained neutral-saline groups.
After 10 weeks of resistance training, trained groups (RTN and RTA) demonstrated significantly higher maximum load carrying capacity than untrained groups, with a large effect size.
Prior to pain induction, the RTA group showed higher maximum load carrying test results than the RTN group.
Acid saline injection increased skeletal muscle IL-6 expression in both untrained and trained acid-saline groups compared to neutral saline groups, with a large effect size.

Resistance training prevented the acid saline-induced increase in muscle IL-6, as the RTA group showed lower IL-6 than the untrained acid-saline group and did not differ from the trained neutral-saline group.
The untrained acid-saline group exhibited higher muscle IL-10 levels than the untrained neutral-saline group, possibly as a compensatory response to IL-6 release.
Resistance training prevented the acid saline-induced increase in muscle IL-10, with the RTA group showing reduced IL-10 compared to the untrained acid-saline group, with a large effect size.

The untrained acid-saline group showed lower thalamic serotonin concentration compared to the trained acid-saline group, with a large effect size, suggesting resistance training prevented the acid saline-induced serotonin decrease.
The untrained acid-saline group showed a non-significant downward trend in thalamic serotonin compared to the untrained neutral-saline group.
A prior study identified a significant rise in BOLD signal at the onset of fMRI runs that is much larger in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls, where it was not significant.

In the FM stim condition, initial BOLD rise was significantly larger than in FM rest in the insular cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, periaqueductal grey, thalamus, and parabrachial nucleus.
FM stim participants showed significantly larger initial BOLD rise than HC stim participants in the insular cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and thalamus.
FM stim participants showed significantly larger initial BOLD rise than HC rest participants in the insular cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, frontal orbital cortex, and anterior cingulate cortex.
No significant differences in initial BOLD rise were found between HC rest and HC stim, nor between FM rest and either HC condition, across regions of interest.

Using a 0.25% signal-change threshold, the initial BOLD signal rise occurred exclusively within grey matter regions, and the right posterior insular cortex showed the largest increase in the FM stim group.
Ciuffini et al. found that FM patients exhibited heightened neural activation and increased emotional arousal in response to negative emotional/unpleasant stimuli compared to controls.
Frumer et al. found that maladaptive emotional regulation responses are associated with FM symptoms and its comorbidity with stress and depression.
Samartin-Veiga et al. found no evidence of increased auditory sensitization in FM patients compared to healthy controls across varying sound intensities and sequences.
Carrillo-de-la-Pena et al. found heightened sensory responses to non-painful auditory stimuli only appeared during later stages of sensory integration after prolonged exposure in FM patients.
Increased functional connectivity within visual networks in FM was linked to increased fatigue, reduced emotional and cognitive processing, and greater symptom severity.

Pomares et al. found grey matter reductions in the posterior and anterior cingulate cortex of FM patients were explained by decreased tissue water content (T1 relaxation), whereas increased GABA receptor concentration was associated with grey matter increases.
Caumo et al. found that elevated BDNF suppresses GABAergic transmission in FM patients, producing hyperexcitability of neural circuits and central sensitization.

Inferrera et al. found mitochondrial structural changes in FM skeletal muscle, including reduced citrate synthase and cytochrome-c oxidase activity, decreased oxidative phosphorylation efficiency, downregulated Mitofusin 2, and reduced Coenzyme Q10.

Huang et al. found elevated lipid peroxidation and reduced glutathione and superoxide dismutase activity in FM, and reported that Boswellia Serrata improved mitochondrial biogenesis by promoting PGC-1α nuclear translocation.
Martinez-Lara et al. found irregular mitochondrial homeostasis in blood samples of FM patients, indicating oxidative stress and impaired cellular function compared to healthy controls.

Higher baseline PASI and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) were independently associated with increased risk of guselkumab discontinuation.

MDA achievement at 12 months was significantly higher in bDMARD-naive patients (60%) compared to those failing one (22%) or two or more prior bDMARDs (22%).

No significant differences in drug retention time were found across guselkumab treatment lines (bDMARD-naive, one prior bDMARD failure, ≥2 prior bDMARD failures) or between monotherapy and combination csDMARD treatment.

Itch-related sleep disturbances were reported by 75% of SFN patients with itch, with over half reporting both difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep.
Warm temperatures were the most commonly reported factor exacerbating itch, while cold temperatures/showers were the least likely to exacerbate itch.
Scratching and distraction were the most effective alleviating strategies for itch in SFN patients.

Itch symptoms in SFN were most frequently reported in the distal extremities, with the shins the most commonly affected site, and showed a slightly more proximal distribution than typical stocking-glove pain.
The spatial correlation between reported itch locations and reported pain locations was generally weak in SFN patients.
Stabbing-quality itch was significantly more common in SFN patients with biopsy-confirmed reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density compared to those with a normal skin biopsy.

No significant differences in itch severity, frequency, timing, exacerbating/alleviating factors, or location were found between SFN patients with sodium channel gene variants versus other SFN etiological subgroups.
SFN patients described their itch as tingling significantly more often than non-SFN patients referred for suspected SFN.
SFN patients reported itch in the hands and feet significantly more often than non-SFN patients, suggesting this location may be a diagnostic clue for SFN.
SFN patients were significantly older, had more severe pain, and later symptom onset compared to non-SFN patients.
Among SFN patients, those with itch were younger, had earlier symptom onset, and had more severe pain than those without itch.
The proportion of SFN patients with an identifiable underlying condition did not differ between those with and without itch, and no underlying cause was found in 61% of SFN patients overall.

The authors speculate that differential involvement of hairy-skin itch neurons (MrgprA3+/MrgprD+) versus glabrous-skin itch neurons (MrgprC11+) could partly explain the more proximal, rather than distal, distribution of itch relative to pain in SFN.
Isolated abnormalities in cold detection threshold (CDT) or warm detection threshold (WDT) alone showed relatively low diagnostic accuracy for small fiber impairment.
Combined abnormalities in CDT and WDT achieved 69% sensitivity and 70% specificity for detecting small fiber impairment in distal symmetric polyneuropathy.
For diagnosing small fiber neuropathy (SFN), the combination of CDT and WDT yielded 78% sensitivity, 70% specificity, and a 94% negative predictive value.
Integrating CDT or WDT abnormalities with small-fiber-related clinical abnormalities improved diagnostic accuracy for SFN to 78% sensitivity and 100% specificity.
Among 138 patients with polyneuropathy diagnosed via ACTTION criteria, 36 had SFN, 91 had mixed fiber polyneuropathy, and 11 had pure large fiber polyneuropathy.
Allodynia with preserved large-fiber sensory modalities (joint position sense, vibration) was a distinctive clinical feature seen in half of the patients, useful for differentiating AIP from GBS.

The authors note that prior literature confirms small fiber neuropathy in AIP via skin biopsy showing markedly decreased intra-epidermal nerve fiber density, consistent with the allodynia observed in this cohort.
All but one patient developed hemodynamic instability (tachycardia or hypertension), reflecting autonomic dysregulation during acute porphyric attacks.
Abdominal pain, reported by all patients, was identified as the most frequently reported manifestation of dysautonomia in AIP, likely related to intestinal spasm, dilation, or ischemia.
Two of six patients carried the pathogenic HMBS splice site variant c.826-2A>T.
One of six patients carried the pathogenic HMBS splice site variant c.706-2A>T.
A missense HMBS variant, c.275T>C, was detected in one patient.
A nonsense HMBS variant, c.874C>T, was detected in one patient.
Patient 3 carried an HMBS deletion resulting in a premature stop codon, previously reported in a Saudi patient presenting with abdominal pain, seizures, psychiatric symptoms, and lower limb weakness.
Five of six patients had elevated urine porphobilinogen (PBG) levels, tested at a median of 5 weeks (range 1–22 weeks) after onset of acute quadriparesis.
All patients with acute porphyric neuropathy manifested electrolyte impairment in the form of hyponatremia and hypomagnesemia, alongside abdominal pain.
Cranial nerve involvement (facial weakness and dysphagia) was observed in two of six patients, consistent with prior reports of trigeminal, facial, vagus, and hypoglossal nerve involvement in AIP.

Initial nerve conduction studies showed predominantly motor axonal polyneuropathy with sparing of motor conduction velocities and distal latencies, and relative sparing of tibial CMAP amplitudes in two patients.

Serial NCS in patient 3 revealed a 'coasting phenomenon' with normal initial NCS but interval reduction of upper extremity CMAP amplitudes at 4 months, consistent with prior reports of progressive CMAP decline for up to 3-5 months post-diagnosis.

Serial NCS in patient 2 showed interval reduction of lower extremity SNAP amplitudes 7 months after the initial attack, with sparing of upper extremity sensory responses, a pattern differing from a prior single-case report showing bilateral involvement.
Five of six patients were initially misdiagnosed as Guillain-Barré syndrome, resulting in diagnostic delay and, in three cases, exposure to IVIg or plasmapheresis before AIP was recognized.

All patients were treated with haem arginate infusions (median 4.5 weeks, range 2.5–28 weeks after onset); early administration is described as crucial for shortening attack duration and improving neuropathic weakness, though delays commonly occurred due to diagnostic confusion with GBS.
At follow-up (median 16 days, range 8-30 days), five of six patients showed distal predominant weakness, and four of six were dependent on ambulation aids.
Electroacupuncture (EA) at ST36 significantly mitigated diabetes-associated weight loss, with EA-treated rats' final body mass 11.4% higher than DGP controls at week 10.
EA did not significantly modulate non-fasting blood glucose levels, which remained elevated (>16.7 mmol/L) in both DGP and EA groups.
DGP rats showed significantly reduced gastric slow wave discharges compared to Sham controls, which EA intervention restored to near-normal levels.
DGP rats showed impaired gastric emptying and intestinal propulsion rates versus Sham controls, both significantly improved by EA treatment.
PET-CT imaging quantitatively confirmed EA-accelerated gastric emptying, with only 66.1% radioactivity remaining at 3600 seconds in EA rats versus 80.9% in DGP and 54.5% in Sham controls.

DGP rats exhibited marked gastric mucosal degeneration, glandular atrophy, inflammatory infiltrates, submucosal fibrosis, and disrupted smooth muscle organization, which was significantly mitigated by EA treatment.
EA significantly upregulated nNOS protein expression in gastric tissue compared to DGP controls.
EA significantly upregulated C-kit (KIT), a marker of interstitial cells of Cajal, in gastric tissue compared to DGP controls, confirmed by both western blot and immunofluorescence.
EA significantly upregulated SCF (KIT ligand) protein expression in gastric tissue compared to DGP controls.
EA induced upregulation of the cholinergic marker ChAT in gastric tissue compared to DGP controls.
EA induced upregulation of α7nAChR in gastric tissue compared to DGP controls.
DGP rats showed significant suppression of gastrin compared to Sham, which EA intervention significantly increased.
DGP rats showed significant suppression of motilin compared to Sham, which EA intervention significantly increased.
DGP rats showed a paradoxical elevation of inhibitory VIP compared to Sham, which EA intervention significantly reduced.

ChAT levels were elevated in DGP rats compared to Sham at ST36 skin, spinal L4-L6, and NTS, further increased by EA and mimicked by the ChAT agonist PA, but abolished by co-administration of the ChAT antagonist AP with EA.
EA increased α7nAChR expression in ST36 skin, L4-L6 spinal cord, and NTS, an effect attenuated by co-treatment with the ChAT antagonist AP.
EA and the ChAT agonist PA induced robust c-FOS neuronal activation in the L4-L6 spinal segments, which was suppressed by co-treatment with the ChAT antagonist AP.

EA and PA significantly elevated c-FOS expression in the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), with EA+AP rats showing reduced activation, supporting NTS as a central integration site for EA's vagal effects.

Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy (SDV) significantly reduced gastric ChAT and α7nAChR expression versus DGP controls, and abolished EA-induced upregulation of both proteins, demonstrating dependence on intact vagal efferent signaling.

Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy attenuated EA's restoration of gastric slow wave discharges and negated EA's improvements in gastric emptying and small intestinal propulsion, with PET-CT showing SDV increased residual gastric content to 82.2% versus 67.8% in EA alone.

Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy counteracted EA's histological benefits, sustaining submucosal collagen deposition and mild smooth muscle disorganization, and reduced nNOS, C-kit, and SCF protein expression compared to EA-treated rats.
Subdiaphragmatic vagotomy reversed EA-mediated upregulation of gastrin and motilin and suppression of VIP, indicating vagal efferent dependence of EA's peptide-normalizing effects.

Intratracheal bleomycin instillation induced CTD-ILD-like lung injury in mice, with alveolar atrophy, interstitial fibrous proliferation, alveolar septal thickening, inflammatory infiltration, and collagen deposition.
Serum MUC5B, a mucin whose overproduction is linked to ILD risk, was significantly increased in bleomycin-treated model mice compared to controls.
Serum TOLLIP showed a borderline decrease in the bleomycin model group compared with controls, consistent with reduced protection against lung injury.
Serum KL-6 and SP-D, markers of epithelial dysfunction and matrix remodeling, were significantly higher, and RCN3 (protective) was lower, in model mice versus controls.
RCN3, reported to be protective against lung lesion, was reduced in serum of bleomycin model mice compared with controls.
Serum IL-6, CCL18, and ferritin (SF), immunoinflammatory and fibrosis-associated markers, were elevated in bleomycin model mice compared with controls.

PD + Cur treatment (and positive control nintedanib) improved alveolar lesions, interstitial thickening, and collagen deposition in bleomycin model mice, with no significant dose-dependence among high, medium, and low doses.
PD + Cur significantly reduced serum MUC5B and increased serum TOLLIP compared to the model group, reversing the disease-associated pattern.
PD + Cur reversed the disease-associated changes in serum KL-6, SP-D, and RCN3 compared with the model group.
PD + Cur downregulated serum IL-6, CCL18, and ferritin compared with the model group.

RNA-seq showed PD + Cur modulated immunoinflammation-related signaling pathways (IL-8 signaling, IL-15 production, macrophage nitric oxide/ROS production, phagosome formation) in bleomycin-treated lung tissue.
Untargeted proteomics indicated PD + Cur's improvement of lung injury was associated with PI3K signaling in B lymphocytes, macrophage NO/ROS production, and TGF-beta receptor complex signaling.

Metabolomics indicated that amino acid metabolism pathways (tyrosine biosynthesis, phenylalanine degradation, tryptophan catabolism, amine-derived hormone metabolism, phenylalanine/tyrosine metabolism) were altered in relation to disease modeling and PD + Cur intervention.

The GABBR agonist baclofen alone reduced interstitial thickening, alveolar atrophy, and fibrillar collagen, and reversed serum MUC5B, TOLLIP, KL-6, SP-D, RCN3, IL-6, CCL18, and SF in bleomycin model mice, mimicking PD + Cur's effects.
PI3-kinase subunit p85-alpha (PI3KR1), the activation subunit of PI3K, was significantly upregulated in lung tissue of the bleomycin model versus control.
PI3KR1 protein expression was significantly downregulated in lung tissue after intervention with either PD + Cur or baclofen compared with the model group.
PRM-based targeted proteomics showed AKT and TGFβR3 protein levels were increased in lung tissue of model mice compared with controls, then decreased after PD + Cur or Baclofen intervention.
Co-administration of the GABBR antagonist CGP52432 with PD + Cur blocked PD + Cur's downregulation of AKT and TGFβR3, indicating the effect is GABBR-dependent.
The authors conclude that PD + Cur inhibits the PI3K/AKT/TGF-β pathway by targeting and activating GABBR, thereby reducing excessive immune-inflammatory response and fibrosis in CTD-ILD lung tissue.
Among the 60 fibromyalgia patients enrolled, 76.6% fulfilled Rome IV diagnostic criteria for at least one disorder of gut-brain interaction.
16.7% of fibromyalgia patients met Rome IV criteria for irritable bowel syndrome.
28.3% of fibromyalgia patients met Rome IV criteria for functional dyspepsia.
31.7% of fibromyalgia patients met Rome IV criteria for both IBS and functional dyspepsia overlap.
Six months of Bedrocan® medical cannabis treatment was associated with a significant month-by-month decrease in fibromyalgia severity as measured by the FIQR.

During the 6-month Bedrocan® cannabis treatment, GI symptoms including epigastric pain, epigastric burning, abdominal pain, abdominal distension, and bloating showed a significant month-by-month reduction in intensity-frequency scores.
In a real-world cohort study, treatment with dupilumab for atopic dermatitis was associated with a reduced risk of developing irritable bowel syndrome.
Both 2D and 3D hPSC-derived ENS differentiation systems efficiently generated enteric neurons, yielding more than 80% TUBB3-positive cells.
Subclustering of NOS1-expressing enteric neurons in hPSC-derived ganglioids revealed five molecularly distinct nitrergic (NO) neuron subtypes, mirroring subtypes found in primary human ENS datasets.
Expression of the neuronal activity marker cFOS increased in enteric ganglioids as they matured from day 40 to day 80 of differentiation, indicating growing functional maturity.

Optogenetic blue-light stimulation of hSYN-ChR2-eYFP-expressing enteric ganglioids increased electrical firing rates measured by microelectrode array, confirming that hPSC-derived enteric neurons are synaptically mature and electrically excitable.

Live calcium imaging showed that hPSC-derived enteric neurons respond to acetylcholine, GABA and serotonin with increased cytosolic calcium, with the strongest responses to acetylcholine, and also responded to mechanical stimulation via fluid injection.
A high-throughput cFOS induction screen of 582 neuromodulators identified 20 compounds that increased the proportion of cFOS-positive NO neurons in enteric ganglioids (z-score > 1.5).
A complementary colorimetric NO-release screen of the same neuromodulator library identified 17 compounds that markedly increased NO release from 2D ENS cultures (z-score > 2.0).

Ex vivo testing of screen-derived candidate compounds on mouse colon identified aripiprazole, dexmedetomidine, matrine and MPEP as shortening colonic migrating motor complex (CMMC) intervals relative to untreated colon.

The adrenergic agonist dexmedetomidine decreased CMMC intervals in 4 of 5 mouse colon samples, and this effect was abolished by co-treatment with the NOS1 inhibitor l-NAME, indicating an NO-dependent mechanism.

Dexmedetomidine decreased the total number of longitudinal contractile events (LCEs) with a trend toward increased LCE duration; this effect was reversed by drug removal and blocked by l-NAME co-treatment.

In an organ myobath assay, dexmedetomidine reduced baseline colonic muscle tone in wild-type tissue but failed to reduce tone in Nos1-knockout tissue, and contraction frequency was abolished in Nos1-/- tissue, confirming a nitrergic mechanism of action.
A screen of 1,694 small-molecule inhibitors on enteric crestospheres identified 12 hit compounds that increased the proportion of NOS1+ neurons by at least eightfold.

PP121, a multi-targeted RTK inhibitor and second-highest ranked screen hit, showed a dose-dependent increase in NO neuron induction efficiency, with treatment during days 15-20 of differentiation producing the highest induction efficiency.

PP121 treatment increased the proportion of NO neurons without altering their transcriptional identity, but reduced cholinergic marker expression, suggesting NO neuron enrichment occurs partly at the expense of cholinergic neurons.

Treatment with the PDGFR agonist PDGF decreased NO neuron induction, whereas the PDGFR/VEGFR antagonist sunitinib increased NO neuron induction, implicating PDGFR signalling as a negative regulator of nitrergic fate.

The ERBB agonist NRG1 and antagonist sapitinib showed no significant effect on NO neuron induction, indicating that ERBB signalling, unlike PDGFR signalling, does not regulate nitrergic fate in this system.

CRISPR-Cas9 knockout of PDGFRA or PDGFRB individually enriched NO neurons in enteric ganglioids, with a greater enrichment effect from double knockout of both receptors, confirming PDGFR's role in restraining nitrergic fate.

BNC2 expression, associated with cholinergic lineage, was higher in the PDGFR-high ENCC 4' cluster, whereas ETV1 expression, linked to the nitrergic lineage, was elevated in other ENCC clusters with lower PDGFR expression, consistent with PDGFR signalling biasing progenitors away from the nitrergic fate.

Nos1-/- mouse colons transplanted with PP121-enriched NO ganglioids showed a significantly higher percentage of engrafted human NO neurons (NOS1+HuC/D+SC121+) than colons transplanted with standard (non-enriched) ganglioids.

Nos1-/- mice transplanted with NO-enriched enteric ganglioids showed a significant reduction in total GI transit time compared to sham-operated Nos1-/- mice, despite transplantation being limited to the distal colon.
Colonic tissue from Nos1-/- mice transplanted with enteric ganglioids showed increased baseline contractility compared to sham-operated tissue.
Electrical field stimulation-induced NANC relaxation in transplanted colonic tissue was significantly greater in mice receiving NO-enriched ganglioids than standard ganglioids or sham surgery.

The degree of human cell engraftment (SC121+ signal) in the distal colon was positively correlated with the magnitude of NANC-induced tissue relaxation, indicating that greater engraftment associates with stronger functional rescue.
In a case-control study of 122 females with IC/BPS versus 122 age-matched controls, IC/BPS patients were significantly more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for IBS.
Multiple independent studies report IBS co-occurring in roughly 38-44% of IC/BPS patients.
In a cohort of 872 IC/BPS patients vs 558 controls, IBS was the strongest single comorbidity distinguishing cases from controls, with an odds ratio of 4.1.
The largest cohort study of IC/BPS (n=2,682) found IBS diagnosed in 30.2% of patients.
Among 276 females with IC/BPS, the 46% with comorbid IBS had a 6-point lower SF-36 quality-of-life score than those without IBS.
IBS comorbidity is more prevalent in non-Hunner-type IC/BPS than in Hunner-type IC/BPS.
In a large matched nationwide cohort (85,359 per arm), patients with a prior IBS diagnosis had an increased hazard of subsequently developing IC/BPS.
IBS patients show elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines and oxidative stress markers alongside reduced anti-inflammatory cytokine and antioxidant capacity.
Fibromyalgia is diagnosed in roughly 12-18% of IC/BPS patients compared to 0-3% of controls.
Two nationwide studies found that IC/BPS patients are 3-7 times more likely to have fibromyalgia than non-IC/BPS controls.
Fibromyalgia prevalence differs markedly by IC/BPS subtype, being much higher in non-Hunner than Hunner-type disease.
In a study of 276 females with IC/BPS, comorbid fibromyalgia (present in 20%) was significantly associated with lower SF-36 quality-of-life scores.

Clauw et al. found that 23-27% of fibromyalgia patients also present with clinical symptoms typical of IC/BPS, and direct comparison of 60 FM, 30 IC/BPS, and 30 healthy controls showed diffusely increased peripheral nociception in both FM and IC/BPS patients.
In a pilot study of 11 IC/BPS patients, small fiber polyneuropathy and fibromyalgia were far more prevalent in non-Hunner than Hunner-type IC/BPS.
A larger 2020 study confirmed that small fiber polyneuropathy is markedly more common in IC/BPS patients than in the general population.
Fibromyalgia patients show elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines, mast cell activation, reduced antioxidant enzyme activity, increased lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial superoxide.
A Taiwanese nationwide study of 1,095 IC/BPS patients found significantly increased risk of developing several autoimmune diseases.
A study of 9,269 IC/BPS subjects and 46,345 controls found a significantly increased odds of prior rheumatoid arthritis in IC/BPS patients.
A population-based cohort study found a 2.26-fold higher incidence of IC/BPS in females with SLE compared to those without.
A nationwide study of 11,526 Sjogren's syndrome patients found significantly increased risk of developing IC/BPS, particularly in younger, female, and dry-eye/dry-mouth-treated patients.

Bladder biopsies from IC/BPS patients share a gene expression signature of increased IL7R, KLRB1, PSMB9, CD38, and ITGAL with patients of other autoimmune diseases, supporting an autoimmune origin for IC/BPS.
IC/BPS patients report higher prevalence of childhood sexual abuse than controls, and those with abuse history report greater pain and worse quality of life.
IC/BPS patients with concurrent PTSD reported increased pain, greater emotional distress, and lower quality of life than IC/BPS patients without PTSD.

A case-control study at West China Hospital found significantly higher rates of metabolic syndrome, diabetes, and hypertension, plus elevated fasting glucose, cystatin-C, and triglycerides, in IC/BPS patients versus matched controls.
Urinary oxidative stress markers 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane are elevated in non-Hunner IC/BPS patients versus healthy controls and correlate with glomerulation grade and reduced bladder capacity.
HIC/BPS bladders show overexpression of cGAS and STING along with elevated IFN-I and TNF-alpha, suggesting accumulation of cytosolic mitochondrial DNA driving inflammation.
In a cyclophosphamide-induced mouse model of IC/BPS, pharmacologic NLRP3 inhibition reduced bladder injury by decreasing immune cell infiltration and systemic cytokines via NF-κB pathways.
Low-energy shock wave therapy reduced symptom severity and pain, improved quality of life, and decreased urinary IL-4, IL-9, and VEGF in human IC/BPS patients.
Increased levels of uro-damaging purine metabolites and high xanthine oxidase activity were observed in IC/BPS patients, with and without Hunner's lesions, compared to healthy controls.
Increased expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase, which enhances ROS production, was found in the urothelium and inflammatory infiltrates of HIC/BPS lamina propria.

Two studies reported reduced total antioxidant capacity and increased oxidative stress markers (8-isoprostane, oxidized guanine species) in serum and urine of IC/BPS patients, with no difference between HIC and NHIC and no correlation with inflammation or severity.

Jiang et al. found significantly elevated urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane in NHIC/BPS patients compared to healthy controls, with higher 8-OHdG in patients with glomerulations, and both markers positively correlating with glomerulation grade and negatively with maximal bladder capacity.

A follow-up study confirmed elevated oxidative stress markers and found a positive correlation between urinary 8-OHdG and pain intensity (VAS), but no difference in oxidative markers between HIC and NHIC patients or correlation with inflammatory markers or histopathology.
Urine samples from IC/BPS patients consistently show elevated pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines compared to healthy controls, reflecting the disease's inflammatory nature.
Systemic inflammation in IC/BPS is suggested by increased serum/plasma levels of CRP, IL-6, CCL11, and IFNα.

HIC/BPS patients exhibit significantly higher levels of IL-6, IL-8, CXCL1, CXCL10, and CCL11 in urine and/or serum compared to NHIC/BPS patients, with urinary CXCL10 correlating with symptom severity and inflammatory cell infiltration in HIC/BPS.

Tian et al. identified CCL11, CCL2, TNF-α, 8-OHdG, and 8-isoprostane as candidate urinary biomarkers (AUC ≥0.60), with lower levels predicting favorable treatment outcomes, while IL-6, IL-8, CXCL10, and CCL11 best distinguished HIC/BPS from other IC/BPS cases.

In NHIC/BPS, urinary CCL2, CCL5, CCL11, and CXCL10 correlate positively with glomerulation grade and negatively with maximal bladder capacity, suggesting local inflammation contributes to bladder wall remodeling.

K-means clustering identified four NHIC/BPS subgroups by inflammatory and oxidative stress biomarkers; one cluster, comprising 85% of NHIC/BPS patients with glomerulations, showed the highest inflammatory and oxidative markers and was associated with the lowest bladder capacity and highest pain scores.
Restraint stress elevates oxidative stress and disrupts expression of core clock genes (PER2, BMAL1, NR1D1), altering circadian regulation of bladder function in mice.

Humans working rotating night shifts, who experience circadian disruption and elevated oxidative stress, show increased nocturia, likely due to impaired circadian control of bladder and kidney function.

Wang et al. demonstrated that bladder-resident macrophages are subject to circadian regulation via clock-controlled genes that modulate pattern recognition receptors, inflammatory mediators, and cell trafficking molecules.

Mechanosensors PIEZO1 and TRPV4, and the gap junction protein connexin 43, expressed in the bladder mucosa and urothelium, exhibit diurnal variation in expression, potentially affecting barrier integrity and inflammatory threshold.
Approximately 5-8% of the macrophage transcriptome, including key pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1β, is regulated by the circadian clock.

Patients with IC/BPS, particularly HIC/BPS, have significantly increased expression of HIF-1α and its downstream target VEGF, associated with bladder inflammation; VEGF correlates with symptom severity and glomerulations.

Zhang et al. reported decreased mRNA and protein expression of VEGF and HIF-1α in 38 IC/BPS patients after hyperbaric oxygen therapy, with improvements in voiding frequency, nocturia, and symptom severity.

The blood-urine barrier in IC/BPS is compromised via a diminished glycocalyx layer, disassembly of tight junctions with deregulated expression of ZO-1, occludin, claudins 1/4/8, adherens junction protein E-cadherin, and reduced uroplakin expression.

Scanning electron microscopy revealed severe defects in superficial umbrella cell integrity with increased pleomorphism and decreased microplicae in IC/BPS, with greater damage associated with increased disease severity and inflammatory infiltrates.

Using single-cell RNA sequencing, Peng et al. showed a significant reduction in uroplakin 3A-positive umbrella cells in HIC/BPS bladders leading to impaired urothelial regeneration, with TLR3 and NR2F6 identified as key pathways in umbrella cell injury.

Elevated ROS production in urothelial cells is associated with upregulation of TRPM8, linked to increased bladder emptying frequency, iNOS, membrane phospholipid peroxidation, MDA formation, decreased antioxidant capacity, and mitochondrial ultrastructural alterations with lipofuscin accumulation.
An acute oxidative stress stimulus dramatically increases intracellular calcium in urothelial cells, and this response can be attenuated by the ROS scavenger NAC.
IC/BPS patients, both with and without Hunner's lesions, show increased uro-damaging purine metabolites and elevated xanthine oxidase activity compared to healthy controls.
Expression of inducible nitric oxide synthase, which enhances ROS production, is increased in the urothelium and inflammatory infiltrates of patients with HIC/BPS.

IC/BPS patients showed reduced total antioxidant capacity and increased serum/urine oxidative stress markers, but these did not differ between HIC and NHIC subtypes nor correlate with inflammation or disease severity.

NHIC/BPS patients had significantly elevated urinary 8-OHdG and 8-isoprostane compared to healthy controls, with higher 8-OHdG in patients with glomerulations, and both markers correlated positively with glomerulation grade and negatively with maximal bladder capacity.

A follow-up study confirmed elevated urinary oxidative stress markers in IC/BPS and found a positive correlation between urinary 8-OHdG and pain intensity (VAS), though no significant differences were seen between HIC and NHIC subtypes.

HIC/BPS patients show significantly higher urinary and/or serum levels of IL-6, IL-8, CXCL1, CXCL10, and CCL11 compared to NHIC/BPS patients, and urinary CXCL10 correlates with symptom severity and inflammatory infiltration.

A urinary biomarker panel (CCL11, CCL2, TNF-α, 8-OHdG, 8-isoprostane; AUC ≥0.60) was identified for IC/BPS, with lower levels predicting favorable treatment outcomes, and IL-6, IL-8, CXCL10, and CCL11 best distinguishing HIC/BPS from other IC/BPS cases.

K-means clustering identified four NHIC/BPS subgroups by inflammatory/oxidative markers; the largest cluster (85% with glomerulations) had the highest inflammatory and oxidative stress marker levels, lowest maximal bladder capacity, and highest pain scores.
Restraint stress elevates oxidative stress and disrupts expression of core circadian clock genes (PER2, BMAL1, NR1D1), altering circadian regulation of bladder function in mice.

Humans working rotating night shifts, who experience circadian disruption and elevated oxidative stress, show increased nocturia, likely due to impaired circadian control of bladder and kidney function.

Bladder mucosal/urothelial mechanosensors PIEZO1 and TRPV4, and the gap junction protein connexin 43, exhibit diurnal variation in expression, potentially affecting barrier integrity and inflammatory threshold.

Patients with IC/BPS, particularly HIC/BPS, show significantly increased expression of HIF-1α and its downstream target VEGF, which is associated with bladder inflammation, and VEGF levels correlate with symptom severity and glomerulations.
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy decreased mRNA and protein expression of VEGF and HIF-1α in 38 IC/BPS patients, along with improvements in voiding frequency, nocturia, and symptom severity.

Single-cell RNA sequencing showed a significant reduction in UPK3A-positive umbrella cells in HIC/BPS bladders, impairing urothelial regeneration and driving chronic inflammation, with TLR3 and NR2F6 pathways implicated in umbrella cell injury.

Elevated ROS production in urothelial cells is associated with upregulation of TRPM8, increased bladder emptying frequency, elevated iNOS, lipid peroxidation, MDA formation, decreased antioxidant capacity, and mitochondrial lipofuscin accumulation.
An acute oxidative stress stimulus dramatically increases intracellular calcium in urothelial cells, and this response can be attenuated by the ROS scavenger NAC.
Mice lacking the antioxidant enzyme NQO1 developed IC/BPS-like symptoms including disrupted energy metabolism, mitochondrial damage, and increased ROS and apoptosis in the urothelium.

Cell-free/oxidized mtDNA released from damaged cells is recognized by AIM2, NLRP3, cGAS, and TLR9 pattern recognition receptors in bladder urothelial cells, and AIM2/NLRP3 engagement leads to inflammasome formation and release of IL-1β/IL-18, promoting mast cell recruitment; elevated IL-1β, IL-18, and mast cell infiltration are well-established features of IC/BPS.

In a cyclophosphamide-induced mouse model of IC/BPS, NLRP3 inhibition reduced bladder injury by decreasing mast cell, T cell, and neutrophil infiltration and lowering systemic cytokine levels via NF-κB pathways.
HIC/BPS bladders show overexpression of cGAS and STING along with elevated IFN-I and TNF-α, indicating accumulation of cytosolic DNA likely of mitochondrial origin due to cell damage or death.

In a ketamine-induced cystitis model, cGAS and STING were upregulated in bladder tissue and urothelial cells, and STING knockdown inhibited NF-κB and IRF3 nuclear translocation, reducing IL-6, IL-8, CXCL10, and IFN-I; mtDNA depletion impaired cGAS-STING activation while mtDNA reintroduction partially restored the inflammatory response.
The authors' own study found that TNF-α stimulation of urothelial cells activated both NF-κB and cGAS-STING-IRF3 pathways, based on transcriptomic data (GSE202576).

HIC/BPS bladders show Th1/17-polarized immune responses with prominent overexpression of IFN-γ, a pattern also implicated in other inflammatory and autoimmune diseases comorbid with IC/BPS such as SjS, SLE, RA, IBS, and diabetes.
Single-cell RNA sequencing of the IC/BPS bladder microenvironment found increased macrophages and a Th1-biased response, with decreased immunosuppressive regulatory T cell (Treg) populations.

Peng et al. identified 22 immune subpopulations in IC/BPS bladders, with significant increases in M2-like macrophages, inflammatory CD14+ macrophages, dendritic cells, central memory CD4+ T cells, activated B cells, and neutrophils, nearly all enriched in the urothelial region compared to control bladders.

scRNA-seq identified a predominant population of immunoglobulin heavy constant delta-expressing naive B cells and upregulated IRF2, IRF4, and IRF8 in NHIC/BPS bladder biopsies (absent in HIC/BPS), suggesting an under-recognized IFN-I-driven inflammatory component in NHIC/BPS, challenging its traditional classification as non-inflammatory.

The authors' own work showed TNF-Ρ-stimulated urothelial cells induce stress fiber formation and actin remodeling, increasing permeability, and increase ROS, COX-2 expression while decreasing NRF2, SOD1, and HO1 antioxidant defenses.

In rats with acute cystitis, low-energy shock wave therapy improved bladder function by modulating ATP production, inhibiting ROS, and decreasing IL-6, TNF-α, and NF-κB expression along with inflammatory infiltrates and edema.
In human IC/BPS patients, low-energy shock wave therapy reduced symptom severity scores and pain, improved quality of life, and decreased urinary levels of IL-4, IL-9, and VEGF.
Human platelet lysate (PRP) decreased ROS and HIF-1α expression in urothelial cells, thereby inhibiting apoptosis during ischemia/hypoxia in vitro.
PRP decreases IL-6 expression via the NF-κB/COX-2 signaling pathway and modifies expression of the tight junction protein ZO-1, promoting urothelial cell regeneration.

Repeated PRP injections in refractory IC/BPS patients improved symptom score, bladder pain, and decreased daytime frequency and nocturia, while increasing ZO-1 and E-cadherin expression and decreasing inflammatory cell infiltration.

In rats with lipopolysaccharide-induced cystitis, N-acetylcysteine (NAC) significantly improved voiding parameters, reduced mast cell infiltration, and reversed histological damage including fibrosis.

A case report of intravenous NAC infusions over 5 months in a patient with refractory IC/BPS achieved complete clinical remission with minimal adverse events, alongside reduced plasma IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α.

Melatonin treatment attenuated the severity of cyclophosphamide-induced cystitis in rats by preserving urothelium, reducing mast cell proliferation/activation, decreasing TNF-α and IL-1β, lowering MDA, and upregulating HO1.
Various flavonoids showed anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anti-apoptotic effects in cyclophosphamide-induced cystitis in rats by inhibiting TXNIP/NLRP3 and NF-κB signaling.
In two open-label clinical trials, IC/BPS patients receiving dietary quercetin supplementation experienced significant improvement in clinical symptoms and VAS pain scores.

Pre-treatment with taurine in cyclophosphamide-induced cystitis in rats significantly reduced bladder wall thickness, vascular congestion, bleeding, and lipid peroxide levels, and increased glutathione levels.
In a rat model of diabetic bladder dysfunction, taurine attenuated transitional epithelium edema and reduced oxidative stress biomarkers MDA and 8-deoxyguanosine.

The PPAR-γ agonist pioglitazone increased superoxide dismutase activity, decreased MDA, 8-OHdG, and CRP, decreased NF-κB expression, and improved mitochondrial structure/function of cardiomyocytes in diabetic rabbits.
Pioglitazone improved bladder function and urothelial cell integrity in rats with cyclophosphamide-induced cystitis.
PPAR-γ is abundantly expressed in urothelial cells and plays an important role in urothelial cell differentiation, including production of barrier proteins such as uroplakin.

Trained immunity involving epigenetic reprogramming of urothelial stem cells after prior UTI is proposed to increase susceptibility to future infections and chronic bladder disease, supported by elevated AIM2 inflammasome expression in sensitized urothelia.

Genome-wide metabolic flux modeling of muscle transcriptomes showed that alanine and aspartate metabolism was the most significantly down-regulated pathway in ME/CFS patients compared to healthy controls.
Two reactions in arginine and proline metabolism (4HGLSDm and PHCHGSm) were significantly down-regulated in the muscle of ME/CFS patients.
The pentose phosphate pathway, including reactions G6PDH2r, PGL, RPE, RPI, TKT1, TKT2, and GND, was significantly up-regulated in the muscle of ME/CFS patients.
Pyrimidine catabolism was significantly down-regulated in the muscle metabolic network of ME/CFS patients relative to controls.
Aminosugar metabolism was significantly down-regulated in the muscle metabolic network of ME/CFS patients relative to controls.
Flux analysis showed reduced urea secretion together with a potential increase in ammonia (NH4) secretion in the muscle urea cycle of ME/CFS patients.

In silico all-against-all metabolite knockout modeling identified asparagine and aspartate as top agonist metabolites, suggesting their administration could potentially rescue the metabolic flux changes seen in ME/CFS muscle.
In Long COVID patients, muscle levels of asparagine and dihydroxyacetone-phosphate were significantly lower during post-exertional malaise compared with healthy controls.
In blood samples of Long COVID patients, asparagine ranked as the top down-regulated metabolite following post-exertional malaise relative to controls.
The consistent down-regulation of ASN/ASP metabolism in muscle across both the ME/CFS and Long COVID datasets suggests a shared metabolic disruption underlying these conditions.

The authors propose the combination L-ornithine L-aspartate (LOLA) as a candidate therapeutic to replenish deficient ASN/ASP and arginine/proline metabolism, enhance urea cycle efficiency, support mitochondrial function, and reduce ammonia dysregulation in ME/CFS and Long COVID.

The bile acid derivative sulfochenodeoxycholate (HC02220), a sulfoconjugated form of chenodeoxycholic acid, was also identified as an agonist metabolite in the knockout analysis, and is discussed as a potential lead relevant to insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial support via its relationship to TUDCA.
