Ammonia dysregulation is implicated as a contributor to fatigue and cognitive dysfunction in both ME/CFS and Long COVID, consistent with known effects of hyperammonemia on energy production and neuroinflammation.
CD38 is highly expressed on plasmablasts and short- and long-lived plasma cells, and also on NK cells, providing the rationale for daratumumab as a plasma-cell targeting agent in ME/CFS.
In the pooled cohort of 10 patients, SF-36 Physical Function, DSQ-SF symptom score, and Function level all improved significantly from baseline through follow-up after daratumumab treatment.
Six of 10 patients experienced clinical improvement after daratumumab, and five of these had major, durable symptom improvement sustained through 12-24 months of follow-up.
Serum IgG levels fell by a mean of 48% from baseline during follow-up after daratumumab, with a greater reduction in patients who showed clinical improvement (54%) than in non-responders (40%).
Peripheral NK cell numbers dropped rapidly after the first daratumumab injection, consistent with CD38 expression on NK cells, and slowly recovered to normal range by 15-21 months.
Higher baseline peripheral NK cell numbers were significantly correlated with greater clinical improvement (maximum SF-36 Physical Function increase) after daratumumab.
Baseline NK cell numbers were not significantly correlated with the maximum relative reduction of serum IgG during follow-up.
Daily step counts measured by Fitbit increased across the cohort after daratumumab, with a much larger increase among clinically improved patients than non-improvers.
Baseline resting heart rate was higher in patients who did not clinically improve compared with those who later showed clinical benefit from daratumumab.
Subcutaneous daratumumab was well tolerated in ME/CFS patients, with only mild (grade 1-2) adverse events and no serious adverse events.
IgG4 showed the largest relative reduction of all IgG subclasses after daratumumab, with a markedly greater decline in clinically improved patients than in non-improvers.
Screening for common clinical autoantibodies was largely negative, with only one patient positive for anti-TPO (normal thyroid function) and one positive for ANA, anti-CCP IgG and ribosomal P IgG.

Protective antibody levels to SARS-CoV-2, diphtheria and tetanus remained protective or probably protective in all patients both at baseline and after 12 months of follow-up despite plasma-cell depletion.
Broad T-cell (CD3, CD4, CD8) and B-cell (CD19) subset counts in peripheral blood showed no systematic changes during follow-up after daratumumab.
A prior meta-analysis found reduced NK-cell cytotoxicity to be the most consistent immune abnormality in ME/CFS, though with high inter-study heterogeneity.
A cited study using Rapid Extracellular Antigen Profiling found no significant difference in autoantibody reactivities to the exoproteome between ME/CFS patients and healthy controls.
A prior randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of the anti-CD20 antibody rituximab showed no difference from placebo in ME/CFS, despite earlier open-label signals of benefit.
An earlier open-label trial of six cyclophosphamide infusions in moderate-to-severe ME/CFS patients showed clinical responses in 55% of patients with apparent long-term benefit.
A review summarizing 38 publications on 83 patients treated with daratumumab for refractory autoimmune diseases (other than ME/CFS) found an 81% response rate of remission or improvement.
One ME/CFS patient with known POTS experienced a marked rise in resting heart rate coinciding with a partial relapse of her transient clinical improvement after daratumumab.
Two ME/CFS patients with pre-existing POTS experienced episodes of increased palpitations during daratumumab treatment, one requiring a temporary increase in metoprolol.
Patients with ME/CFS showed significantly higher lactate concentrations than healthy controls in the pregenual anterior cingulate cortex (pgACC).
Patients with ME/CFS showed significantly higher lactate concentrations than healthy controls in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), similar to the pgACC finding.
A trend toward higher pgACC lactate in ME/CFS compared with long COVID patients approached but did not reach statistical significance.
Long COVID patients had significantly lower total choline concentrations in the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) than healthy controls.
Total choline in dACC was significantly lower in long COVID patients than in ME/CFS patients.
The study failed to replicate the pilot finding of decreased pgACC creatine in ME/CFS compared with healthy controls.
No significant between-group differences in GSH were found in ME/CFS or long COVID compared with healthy controls, failing to replicate the pilot study's finding of decreased GSH in ME/CFS.
Muscle carnosine showed a non-significant trend toward being lowest in ME/CFS, intermediate in long COVID, and highest in healthy controls.

No significant between-group differences were found in muscle creatine, acetyl-carnitine, TMA-containing compounds, intramyocellular lipids, or extramyocellular lipids across ME/CFS, long COVID, and healthy controls.
ME/CFS patients performed significantly worse than healthy controls on the Tower of London executive function task, the only significant cognitive difference found.
In long COVID patients, dACC total choline levels correlated positively with the length of illness.
In ME/CFS, lactate levels did not correlate with fatigue scores, anxiety, depression ratings, or length of illness.
Both ME/CFS and long COVID patients had substantially higher fatigue ratings on the Chalder Fatigue Scale than healthy controls.

Long COVID patients had modestly increased anxiety (STAI) scores compared with controls, similar in magnitude to ME/CFS patients, though the ME/CFS-control difference was not statistically significant.

Both ME/CFS and long COVID patients had higher BDI-II depression scores than healthy controls, but no patient met DSM-5 criteria for major depression, with elevated scores driven mainly by fatigue- and cognition-related items.

The authors developed a cylindrical carbon nanotube-paper composite capacitive sensor-based eye tracker integrated into eyeglasses to noncontact-monitor blink rate and eye closure as digital markers for chronic fatigue assessment.

A 15-minute protocol combining cognitive tasks and noise exposure was designed to induce acute fatigue, with machine learning models applied to digital eye-tracking markers to evaluate accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity for identifying chronic fatigue.

Patients receiving care from providers trained through the LC&FIRP tele-mentoring program, which integrates lived-experience experts, reported validation of their illness experience as one of the top perceived benefits of the program.

Almost half of interviewed patients reported that participating in LC&FIRP changed their attitudes and beliefs about their illness, including reducing prior self-doubt that symptoms were purely psychological.

A lived-experience expert who is a healthcare provider with ME/CFS noted that dysautonomia and POTS are common comorbid conditions in patients with Long COVID/ME_CFS/PAIS and cautioned that misdiagnosing depressed mood as clinical depression can lead to psychiatric medications that worsen these comorbidities.

Nearly all interviewed patients reported making self-care behavior changes (exercise, dietary changes, mask-wearing, use of activity/sleep trackers) as a result of participating in the LC&FIRP program, consistent with lived-experience experts' emphasis on pacing and self-management.

About a third of interviewed patients reported unmet needs and dissatisfaction due to difficulty scheduling appointments with specialists and therapists referred through the program, indicating a gap between lived-experience experts' referral recommendations and actual referral care access.

Lived-experience experts educated providers that fluctuating, dynamic chronic illness such as Long COVID/ME_CFS/PAIS can qualify as a disability under the ADA/Section 504/Section 1557, entitling patients to workplace accommodations and disability benefits, but some patients reported unmet needs regarding disability and employment benefit filing and health insurance coverage.
The authors state that no clinical biomarker for long Covid has yet been identified despite five years of research.
The authors note that no effective therapy for long Covid has been developed despite five years of investigation.
The paper describes growing recognition of overlap between long Covid and myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome.
The authors report that for most people, long Covid symptoms progressively resolve over time.
Recurrent Covid-19 infections are described as an increasingly important contributor to the population affected by long Covid.
Long Covid symptoms limit activity in up to 20% of affected individuals, while complete inability to work is less common.
The anticipated surge in disability claims among insured individuals with long Covid has not occurred.
COVID-19 patients hospitalized during acute infection had a 46% higher risk of new-onset CFS/ME compared to COVID-negative patients over up to four years of follow-up.
Non-hospitalized COVID-19 patients (mild disease) had a 56% higher risk of new-onset CFS/ME compared to COVID-negative patients, similar to hospitalized patients.
Patients who received at least one COVID-19 vaccine dose prior to their index date had a higher risk of subsequent new-onset CFS/ME.
Female sex was associated with a higher risk of developing new-onset CFS/ME compared to males.
Pre-existing liver disease was associated with elevated risk of new-onset CFS/ME.
Pre-existing autoimmune disease was associated with elevated risk of new-onset CFS/ME.
Pre-existing depressive disorder showed a trend toward elevated risk of new-onset CFS/ME that did not reach statistical significance.
Pre-existing anxiety disorder was associated with elevated risk of new-onset CFS/ME.
Black patients had a lower risk of new-onset CFS/ME compared to non-Hispanic White patients.
Patients of other (non-Black, non-White) racial groups had a lower risk of new-onset CFS/ME compared to non-Hispanic White patients.

Age, most pre-existing comorbidities (hypertension, T2DM, COPD, CKD, cardiovascular disease), insurance type, and neighborhood median income were not significantly associated with risk of incident CFS/ME.
Blood-based biomarkers measured during acute COVID-19 hospitalization were not associated with subsequent long-term risk of incident CFS/ME.
SARS-CoV-2 re-infection was not associated with increased risk of incident CFS/ME.
The elevated risk of new-onset CFS/ME associated with COVID-19 vaccination was present only among those vaccinated during 2020-2021 (early rollout) and not among those vaccinated from 2022 onward.
Cumulative incidence of new-onset CFS/ME per 1000 patient-years was higher in both hospitalized and non-hospitalized COVID+ patients than in COVID- patients over a median 21-month follow-up.
Subgroup analysis suggested that the association between COVID-19 and incident CFS/ME was more pronounced among White patients compared to other racial/ethnic groups.

The paper argues that the previously reported 4.5% incidence rate of post-COVID ME/CFS onset from the RECOVER study reflects selection bias in the underlying cohort rather than a valid population estimate.
Cluster B personality disorders were markedly more prevalent in fibromyalgia patients than healthy controls, showing the highest relative risk among all diagnoses examined.
Personality disorders overall were substantially more prevalent among fibromyalgia patients than healthy controls.
PTSD was over 22 times more prevalent among fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls.
Adjustment disorder diagnoses were about eight times more common among fibromyalgia patients than healthy controls.
Anxiety disorders were 4.5 times more prevalent in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
Depression was about five times more prevalent among fibromyalgia patients than healthy controls.
Fibromyalgia patients used antidepressant medication far more often than healthy controls.
Anxiolytic medication use was more than three times higher in fibromyalgia patients than in healthy controls.
OCD spectrum-related disorders (excluding OCD itself) had a relative risk of about 12 in fibromyalgia patients compared with healthy controls despite lower absolute prevalence.
Mood stabilizer use, though relatively uncommon overall, showed a notably high relative risk in fibromyalgia patients versus healthy controls.
Antipsychotic use showed a high relative risk in fibromyalgia patients relative to healthy controls despite lower absolute prevalence.
Fibromyalgia patients had modestly but significantly higher rates of depression than chronic pain patients.
Anxiety disorder prevalence was slightly but significantly higher in fibromyalgia than chronic pain patients.
Schizophrenia spectrum disorders were more prevalent among chronic pain patients than fibromyalgia patients.
Antidepressant use was higher among fibromyalgia patients than chronic pain patients.
PTSD was about three times more prevalent in fibromyalgia patients than in chronic fatigue syndrome patients.
Adjustment disorder rates were higher in fibromyalgia patients compared with chronic fatigue syndrome patients.
Dysthymia prevalence did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome patients.
Schizophrenia spectrum disorders were more prevalent in chronic fatigue syndrome patients than fibromyalgia patients.
Antidepressant use was substantially higher in fibromyalgia patients than in chronic fatigue syndrome patients.
Anxiolytic use was higher in fibromyalgia patients than in chronic fatigue syndrome patients.
Anxiety disorders were roughly twice as prevalent in fibromyalgia patients as in rheumatoid arthritis patients (55.1% vs 26.7%).
Personality disorders were about four times more prevalent in fibromyalgia patients than in rheumatoid arthritis patients (5.7% vs 1.4%).
Antidepressant use was more than twice as common in fibromyalgia patients as in rheumatoid arthritis patients (90% vs 41.7%).
Mood stabilizer use was nearly three times more common in fibromyalgia patients than in rheumatoid arthritis patients (12.9% vs 4.5%).
Despite a relatively low prevalence of use (13%), fibromyalgia patients showed a markedly elevated relative risk (RR 5.4) of mood stabilizer use compared with healthy controls.
Antipsychotic use had a notably high relative risk (RR 4.5) in fibromyalgia patients versus healthy controls despite only 21% prevalence.
Psychotic disorder diagnoses were more common in fibromyalgia than healthy controls but less common than in chronic pain or chronic fatigue syndrome patients.

Somatization disorder diagnoses were similar between rheumatoid arthritis patients and healthy controls but 4-5 times more prevalent in fibromyalgia, chronic pain, and chronic fatigue syndrome, conditions lacking clear biomarkers.

A cited Israeli survey of rheumatologists found only 53% were willing to accept fibromyalgia patients compared with 98% for rheumatoid arthritis patients, with FM perceived as more severe and burdensome.
Physical fatigue was reported by nearly all IBS-CFS patients compared to a small minority of IBS-U patients.
Sleep disorders were twice as common in IBS-CFS patients compared to IBS-U patients.
Bowel habit patterns differed between groups, with constipation predominating in IBS-CFS and diarrhea predominating in IBS-U.
IBS-CFS patients showed a high burden of fatigue symptoms on the Chalder Fatigue Questionnaire (CFQ-11).
IBS-CFS patients showed significant functional impact of fatigue on daily activities as measured by the Fatigue Severity Scale.
Breath methane concentrations at 90 and 180 minutes were significantly higher in IBS-CFS patients than IBS-U patients, suggesting greater methanogen activity.
Both groups showed hydrogen breath rises exceeding the SIBO diagnostic threshold at 90 minutes, with the increase higher in the IBS-U group.
All patients had an altered microbiome profile relative to the normobiotic reference, but the dysbiosis index did not differ between IBS-U and IBS-CFS groups.
Shannon alpha diversity of the gut microbiome was significantly higher in the IBS-CFS group compared to the IBS-U group.
Relative abundance of Bacteroidetes was significantly higher in IBS-U than in IBS-CFS, the only taxon showing a statistically significant between-group difference.
Apart from Bacteroidetes, other pro- and anti-inflammatory bacterial taxa did not differ significantly between IBS-U and IBS-CFS groups.
Urinary 3-indoxyl sulfate, a microbial indole pathway metabolite, was significantly higher in IBS-CFS patients than IBS-U patients.
Urinary homovanillic acid, a dopamine metabolite, was significantly higher in IBS-CFS patients than IBS-U patients.
Urinary quinolinic acid, a neurotoxic kynurenine pathway metabolite, was significantly higher in IBS-CFS patients than IBS-U patients.
Urinary xanthurenic acid, a neurotoxic kynurenine pathway metabolite, was significantly higher in IBS-CFS patients than IBS-U patients.
Urinary 5-HIAA, a serotonin degradation metabolite, was significantly lower in IBS-CFS patients than IBS-U patients, suggesting impaired serotonin turnover.
Urinary kynurenine levels were slightly but significantly lower in IBS-CFS patients than IBS-U patients, though the effect size was small and did not survive multiple testing correction.
Urinary kynurenic acid and hydroxyphenylacetic acid did not differ significantly between IBS-U and IBS-CFS patients.
Higher urinary xanthurenic acid levels correlated significantly with greater fatigue severity scores.
Higher urinary quinolinic acid levels showed a weaker but significant correlation with greater fatigue severity scores.
Standard laboratory parameters relevant to fatigue (vitamins, glucose, thyroid function, inflammatory markers) did not differ significantly between IBS-U and IBS-CFS groups.
Patients diagnosed with influenza had a significantly higher risk of subsequently developing chronic fatigue syndrome than matched individuals without influenza.
Among influenza patients, those aged 40-64 years had a higher risk of CFS than those aged 20-39 years.
Patients aged 65 and older had an even higher risk of CFS after influenza compared to the 20-39 age group.
Male sex was associated with a slightly lower risk of CFS than female sex.
A pre-existing history of insomnia was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
A pre-existing history of anxiety was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
A pre-existing history of peptic ulcer disease was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
A pre-existing history of gout was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
A pre-existing history of dyslipidemia was independently associated with a modestly increased risk of subsequent CFS.
A pre-existing history of irritable bowel syndrome was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
Chronic hepatitis B virus infection was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
Hepatitis C virus infection was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
A pre-existing diagnosis of fibromyalgia was independently associated with increased risk of subsequent CFS.
Among influenza patients, receiving an influenza vaccine (before or after infection) was associated with a lower subsequent risk of CFS compared to being unvaccinated.

In influenza patients who did not require mechanical ventilation (mild illness), vaccinated individuals had a significantly lower incidence of CFS than unvaccinated individuals, regardless of vaccine timing before or after infection.
Influenza patients who required mechanical ventilation (a proxy for severe illness) had a higher risk of subsequently developing CFS than those who did not require ventilation.
Among influenza patients who required mechanical ventilation (severe illness), prior vaccination did not significantly reduce the risk of subsequent CFS.
Pre-existing renal disease was associated with a significantly reduced adjusted risk of subsequent CFS, in contrast to the crude (unadjusted) comparison which showed no difference.
Untreated hypothyroidism was not independently associated with CFS risk after adjustment, despite a significant unadjusted association.
Diabetes mellitus was not independently associated with CFS risk after adjustment, despite a significant unadjusted association.
Overall baseline comorbidity burden (Charlson Comorbidity Index) was not independently associated with CFS risk after full adjustment, despite significant crude associations.
Influenza vaccination was associated with an overall protective effect against subsequent CFS in the influenza cohort.

Among influenza patients who did not require mechanical ventilation (milder disease), vaccinated individuals had significantly lower CFS incidence than unvaccinated individuals, regardless of timing of vaccination.
Among influenza patients who required mechanical ventilation (severe disease), prior vaccination did not significantly reduce CFS risk.
Patients requiring mechanical ventilation during influenza illness (a proxy for severe infection) had a higher subsequent risk of CFS than non-ventilated influenza patients.
Kaplan-Meier analysis showed the influenza cohort had a significantly higher cumulative incidence of CFS over the follow-up period than the non-influenza cohort.

The elevated CFS risk associated with influenza persisted consistently across subgroups stratified by age, sex, CCI comorbidity burden, and presence/absence of comorbidities, with adjusted hazard ratios generally between 1.4 and 1.6.
CXCL10 (IP-10) is the only cytokine reported as elevated in both severe influenza and severe CFS in cited literature, suggesting a possible shared inflammatory link.
CXCL9 (MIG), which is strongly elevated in severe influenza, has been reported to be inversely correlated with fatigue duration in CFS, i.e., higher CXCL9 is linked to shorter fatigue duration.
Cited studies show CFS patients tend to have significantly shorter leukocyte telomeres compared to healthy controls, proposed as a mechanism of reduced resilience to infection.

Longer telomeres in B cells and in influenza-specific CD8+ T cells (e.g., targeting M1 protein) have been associated with better antibody responses and more robust expansion upon activation in older adults, proposed as a link to reduced influenza complication susceptibility.

The authors propose that a genetic predisposition toward B-cell autoreactivity, triggered by a significant infection such as influenza, could induce an autoimmune response against self-antigens (possibly involving energy metabolism/mitochondrial components), manifesting clinically as CFS.

Cited literature indicates that more than half of ICU survivors report chronic fatigue lasting 6 to 70 months after discharge, attributed to muscle deconditioning, malnutrition, rehabilitation demands, and sleep disturbance, offered as an explanation for why vaccination does not mitigate CFS risk after severe influenza requiring ventilation.
Vaccinated patients (particularly those reinfected after vaccination) had significantly shorter symptom duration than unvaccinated patients.

Certain pre-existing symptoms including anger, insomnia, chest pain, joint pain, abdominal pain, and especially chronic fatigue were associated with increased odds of COVID-19 reinfection after vaccination.
Irritability, fragmented sleep, sore throat, and muscle aches were associated with lower odds of COVID-19 reinfection after vaccination.
Vaccination status, migraine, and naproxen use were independently associated with increased odds of prolonged (>2 week) long COVID symptoms.
Pre-infection vertigo, hospitalization, anaemia, hypertension, lower BMI, aspirin, azithromycin, and steroid use were each associated with reduced odds of prolonged long COVID symptoms.
Paracetamol, ibuprofen, antioxidants, type-2 antihistamines, omega-3 use, and IBS showed no significant association with prolonged symptom duration.

Runny nose increased the odds of prolonged symptoms by 25%, while brain fog, anxiety, anger, loss of smell, tachycardia, loss of appetite, shortness of breath, dry cough, and abdominal pain reduced the odds by 22-40%.

Using IOM ME/CFS criteria, CFS was associated with mental health disorders, vertigo/dizziness, smoking, hospitalization, vitamin D deficiency, asthma, type 2 diabetes, nightmares, and paracetamol use, with vitamin D deficiency and vertigo/dizziness showing the strongest associations.
Male sex, good pre-COVID health, and anti-H1 antihistamine use were associated with reduced risk of ME/CFS after COVID-19.
Chronic fatigue score was associated with brain fog, anxiety, depression, insomnia, palpitations, loss of appetite, joint pain, and muscle aches, while altered smell was associated with reduced risk.

Depression risk was independently increased by age 40-49, healthcare work, poor pre-COVID health, prior mental health diagnosis, tinnitus, vertigo, smoking, oxygen support, anemia, diabetes, migraine, IBS, insomnia, nightmares, aspirin, and omega-3 use, with prior mental health diagnosis showing the strongest association.
Male sex, excellent pre-COVID health, vision problems, paracetamol use, and anti-H2 histamine use were associated with lower depression risk.
In a second model, depression risk was increased by migraine, tinnitus, vertigo, brain fog, anger, emotional instability, insomnia, tachycardia, and abdominal pain.
Reproductive/urinary symptoms and sore throat were associated with lower depression risk.
Regular menstrual cycles were independently associated with prolonged (>2 week) COVID-19 symptoms in women.
Pregnancy status had no significant impact on COVID-19 symptom duration, though the authors caution this may reflect a small sample of pregnant participants.

Density-based clustering (HDBSCAN) of 50 outcome variables failed to identify meaningful patient subgroups, classifying most patients as noise, and PCA yielded only three components explaining 30% of variance without clear separation.

Deep learning latent representations (SCARF contrastive embedding and autoencoder bottleneck) showed strong correlations across nearly all long COVID outcome variables, suggesting shared underlying multisystemic features rather than distinct symptom subgroups.

In a linear regression on the autoencoder latent (bottleneck) variable, pre-COVID tinnitus, vertigo, dizziness, hospitalization, and insomnia were positively associated, while male sex, antihistamine use, and vitamin D deficiency were negatively associated.

In a linear regression on the SCARF two-dimensional embedding, pre-COVID tinnitus, vertigo, and hospitalization were positively associated, whereas antihistamine use and mood-related irritability were negatively associated.
An AutoML-selected gradient boosting model for predicting symptom duration achieved high discrimination (AUC 0.87) but low balanced accuracy and poor negative predictive value.
An AutoML-selected model for predicting chronic fatigue achieved good discrimination and balanced accuracy, outperforming the no-information rate.
Density-based clustering (HDBSCAN) applied to 50 outcome variables failed to identify meaningful, distinct patient subgroups within the long COVID cohort, classifying most participants as noise.
Principal component analysis of the 50 outcome variables yielded three principal components explaining only 30% of the total variance, without clear separation between patients.

Deep learning latent feature extraction (autoencoder bottleneck and SCARF contrastive embeddings) showed strong correlations among the diverse long COVID outcome variables, suggesting shared underlying features rather than distinct clinical subgroups.

The first SCARF latent feature correlated positively with nearly all long COVID outcome variables except reproductive and urinary symptoms, and was highly similar to encoder outputs, reinforcing a multisystemic model of COVID-19 sequelae.

In a linear model of the autoencoder bottleneck latent variable, pre-COVID tinnitus, vertigo, dizziness, hospitalization, and insomnia were positively associated with the latent long COVID severity score, while male sex, antihistamine use, and vitamin D deficiency were negatively associated; the model explained 35% of variance.

In a linear model of the SCARF embedding, pre-COVID tinnitus, vertigo, and hospitalization were positively associated with the embedding score, whereas antihistamine use and mood-related irritability were negatively associated; the model explained 40% of variance.

The AutoML-selected GBM model for predicting long COVID symptom duration achieved high discrimination (AUC 0.87) but poor accuracy relative to the no-information rate, with very high PPV but very low NPV, indicating imbalanced predictive performance.

The AutoML-selected model for predicting chronic fatigue outperformed the no-information rate with balanced sensitivity, specificity, and PPV/NPV, representing the best-calibrated of the three prediction models.
The AutoML-selected model for predicting depression showed only moderate discrimination, similar to the no-information rate, with low PPV and notable false positive/negative imbalance.

Migraine prevalence in this post-COVID-19 cohort (18.0%) was higher than the estimated 10-15% prevalence in the general population, consistent with reports linking COVID-19 to increased migraine risk.
A substantial majority of participants (90.3%) reported reproductive or urinary symptoms following COVID-19, highlighting a marked impact on the genitourinary system.
Calibration assessment showed good predictive performance for the chronic fatigue model and moderate accuracy for the symptom duration and depression models, based on Brier scores.
Median arcuate ligament syndrome (MALS) was found to co-occur strikingly with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS) in a series of 45 patients.
The vast majority of patients with concurrent MALS/hEDS were female and most were 20-40 years old.
Postural relief of pain and postprandial pain were reported by the great majority of patients with MALS/hEDS, and over a third had significant weight loss.
May-Thurner syndrome was identified for the first time as co-occurring with hEDS in 11 of 45 patients, with 4 also having concurrent MALS.
Surgical resection of the median arcuate ligament combined with celiac plexus neurectomy resulted in total pain relief in 28 patients treated so far.
The majority of patients (80%) underwent genetic testing panels of 5-37 connective tissue disorder genes and up to 19 aneurysm genes as part of workup.

In an 18-year-old woman with EDS and bilateral midcarpal instability, triangular ligament reconstruction using cadaveric tendon allografts (semitendinosis on the right, gracilis on the left) improved grip strength, active range of motion, pain control, and daily function at 8 weeks compared with preoperative measures.
At 18 months after surgery, the patient maintained a satisfactory functional outcome from the cadaveric tendon graft reconstruction of the midcarpal joint.
No surgical complications occurred in either wrist following bilateral cadaveric tendon graft reconstruction for midcarpal instability.
Midcarpal laxity affects approximately 70% of EDS patients, particularly those with the hypermobile subtype (EDS-HT, type III), the most common form of EDS.

The authors propose that autologous tendon grafts in EDS patients carry a higher risk of loosening over time due to intrinsic abnormalities in collagen metabolism, whereas cadaveric (allograft) tendon retains normal tendon structure and quality and may better maintain midcarpal stability.
The majority of hEDS survey respondents reported experiencing a mental health burden every day, with fewer reporting it weekly, monthly, or never.
Patients who received EDS-tailored physical therapy were more likely to report improved posture than those who received standard physical therapy.
EDS-tailored physical therapy was rated as more helpful by patients than standard physical therapy.
Patients receiving EDS-tailored physical therapy attended therapy for a longer duration than those receiving standard physical therapy.
Among hEDS patients undergoing orthopaedic surgery for joint instability or pain, more than a third reported complications.
Spine surgeries in hEDS patients had an even higher reported complication rate than joint surgeries.
Physical therapy was the only nonoperative treatment whose median reported helpfulness sometimes equaled or exceeded that of joint or spine surgery in hEDS patients.
About two-thirds of EDS survey respondents reported sleeping less than 8 hours per night, below CDC sleep recommendations.
The proportion of EDS respondents sleeping less than 6 hours per night (26.2%) was slightly higher than the 23% reported in the general US population.
EDS respondents reported markedly longer sleep latency than the general population, with the majority taking over 30 minutes to fall asleep.
Sleep apnea diagnosis prevalence in the EDS sample was similar to general population values and did not appear to explain the reduced sleep duration and increased sleep latency observed.
Pain was reported to affect sleep quality every day by over a third of EDS respondents, and daily pain overall was reported by the majority.
Sleeping fewer than 8 hours per day was not a significant predictor of reporting more than 14 days per month of poor physical or mental health.

After adjusting for age and gender, sleeping less than 6 hours was significantly associated with increased odds of reporting more than 14 days of poor physical health per month, while sleeping more than 6 hours decreased those odds by 32%.
Women aged 65-74 with EDS had significantly decreased odds of reporting more than 14 days of poor physical health compared to other age groups.

After adjusting for age and gender, sleeping less than 6 hours was significantly associated with increased odds of reporting more than 14 days of poor mental health per month, while sleeping more than 6 hours decreased those odds by 26%.
Positioning pillows/wedges were the most commonly used sleep aid among EDS patients, while ear plugs were the least commonly used.
Overall, use of various sleep aids did not significantly predict the odds of sleeping more than 8 hours per day, though weighted blanket use individually was associated with 23% increased odds.
White noise machine use was individually associated with decreased odds of sleeping more than 8 hours per night, despite the overall sleep aid model being non-significant.
Use of sleep aids did not significantly predict the odds of sleeping more than 6 hours per night, and no individual sleep aid had a significant effect in this model.
Prescription sleep medication use was substantially more common among EDS respondents than in the general population.
A previously cited study found that the majority of EDS patients report poor sleep quality.

A previously cited study found high prevalence of severe fatigue among EDS patients, with severely fatigued individuals reporting more sleep disturbance, concentration problems, pain, and psychological distress.
A previously cited study of children with EDS found a high prevalence of multiple sleep disorder types, with about a third requiring behavioral sleep medicine management.

A patient with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome developed severe kinking of an ascending aortic prosthesis five years after type A aortic dissection repair, which was associated with thrombus formation leading to an embolic cerebellar stroke.

During elective redo surgery, multiple fresh thrombi were found at the same site of the severe prosthetic kink despite prior treatment with clopidogrel, supporting the kink as the causal source of thromboembolism.
Intravenous thrombolysis rapidly improved the patient's acute stroke symptoms, and follow-up CT two days later showed no residual thrombus.

Redo surgical replacement of the ascending aortic prosthesis using separate anastomosed proximal and distal segments (avoiding a single long kinked graft) eliminated the kink and prevented further thromboembolic events.

The authors note that anatomical angulation between the aortic root and arch (nearly 90 degrees) combined with use of a single continuous overlong prosthetic graft can result in severe mid-ascending kinking, particularly relevant in connective tissue disorders like vascular EDS undergoing aortic repair.

In a similar prior case from the authors' practice, severe kinking of an ascending prosthesis caused a mid-ascending pseudocoarctation leading to progressive heart failure, and resection of the kink restored left ventricular function.

A hypermobile (mobile) cecum, caused by failure of embryological fixation to the posterior abdominal wall, can present with recurrent right lower quadrant pain, distension, pseudo-obstruction, and volvulus, mimicking acute appendicitis.

CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was diagnostic, revealing cecal volvulus and a hypermobile cecum with the caecal pole displaced to the left of midline at the level of the umbilicus, ruling out acute appendicitis, whereas ultrasound was inconclusive due to overlying bowel gas.

Abdominopelvic ultrasound findings for mobile cecum are generally non-specific and were inconclusive in this patient due to overlying bowel gas, whereas CT is reported to be highly specific for mobile cecum diagnosis.

Emergency laparoscopy with untwisting of the volvulized cecum showed complete bowel recovery, after which appendectomy and cecopexy were performed; the patient recovered well and was discharged on the fourth post-operative day.

Patients whose 15-point Tulane-modified Beighton score was 11 or greater consistently failed standard open or arthroscopic capsular shift surgery, whereas those with scores of 7 or lower had successful outcomes with standard surgery.
UCLA shoulder strength scores improved significantly from preoperative to postoperative assessment after double-allograft reconstruction.
American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) scores improved significantly after double-allograft reconstruction.
Bankart scores improved significantly after double-allograft reconstruction.
Constant-Murley scores improved significantly after double-allograft reconstruction.
Visual analog scale (VAS) pain scores decreased significantly after double-allograft reconstruction.
Self-reported activity level increased significantly after double-allograft reconstruction.
Postoperative improvement across all PRO measures was statistically comparable between patients with genetically confirmed EDS and those without a confirmed EDS diagnosis.
Female patients showed a numerically larger improvement in Constant-Murley score than male patients, but the difference did not reach statistical significance.
Among 46 operative shoulders, complications occurred in 7 cases, consisting of recurrent subluxation and continued pain.
Five of 46 shoulders (10.9%) required revision surgery after double-allograft reconstruction, occurring on average 5.36 years postoperatively.
Complication rates after double-allograft reconstruction did not differ significantly between patients with and without genetically confirmed EDS.
Complication rates did not differ significantly between patients aged ≤27 years and those older than 27 years.
Complication rates did not differ significantly between male and female patients.

The authors describe patients with EDS as having abnormal/poor-quality collagen underlying multi-joint laxity, and propose that allograft tendon substitutes for this deficient native collagen to restore shoulder stability.
Only 13 of 46 shoulders (28.3%) had a formally charted, genetically tested positive diagnosis of EDS, despite all patients meeting hyperlaxity criteria.
The majority of patients undergoing double-allograft reconstruction had already failed one or more prior shoulder stabilization surgeries.
Connective tissue diseases including Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, along with Marfan syndrome and polycystic kidney disease, are listed as risk factors for diverticular disease.

A 12-year-old boy with Stickler syndrome presented with bilateral ankle pain due to distal tibial recurvatum-valgus deformity and distal tibial slipped epiphysis, a condition not previously reported in Stickler syndrome.
The patient underwent osteotomy along the true plane of deformity with internal fixation, resulting in decreased pain and improved clinical and radiographic alignment at latest follow-up.

Quadriceps muscle strength, assessed as limb symmetry index (LSI) and peak torque relative to body weight, did not differ significantly between GJH patients who sustained a second ACL injury and matched GJH controls at 10 weeks, 4, 8 or 12 months after primary ACL reconstruction.
Hamstring muscle strength (LSI and peak torque relative to body weight) showed no significant differences between the second ACL injury group and controls at any postoperative follow-up.

At 8 months after primary ACL reconstruction, patients with GJH who later sustained a second ACL injury reported significantly higher ACL-Return to Sport Index (ACL-RSI) scores, indicating greater confidence and lower negative emotion/risk appraisal toward return to sport, compared with matched controls who did not sustain a second injury.

At 8 months after primary ACL reconstruction, patients who later sustained a second ACL injury reported a higher level of knee-strenuous activity (Tegner score) than matched controls who did not sustain a second injury.

Despite reporting greater knee-strenuous activity levels, patients who sustained a second ACL injury did not show a significantly greater proportion achieving dichotomised return-to-sport status (Tegner ≥6) compared with controls.

Knee self-efficacy (K-SES18, present and future subscales) showed no significant differences between the second ACL injury group and controls at any follow-up other than the ACL-RSI and Tegner differences noted at 8 months.

General ligamentous hyperlaxity, along with Lisfranc joint arthritis, older sedentary age, and prior hallux valgus recurrence, is cited as a clinical factor supporting selection of the Lapidus procedure over other hallux valgus corrections.
Patients with hallux valgus deformity showed significantly increased first ray sagittal plane motion compared with those without the deformity.
Using the Klaue caliper device, first metatarsal head elevation was greater in hallux valgus patients than in those without the deformity, indicating increased first ray hypermobility.
First metatarsal coronal-plane pronation, assessed via weight-bearing CT, was present in the large majority of hallux valgus deformities, supporting the triplanar model of the deformity.
Athletes undergoing Lapidus-type procedures had a somewhat higher rate of failing to return to preoperative activity levels than sedentary patients.

In a retrospective series of modified Lapidus arthrodesis for hallux valgus with first ray hypermobility (32 feet, 25 patients), most patients rated the surgery as effective, but athletic return-to-activity was poor and several nonunions/delayed unions occurred.

A more recent retrospective study of 48 athletes undergoing modified Lapidus arthrodesis for hallux valgus with first ray hypermobility reported high subjective satisfaction and sport resumption rates, with a modest complication rate.
In a comparison of 143 patients undergoing Lapidus arthrodesis, dorsomedial locking plate fixation achieved a higher union rate and faster time to full weight-bearing than crossed screw fixation.
In a case series of revision bone block TMT arthrodesis for prior nonunion, most patients achieved union, and smoking was identified as a statistically significant predictor of nonunion.
Nonunion rates after Lapidus arthrodesis have historically been 6-12%, and this risk rises substantially when the procedure is performed bilaterally and simultaneously.
Arthroscopic Lapidus fusion in a small case series achieved good radiographic correction and universal fusion with minimal first ray shortening.
A large cohort using external fixation for Lapidus arthrodesis reported rapid unassisted weight-bearing and fusion with no nonunion, though outcomes varied in other smaller series.

Fibromyalgia patients showed significantly longer latency and lower amplitude of foot and hand sympathetic skin response compared with healthy controls, with 7 patients having unobtainable foot SSR, indicating small fiber pathology.

Fibromyalgia patients had significantly earlier onset latency, longer duration, and more delayed offset latency of the cutaneous silent period compared with controls, consistent with small fiber pathology.
Fibromyalgia patients with the COMT A/A genotype had significantly higher pain severity scores (McGill and Visual Analog Scale) than those with the G/G genotype.

Fibromyalgia patients with COMT A/A and A/G genotypes had significantly higher neuropathic pain scores (painDETECT and Small Fiber Neuropathy Symptoms Inventory-like scale) compared with G/G genotype carriers.
The frontal QRS-T angle did not differ significantly between fibromyalgia patients and healthy controls.
Resting heart rate did not differ significantly between FMS patients and healthy controls.
QRS complex duration on ECG did not differ significantly between FMS patients and controls.
Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQ) severity scores showed no significant correlation with the frontal QRS-T angle among FMS patients.
Frontal QRS-T angle measurements did not differ significantly between FMS patients using duloxetine and those not using it.
Serum magnesium levels were significantly lower in fibromyalgia patients with poor sleep quality (PSQI >5) compared to good sleepers.
Fibromyalgia patients with poor sleep quality had significantly higher tender point counts than good sleepers.
Poor sleepers reported significantly higher pain intensity on the VAS compared to good sleepers.
Poor sleepers had significantly higher Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores, indicating greater functional impairment, than good sleepers.
Age did not differ significantly between good and poor sleeper subgroups of fibromyalgia patients.
Body mass index did not differ significantly between good and poor sleeper subgroups of fibromyalgia patients.
Serum magnesium levels were negatively correlated with tender point count in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum magnesium levels were negatively correlated with Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire scores.
Serum magnesium levels were negatively correlated with VAS pain scores in fibromyalgia patients.
Serum magnesium levels were negatively correlated with PSQI sleep quality scores, i.e. lower magnesium was associated with poorer sleep.
Tender point count was positively correlated with FIQ scores in fibromyalgia patients.
Tender point count was positively correlated with VAS pain scores in fibromyalgia patients.
PSQI sleep quality scores were positively correlated with VAS pain scores in fibromyalgia patients.
PSQI sleep quality scores were positively correlated with tender point count in fibromyalgia patients.
PSQI sleep quality scores were positively correlated with FIQ scores in fibromyalgia patients.
Female MCAS patients self-reported a mean of 10.0 neurologic disorders/symptoms versus 2.5 in female controls.
Male MCAS patients self-reported a mean of 7.0 neurologic disorders/symptoms versus 0.5 in male controls.
Cognitive dysfunction showed the highest odds ratio (23.5) among female MCAS patients versus female controls.
Fatigue was strongly associated with MCAS in females with an odds ratio of 22.3.
Non-epileptic seizure-like activity was associated with MCAS in females with an odds ratio of 15.3.
Odor sensitivity showed the highest odds ratio (28.0) among male MCAS patients versus male controls.
Light sensitivity was associated with MCAS in males with an odds ratio of 23.4.
Fatigue was associated with MCAS in males with an odds ratio of 18.6.
Female MCAS patients self-reported a mean of 3.8 psychiatric disorders versus 1.3 in female controls.
Male MCAS patients self-reported a mean of 2.9 psychiatric disorders versus 0.9 in male controls.
Hallucinations had the highest psychiatric odds ratio (12.3) among female MCAS patients.
Suicidal ideation was associated with MCAS in females with an odds ratio of 7.4.
PTSD showed the highest psychiatric odds ratio (8.3) among male MCAS patients.
POTS was substantially more prevalent in female MCAS patients than in female controls.
Restless legs syndrome was more prevalent and strongly associated with MCAS in both females and males.
Tinnitus was highly prevalent and strongly associated with MCAS in both sexes.
Among treatments tried, antihistamines received the highest self-rated global health improvement score, followed by LDN and benzodiazepines.
Antihistamines were reported to help cognitive dysfunction, migraine, fatigue, and insomnia in a subset of MCAS patients who used them.
LDN was reported to help fatigue/myalgia, cognitive dysfunction, neuropathy, and RLS in a subset of MCAS patients who used it.
Benzodiazepines were reported to help chronic severe insomnia, resting tremors, RLS, pain hypersensitivity, and myalgia in a subset of MCAS patients who used them.
Benzodiazepines showed the highest efficacy ratings among the three drug classes for anxiety disorder, panic disorder, agoraphobia, OCD, PTSD, and anger management problems.
Side effects were reported at similar rates across the three medication classes used for MCAS-related NP symptoms.
IL-12, a key mediator of neuroinflammation, is proposed to contribute to neuropsychiatric symptoms in MCAS by altering neurotransmitter systems and activating microglia.
Aberrantly excessive histamine release by dysfunctional mast cells is proposed to drive central and peripheral neuronal dysfunction via histamine H1, H2, and H4 receptors expressed on neurons.
Unlike histamine, mast cell mediators IL-6 and TNF-alpha readily cross the blood-brain barrier, providing a route for peripheral mast cell activation to affect the CNS.
Degranulation of meningeal mast cells is thought to sensitize trigeminal vascular afferent processing, contributing to migraine pathophysiology, which is a common MCAS comorbidity.
A prior study found that 42% of patients initially diagnosed with POTS had additional symptoms and at least one elevated mast-cell-related biochemical marker suggesting comorbid MCAS.
In a case series of 47 patients with refractory MCAS treated with various GLP-1 receptor agonists, 89% reported clinical benefit across a broad range of MCAS-associated problems.
GLP-1 receptors are expressed on mast cells among many other cell types, providing a rationale for GLP-1RA drugs to modulate mast cell activity.
Clarithromycin reduced secretion of inflammatory mediators from airway epithelial cells stimulated with LPS plus IL-13.
Clarithromycin modulated the balance between type 2 and type 17 inflammatory responses induced by IL-13 plus TNF-α or by IL-17A.
Clarithromycin directly inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell activation in vitro.
Clarithromycin reduced pseudo-allergic reaction in vivo, consistent with inhibition of MRGPRX2-driven mast cell activation.
Clarithromycin inhibited the activation and proliferation of mast cells cultured with supernatant from LPS+IL-13-stimulated epithelial cells.

In an LPS/OVA-induced severe steroid hyporesponsive asthma mouse model, clarithromycin attenuated pulmonary inflammation, BALF cytokine release, airway hyperresponsiveness, and overall disease symptoms.
Patients with hymenoptera venom allergy who present with anaphylaxis marked by cardiovascular symptoms and absence of cutaneous symptoms may have an underlying clonal mast cell disease.
Patients with hymenoptera venom allergy and clonal mast cell disease usually have low mast cell burden, requiring highly sensitive techniques to detect clonality.
The management approach and duration of venom immunotherapy differs between patients with hymenoptera venom allergy who have an associated clonal mast cell disease versus the general population.
Patients with clonal mast cell diseases may experience bone mass loss as a complication in addition to typical mast cell-mediator release symptoms.
The review identifies mast cell activation syndrome as one of the chronic inflammatory pathways contributing to autoimmune disease development in Long COVID.
Cytokine storm-related pro-inflammatory responses are described as contributing to systemic chronic inflammation and autoimmune disease pathogenesis in Long COVID.
Changes in the gut microbiota are cited as a pathway contributing to autoimmune disease development in Long COVID.
Molecular mimicry between viral and host antigens is proposed as a mechanism linking SARS-CoV-2 infection to autoimmune disease in Long COVID.
Reactivation of latent viruses (e.g., herpesviruses such as EBV) is described as one pathway contributing to autoimmune disease in Long COVID.
Coagulation abnormalities are listed as a chronic inflammatory pathway contributing to autoimmune disease pathogenesis in Long COVID.
The authors describe intervention approaches for Long COVID-related autoimmune disease including probiotics, immunoglobulins, the RECOVER clinical trial model, and immunomodulatory drugs.
Whole-exome variant counts did not differ significantly between MCS patients and controls under any of three filtering conditions (raw QC, coding low-frequency, non-intronic low-frequency).
Rare homozygous variants across the SLC gene superfamily (Group C) were significantly more frequent in MCS patients than controls, with every patient carrying at least one such variant.
Rare heterozygous CYP2D6 variants were more frequent in controls than in MCS patients, opposite to the expected direction for a susceptibility gene.

Across the 17 detoxification/oxidative-stress genes (Group A) as a whole, heterozygous rare variant frequency did not differ significantly between patients and controls, trending non-significantly toward more variants in controls.
Heterozygous rare PKD1 variants were numerically more frequent in MCS patients than controls, though statistical significance could not be determined.
Among the 19 GWAS-derived risk/protective genes (Group D), heterozygous rare variant frequency showed no significant difference between MCS patients and controls.
When analyzed as a whole (all 66 SLC families), heterozygous rare variant frequency showed no significant difference between patients and controls.

Restricting the SLC analysis to 12 gene families directly involved in neurotransmitter synthesis, release, and clearance, heterozygous rare variants were significantly more frequent in MCS patients than controls.

Among the restricted SLC neurotransmitter-related gene list, controls showed heterozygous variants preferentially in regulatory regions while patients did not; synonymous coding variants differed significantly between groups and non-synonymous variants approached significance.

The rare SLC6A1 variant rs41293373, located in the 3'UTR regulatory region and with very low population frequency, was found heterozygous in two patients and homozygous in a third, but absent from all controls.

Three closely located rare SLC9B1 SNP variants were shared by three to four MCS patients and absent from all controls, with five of six patients carrying at least one, often alongside an SLC6 family variant.

Two SLC1A2 variants appeared in three of six patients but also in one control individual, so did not meet the criterion of being patient-exclusive despite SLC1A2 being the human ortholog of the Drosophila eaat2 gene implicated in olfactory hyper-reactivity.

A high-frequency chromosome 11 variant region belonging to the MTCH2/SLC25A50 mitochondrial transporter gene was shared by both patients and controls and was deemed uninformative for MCS association, partly because some variants lacked population frequency data and thus escaped the rare-variant filter.
GO Biological Process enrichment analysis of 13 candidate SLC genes showed significant enrichment for transmembrane ion transport processes and regulation of intracellular pH.
GO Molecular Function enrichment analysis of the same candidate SLC genes highlighted transmembrane transporter activity and symporter activity as the most enriched categories.

Homozygous rare variants clustered within the same gene family across several MCS patients, specifically SLC6A1/SLC6A14 and SLC13A3/SLC13A4, though no two patients shared homozygosity for the exact same gene.

As background evidence cited from a prior case report (not this study's own data), levetiracetam, which reduces presynaptic neurotransmitter release including glutamate, eliminated MCS symptoms in a 23-year-old woman with comorbid parietal lobe epilepsy.

A prior blind GWAS study cited by the authors found risk and protective SNPs in MCS patients pointing to immune function and mast cell activation as implicated biological processes; this study's own dataset (Group D genes) did not reproduce a significant association.
Neochamaejasmin B (NCB) inhibited MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell degranulation in vitro.
NCB demonstrated a strong binding affinity for MRGPRX2 as measured by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and surface plasmon resonance.
NCB inhibited activation of the NF-κB signalling pathway downstream of MRGPRX2.
Systemic administration of NCB reduced pathogenesis and inflammation in an LL-37-induced rosacea mouse model by inhibiting mast cell activation.
MRGPRX2 is described as a key receptor implicated in the pathogenesis and inflammation of rosacea.
None of the 68 pediatric CM patients had hereditary α-tryptasemia (HαT), in contrast to the 12–21% prevalence reported in adult systemic mastocytosis.
A markedly higher proportion of pediatric CM patients carried at least one α-tryptase-encoding allele compared with the general population.
All pediatric CM patients presenting with pruritus were carriers of at least one α-tryptase-encoding allele.
Only a minority of CM patients had pure beta-tryptase genotypes, a substantially lower frequency than expected in the general population.
Patients with a tryptase gene deletion genotype had significantly lower basal serum tryptase levels than patients with other tryptase genotypes.
KIT p.D816V mutation was detected in peripheral blood leukocytes of 10.3% of pediatric CM patients.
Among KIT p.D816V-positive patients, the median variant allele frequency in peripheral blood was very low, with most having an allele burden ≤0.01%.
KIT p.D816V positivity in peripheral blood was significantly associated with the monomorphic maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis clinical phenotype.
Pruritus was significantly more common among KIT p.D816V-positive children than KIT-negative children with cutaneous mastocytosis.
Median basal serum tryptase levels were comparable between KIT p.D816V-positive and KIT-negative CM patients.

Bone marrow biopsy in a KIT p.D816V-positive child with monomorphic MPCM revealed spindle-shaped mast cell infiltrates and CD2/CD25 expression, fulfilling three minor criteria and leading to a diagnosis of indolent systemic mastocytosis.
A second child with monomorphic MPCM fulfilled two minor criteria (KIT p.D816V in PBL and CD25/CD2 expression) and was diagnosed with monoclonal mast cell activation syndrome (MMAS).
The one patient with elevated basal serum tryptase (14.5 ng/mL) was also KIT p.D816V-positive in blood and was subsequently diagnosed with indolent systemic mastocytosis after bone marrow analysis.
Multivariate linear regression showed that the presence of cutaneous mast cell activation symptoms was the only significant positive predictor of basal serum tryptase level.
KIT p.D816V showed only a non-significant positive trend as a predictor of basal serum tryptase in the multivariate regression model.
KIT p.D816V was found in peripheral blood of one patient with isolated cutaneous mastocytoma, a phenotype in which the mutation is very rarely detected even in skin biopsies.
A prior Polish pediatric cohort found KIT p.D816V in peripheral blood at a higher rate than the present study, with most KIT-positive individuals showing bone marrow changes.
Despite mastocytoma being the most common phenotype in this cohort, the study could not confirm a previously reported association between hereditary α-tryptasemia and mastocytoma.
Male sex predominance was confirmed in this pediatric cutaneous mastocytosis cohort, consistent with prior reports.
Young females had lower cerebral pulsatility index in both the left and right internal carotid arteries compared with young males.
Older females had greater pulsatility index in the right internal carotid artery than older males, with no significant difference in the left ICA.
Middle-aged females had significantly lower pulsatility index in the right ICA compared with middle-aged males, with no significant difference in the left ICA.

There were significant age-by-sex interactions and main effects of age and sex for PI in both left and right ICAs, with females showing lower PI than males at young age, similar PI around middle-age, and greater PI at older age.
Older females had greater pulsatility index in the right MCA compared with older males, but not in the left MCA, and no sex differences were seen in young or middle-aged groups.
When modeling PI with continuous age and sex, MCAs showed only a main effect of age (both sexes increased PI with age) with no significant age-by-sex interaction or main effect of sex.
There were no sex differences in basilar artery pulsatility index in young, middle-aged, or older groups, and only a main effect of age was observed with no age-by-sex interaction.
There were no sex differences in within-ICA damping factor in young, middle-aged or older groups, though a significant main effect of age was seen in both left and right ICAs.

Young females had lower right ICA-to-MCA damping factor compared with young males, with a significant age-by-sex interaction and main effect of sex overall, but no other significant sex differences at middle-age or older age.
There were no sex differences in left ICA-to-MCA damping factor across young, middle-aged, or older groups, and no significant age-by-sex interaction or main effects of age or sex.
Pulse pressure was greater in young males compared with young females.
TMEM150A mRNA expression was significantly higher in glioma tissues than in normal tissues based on TCGA and XENA database analysis.
TMEM150A expression increased progressively with higher WHO glioma grade (G3 and G4 higher than G2).
TMEM150A was more highly expressed in IDH wild-type glioma tissue than in IDH mutant glioma tissue.
TMEM150A expression was higher in glioma tissue without 1p/19q codeletion compared to tissue with codeletion, and also higher in patients aged >60 years compared to ≤60 years.
TMEM150A showed strong diagnostic performance for distinguishing glioma from normal tissue by ROC analysis in both TCGA and XENA datasets.
TMEM150A overexpression was significantly associated with shorter overall survival, disease-specific survival, and disease progression in glioma patients.
In subgroup analyses stratified by grade, IDH status, codeletion, sex, and age, TMEM150A overexpression remained significantly associated with worse survival in all subgroups (HR>1).
Time-dependent ROC analysis showed good predictive accuracy of TMEM150A for 1-, 3-, and 5-year overall survival, disease-specific survival, and disease progression.

Multivariate Cox regression identified WHO classification, IDH status, 1p/19q codeletion, age, and TMEM150A overexpression as independent risk factors for shorter overall, disease-specific, and progression-free survival, and these were incorporated into a prognostic nomogram.

502 genes were identified as co-expressed with TMEM150A (|correlation coefficient| > 0.6), with GUSB, DTX2, TCIRG1, SRA1, CTSA, TP53I13, CASP6, CNPY4, and TPRA1 showing the strongest correlations, implicated in immune response, necrotic cell death, myeloid leukocyte activation, mast cell activation, and cell adhesion/proliferation pathways.
siRNA knockdown of TMEM150A in glioma U251 cells significantly reduced TMEM150A mRNA and protein levels.
TMEM150A knockdown significantly suppressed proliferation, migration, and invasion of glioma U251 cells.
TMEM150A knockdown decreased Snail protein and increased E-cadherin protein, consistent with reversal of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in glioma cells.
TMEM150A overexpression was positively correlated with the glioma tumor microenvironment estimate score, immune score, and stromal score.

TMEM150A expression in glioma tissue was negatively correlated with tumor-infiltrating mast cell abundance, in contrast to its positive correlation with several other immune cell types such as macrophages and neutrophils.
Small-fiber neuropathy in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases is histopathologically characterized by reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density on skin biopsy.
Small-fiber neuropathy is increasingly reported in systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren's syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, and sarcoidosis.
Damage to autonomic small fibers in SFN contributes to systemic manifestations such as fatigue, orthostatic intolerance, and gastrointestinal dysmotility.
Anti-Ro/SSA autoantibodies in Sjögren's syndrome have been proposed as a mediator of direct immune-mediated small-fiber nerve damage.
Reduced heart rate variability, reflecting sympathetic-vagal imbalance, is one of the most consistent autonomic findings in rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Sjögren's syndrome.
PET imaging with TSPO ligands, a marker of microglial activation, shows increased uptake in patients with chronic pain and fatigue, including fibromyalgia and systemic autoimmune diseases.
IL-6 is able to cross the blood-brain barrier and alter neurotransmitter metabolism, contributing to fatigue, mood disorders, and pain amplification.
TNF-α can sensitize nociceptors and promote central sensitization via action on spinal cord neurons and glial cells.
IL-17 has been implicated in altering blood-brain barrier integrity and promoting neuroinflammation, in addition to its peripheral pro-inflammatory role.
Dysregulated expression of miR-146a, miR-155, and miR-124 has been reported in SARDs and is associated with systemic inflammation and neuroinflammatory signaling.
P2X7 receptor activation by ATP opens non-selective cation channels and promotes release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, playing a key role in pain development.
TLR signaling has recently been linked to nociceptive pain in fibromyalgia via microglial activation and M1/M2 polarization.
Calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) has vasodilatory and immunoregulatory functions and is elevated in chronic pain conditions.
Central sensitization is associated with poor response to conventional anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive therapies, prompting pain-phenotyping approaches to guide treatment.
Strategies to improve vagal tone, such as biofeedback, neuromodulation, and exercise training, have shown promise in modulating autonomic function and inflammatory responses in SARDs.

Nerve growth factor (NGF) is upregulated in chronic inflammation and pain, acting as a potent nociceptor sensitizer linked to peripheral and central sensitization; anti-NGF monoclonal antibodies have shown promise in osteoarthritis pain.

In a mixed-methods survey of ME/CFS patients, 9.27% of qualitative respondents spontaneously reported voice or speech changes (e.g., hoarseness, slurred words, loss of speech) as part of their disease experience, including during post-exertional malaise.

A cited pilot 10-week program combining mindfulness, breathing retraining, vocal exercises, and singing in 27 long COVID patients was associated with improved breathing and well-being, and 14.3% of participants who initially met ME/CFS criteria no longer met them after the intervention.
Exploratory factor analysis of 13 DSQ-1 neurocognitive items in ME/CFS patients yielded a two-factor solution: Factor 1 (concentration/memory) and Factor 2 (sensory/perceptual disturbances).
In PASC patients, the same 13 DSQ-1 neurocognitive items also yielded a similar two-factor solution mirroring the ME/CFS structure.
In the ME/CFS sample, participants with severe functional impairment had significantly worse Factor 1 (concentration/memory) scores than those with moderate impairment.
In the ME/CFS sample, participants with severe functional impairment had significantly worse Factor 2 (sensory/perceptual disturbances) scores than those with moderate impairment.
In the PASC sample, participants with severe functional impairment had significantly worse Factor 1 (concentration/memory) scores than those with moderate impairment.
In the PASC sample, participants with severe functional impairment had significantly worse Factor 2 (sensory/perceptual disturbances) scores than those with moderate impairment.
In the ME/CFS sample, the two neurocognitive factors (concentration/memory and sensory/perceptual disturbances) were moderately correlated.
In the PASC sample, the two neurocognitive factors were also moderately-to-strongly correlated.
Cited prior work reports reduced cerebral blood flow in both ME/CFS and PASC, which may contribute to fatigue and cognitive symptoms.
Cardiopulmonary exercise testing reportedly revealed 'preload failure' (impaired venous return to the heart, reduced cardiac output and muscle blood supply) in patients with ME/CFS and PASC.
Cited prior neuroimaging work found decreased central executive network and salience network functional connectivity in ME/CFS patients compared with controls.
Cited prior work (Manca et al.) found increased activation of the salience network in patients with ME/CFS, proposed to underlie sensory hypersensitivity symptoms.
Cited prior work (Sharetts et al.) found taste dysfunction in nearly one-third of individuals with COVID-19.
Cited prior work (Maeda et al.) found that sensory hypersensitivities were common among patients with ME/CFS.

The multi-omics model identified altered associations between microbial metabolism (including short-chain fatty acids, branched-chain amino acids, tryptophan, and benzoate) and health status in ME/CFS.
Plasma lipids and bile acids showed altered associations with the microbiome and immune system in ME/CFS compared to health.
Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells showed heightened inflammatory activity, secreting IFN-γ and granzyme A, in ME/CFS.
γδT cells showed heightened inflammatory activity, secreting IFN-γ and granzyme A, in ME/CFS.

BioMapAI, a supervised deep neural network integrating gut metagenomics, plasma metabolomics, immune profiling, and blood laboratory data, successfully classified ME/CFS patients in both held-out and independent external cohorts.

BioMapAI identifies disease- and symptom-specific biomarkers by integrating gut metagenomics, plasma metabolomics, immune cell profiling, blood laboratory data and clinical symptoms from a 4-year longitudinal multi-omics dataset of 249 participants.
The incidence of chronic fatigue in the year following acute COVID-19 is four to five times higher than in matched non-COVID controls and higher than after influenza.
Consistently reported risk factors for developing long COVID include older age, lower socioeconomic status, female sex, and more severe acute infection.
An estimated 13%-45% of people with long COVID meet the National Academy of Medicine case definition for ME/CFS.
A large GWAS of long COVID identified three genome-wide significant loci, and Mendelian randomization suggested causal roles for these loci in both long COVID and ME/CFS.

A whole-genome sequencing study using a deep learning algorithm identified 115 risk genes for ME/CFS, most exhibiting reduced expression in transcriptomic studies, with gene expression patterns correlating with specific symptom groups.

Combinations of polymorphisms associated with long COVID and ME/CFS were confirmed in a second large population, and similar genes/gene expression patterns are also found in fibromyalgia and major depression.
Autonomic dysfunction leading to reduced cerebral blood flow, particularly during orthostatic stress, can directly impair cognitive performance in long COVID and ME/CFS.
Endothelial dysfunction can cause vascular spasm and coagulopathy that reduce cerebral blood flow and disrupt the blood-brain barrier, which could directly impair cognitive performance.
Residual viral antigens may trigger formation of amyloid fibrin micro-clots that impair the microcirculation in long COVID.
A few small studies reported symptom relief with autoantibody-depleting therapies in long COVID/ME-CFS, but larger controlled trials are needed.
Elevated plasma neurofilament light chain, a marker of neuroaxonal damage, has been found in people with long COVID (but not those who fully recovered) as well as in ME/CFS.
SARS-CoV-2 spike protein can be detected in plasma for up to 2 years after acute infection, likely leaking from tissue reservoirs.
SARS-CoV-2-specific activated T cells persist for many months in some people with long COVID, remain in the brainstem and spinal cord for at least 2 years, and display markers of exhaustion.
Compared with people who recover fully, people with long COVID have lower neutralizing antibody levels and increased expression of co-inhibitory receptors PD-1 and TIM-3.
Observational studies found that immunization against SARS-CoV-2 is strongly associated with a lower prevalence of persisting (long COVID) symptoms.
Observational studies and one large randomized trial found that antiviral treatment of acute COVID-19 reduces the incidence of persisting symptoms over the following year.
The degree of EBV reactivation correlates with the level of fatigue and cognitive impairment in long COVID/ME-CFS.
A study of 55 people with long COVID with neurological symptoms found autoantibodies directed at human and rodent neural antigens, with specific autoantibodies correlating with particular symptoms.

Circulating micro-clots similar to those seen in long COVID have also been noted in ME/CFS, suggesting similar persisting fibrin-mediated pathology, though confirmation by multiple laboratories is still needed.
There is indirect evidence of mTOR pathway activation in people with ME/CFS.
SARS-CoV-2 infection inhibits expression of nuclear oxidative phosphorylation genes and increases mitochondrial reactive oxygen species production in rodents and humans.
The level of viral replication during acute COVID-19 is associated with both more severe acute infection and the subsequent development of long COVID.
Gut microbiota dysbiosis with a resulting low-level inflammatory state causing gut-blood barrier breaches ('leaky gut') has been documented in both long COVID and ME/CFS.
Global genome-wide DNA methylation levels were similar across healthy controls, ME/CFS, and Long COVID cohorts, with hypermethylation predominant overall.
Promoter regions were predominantly hypomethylated across all three cohorts, in contrast to intronic/exonic regions which were predominantly hypermethylated.
Principal component analysis of shared differentially methylated fragments separated healthy controls, ME/CFS, and Long COVID patients into three distinct, tightly clustered groups.
Comparing Long COVID patients to healthy controls identified 429 differentially methylated fragments, with 148 hypomethylated and 281 hypermethylated.
Comparing ME/CFS patients to healthy controls identified 214 differentially methylated fragments, with 69 hypomethylated and 145 hypermethylated.

Long COVID patients showed a greater number of differentially methylated fragments than the age/sex-matched ME/CFS patients, suggesting more abundant methylation changes at this earlier disease stage.

118 differentially methylated fragments were common to both the LC-vs-HC and ME/CFS-vs-HC datasets, with a high correlation (Pearson R=0.88) between methylation values at these shared sites in the two conditions.
Nine gene promoters (LGALS3, SLC38A8, SLFN13, CCDC130, HSPB6, CTSZ, MYL9, DOM3Z, CACNA2D4) were hypermethylated in both LC and ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
The gene promoters of IRF2BPL and NMRAL1 were hypomethylated in both LC and ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, with HC median methylation of 25% and 75% respectively.

The FGD2 gene promoter was hypermethylated specifically in Long COVID patients (increasing from 52% to 81%) but remained unchanged (~50%) in ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls, marking a condition-specific difference.
Exonic regions of ITPKB, KIF26B, and CHD7 were hypomethylated in both LC and ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
Exonic regions of STAT5A and ABCA7 were hypermethylated in both LC and ME/CFS patients compared with healthy controls.
The HSPA12B exon showed hypermethylation in Long COVID but hypomethylation in ME/CFS relative to healthy controls, an opposite-direction change between the two conditions.

Among the 118 DMFs shared between the two conditions, 26 showed >10% methylation difference between LC and ME/CFS, with LC generally showing the greater degree of change (16 of 20 same-direction DMFs), while six DMFs changed in opposite directions between the two cohorts.

Pathway enrichment analysis identified shared pathways between LC and ME/CFS DMF-associated genes, including Response to Wounding, Regulation of System Process, Cellular Response to Cytokine Stimulus, Regulation of Small GTPase-Mediated Signal Transduction, and Growth Regulation.
Long COVID-specific DMF-associated pathways included blood vessel morphogenesis, muscle organ development, the AGE-RAGE pathway, and neutrophil degranulation, distinct from ME/CFS-specific pathways.

ME/CFS-specific DMF-associated pathways included thyroid hormone production, leukocyte differentiation, negative regulation of T cell receptor signalling, heart development, and blood circulation, distinct from LC-specific pathways.

Sankey pathway categorization showed four shared broad functional categories affected by differential methylation in both LC and ME/CFS (transcription, immune function, signal transduction, cytoskeleton), with LC additionally showing lncRNA changes and ME/CFS additionally showing ion channel changes.
One ME/CFS patient (ME028), the youngest in the cohort with the shortest time from onset to study, separated from the other ME/CFS patients in both PCA and hierarchical clustering analyses.

While an older healthy control separated from other healthy controls in PCA by age, the older ME/CFS and LC patients remained tightly clustered with their respective disease cohorts, suggesting disease-driven methylation changes outweigh age-related methylation changes.

A prior crossover study found downregulation of ACE2 (but not the homologous ACE) expression via DNA methylation in ME/CFS patients, relevant because high ACE:ACE2 ratios have been linked to severe COVID outcomes.
Combined CoQ10 and NADH supplementation significantly lowered Fatigue Impact Scale (FIS-40) scores in ME/CFS patients.
CoQ10 plus alpha-lipoic acid supplementation decreased fatigue levels on the Fatigue Severity Scale (FSS).
Melatonin and zinc supplementation significantly reduced FIS-40 fatigue scores in ME/CFS patients.
