CoQ10 plus selenium supplementation significantly decreased fatigue levels post-intervention.
Hydrogen water supplementation produced a small but statistically significant reduction in perceived fatigue measured by the FSS.
Ginkgo and Cistanche combination therapy significantly reduced perceived fatigue in both treatment groups with a dose-dependent effect.
AEO supplementation decreased fatigue levels across three dosage/frequency subgroups in an open-label trial.
Sodium dichloroacetate treatment resulted in significantly lower fatigue levels in ME/CFS patients.
Wasabi supplementation showed no significant improvement in fatigue levels but did improve overall performance status.
GAA supplementation significantly increased muscular creatine levels, muscular strength, and aerobic power but did not significantly change pain in a cross-over RCT.
D-ribose supplementation was associated with significant improvements in energy, sleep, mental clarity, and overall well-being.
Porcine peptide serum treatment resulted in significant improvements in energy, well-being, sleep, cognition, anxiety, gastrointestinal health, and pain in ME/CFS patients.
Porcine serum polypeptide treatment significantly reduced Revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQR) scores, indicating improved functional status.
In a study assessing maximum heart rate during cycle ergometer testing, the CoQ10/NADH active group had a significant reduction in maximum heart rate compared to baseline/placebo.
Probiotic supplementation significantly improved mental fatigue levels and decreased inflammatory cytokines post-treatment in ME/CFS patients.
Probiotic supplementation increased urinary free cortisol, fecal calprotectin, and DHEA-S, and decreased C-reactive protein in ME/CFS patients.
CoQ10 and selenium supplementation increased total antioxidant capacity and reduced lipid peroxidase levels but had no effect on inflammatory cytokines.
Ginkgo and Cistanche significantly improved general health-related and sexual quality of life and reduced blood ammonia and lactic acid levels.
Wasabi supplementation improved self-reported vigor and reduced brain fog, photophobia, and word-finding difficulty, along with improved vitality-related HRQoL.
Melatonin and zinc supplementation increased melatonin metabolite excretion but did not significantly improve sleep or anxiety.
Exposing healthy 3D skeletal muscle tissues to ME/CFS or Long COVID-19 patient sera for 48 hours significantly reduced muscle contractile strength.
Transcriptomic analysis of muscle tissue exposed to patient sera showed upregulation of protein translation machinery genes.
Glycolytic enzyme genes were upregulated in muscle tissue during early adaptation to patient sera, suggesting an initial glycolytic shift.
Transcriptomic analysis revealed disturbances in calcium homeostasis pathways in muscle tissue exposed to patient sera.
Structural analyses confirmed myotube hypertrophy in muscle tissue exposed to ME/CFS sera.
Mitochondrial oxygen consumption was elevated in muscle tissue exposed to ME/CFS sera.
Mitochondria displayed hyperfusion at the transcriptomic/structural level during early sera exposure, indicating altered mitochondrial dynamics.
Prolonged exposure (96-144 hours) of 3D skeletal muscle tissues to ME/CFS and Long COVID-19 patient sera caused muscle fragility and weakness following the initial adaptive phase.
With prolonged serum exposure, mitochondria in the 3D skeletal muscle tissues transitioned from a hyperfused state to a fragmented toroidal (ring-shaped) conformation.

The authors propose that skeletal muscle tissue in ME/CFS and Long COVID-19 progresses through an initial hypermetabolic adaptive state that ultimately leads to severe muscular and mitochondrial deterioration.
This study presents the first in vitro 3D skeletal muscle model developed to study muscle wasting, peripheral weakness, and potential therapies relevant to ME/CFS and Long COVID-19.
No significant differences in absolute circulating levels of any of the 17 measured steroids were found between ME/CFS patients and controls in the combined cohort.
Androsterone levels were significantly higher in male participants than female participants across the combined ME/CFS and control cohorts.
DHEA levels were significantly higher in male participants than female participants across the combined ME/CFS and control cohorts.
17-OHP levels were significantly higher in male participants than female participants across the combined ME/CFS and control cohorts.
Testosterone levels were significantly higher in male participants than female participants across the combined ME/CFS and control cohorts.
When stratified by gender, no significant differences in absolute steroid levels were found between ME/CFS and controls in the female-only cohort.
When stratified by gender, no significant differences in absolute steroid levels were found between ME/CFS and controls in the male-only cohort.
No correlation was found between participant age and steroid levels, so no age-based subgroup analysis or adjustment was performed.

The cortisol-to-pregnanolone ratio was significantly higher in ME/CFS patients than controls, driven mainly by lower pregnanolone rather than changed cortisol, though this did not survive FDR correction.
The pregnanolone-to-progesterone ratio was significantly lower in ME/CFS patients than controls, driven by changes in both steroids, but this did not survive FDR correction.

Steroid-steroid partial correlation network analysis revealed a marked collapse of hormone interrelationships in ME/CFS, with 52 significant direct partial correlations among steroids in controls but only one (cortisol-corticosterone) in ME/CFS.
Comparing partial correlation coefficients directly between groups showed 57 steroid-pair relationships that differed significantly between ME/CFS and controls.

Despite unchanged absolute levels, cortisone became a highly central, connected node in the ME/CFS steroid correlation network while remaining peripheral in controls, suggesting a compensatory regulatory role.
Progesterone showed markedly reduced network integration/centrality in the ME/CFS steroid correlation network compared to controls, suggesting dysregulation of the progestogen pathway.
OPLS-DA modelling of the combined steroid panel showed only modest group separation between ME/CFS and controls with poor cross-validated predictive power, indicating overfitting.
OPLS-DA modelling restricted to the female cohort showed a stronger apparent group relationship but poor and negative predictive power, indicating significant overfitting.
OPLS-DA modelling restricted to the male cohort showed a moderate apparent group relationship but very poor negative predictive power.

Pregnanolone showed a moderate effect size difference between ME/CFS and controls consistently in both combined and sex-stratified analyses, with power calculations indicating current sample sizes were too small to reach significance.

In the small male ME/CFS subgroup, exploratory correlations suggested fatigue scale scores were positively associated with cortisone, corticosterone and 11-deoxycorticosterone levels, but these did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
Hypothyroidism and Fibromyalgia were the two most common comorbidities among the ME/CFS patients, with Irritable Bowel Syndrome also frequently present.

Among recorded disease-triggering infections preceding ME/CFS onset, flu and upper respiratory infection were most common, alongside neuroborreliosis, TWAR, Epstein-Barr virus, gastroenteritis, and meningitis.

The larger Cohen's d for cortisol observed in the male ME/CFS subgroup of this study is directionally consistent with a prior steroidomics study that found lower cortisol only in males with mild/moderate ME/CFS versus controls.
HERV-W ENV antigenemia was detected in nearly half of post-COVID-19 condition cases compared to only a small fraction of healthy controls.
HERV-W ENV antigenemia was also detectable in ME/CFS, FM, and co-diagnosed patient subgroups, though at lower prevalence than in post-COVID-19 condition.
Anti-spike IgG levels were significantly increased specifically in the post-COVID-19 condition group.
Anti-spike IgA levels were significantly increased in the co-diagnosed (ME/CFS+FM) group.
Total IgM antigenemia against SARS-CoV-2 was detected in all disease groups with the most prominent anti-spike IgM signal in post-COVID-19 condition, possibly reflecting viral reservoirs.
Total and anti-spike IgE antigenemia against SARS-CoV-2 were significantly increased specifically in the post-COVID-19 condition group compared to healthy controls and other patient groups.
SARS-CoV-2 immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgE) did not differ significantly when samples were stratified by HERV-W ENV expression status.
IL-6 levels were elevated in ME/CFS, FM, and co-diagnosed groups relative to healthy controls, but not in the post-COVID-19 condition group.
IL-8 levels were significantly higher in FM and co-diagnosis groups compared to ME/CFS.
IL-10 was elevated in post-COVID-19, FM, and co-diagnosis groups but not in ME/CFS.
IFNγ levels were specifically reduced in the post-COVID-19 condition group compared to healthy controls and the other patient groups.
No significant differences were found across patient groups and controls for neurofilament light chain (NFL) or TNFα levels.
Cytokine (IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IFNγ, TNFα) and NFL levels did not differ when stratified by HERV-W ENV expression status.
Ferritin levels were significantly lower in the post-COVID-19 condition group compared to all other patient groups.
MCHC was significantly higher in the post-COVID-19 condition group compared to all other patient groups.
Hemogram parameters and platelet counts did not differ significantly when stratified by HERV-W ENV expression levels.
A two-variable diagnostic model combining ferritin and MCHC distinguished post-COVID-19 condition from other groups with high sensitivity and acceptable specificity.
Adding IgE and IFNγ to the ferritin/MCHC ROC model increased sensitivity to 100% but reduced specificity to 70.8%.
HERV-W ENV levels showed a moderate-to-strong negative correlation with IFNγ specifically within the post-COVID-19 condition group.
HERV-W ENV levels showed a moderate-to-strong negative correlation with MCHC specifically within the post-COVID-19 condition group.
Adding HERV-W ENV as a fifth variable to the four-marker diagnostic model modestly improved AUC and reduced the false positive rate for post-COVID-19 condition classification.
Lower MCHC values correlated with worse symptom scores in post-COVID-19 patients, including higher total FIQ, higher MFI reduced-activity scores, and lower SF-36 Role Physical scores.
Higher ferritin levels correlated strongly with worse COMPASS-31 secretomotor dysautonomia scores in post-COVID-19 patients.
Higher HERV-W ENV levels correlated negatively with the COMPASS-31 Pupillomotor domain, suggestive of vision problems or neurodegeneration.
Higher anti-SARS-CoV-2 IgE antigenemia correlated with worse SF-36 Bodily Pain and Mental Health scores in post-COVID-19 patients.
Post-COVID-19 condition patients differed significantly from the co-diagnosed group in most SF-36 and COMPASS-31 subdomains, but showed fewer differences in FIQ pain and MFI fatigue subdomains.
The FM and co-diagnosed groups showed the highest COMPASS-31 dysautonomia scores among all study groups, indicating greater autonomic dysfunction.
Lower MCHC (hemoglobin concentration) values correlated with worse Total FIQ scores in the post-COVID-19 condition group, indicating poorer overall health status.
Lower MCHC values strongly correlated with worse MFI 'Reduced Activity' fatigue subdomain scores in the post-COVID-19 condition group.
MCHC also correlated with the SF-36 'Role Physical' domain, with lower MCHC values associating with lower (worse) Role Physical scores in post-COVID-19 condition.

Lower circulating IFN-γ levels were associated (moderate trend) with worse FIQ 'Overall'/'Symptoms' and MFI 'Physical Fatigue'/'Reduced Activity' scores, and positively with SF-36 Vitality, in post-COVID-19 condition.

Ferritin levels strongly correlated with the COMPASS-31 'Secretomotor' subdomain, suggesting elevated ferritin associates with greater secretomotor dysautonomia (sweat/salivary gland dysfunction) in post-COVID-19 condition.
Higher HERV-W ENV levels negatively correlated with the COMPASS-31 Pupillomotor domain in post-COVID-19 condition, suggesting a link to vision problems or neurodegeneration.
SARS-CoV-2 anti-spike IgE antigenemia moderately correlated with worse SF-36 'Bodily Pain' and 'Mental Health' subdomain scores in post-COVID-19 condition.

None of the five candidate diagnostic variables (HERV-W ENV, IgE, IFN-γ, Ferritin, MCHC) showed significant correlations with symptom questionnaire subdomains in the ME/CFS, FM, or co-diagnosed groups, unlike in post-COVID-19 condition.
The study's finding of reduced IFN-γ in post-COVID-19 condition agrees with Williams et al. (2022) but disagrees with Queiroz et al. (2022), who reported no change in this cytokine.

The study's finding of elevated IL-10 in post-COVID-19 condition contradicts two prior studies (Queiroz et al. 2022; Williams et al. 2022) which reported decreased and unchanged IL-10 levels, respectively.

In contrast to Williams et al. (2022), who found significantly decreased IL-6 and IL-8 in long COVID patients, this study found no significant differences in these cytokines in the post-COVID-19 condition group.
Unchanged TNFα levels in post-COVID-19 condition were consistent with both prior comparator studies (Queiroz et al. 2022; Williams et al. 2022).
The elevated MCHC finding in post-COVID-19 condition contrasts with results reported by Alfadda et al. (2022).
The lower ferritin finding in post-COVID-19 condition is inconsistent with six other prior studies that themselves reported inconsistent ferritin findings in long COVID.
Negative affect (PANAS) decreased significantly after a single 3-hour forest bathing session compared to baseline.
State anxiety (STAI-state) decreased significantly after the forest bathing session, with a large effect size.
Anger (POMS subscale) decreased significantly after the forest bathing session.
POMS fatigue subscale decreased significantly after the forest bathing session, though with a small-to-moderate effect size.
Tension (POMS subscale) decreased significantly after the forest bathing session, with a large effect size.
Depressive mood (POMS subscale) decreased significantly after the forest bathing session, with a large effect size.
Positive affect (PANAS) increased significantly after the forest bathing session, with a large effect size.
Vigor (POMS subscale) increased significantly after the forest bathing session, with a large effect size, mirroring the reduction in fatigue.
Friendship/friendliness (POMS subscale) increased significantly after forest bathing, with a small effect size.
State mindfulness of body increased significantly after the forest bathing session.
State mindfulness of mind increased significantly after the forest bathing session.
Self-reported fatigue on the Visual Analog Scale decreased significantly after the forest bathing session, with a moderate effect size, consistent with the reduction on the POMS fatigue subscale.
Self-reported pain intensity on the Visual Analog Scale did not significantly change after the forest bathing session.
Most participants (80.4%) carried dual diagnoses of both fibromyalgia and CFS/ME, reflecting high comorbidity between the two conditions.
At baseline, a large proportion of participants exhibited severe or extremely severe levels of depression, anxiety, and stress symptoms on the DASS-21.
Gut microbiota composition (Jaccard) and structure (Bray-Curtis) showed distinct clustering between controls and Long COVID/COVID-19 subjects at each visit.
Gut microbiome beta-diversity profiles differed significantly between males and females at both study visits.
The relative abundance of the phylum Bacteroidota was significantly reduced in male COVID-19/Long COVID subjects compared to male controls at Visit 2.
The relative abundance of the phylum Bacillota (Firmicutes) was significantly increased in both male and female COVID-19/Long COVID subjects compared to controls at both visits.
Microbial alpha-diversity (Chao1, Shannon, inverse Simpson) did not differ significantly between controls and Long COVID subjects, by sex or by visit.
In female Long COVID patients, Fusicatenibacter, Ruminococcus, Ruminococcaceae, Agathobacter, and Blautia ASVs were enriched compared to sex-matched controls at both visits.

In female Long COVID patients, Lachnospiraceae, Granulicatella, Gemella, Bacteroides, Lachnoclostridium, Enterobacteriaceae, Streptococcus, Escherichia/Shigella, Peptostreptococcus, and Veillonella showed more than 5-fold decreases in abundance across visits compared to controls.
In male Long COVID patients, specific Blautia ASVs and Eubacterium were enriched at both visits relative to sex-matched controls.

In male Long COVID patients, Blautia, Ruminococcus, Lachnoclostridium, Lactobacillaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, Streptococcus, Escherichia/Shigella, Peptostreptococcus, Bacteroides, and Veillonella ASVs were significantly less abundant than in controls.
In male Long COVID patients, serum TNF-α levels correlated strongly and positively with the relative abundance of specific gut ASVs (CAG.56, Roseburia, Lachnospiraceae) at Visit 1.
In female Long COVID patients, Lachnospiraceae_ASV_0171 showed a strong positive correlation with TNF-α at Visit 1.

In male Long COVID patients, IP-10 (CXCL10) levels correlated strongly and positively with Streptococcus, Alistipes, and Butyricicoccus ASVs at Visit 1, with Butyricicoccus association persisting at Visit 2.

In female Long COVID patients, IP-10 correlated positively with Blautia_ASV_0011 but negatively with Butyricicoccus_ASV_0414 and Agathobacter_ASV_0119, with the Agathobacter association persisting at Visit 2.
Predicted microbial metabolic pathways for amino acid degradation and tetrapyrrole biosynthesis were downregulated more than two-fold in male Long COVID patients at both visits relative to controls.

A broader set of predicted metabolic pathways, including carbohydrate degradation, nucleotide biosynthesis, amino acid degradation, tetrapyrrole biosynthesis, glycan and lipid biosynthesis pathways, were downregulated in female Long COVID patients, more markedly at Visit 2 than Visit 1.
The authors cite prior work identifying an ancient (Neanderthal-derived) OAS1 isoform that reduces COVID-19 susceptibility and severity in some individuals of European descent.
The authors note rintatolimod, an as-yet-unapproved drug touted to increase OAS levels without helicase activation, as a potential intervention for CFS/ME.
A historical trial of acyclovir for chronic atypical fatigue illness was undertaken but was not successful.

Among US veterans, chronic fatigue syndrome was reported to be about 18-fold more prevalent (by odds ratio) in deployed versus non-deployed populations, with a related but smaller effect for fibromyalgia.
Patients with chronic fatigue showed a trend toward lower serum iron saturation compared to controls, though this did not reach statistical significance.
Vitamin D levels differed between chronic fatigue patients and controls at a trend level of significance.
Rintatolimod is described as an as-yet unapproved drug purported to increase OAS levels without activating helicase activity, proposed as a potential intervention for CFS/ME and related conditions.

Lerner and colleagues implicated a subset of CFS patients with coinfection by both CMV and EBV, with myocardial biopsy evidence of incomplete viral replication causing non-inflammatory progressive myocytic apoptosis and associated EKG changes.
The authors note that prior external work (Horvath et al., 2024) reported decreases in Ruminococcaceae abundance following COVID-19 infection, contextualizing their own gut microbiome findings.

In the discussion, the authors state that COVID-19 resulted in decreased abundance of Bacillota in both males and females, which appears to contradict their own Results section reporting increased Bacillota abundance in COVID-19 males and females at both visits.

The literature on tonsillectomy history and COVID-19 risk is conflicting, with some studies suggesting a tendency toward higher fever and others finding no increased risk of contracting COVID-19 or greater severity.

A cited review discussed ivermectin as a proposed treatment for acute and chronic COVID-19 and CFS, but the authors of that review considered the supporting publications skeptically and rated them as low grade.
It has been postulated that COVID-19 vaccines may exacerbate pulmonary disease severity in cells expressing an Fc receptor, potentially linking to vaccination-related myocarditis.
A review of 61 Long COVID papers found that only one study included a healthy control comparison group, which the authors identify as a serious methodological flaw across the field.

Cotton-top and common marmosets (and a saddleback tamarin with a coronavirus-associated bronchopneumonia/nephritis phenotype) were found to express p87, CEACAM-1 (a mouse hepatitis coronavirus ligand), and p38 MAPK antigens, suggesting potential utility as a non-human primate model for COVID-19.
Acupressure significantly reduced fatigue severity compared to the control group, which showed an increase in fatigue severity.
Acupressure significantly improved depressive symptoms in CFS patients as measured by the Beck Depression Scale.
Acupressure significantly improved the physical function sub-parameter of quality of life in CFS patients.
Acupressure significantly improved physical role difficulty on the SF-36 in CFS patients.
Acupressure significantly improved emotional role difficulty on the SF-36 in CFS patients.
Acupressure significantly improved the energy sub-parameter of quality of life in CFS patients.
Acupressure showed a borderline significant improvement in the mental health sub-parameter of quality of life in CFS patients.

A patient with hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome initially diagnosed with vocal fold immobility attributed to vocal fold paralysis was found on dynamic CT imaging to actually have intermittent arytenoid subluxation.
The authors suggest that vocal fold immobility in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome may require further diagnostic investigation before surgical intervention is undertaken.
An 11-year-old boy with genetically diagnosed kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS VI) presented with acute retroperitoneal hemorrhage extending from T10 to lower sacral vertebrae.

The kyphoscoliotic variant of EDS results from a defect in the PLOD1 gene, which encodes lysyl hydroxylase 1 (LH1) required for lysine hydroxylation and collagen cross-link formation, leading to defective connective tissue including vascular fragility.
CT Aortogram revealed a sizable bilobed aneurysm measuring 13 x 32 mm closely adjacent to the celiac artery, with an increasing hematoma volume over time.

The multidisciplinary team chose conservative management (strict blood pressure control, blood transfusion, pain management, and monitoring) over surgical/endovascular intervention, resulting in stabilization and discharge without complications.
An increased urinary deoxypyridinoline/pyridinoline ratio is described as a quick, cost-effective test with high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing kyphoscoliotic EDS.

The authors report this as the first known documented case of vascular rupture presenting in the pediatric age group specifically within the kyphoscoliotic variant of EDS, despite vascular rupture being previously described in this variant's spectrum in adults.
Heterozygous pathogenic variants in COL3A1 cause vascular EDS by significantly reducing production of type III (pro)collagen, leading to generalized tissue friability.

Earlier literature reported a median life expectancy of 51 years for vEDS patients and a vascular complication rate as high as 80% by age 40, though the authors note this likely reflects a bias toward publishing severe cases.

More recent studies (Frank et al., Bowen et al.) using more extensive predictive genetic testing identified milder vEDS cases and reported lower vascular complication rates than earlier cohorts, revealing significant intra- and interfamilial variability.

Next-generation sequencing combined with copy number variation analysis accurately detected a wide range of pathogenic COL3A1 variants in patients with typical and atypical vEDS presentations, including some initially suspected of having Loeys-Dietz syndrome.

The 2010 BBEST randomized trial in 53 individuals (33 with molecular confirmation of vEDS) showed that Celiprolol, a cardioselective beta-blocker, reduces the risk of vascular events by stabilizing hemodynamics and reducing arterial wall fragility.

A follow-up study by Baderkhan et al. in 40 genetically confirmed vEDS patients found an annual major vascular event risk of 4.7% under Celiprolol, similar to the BBEST treatment arm (5%) and lower than the BBEST control arm (12%).

A 12-year Italian study found that despite Celiprolol therapy at up to the maximum dose of 400mg daily, vEDS patients still faced an 8.8% yearly risk of symptomatic vascular events and a 6.4% yearly risk of life-threatening events.

Mouse models of vEDS suggested that angiotensin II receptor blockers and pharmacologic inhibitors of ERK1/2 or PKCβ signaling have beneficial properties, though further validation in molecularly confirmed human vEDS cohorts is needed.
Combined therapy with a beta-blocker and an angiotensin II receptor blocker appeared to further reduce vascular events in vEDS patients.

COL3A1 glycine substitution and splice site variants act via a dominant-negative mechanism causing an 87.5% decrease in (pro)collagen type III production and are associated with more severe vEDS phenotypes warranting shorter surveillance intervals.

COL3A1 variants causing haploinsufficiency (50% reduction in pro-collagen type III via complete deletion of one allele) are associated with a milder vEDS phenotype, life expectancy close to the general US population, and significantly fewer obstetric and bowel complications.

Recent reports suggest endovascular repair may be viable in select vEDS patients with null COL3A1 variants, which are associated with milder disease phenotypes due to less severely reduced collagen III production, potentially improving surgical outcomes.
Pregnant women with vEDS face elevated risk of complications such as uterine rupture and major aortic events, with an estimated maternal mortality rate of approximately 5.3%.

VASCERN recommends non-invasive imaging (MRA/CTA) as preferred surveillance modalities for vEDS, with most expert centers adopting monitoring intervals of 1.5 to 3 years depending on clinical features and the patient's specific COL3A1 variant.
Total Beighton score decreased significantly across three annual measurements in children aged 6-11 years, with significant post-hoc differences between each consecutive measurement.
Knee and elbow range of motion (hyperextension) decreased significantly over the three measurements, while MCP-V (little finger) ROM did not change significantly.
A significant time-by-sex interaction was found for right elbow ROM, with girls showing progressive decreases at each measurement point while boys showed no change between measurements two and three.
The decrease in left knee ROM over the study period was greater in girls than boys.
There was no significant main effect of sex on total Beighton score, and no significant time-by-sex interaction for the overall score.
Beighton item 5 (hands flat on floor), which reflects muscle length rather than joint laxity, was the only item showing an increase in positive scores over the three measurements.
Children gained significantly in weight and height over the two-year study period, with the rate of growth being higher in girls than boys.
At baseline, excess range of motion summed over six joints was greater in the hypermobile group than the mobile group.
In children classified as hypermobile at baseline, mean excess ROM beyond the Beighton cut-off decreased substantially across the three measurements.
Knee ROM decreased more over time in children classified as hypermobile or mobile compared to children with normal mobility.
Baseline muscle strength (functional and isometric) and proprioception did not significantly predict changes in excess ROM, knee ROM, or total Beighton score over the study period.
Over the two-year study, most children (73.1%) became less mobile in terms of excess ROM, while 19% became more mobile and 7.9% showed no change.

Among children classified as normal mobility at baseline, a notable minority still showed localized excess range of motion, mainly at the MCP-V and elbow joints, without meeting Beighton criteria for hands-on-floor or thumb-to-forearm.

Among children classified as hypermobile at baseline, only a small proportion showed a large increase (>10 degrees) in ROM over the study, driven mainly by the MCP-V joint, with minimal change at the elbows and none at the knee.
Genetic testing identified a mutation in the COL3A1 gene, confirming a diagnosis of vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome in the patient.

The patient presented with spontaneous sigmoid colon perforation and faecal peritonitis, later attributed to previously undiagnosed vascular EDS, consistent with colonic perforation being the most common digestive complication of this condition.
Approximately 31% of vascular EDS patients experience recurrent colonic perforations, along with complications such as impaired wound healing and anastomotic leak.
vEDS patients face an increased risk of life-threatening complications at a young age, resulting in a reduced life expectancy with a mean survival age of approximately 50 years.

The patient developed multiple thrombotic complications, including left renal artery thrombosis causing kidney infarction, left radial artery occlusion, and right lower lobar pulmonary embolism, despite a negative thrombophilia and autoimmune workup.

Angiography revealed arterial microaneurysms in the hepatic, perigastric, and mesenteric arteries initially suggestive of polyarteritis nodosa, but a subsequent PET scan showed no signs of vasculitis, favoring vEDS-related vascular fragility as the underlying cause.
Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed nonspecific leukoencephalopathy, classified as possible leukodystrophy, which prompted the genetic workup that identified the COL3A1 mutation.
The patient had a history of non-traumatic recurrent shoulder dislocations, and imaging later showed a Hill-Sachs lesion related to the joint luxations, consistent with joint laxity seen in EDS.
Some experts suggest that total colectomy with ileostomy may help prevent recurrent colonic perforations in vEDS patients, although prognosis after such treatment remains poor.
The patient developed a colonic wall hematoma and subsequently an enterocutaneous fistula near the anastomosis site postoperatively, consistent with impaired wound healing described in vEDS.
The patient's mother died at a young age from an unclear acute gastrointestinal incident, suggesting a possible hereditary component consistent with the later-diagnosed COL3A1 mutation.
The majority of surveyed EDS participants reported a history of voice problems.
Women with EDS reported voice problems at a significantly higher rate than men or those identifying as other genders.
Age was not significantly different between EDS participants who reported voice problems and those who did not.
Education level did not significantly differ between EDS participants who reported voice problems and those who did not.
Acute voice problems were significantly more commonly reported than chronic voice problems among EDS participants.
The majority of EDS participants with current voice problems reported social limitations or absences from school or work due to their voice.
Only a small minority of EDS participants with current voice problems sought speech-language pathology services despite high rates of functional impact.
EDS participants who sought speech-language pathology services reported more frequent hoarseness and throat clearing than those who did not seek such services.
Overall upper and lower GI dysmotility rates on comprehensive motility testing did not differ significantly between patients with HSD and those without HSD.
Esophageal dysmotility rates were similar between HSD (36%) and non-HSD (23%) patients on esophageal manometry.
Delayed gastric emptying rates did not differ significantly between HSD (67%) and non-HSD (76%) patients.
Antro-duodenal dysmotility rates were not significantly different between HSD (40%) and non-HSD (29%) patients.
Colonic dysmotility and delayed colonic transit rates were similar between HSD and non-HSD patients.

GI symptom severity scores (GSRS subscales for abdominal pain, regurgitation, indigestion, diarrhea, constipation) did not differ significantly between HSD and non-HSD groups, nor across Beighton score cut-offs.

Anxiety and depression rates (HADS) and quality of life scores (SF-36) did not differ significantly between HSD and non-HSD patients despite overall high anxiety/depression prevalence and reduced QoL in the total population.
Patients with a Beighton score ≥6 (more extensive hypermobility) had significantly higher laxative use than those with Beighton <6.
All patients with a Beighton score ≥6 had at least one abnormal GI motility test, compared to 78% of those with Beighton <6, though the difference was not statistically significant.

No correlation was found between GI symptoms, anxiety/depression, or quality of life scores and the outcomes of the motility analysis, either in the total population or when comparing hypermobility/HSD to non-hypermobility/non-HSD groups.
No correlation was found between symptoms (GI, anxiety/depression, quality of life) and higher Beighton score in the total population.
Patients with Beighton score ≥4 were significantly younger than those with Beighton <4, and this age difference was also present between the ≥6 and <6 groups.

Six months after modified Karlsson repair, patients with generalized joint laxity (GJL) had significantly greater residual anterior talar displacement on ADT than non-hypermobile patients, despite similar preoperative laxity.
Postoperative AOFAS ankle scores were significantly lower in the hypermobile group than the non-hypermobile group at 6 months.
Postoperative Karlsson scores were significantly lower in the hypermobile group than the non-hypermobile group at 6 months.
A markedly smaller proportion of hypermobile patients achieved ADT normalization (≤3mm displacement) at 6 months compared to non-hypermobile patients.
The distribution of postoperative ADT grades (A-D) differed significantly between hypermobile and non-hypermobile groups, with hypermobile patients skewed toward worse grades.
Postoperative talar tilt angle remained significantly higher (worse) in the hypermobile group compared to the non-hypermobile group despite improvement in both groups.

Concomitant intra-articular pathologies (osteochondral lesions, synovitis, osteophytes) had comparable prevalence between hypermobile and non-hypermobile groups and did not significantly alter postoperative AOFAS or Karlsson score improvement.
Minor complications, specifically superficial wound dehiscence, were more frequent in the hypermobile group but the difference did not reach statistical significance.

Both hypermobile and non-hypermobile groups showed significant within-group improvement in ADT displacement, AOFAS score, and Karlsson score from preoperative baseline to 6-month follow-up after the modified Karlsson procedure.
Children with generalized joint laxity (Beighton score ≥4) are reported to have a 2.3-fold higher risk of delayed motor milestones (e.g., walking, balance) compared to non-hypermobile peers.
The incidence of generalized joint laxity is reported to be approximately 10% in Western populations and about 25% in other ethnic groups.

The authors propose that abnormal collagen structure (thinner, less organized fibers) and reduced ligament tensile strength in GJL patients contributes to persistent postoperative laxity after ligament repair.
Hypermobile individuals are reported to have poorer neuromuscular control, which may further exacerbate joint instability even after successful anatomical ligament repair.

The ŌNŌ transcatheter retrieval system successfully performed a partial thrombectomy of a large, mobile right atrial thrombus in an 8-year-old boy, encapsulating and removing the mobile portion of the thrombus without embolisation.
Attempted thrombolysis with alteplase was abandoned after the patient developed anaphylaxis (scratchy throat, hives, wheezing, emesis) five minutes after initiation.
Cited retrospective analyses in adults with right heart thromboemboli reported lower mortality with thrombolysis compared with anticoagulation alone or surgical embolectomy.

In adults undergoing cardiac surgery, those with malignancy had significantly higher rates of red blood cell transfusion, reintubation, sepsis, and anticoagulation-related complications compared with those without malignancy.

Following partial thrombectomy and sequential anticoagulation (heparin, enoxaparin, rivaroxaban), the residual right atrial thrombus progressively decreased in size and became calcified over 7 months without recurrence.
Dystonia severity decreased at follow-up in four participants, all of whom had received intrathecal baclofen treatment.
Signs of spasticity (exaggerated tendon reflexes) were less pronounced at follow-up in five participants, four of whom had received intrathecal baclofen.
Shoulder joint range of motion limitations affecting function (grades 3-4) were common, seen in 30% of participants for shoulder flexion and 40% for shoulder abduction.
Many participants showed hypermobility (excess joint laxity) in shoulder outward rotation, with 87% having no measurable limitation.
In contrast to outward rotation, shoulder inward rotation showed limitations in 63% of participants (grades 2-4).
Lower extremity range-of-motion limitations affecting function were common, most notably in hip flexion (40%), hip abduction (47%), hamstring muscles (67%), and knee extension (57%).
Compared to a younger cohort with dyskinetic CP, an older adult DCP group showed significantly more limitation in shoulder outward rotation, hip abduction, and hip outward rotation.
Pain was reported by 47% of participants at follow-up, a similar proportion to first examination though not in the same individuals.
Anarthria (no intelligible speech) persisted from childhood to adulthood in 10 of 11 participants originally classified as anarthric, with only one gaining minimal speech function.
Nearly half of participants (7 of 15) were classified as underweight by BMI at follow-up, representing a non-significant trend toward deterioration from the first assessment.
Waist circumference values were low across the cohort (median 72 cm, range 63-90 cm).
Among orally-fed participants, most had significant eating/drinking difficulties requiring assistance, per EDACS classification.

Health-related quality of life was poor across most RAND-36 dimensions, with physical functioning most affected (score 24), followed by general health (56.8) and vitality (54.7); all values were below Swedish reference data for the same age group.
Clinically significant fatigue (score above the FSS cut-off of 4.0) was present in nearly two-thirds (64%) of participants.
Nearly half of participants (47%) were treated with intrathecal baclofen, initiated between ages 10 and 17 years.
More than half of participants (53%) had a gastrostomy for feeding.
Upper gastrointestinal disorders such as reflux and esophagitis required treatment in 40% of participants; lower GI problems were mainly obstipation.

Respiratory disorders, including recurrent phlegm and pneumonia (some aspiration-related), were reported in 40% of participants and were managed with respiratory support devices ranging from inhalation to ventilators.
Orthopedic surgery was common: 33% had scoliosis surgery and 60% had lower extremity surgery, mainly hip and Achilles tendon procedures.

Fractures, sometimes occurring spontaneously or after minor trauma, were sustained by 40% of participants, some repeatedly, consistent with risk factors for poor bone health (low mobility, nutritional deficiency, anticonvulsant treatment).
Most participants (93%) reported sleeping well, and psychiatric or neuropsychiatric conditions, including autism, anxiety, and depression, were reported in four (27%) of the participants.

In the original population-based cohort of 43 individuals with DCP, seven (three male) had died by follow-up at a mean age of 17.8 years, most having severe motor and intellectual impairment and epilepsy.
Most participants (60%) took anti-epileptic medication.

More than half of participants (53%) still lived with their parents in young adulthood, consistent with severe motor impairment being associated with parental co-residence in a national Swedish CP registry.
Knockdown of USP5 in mast cells inhibited IgE-induced release of β-hexosaminidase and histamine.
USP5 knockdown attenuated allergic inflammation in a mouse model.
USP5 binds FcεRIγ in mast cells and deubiquitylates it, leading to its stabilization.
USP5 reverses K48-linked polyubiquitylation of FcεRIγ, a modification that normally targets it for degradation.
USP5 knockdown in mast cells or HEK293T cells increased binding of the E3 ubiquitin ligase Cbl-b to FcεRIγ, resulting in increased FcεRIγ polyubiquitylation and degradation.
The USP5 inhibitor WP1130 attenuated IgE-mediated mast cell activation and allergic inflammation in mice.
The authors propose the USP5-FcεRIγ axis as a potential drug target for therapy of IgE/FcεRI-mediated allergic diseases.
Hereditary alpha tryptasemia is caused by congenital copy number gains in a single allele of the TPSAB1 gene encoding alpha tryptase, leading to elevated serum basal tryptase.
HAT has an estimated prevalence of 4%-6% in the general population across multiple studies.
HAT is the most common cause of pathologically elevated serum basal tryptase, accounting for 64%-72% of such cases in the general population.

In one study, symptom burden among HAT individuals was distributed with one-third asymptomatic (similar to healthy individuals), one-third with mild-to-moderate symptoms, and one-third with significant symptoms.
Approximately half of affected HAT individuals report irritable bowel syndrome-like symptoms such as cramping abdominal pain and diarrhea.
Duodenal and terminal ileum biopsies from HAT patients showed a higher mast cell density than in healthy individuals.
Recurrent skin symptoms including flushing and itching occur in about half of symptomatic HAT cases, usually spontaneously but sometimes triggered by vibration or mild trauma.
Mood changes, chronic fatigue/pain, joint hypermobility, and autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, tachycardia, presyncope, syncope) are additionally reported clinical features of HAT.
HAT prevalence is 2-3 times higher (12%-21%) in patients with systemic or cutaneous mastocytosis compared to the general population in Europe.
Venom allergy prevalence is 3-fold higher in patients with both systemic mastocytosis and HAT compared to patients with systemic mastocytosis alone.
The rate of venom anaphylaxis in HAT patients is not higher than in the general population, although reactions are more severe when they occur.

Serum basal tryptase levels increase in a dose-dependent manner with additional TPSAB1 alpha gene copy numbers: ~15±5 ng/mL with one extra copy, ~24±6 ng/mL with two extra copies, and ~37±14 ng/mL with four extra copies.
Digital droplet PCR is the most reliable method for detecting TPSAB1 copy number variation, with 100% sensitivity and 90% specificity.

In an initial study of 13 symptomatic HAT patients, omalizumab produced a 100% response rate for urticaria and anaphylaxis, and a 50% response rate for itching, rash, fatigue, nausea, and abdominal pain.
In a second study of 18 HAT patients, omalizumab achieved a 100% response rate for urticaria and 80% response rate for anaphylaxis.
Combination H1 and H2 antihistamine therapy provides symptomatic relief, particularly for gastrointestinal symptoms, in HAT patients.
Mast cell stabilizers such as cromoglycate or the flavonoid quercetin have been observed to alleviate intestinal symptoms in some HAT patients.

AK002, an antibody that binds and inactivates the inhibitory receptor Siglec-8 on mast cells and eosinophils, is a candidate treatment for HAT and other mast cell disorders currently under investigation for safety and efficacy.

A non-competitive inhibitor antibody developed by Maun et al binds human alpha and beta tryptase, dissociating the active tetramer into monomers, and potently inhibits active beta tryptase in vivo, suggesting a potential treatment for HAT.

A serum acute tryptase to serum basal tryptase ratio of 1.685 or higher has been proposed as an improved diagnostic threshold for anaphylaxis, including in patients with HAT and systemic mastocytosis.

Serum tryptase values are elevated in myeloid neoplasms (AML, CML, myeloproliferative neoplasms, MDS, CMML, chronic eosinophilic leukemia) and mast cell diseases, but generally remain stable in lymphoid neoplasms.

A lower serum basal tryptase threshold of 8.0 ng/mL has been recommended for HAT screening since some HAT-positive individuals have basal tryptase levels between 8.0-11.3 ng/mL, below the traditional cutoff.
Dural mast cells regulate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow dynamics at arachnoid cuff exit (ACE) points, sites of CSF-dura exchange around bridging veins.
Mast cell degranulation releases histamine, which induces vasodilation of bridging veins and reduces the perivascular spaces critical for CSF drainage.
During bacterial meningitis, pathogens exploit the arachnoid cuff exit (ACE) points to gain access to the brain.
Activation of mast cells redirects CSF flow and recruits neutrophils, thereby limiting bacterial invasion of the brain during meningitis.
Mice lacking dural mast cells show impaired immune responses and higher bacterial loads in the brain compared with mice possessing intact dural mast cell populations.
Acute hyperbaric oxygenation significantly reduced A1R agonist (CCPA)-induced vasoconstriction of middle cerebral arteries compared to control and intermittent HBO2 groups.
Acute HBO2 significantly reduced A2aR agonist (CGS-21680)-induced vasodilation of middle cerebral arteries at higher drug concentrations compared to control and intermittent HBO2 groups.
Flow-induced dilation (FID) of the middle cerebral artery was attenuated in the acute HBO2 group compared to control and intermittent HBO2 groups.
Application of the A1R agonist CCPA or antagonist DPCPX did not significantly alter flow-induced dilation in either the acute or intermittent HBO2 groups.
In the intermittent HBO2 group, the A2aR agonist CGS-21680 significantly reduced flow-induced dilation compared to baseline at higher pressure gradients (Δ60-Δ100 mmHg).
Hypoxia-induced dilation (HID) was significantly decreased in rats exposed to acute HBO2 in the absence of adenosine receptor agonists/antagonists.
In the presence of the A2aR agonist CGS-21680, hypoxia-induced dilation was significantly more pronounced in intermittent HBO2 rats compared to acute HBO2 rats.
A1R gene expression in cerebral blood vessels was significantly increased in the intermittent HBO2 group compared to control, with similar expression between acute and intermittent HBO2 groups.

A2aR gene expression in cerebral blood vessels was significantly increased following intermittent HBO2 compared to both control and acute HBO2 groups, with no difference between control and acute HBO2.
A1R protein expression in cerebral blood vessels was significantly reduced in acute HBO2 rats compared to intermittent HBO2 rats.

A2aR protein expression in cerebral blood vessels was significantly reduced in the acute HBO2 group compared to both control and intermittent HBO2 groups, while intermittent HBO2 protein expression was similar to control.
There were no statistically significant differences among CTRL, Ac-HBO2, and In-HBO2 groups in body mass, resting MCA diameter, maximal MCA diameter, or active vascular tone.
Microvesicles derived from activated T cells, but not resting T cells, significantly enhanced human mast cell chemotaxis in a transwell migration assay.
